1) Evidence: The best result so far is the RNA-only pca_n2000 avgpool multiprofile model (config_024: 0.725 accuracy, 0.685 F1). It cost only 1.34 GPU hours. The multimodal pca_n2000 version with resnet50 (config_009) scored slightly lower at 0.715, despite costing 36.42 GPU hours. So the images do not appear to help, and pca_n2000 is clearly the strongest RNA encoder tested. Aggregation is the main design choice not yet tested in this setting. With scvi multimodal, transformer and avgpool were close (0.579 vs 0.591), which is a single, small comparison and not conclusive for the much stronger pca features. 2) Test: config_051 changes only the aggregation of the current best configuration, from avgpool to transformer. This shows whether attention-based multiprofile aggregation can extract more from the 2000-dimensional PCA features. 3) Why now: It directly exploits the leading direction while settling an open design choice. It is expected to be cheap, roughly 1.5–3 GPU hours, which is far below any multimodal pca run. That keeps total compute low and leaves two experiments for follow-up, such as single-profile RNA-only.

1. Evidence: The pca_n2000 RNA encoder is clearly the strongest. RNA-only multiprofile avgpool (config_024) gives 0.725 accuracy for 1.34 GPU h. Adding ResNet50 images (config_009) did not help, scoring 0.715 for 36 GPU h. Transformer aggregation underperformed avgpool, and weighted fusion was clearly worse than concat. Image modality and alternative fusion choices therefore look unpromising. Profile setting is the one major design axis that remains completely untested: every run so far has been multiprofile. 2. Test: config_017 runs the best known encoder (pca_n2000, RNA-only) in the single-profile setting. This checks whether multiprofile aggregation is actually needed, or whether a simpler single-profile model matches or beats 0.725. 3. Why this experiment: It is the most informative remaining test that still has a real chance of beating the current best. It is also very cheap, expected around 1 GPU h or less, since it has no aggregation and no image branch. That cost is far below the expensive multimodal alternatives such as pca with imagenet_vit_l, which the evidence suggests add little accuracy. It leaves budget for one final exploitation step.

1) Evidence: pca_n2000 is clearly the strongest RNA encoder, reaching 0.715 to 0.725, versus at most 0.653 for scgpt and 0.591 for scvi. Concat fusion beats weighted fusion by a wide margin (0.653 vs 0.421). ResNet50 beats ViT-L (0.579 vs 0.540), and avgpool or no aggregation beats transformer aggregation. Single-profile RNA-only (0.721 at 0.04 GPU hours) nearly matches multiprofile RNA-only (0.725). Multiprofile multimodal pca+ResNet50+concat reached 0.715 but cost 36 GPU hours. 2) Test: config_032 combines the best components (pca_n2000, ResNet50, concat) in the cheaper single-profile setting. It checks whether adding image features without multiprofile aggregation can push past the 0.725 RNA-only best. 3) Why this choice for the last run: every other option includes a component already shown to be weaker (weighted fusion, transformer aggregation, ViT-L, or a non-pca encoder). This makes config_032 the best remaining chance at a new top score. Expected cost is low to moderate: far below the 36 GPU hours of multiprofile multimodal, likely a few GPU hours at most.

1) Evidence: no experiments have been run yet, so the main uncertainty is whether combining RNA and image data (multimodal) and pooling several profiles per sample (multiprofile) actually help. Domain priors suggest both should beat RNA-only, image-only and single-profile setups. 2) Test: this run sets a central, mid-cost anchor in the region most likely to score well: multimodal, multiprofile, the compact scVI 200-dimensional RNA embedding, the ResNet50 image encoder, simple average pooling and concatenation fusion. Later runs can then change one factor at a time against it: switching to the transformer aggregator, to weighted fusion, to the larger ViT-L image encoder, to the scGPT or PCA-2000 RNA encoders, or dropping to a single modality. 3) Why now: starting at the most plausible region while avoiding the most expensive components (transformer aggregation, ViT-L, scGPT) gives a dependable baseline at moderate GPU cost. If the expensive upgrades help, the remaining 9 runs leave room to escalate to them. Expected relative cost: moderate. Multiprofile multimodal processing adds cost, but the low-dimensional scVI input, the lighter ResNet50 and average pooling keep it well below the ViT-L or transformer-based variants.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: We have only one result so far. config_013 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI-200 + ResNet50, avgpool, concat) reached 0.530 accuracy and 0.515 F1 for 7.27 GPU hours. That gives a baseline but says nothing yet about which design choices matter. 2. What this tests: config_033 is identical except that avgpool aggregation is replaced by transformer aggregation. Aggregation is the main way a multiprofile model combines its profiles, and learned attention over profiles could plausibly beat simple averaging. Because only one factor changes, any difference in accuracy can be attributed to it. 3. Why it is the best next use: Settling aggregation early tells us whether later experiments, such as trying ViT-L image features, scGPT RNA features or weighted fusion, should build on transformer or avgpool. That makes the remaining 8 experiments more efficient. Expected cost is moderately higher than config_013, perhaps around 8 to 10 GPU hours, because of the attention layers. That is still cheaper than switching to the larger ViT-L image encoder.

1. Evidence: with scvi_n200, resnet50 and concat fusion held fixed, transformer aggregation (0.650 accuracy, 0.628 F1) clearly beat avgpool (0.530 accuracy, 0.515 F1). Transformer was also cheaper (5.16 vs 7.27 GPU hours), so it is the anchor to keep. 2. Test: this run keeps the best configuration (config_033) and changes only the image encoder from resnet50 to imagenet_vit_l. That isolates whether a stronger pretrained image backbone adds accuracy on top of transformer aggregation. The image encoder is probably a larger lever than fusion type, which is a smaller tweak left for later. 3. Why now: we have 7 experiments left, and settling the image encoder early tells us which backbone to use for the later RNA-encoder (scgpt vs pca) and fusion comparisons. Expected cost is moderately higher than config_033, roughly 6 to 9 GPU hours, because ViT-L produces larger representations. That is justified because the image backbone could plausibly decide which configuration ends up best.

1) Evidence: Transformer aggregation clearly beat avgpool (0.650 vs 0.530 accuracy, with the same scvi_n200 + resnet50 + concat setup), and the F1 scores agree. ResNet50 slightly beat ViT-L under the transformer (0.650 vs 0.618), but that is a modest single comparison. The RNA encoder is the main untested axis: only scvi_n200 has been tried, and it has three options, so it could plausibly move accuracy more than fusion type. 2) This experiment keeps the best setup (multiprofile, resnet50, transformer, concat) and swaps only the RNA encoder to scGPT. It is a clean one-factor test of whether a foundation-model RNA embedding beats scVI. 3) It explores a high-impact axis while staying in the best-performing region, and the result will tell me whether to test PCA next or move on to weighted fusion (config_003, or its scGPT counterpart config_026). Expected cost is similar to config_033 (about 5 GPU hours), possibly slightly higher if scGPT embeddings are larger. That is still well below the 7.27-hour avgpool run.

1. Evidence: Transformer aggregation clearly beats avgpool (0.650 vs 0.530 with scvi_n200 + resnet50). ResNet50 slightly beats ViT-L (0.650 vs 0.619). scGPT and scVI are essentially tied (0.653 vs 0.650), but scGPT costs much more (9.06 vs 5.16 GPU hours). Fusion is the main design choice still untested: every run so far used concat. 2. Test: config_003 keeps the strong, cheap setup (multiprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, transformer) and changes only fusion to weighted. Compared with config_033, this isolates the effect of fusion. 3. Why now: it reduces uncertainty on an important unexplored dimension with a single controlled change, on the cheaper of two near-equal RNA encoders. If weighted fusion helps, I can then try it with scGPT (config_026). Expected cost is moderate, about 5 GPU hours, similar to config_033 and roughly half of an scGPT run.

1) Evidence: three design choices look clear so far. Transformer aggregation beats avgpool by about 12 points (0.650 vs 0.530). Concat fusion beats weighted fusion by about 11 points (0.650 vs 0.535). ResNet50 edges out ViT-L (0.650 vs 0.619). Among RNA encoders, scGPT and scVI are nearly tied (0.653 vs 0.650, with similar F1), but scGPT cost about 75% more GPU time. The one major design choice still untested is the PCA_n2000 RNA encoder. 2) Test: config_010 places PCA_n2000 inside the best-performing setup (multiprofile, ResNet50, transformer, concat). This tells us whether a simpler, high-dimensional linear RNA representation matches or beats the learned encoders. 3) Why now: it fills the last important gap in the RNA-encoder dimension inside the strongest region of the search space. It therefore has a real chance of setting a new best, and it informs how the remaining 4 experiments are spent. Expected cost: moderate, likely similar to or slightly above the scVI transformer run (about 5–7 GPU hours) and below the scGPT run (about 9 GPU hours).

1. Evidence: transformer aggregation clearly beats avgpool (0.650 vs 0.530). Concat fusion clearly beats weighted (0.650 vs 0.535). PCA is a poor RNA encoder (0.435). scGPT and scVI are about equal (0.653 vs 0.650), and ResNet50 beats ViT-L by about 0.03 with scVI. The one important untested choice is the modality setting: no unimodal baseline has been run, so we do not know whether the image branch adds signal or mostly noise. 2. This experiment runs the RNA-only model with the strongest setup found so far (scGPT encoder, multiprofile, transformer aggregation). It shows how much the image modality contributes and whether dropping it could match or beat the current best of 0.653. 3. Why now: the only untested multimodal concat+transformer option without PCA is config_005 (scGPT + ViT-L). Since ViT-L has underperformed ResNet50, it is unlikely to beat 0.653. The modality ablation is more informative and could reveal a better and cheaper direction, which would guide the last two experiments. Expected cost is moderate: lower than the multimodal scGPT run (9.06 GPU hours) because there is no image encoder, likely around 5–7 GPU hours.

Evidence: transformer aggregation clearly beats avgpool (0.650 vs 0.530), and concat fusion clearly beats weighted (0.650 vs 0.535). The two best runs are scGPT/ResNet50 (0.653) and scVI/ResNet50 (0.650), so the RNA encoder choice between these two matters little, while PCA is poor. The main remaining uncertainty inside the winning recipe (multiprofile, transformer, concat) is the image encoder for scGPT. With scVI, ViT-L scored about 3 points below ResNet50 (0.619 vs 0.650), but that is a single comparison and may not transfer to scGPT features. Test: config_005 (scGPT + ViT-L, transformer, concat) is the only untested combination of the top-performing aggregation, fusion and RNA encoder. It checks whether pairing ViT-L with scGPT can match or beat the current best. Why now: alternatives such as weighted fusion, avgpool, PCA or single-profile models have strong evidence against them or are unlikely to exceed 0.65. This is the highest-upside test with 2 experiments left. Expected cost: moderate-to-high, roughly 5-9 GPU hours. That is similar to config_032, since scGPT runs were the most expensive and the ViT-L run was slightly cheaper than ResNet50.

1) Evidence: The best design so far is multimodal, multiprofile, transformer aggregation with concat fusion and a ResNet50 image encoder. Two runs reach this level: scGPT in config_032 (0.653 acc, 0.628 F1) and scVI in config_033 (0.650 acc, 0.628 F1). One-factor changes from that design consistently hurt. Avgpool dropped accuracy to 0.530, weighted fusion to 0.535, PCA to 0.435, and ViT-L lowered it by about 0.02-0.03. RNA-only scGPT reached only 0.512. The remaining untested multiprofile neighbours of the best config therefore change factors already shown to hurt, such as weighted fusion (config_026) or avgpool (config_040). 2) Question: The largest open design choice is single-profile versus multiprofile input. Config_001 keeps the best components (scGPT, ResNet50, concat) but uses single profiles with no aggregation. This shows whether multiprofile aggregation is truly needed or whether simpler per-profile training does as well or better. 3) Why now: Re-running close variants of the best config is unlikely to give a meaningful gain. Testing the one unexplored axis has the best chance of revealing a new optimum and still leaves one experiment to exploit the answer. Expected cost is low to moderate. With no multiprofile aggregation it should cost well below the 9.06 GPU hours of config_032, probably around 2-4 GPU hours.

1. Evidence: the best result so far is config_001 (singleprofile, scGPT, ResNet50, concat) at 0.678 accuracy and 0.646 F1. It is also the cheapest multimodal run at 1.16 GPU hours, and it beats every multiprofile variant. The other patterns are consistent. ResNet50 beats ViT-L by about 0.02 to 0.03 accuracy. Concat clearly beats weighted fusion (0.650 vs 0.535). scVI and scGPT are nearly tied (0.650 vs 0.653), with scVI costing much less. PCA is clearly worse. 2. This experiment keeps the winning singleprofile, ResNet50, concat setup and swaps the RNA encoder to scVI. It tests whether scVI's near-tie with scGPT carries over to the singleprofile setting and could edge out the current best. 3. On the final run, the other options look weaker. ViT-L variants and weighted fusion are both expected to score lower, so this is the most plausible way to beat 0.678. If it falls short, nothing is lost because config_001 is already recorded. Expected cost is low, about 1 GPU hour or less: no multiprofile aggregation, and scVI was cheaper than scGPT in the multiprofile runs.

1) No experiments have been run yet, so there is no evidence about which design choices matter. Prior expectations are that multimodal fusion and multiprofile aggregation are likely to give the highest accuracy, but their benefit over simpler settings is uncertain. 2) This experiment tests a strong, representative multimodal multiprofile configuration: scVI-200 RNA encoder, ImageNet ViT-L image encoder, avgpool aggregation and weighted fusion. It sets an upper-region baseline. Later experiments can then vary one factor at a time against it: transformer vs. avgpool aggregation, concat vs. weighted fusion, encoder choices, and single-modality ablations. 3) Starting with a likely high performer gives a good best-so-far result early in the 10-experiment budget. Using avgpool instead of a transformer and the compact scVI embedding keeps cost moderate compared with the transformer variants. Expected relative cost is medium-high: multimodal multiprofile processing with ViT-L features costs more than single-modality or single-profile runs, but avgpool makes it cheaper than the transformer-aggregation options.

1) Evidence: there is only one result so far. config_012 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI, ViT-L, avgpool, weighted) reached 0.520 accuracy and 0.479 F1 for 4.82 GPU hours. That gives a reasonable baseline but says nothing yet about which design choices matter. 2) What this tests: config_007 changes only the aggregation, from avgpool to a transformer, and keeps everything else fixed. That isolates whether learned attention across multiple profiles beats simple mean pooling. Aggregation is a key structural choice that affects every multiprofile configuration in the search space, so the answer will guide many later picks. 3) Why now: it is a one-variable change to the current best, so the result is easy to interpret, and it is a plausible way to raise accuracy directly. Encoder and fusion variations can follow once the aggregation question is settled. Expected cost is moderately higher than config_012, roughly 1.3–1.6x (about 6–8 GPU hours), because transformer aggregation adds compute over multiple profiles. I judge that worthwhile given its potential to be the strongest setup.

1) Evidence: with the same scVI + ViT-L + weighted setup, avgpool aggregation reached 0.520 accuracy and 0.479 F1. Transformer aggregation reached only 0.208, so avgpool is the stronger aggregation choice for this setup. This is one pair of runs, but the gap is large enough to act on. 2) Test: keep the winning avgpool + ViT-L + weighted setup and change only the RNA encoder from scVI to scGPT. The RNA representation is the biggest untested design choice and could plausibly drive most of the remaining accuracy gains. This isolates whether a richer foundation-model RNA embedding beats scVI. 3) Why now: it exploits the clearest signal so far (avgpool) while reducing uncertainty about a high-impact factor. The result will guide the remaining 7 experiments: either fine-tune fusion and image encoder around scGPT, or revert to scVI or try PCA. Expected cost is similar to config_012 (about 4.5–5.5 GPU hours), since it is still multiprofile multimodal with ViT-L; scGPT embeddings may add slightly more.

1) Evidence: avgpool aggregation clearly beats transformer (about 0.52 vs 0.21 with an otherwise identical setup). scVI and scGPT RNA encoders perform about the same with ViT-L, weighted fusion and avgpool (0.520 vs 0.514 accuracy). scGPT has the better F1 (0.498 vs 0.479) and was cheaper (2.94 vs 4.82 GPU hours). Fusion type is still completely untested, as are the ResNet50 image encoder and the PCA RNA encoder. 2) This experiment keeps the best-known setup (multiprofile, ViT-L, avgpool) and switches fusion from weighted to concat on the cheaper scGPT backbone. That isolates the effect of fusion in a direct comparison with config_035. 3) Fusion is a key design choice that affects every multimodal configuration, so learning it early narrows the remaining 6 experiments. Using scGPT rather than scVI tests this at lower cost with similar expected accuracy. Expected cost is moderate, about 3 GPU hours, similar to config_035 and cheaper than the scVI equivalent.

1. Evidence: Four multimodal multiprofile runs suggest that avgpool aggregation beats transformer by a wide margin (0.520 vs 0.208). Weighted fusion beats concat (0.514 vs 0.427 with scGPT). The RNA encoder matters little: scVI scored 0.520 and scGPT 0.514, though scGPT had higher F1. All four runs used imagenet_vit_l, so the image encoder choice is completely untested. 2. Test: config_046 keeps the best recipe (scvi_n200, avgpool, weighted fusion) and swaps the image encoder to resnet50. This isolates the effect of the image encoder, the largest remaining uncertainty among the major design choices. 3. Why now: Running pca_n2000 would only refine an axis that already looks flat. The image encoder axis could shift the result in either direction and will guide the remaining 5 experiments. Expected cost is low to moderate, likely below the 4.82 GPU hours of config_012, because ResNet50 features are smaller than ViT-L features and avgpool with weighted fusion is the cheaper aggregation and fusion pairing.

1) Evidence: switching the image encoder from imagenet_vit_l to resnet50 gave the largest gain so far, from 0.520 to 0.688 accuracy (config_012 vs config_046). Avgpool clearly beat transformer aggregation (0.520 vs 0.208), and weighted fusion beat concat (0.514 vs 0.427). With the ViT-L encoder, scGPT matched scVI on accuracy (0.514 vs 0.520), had higher F1 (0.498 vs 0.479) and trained faster (2.94 vs 4.82 GPU hours). 2) Test: config_008 keeps the best known setup (multimodal, multiprofile, resnet50, avgpool, weighted) and swaps only the RNA encoder to scGPT. This shows whether the RNA encoder matters once the stronger image backbone is used, and whether scGPT's F1 edge turns into higher accuracy. 3) Why now: it is a one-factor change from the current best, so it exploits strong evidence while resolving a key remaining choice. Expected cost is similar to or slightly below config_046's 5.90 GPU hours, since scGPT runs were cheaper than scVI under weighted fusion. That is moderate and avoids the costly concat and transformer variants.

1. Evidence: the image encoder is the dominant factor. With avgpool and weighted fusion, ResNet50 beats ViT-L by roughly 0.17 to 0.21 accuracy. Avgpool clearly beats transformer aggregation (0.208 vs 0.520), and weighted fusion beats concat (0.514 vs 0.427). The best result so far is config_008 (scGPT + ResNet50, avgpool, weighted) at 0.725 accuracy and 0.685 F1. The scVI version (config_046) reached 0.688, so the RNA encoder matters, but less than the image encoder. pca_n2000 is the only RNA encoder not yet tried in this strong setting. 2. Test: config_031 keeps the winning setup (ResNet50, avgpool, weighted) and swaps in PCA-2000 RNA features. This completes the RNA-encoder comparison and could beat scGPT, since simple PCA features sometimes rival foundation-model embeddings. 3. Why now: it exploits the clearly best region while still resolving the one remaining open design choice there, and it avoids settings that are already shown to be worse (ViT-L, transformer aggregation, concat). Expected cost is moderate, roughly 4–6 GPU hours, similar to config_008 and config_046. PCA embeddings are cheap, so it should not cost more than the scGPT run.

1) Evidence: The image encoder is the largest effect seen so far. ResNet50 scores 0.69 to 0.72 accuracy, while ViT-L scores about 0.51 to 0.52. Avgpool clearly beats transformer aggregation (0.21 vs 0.52), and weighted fusion beats concat (0.51 vs 0.43). Among RNA encoders, scGPT and scVI are close, and PCA is much worse (0.43). The best result is config_008 (scGPT + ResNet50, avgpool, weighted) at 0.725 accuracy and 0.685 F1. The open question is how much the RNA branch actually contributes, since swapping in a weak RNA encoder hurt performance badly. 2) Test: Image-only ResNet50 with multiprofile avgpool isolates the strong image pathway. It shows whether the RNA modality adds signal or mostly adds noise. If it matches or beats 0.725, it could become the new best and tells us where the last experiment should focus. If it falls short, that confirms fusion is worth keeping, and the last experiment can refine around config_008. 3) Why now and cost: Re-testing concat or transformer variants of the best setup is unlikely to win, given their consistent underperformance. This run answers a key design question with real upside. Dropping the RNA branch should make it cheaper than the multimodal runs, roughly 3 to 4 GPU hours or less.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_008 (scGPT + ResNet50, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted fusion) at 0.725 accuracy and 0.685 F1. Several design choices are fairly consistent. ResNet50 beat ViT-L in every comparison. Weighted fusion beat concat (0.514 vs 0.427). Avgpool beat transformer aggregation (0.520 vs 0.208). scGPT and scVI were close, with scGPT ahead on ResNet50, and PCA was poor. Multimodal clearly beat image-only. The one major axis never tested is profile setting: all 8 runs were multiprofile. 2) Test: config_003 keeps the best encoder pair and fusion (scGPT + ResNet50, weighted) but switches to singleprofile. This directly checks whether per-profile modeling matches or beats multiprofile aggregation. 3) Why this experiment: The other extensions look unlikely to win. Transformer aggregation and concat fusion each did much worse in their only tests, though the transformer result rests on a single run. Unimodal runs also look weaker than multimodal. The profile axis is the largest remaining uncertainty, and its result will inform the final experiment. Expected cost is low, probably below config_008's 4.4 GPU hours and well below the 10–21 hour runs, because singleprofile skips multiprofile aggregation.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_008 (multiprofile, scGPT + ResNet50, avgpool, weighted fusion) at 0.725 accuracy and 0.685 F1. Three patterns stand out. Changing only the fusion from weighted to concat lowered accuracy (0.514 to 0.427 with ViT-L). The one transformer-aggregation run collapsed to 0.208. Image-only multiprofile ResNet50 reached just 0.485, while adding scGPT RNA raised it to 0.725. That suggests RNA carries most of the signal, and an RNA-only model is still untested. 2) This experiment tests whether multiprofile scGPT RNA alone with avgpool matches or beats the multimodal model. If the image branch adds noise, removing it could help. It also measures the image modality's true contribution. 3) The other neighbours of the best config look weaker. config_038 uses concat fusion and config_034 uses transformer aggregation, both of which hurt in earlier runs. So the RNA-only variant is the most plausible remaining chance of improving on 0.725. Expected cost is low, likely about 1-3 GPU hours, since there is no image encoder. That is cheaper than any multimodal multiprofile alternative (about 3-7 GPU hours).

1. Evidence: no experiments have been completed, so there is no data yet. The main uncertainty is whether multimodal fusion and multiprofile aggregation are worth their extra cost; my prior is that combining RNA and image information across multiple profiles is most likely to give the highest accuracy. 2. What this tests: config_032 is a multimodal, multiprofile baseline built from the lighter options in each slot: compact scVI-200 RNA embeddings, a ResNet50 image encoder, avgpool aggregation and weighted fusion. Its result will show whether this region of the search space is strong. Later experiments can then change one component at a time from it, such as swapping in the transformer aggregator, ViT-L, scGPT or concat fusion, or comparing against single-modality and single-profile runs. 3. Why now: it covers the most promising design region at moderate cost, which makes it an informative first anchor. Expected relative cost is medium. Multiprofile multimodal training adds overhead, but ResNet50, small scVI embeddings and avgpool keep it well below ViT-L, scGPT or transformer variants.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: We have one result. config_032 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI, ResNet50, avgpool, weighted fusion) reached 0.422 accuracy and 0.405 F1 for 5.9 GPU hours. That gives a baseline but says nothing yet about which design choices matter. 2. What this tests: config_038 changes only the aggregation, from avgpool to transformer, and keeps everything else fixed. This isolates whether learned attention over the multiple profiles improves on simple averaging. Because it is a one-variable change, the comparison is clean and the result can guide every later multiprofile configuration. 3. Why it is the best next use: aggregation is a central design axis that should be resolved early. The cheaper ResNet50 backbone stays in place, so this costs less than switching to ViT-L. Expected cost is moderately higher than the baseline, roughly 1.2–1.5x (about 7–9 GPU hours), because of the transformer aggregator. Testing the image encoder (ViT-L) can come next, building on whichever aggregation wins.

1) Evidence: with everything else held fixed (multiprofile, scvi_n200 + resnet50, weighted fusion), transformer aggregation reached 0.632 accuracy and 0.607 F1, versus 0.422 and 0.405 for avgpool. That is a large gap, and the two runs cost about the same (~6 GPU hours each), so transformer aggregation looks like the right base. We have no evidence yet on the image encoder, RNA encoder or fusion choice. 2) This run keeps the best configuration and swaps only the image encoder from resnet50 to imagenet_vit_l. A pretrained ViT-L gives a stronger, larger image representation, and the image encoder is plausibly the biggest remaining driver of accuracy. Changing one factor keeps the result interpretable. 3) This is a high-upside test of an important, untested design choice, built on the direction the evidence already supports. RNA encoder (config_041 or config_008) and fusion (config_019) variants can follow in later runs. Expected cost is moderately higher than config_038, roughly 7–9 GPU hours, because of the larger ViT-L backbone, which is justified if it is likely to be the top performer.

1) Evidence: Transformer aggregation beat avgpool by a wide margin with ResNet50 (0.632 vs 0.422 accuracy). Swapping ResNet50 for ImageNet ViT-L then raised accuracy to 0.706 (F1 0.667), and that run was cheaper at 3.6 GPU hours. So aggregation and image encoder look settled for now. The RNA encoder has only been tested as scvi_n200, which makes it the largest remaining uncertainty. 2) This experiment keeps the best setup (multiprofile, ViT-L, transformer, weighted fusion) and changes only the RNA encoder to scGPT. It tests whether pretrained foundation-model RNA embeddings beat scVI. 3) Changing one factor on the current best is the most informative next step. If scGPT helps, it becomes the base for later fusion (concat vs weighted) tests. If it does not, PCA or the fusion variants of the scVI setup remain open. Expected cost: similar to config_050, about 3.5 to 5 GPU hours. That is moderate, and possibly slightly higher if scGPT embeddings are larger.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_050 (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + transformer + weighted, acc 0.706, F1 0.667), and it was also cheap at 3.6 GPU h. A transformer clearly beat avgpool (0.632 vs 0.422 with resnet50). ViT-L beat ResNet50 (0.706 vs 0.632). scVI beat scGPT (0.706 vs 0.525). Fusion is the one design choice not yet varied: every run so far used weighted fusion. 2) Test: config_037 changes only fusion, from weighted to concat, on the best configuration. This isolates the effect of fusion and could directly improve on the current best. 3) Why now: It exploits the strongest region found while resolving the main open design choice, which lets the remaining budget move on to the RNA encoder (pca_n2000, config_046) or an image-only ablation. Expected cost is similar to config_050 (~3.5-4 GPU h), low relative to the ResNet50 multiprofile runs (~6 GPU h).

Evidence: the best result so far is config_050 at 0.706 accuracy and 0.667 F1. It uses the scvi_n200 RNA encoder, the imagenet_vit_l image encoder, transformer aggregation and weighted fusion. Single-factor comparisons each favoured one choice: transformer beat avgpool (0.63 vs 0.42 with resnet50), vit_l beat resnet50 (0.71 vs 0.63), weighted beat concat (0.71 vs 0.52) and scvi beat scgpt (0.71 vs 0.53). Uncertainty: the only RNA encoder never tested is pca_n2000. It is the main design choice left open within the winning setup. Test: config_046 keeps everything from config_050 and swaps only the RNA encoder to pca_n2000. This directly shows whether a simple high-dimensional PCA representation can beat scvi_n200. Why now: this is a focused one-factor extension of the strongest direction, so it has a real chance of setting a new best while also filling the last major gap in the search. Expected cost: moderate, likely about 3.5-5 GPU hours. 1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_050 (scVI + ViT-L, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) at 0.706 accuracy. 1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_043 (scGPT + ResNet50 + transformer aggregation + concat fusion) at 0.706 accuracy and 0.667 F1. Evidence: the best design so far is multiprofile + ViT-L + avgpool + weighted fusion. With scVI it reached 0.540 accuracy and 0.524 F1 (config_026); with PCA it reached 0.537 (config_031). Avgpool beat transformer (0.540 vs 0.471), weighted fusion beat concat (0.540 vs 0.485), and ViT-L beat ResNet50 (0.540 vs 0.512). Swapping the RNA encoder between scVI and PCA barely changed results, while scGPT was worse (0.494). The fused model's gain over a single modality has never been tested, so the image branch may be doing most of the work. Test: config_032 keeps the winning setup (multiprofile ViT-L with avgpool) but drops the RNA branch. This shows whether multimodal fusion adds real value or whether image-only is competitive, possibly even better. Why now: most of the multimodal neighbourhood around the current best is mapped, and the remaining variants are predicted to do worse. The modality question is the largest unresolved design choice, and its answer would guide the last two experiments. Expected cost is relatively low, around 2-4 GPU hours, cheaper than the multimodal avgpool runs (4.8-7.0 GPU hours) because there is no RNA encoder or fusion.

1. Evidence: the best result so far is config_039 (scvi_n200 + resnet50 + transformer + concat, acc 0.713, F1 0.695). Three one-factor changes from it have each made things worse. Switching the image encoder to ViT-L dropped accuracy to 0.639, weighted fusion dropped it to 0.632, and avgpool aggregation dropped it to 0.532. Transformer aggregation, concat fusion and ResNet50 therefore look like the right choices. The RNA encoder is the only design axis not yet varied around the best configuration, so it is the largest remaining uncertainty. 2. Test: config_042 keeps the best backbone and swaps scvi_n200 for scGPT. This isolates whether a pretrained foundation-model RNA representation beats the scVI latent within the winning architecture. 3. Why now: this is a direct exploitation-plus-exploration step along the one untested axis, and it has the most plausible upside of the remaining options. The PCA variant (config_017) is the alternative for this slot; scGPT was preferred because it is more likely to add new information than a linear PCA embedding. Expected cost: similar to or somewhat above config_039 (about 5-7 GPU hours), since the multiprofile transformer is the same and scGPT embeddings may be larger.

1) Evidence: The current best is config_039 (scVI + ResNet50 + transformer aggregation + concat fusion, 0.713 acc / 0.695 F1). Each one-factor change from it has lowered performance. Swapping avgpool for the transformer dropped to 0.532. Swapping ResNet50 for ViT-L dropped to 0.639. Swapping concat for weighted fusion dropped to 0.632. Swapping scVI for scGPT collapsed to 0.224. This shows the RNA encoder choice matters a lot. pca_n2000 is the only RNA encoder not yet tested in the winning setup, and it is the largest remaining uncertainty. 2) Test: config_017 keeps everything from config_039 except the RNA encoder, which becomes pca_n2000. Expected cost is moderate, roughly 5-6 GPU hours, similar to config_039. PCA inputs should cost about the same as scVI and well below the 9 GPU hours scGPT took.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_039 (scvi_n200 + resnet50, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) at 0.713 accuracy and 0.695 F1. Every one-factor change from it has scored lower: avgpool 0.532, ViT-L 0.639, weighted fusion 0.632, PCA 0.507 and scGPT 0.224. The RNA encoder causes by far the largest swings (0.22 to 0.71), while the image encoder shifts accuracy by only about 0.07. This suggests the RNA branch carries most of the signal. Whether the image branch helps at all is untested. 2. Test: config_029 is the RNA-only version of the best setup (scvi_n200, multiprofile, transformer aggregation). It checks whether adding imaging and concat fusion actually improves accuracy, or whether a simpler RNA-only model can match or beat 0.713. 3. Why now: Modality is the last major design choice we have not explored, and this run settles it directly. If RNA-only matches or wins, it becomes a cheaper new best. If it loses clearly, the multimodal design is confirmed and the remaining budget can go to the single-profile comparison and fine-tuning. Expected cost: lower than the multimodal runs (no image encoder or fusion), roughly 3–4 GPU hours versus about 5–9 for the multimodal transformer configurations.

Evidence: config_039 (multimodal, scVI, ResNet50, transformer, concat; 0.713 acc / 0.695 F1) is clearly best. Every one-factor change from it has been tested and lost: avgpool (0.53), ViT-L (0.64), weighted fusion (0.63), PCA (0.51), scGPT (0.22) and RNA-only (0.43). The main untested axes are image-only and single-profile. Single-profile drops the aggregation step, and transformer aggregation gave the largest gain seen so far, so it looks unlikely to win. The poor scGPT and PCA runs show that a weak RNA branch can badly hurt fusion. Test: config_023 (image-only, ResNet50, transformer) measures how much the image branch achieves alone. It shows whether scVI adds real value or whether image-only could match or beat 0.713. Why now: it is the last plausible one-step neighbor of the best config that could beat it, and it tells us how to use the final experiment. Expected cost is low to moderate, likely below the ~5 GPU hours of config_039 because there is no RNA branch or fusion.

1. Evidence: config_039 (scVI-n200 + ResNet50, multiprofile, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) leads at 0.713 accuracy and 0.695 F1. Every single change from it tested so far has hurt: avgpool aggregation (0.532), ViT-L image encoder (0.639), weighted fusion (0.632), PCA RNA encoder (0.507) and scGPT RNA encoder (0.224). The unimodal baselines (RNA-only 0.435, image-only 0.494) show that fusing both modalities matters. The one major design axis never tested is single-profile versus multiprofile.
2. Test: config_010 keeps the best encoders and fusion (scVI-n200, ResNet50, concat) but uses single-profile input with no aggregation. This shows whether multiprofile aggregation itself drives the gain, or whether single-profile modeling is competitive or better.
3. Why now: the remaining multiprofile options combine settings that already underperformed, so they are unlikely to beat 0.713. This is the last unexplored axis that could plausibly win. It is also cheap, likely well under the ~5 GPU hours of config_039, because it skips multiprofile aggregation. If it falls short, the final experiment can still refine around config_039.

1. Evidence: the two best results are nearly tied. Singleprofile scVI+ResNet50 concat (config_010) reached 0.715 at only 0.56 GPU h, and its multiprofile transformer counterpart (config_039) reached 0.713 at 5.16 GPU h. So multiprofile aggregation adds cost without a clear accuracy gain. Among single-factor changes tested in the multiprofile setting, scVI clearly beats PCA and scGPT, and concat beats weighted fusion (0.632 vs 0.713). ViT-L as the image encoder gave a somewhat smaller drop than weighted fusion (0.639 vs 0.713). 2. Test: whether ViT-L image features help in the cheap singleprofile setting, where there is no transformer aggregator to interact with the encoder. This is the one remaining nearby variant of the leading recipe that has not been ruled out. 3. Why this is the best final use: it keeps the strongest known choices (scVI, concat, singleprofile) and changes only the factor with the mildest observed penalty, so it has a modest chance of beating 0.715. The best result found so far is kept regardless of the outcome, and the cost is low, about 0.5–1.5 GPU h. That is roughly an order of magnitude cheaper than any multiprofile multimodal run, so a more expensive alternative is not justified.

1. Evidence: no experiments have been run, so there is no data on modality, profile setting, encoder or aggregation. The usual prior is that multimodal, multiprofile models do best on cellular profiling, but that has not been checked here. 2. Test: config_033 is a strong but moderately priced anchor in that likely-best region. It uses scVI (n200) for RNA, ResNet50 for images, avgpool aggregation and concat fusion. The result will show how well multimodal multiprofile models perform, and later runs can vary one factor at a time from it: transformer vs avgpool, ViT-L vs ResNet50, weighted vs concat fusion, and single-modality or single-profile ablations. 3. Why now: starting in the region most likely to hold the best accuracy leaves 9 runs for exploitation and targeted ablations. Choosing ResNet50, scVI's compact 200-dim embedding and simple avgpool/concat avoids the heaviest components (ViT-L, transformer aggregation, scGPT). Expected cost is medium: more than a single-profile or unimodal run because of multiprofile and multimodal processing, but well below ViT-L or transformer-aggregation variants.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: there is only one result so far. config_033 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI-200, ResNet50, avgpool, concat) reached 0.573 accuracy with matching F1 (0.573), so the classes look balanced. What this tests: config_012 changes only the image encoder, from ResNet50 to the larger pretrained ViT-L, and keeps everything else fixed. 1) Evidence: with the RNA encoder (scvi_n200), aggregation (avgpool) and fusion (concat) held fixed, the ImageNet ViT-L image encoder far outperformed ResNet50 (val acc 0.715 vs 0.573; F1 0.687 vs 0.573). It was also cheaper in measured cost (4.49 vs 7.27 GPU h), so ViT-L is the clear image backbone to build on. The aggregation choice for multiprofile inputs is still completely untested. 2) This experiment keeps the best configuration (config_012) and changes only avgpool to transformer aggregation. It tests whether learned attention across profiles adds accuracy beyond simple pooling. That is likely one of the largest remaining design levers, and the single-variable change keeps the comparison clean. 3) This is a direct exploitation of the strongest result that also resolves a key design choice. The outcome will guide the remaining 7 runs: if transformer helps, later runs will test RNA encoders and fusion on top of it; if not, avgpool stays as the cheaper default. Expected cost is moderate to somewhat higher than config_012 (roughly 5–7 GPU h) because of the transformer aggregator. That is justified because it could plausibly become the best configuration.

1) Evidence: three multiprofile multimodal runs point the same way. ImageNet ViT-L beat ResNet50 (0.715 vs 0.573) and avgpool beat transformer aggregation (0.715 vs 0.532), with F1 agreeing in both cases. These are single runs, so the conclusions are provisional. Every run so far used scvi_n200 as the RNA encoder, so the RNA encoder is the largest untested design choice. 2) Test: config_007 keeps the best setup (ViT-L, avgpool, concat) and swaps scvi_n200 for scGPT. This one-factor change shows whether foundation-model RNA embeddings add accuracy beyond scVI. 3) Why now: RNA representation probably matters more than fusion type, so it is the most informative next step and directly exploits the current best. If scGPT helps, later runs can refine fusion (weighted). If not, the pca_n2000 and weighted-fusion variants stay as options. Expected cost is about 4.5–5 GPU hours, similar to config_012 and well below the ResNet50 run (7.27 GPU hours).

Evidence: config_012 (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l, multiprofile, avgpool, concat) is the clear leader at 0.715 accuracy and 0.687 F1. Each single-factor change from it has hurt: resnet50 gave 0.573, transformer aggregation 0.532, weighted fusion 0.527 and scGPT 0.619. So vit_l, avgpool and concat look strong for now. 1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_012 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI, ViT-L, avgpool, concat), with accuracy 0.715 and F1 0.687. Changing one component at a time from that setup has consistently hurt. PCA dropped accuracy to 0.688, scGPT to 0.619, and ResNet50 to 0.573. Swapping in transformer aggregation (0.532) or weighted fusion (0.527) hurt the most. The local neighborhood around config_012 is now well mapped. Evidence: the best result so far is config_012 (scVI + ViT-L, multiprofile avgpool, concat fusion) at 0.715 accuracy. Single-factor changes from it all scored lower: a transformer aggregator gave 0.53, weighted fusion gave 0.53, a ResNet50 image encoder gave 0.57 and single-profile gave 0.43. Changing the RNA encoder also shifted accuracy noticeably (PCA 0.688, scGPT 0.619). That leaves one important open question: does the RNA branch help at all, or does the ViT-L image signal drive most of the performance? This experiment runs the ViT-L multiprofile avgpool setup image-only to answer that. If it matches or beats 0.715, it could become the best configuration, and it would point the last two experiments toward image-centric variants. If it falls short, that confirms multimodal fusion helps and justifies spending the remaining budget on multimodal refinements. The other untested multimodal variants change components that have already been shown to hurt, so this ablation is the most informative remaining option with a real chance of a new best. Expected cost is low, about 3-4 GPU hours or slightly below the ~4.5 h ViT-L multimodal runs, because the RNA encoder and fusion steps are dropped.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is image-only, ViT-L, multiprofile, avgpool (config_013: 0.725 accuracy, F1 0.685) at only 1.41 GPU hours. Adding RNA did not improve on it: scVI reached 0.715, PCA 0.688 and scGPT 0.619. ViT-L clearly beats ResNet50, multiprofile clearly beats singleprofile, and weighted fusion hurt. Every multimodal ViT-L avgpool concat variant has already been tested. 2. What this tests: The main open question within the best model family is aggregation. Transformer aggregation hurt in one multimodal run (0.53). That single result may reflect overfitting or interference from fusion rather than a general weakness of attention-based aggregation over multiple profiles. This experiment tests transformer aggregation in the image-only setting directly. 3. Why it is the best use of the budget: Other untested branches are unlikely to beat 0.725, including RNA-only, ResNet50 models and weighted fusion. This is therefore the most plausible remaining way to improve on the best result. Expected cost is low, slightly above config_013 (about 1.5 to 2 GPU hours) and far below any multimodal run.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_013 (image-only, ViT-L, multiprofile, avgpool) at 0.725 accuracy. The search is consistent on four design choices: multiprofile beats singleprofile, avgpool beats transformer, concat beats weighted fusion, and ViT-L beats ResNet50 (0.715 vs 0.573). The strongest multimodal run (scVI + ViT-L, avgpool, concat) reached 0.715, slightly below image-only. That leaves RNA alone as the main unmeasured factor, since no RNA-only model has been tested. 2) What it tests: config_032 trains RNA-only on scVI features with multiprofile avgpool, the best-performing aggregation and the best RNA encoder in multimodal runs. It shows whether the RNA modality can stand on its own or whether fusion has been diluting the image signal. 3) Why this one: The other untested options mostly repeat choices that have consistently hurt (transformer aggregation, weighted fusion, ResNet50, singleprofile), so they are unlikely to beat 0.725. This is the one remaining experiment with real uncertainty and some chance of a new best. Its odds of beating 0.725 are modest, given multimodal scored below image-only. Expected cost is low: likely around or below 1.4 GPU hours, similar to or cheaper than the image-only runs, since there is no image encoder or fusion step.

1. Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been run yet, so I am relying only on domain priors. Those priors suggest that combining RNA and image data, and aggregating over multiple profiles, usually beats single-modality or single-profile setups. The main open questions are which encoders and which aggregation and fusion choices work best. 2. What this tests: config_003 is a strong but not maximal anchor. It is multimodal and multiprofile, pairs the compact scVI-200 RNA embedding with the strong ViT-L image encoder, and uses weighted fusion with cheap average-pool aggregation. The result sets a high-quality baseline. Later runs can then change one factor at a time: transformer aggregation, scGPT or PCA for RNA, ResNet50 for images, concat fusion, or single-modality ablations. 3. Why now: Starting near the likely high-performing region raises the chance of a good final best under a 10-run budget. It also avoids the most expensive options (scGPT plus transformer aggregation) until there is evidence they pay off. Expected relative cost is moderate to high: multimodal multiprofile with a large ViT adds cost, while avgpool and the 200-dimensional scVI input keep it below the transformer and scGPT variants.

1) Evidence: there is only one result so far. config_003 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI + ViT-L, avgpool, weighted fusion) reached 0.494 accuracy and 0.453 F1 for 4.82 GPU hours. With one data point, no design choice has been tested yet. 2) This run changes one factor from config_003: avgpool aggregation becomes transformer aggregation, with everything else held fixed. That makes it a clean test of whether learned attention across profiles beats simple averaging. In multiprofile set-ups this is often one of the biggest levers on accuracy. 3) It is the best next step because it isolates a high-impact choice while staying near the only known working configuration. It also has a plausible chance of becoming the new best. The answer will guide later runs: keep the transformer if it helps, or switch to the cheaper avgpool and single-profile or encoder comparisons if it does not. Evidence: with scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l and weighted fusion held fixed, avgpool aggregation (0.494 acc, 0.453 F1) clearly beat transformer aggregation (0.328 acc, 0.288 F1). That gap is large enough to treat avgpool as the working choice for now, though it is still only one comparison. The main open question is which RNA encoder works best, since RNA features likely drive much of the signal. Test: config_025 keeps the best-known setup (multimodal, multiprofile, vit_l, avgpool, weighted) and changes only the RNA encoder, from scvi_n200 to the scGPT foundation-model embeddings. Any change in accuracy can then be credited to the encoder. Why now: it exploits the strong avgpool result while exploring the RNA encoder, which could plausibly give a large gain. Fusion type and image encoder can be tested in later experiments. Expected cost: similar to or slightly above config_003 (~5 GPU hours), because it uses the same multiprofile vit_l avgpool pipeline and scGPT embeddings may be somewhat larger.

1) Evidence so far: the best result is scGPT + ViT-L + avgpool + weighted fusion (0.537 accuracy, 0.518 F1). scGPT beat scVI by about 4 points under matched settings. Avgpool clearly beat transformer aggregation with scVI (0.494 vs 0.328), so avgpool looks like the right aggregation. Fusion type is still completely untested, since every run so far used weighted fusion. 2) This run keeps the best configuration fixed and switches only weighted fusion to concat. That cleanly isolates the effect of fusion on the strongest RNA/image/aggregation setup. 3) Why this is the best next use: fusion is the main untested design choice on the leading branch, and concat could plausibly add accuracy. The result also tells us which fusion to carry into the remaining runs (for example, a ResNet50 image-encoder swap or unimodal baselines). Expected cost is similar to config_025, roughly 3 GPU hours, because concat fusion adds negligible overhead. That makes it cheaper than the scVI ViT-L avgpool run at about 4.8 GPU hours.

1. Evidence: Every run so far used the imagenet_vit_l image encoder. Within that setting, avgpool beat transformer aggregation (0.494 vs 0.328), weighted fusion beat concat (0.537 vs 0.260), and scGPT beat scVI (0.537 vs 0.494). Each of these rests on a single comparison, but together they point to scgpt + avgpool + weighted as the current best (config_025, 0.537 accuracy, 0.518 F1). The image encoder is still a completely untested design choice. 2. Test: config_007 keeps the best configuration unchanged except for swapping the image encoder to resnet50. This isolates the effect of the image backbone and tells us whether a better configuration exists around the current best. 3. Why now: It exploits the strongest region found so far while reducing uncertainty about an important axis that has not been explored. The result will guide the remaining 5 experiments, for example whether to try pca_n2000 or single-profile variants with resnet50 or vit_l. Expected cost: about 3 GPU hours or less, similar to or cheaper than config_025, since resnet50 features are smaller than ViT-L's and avgpool with weighted fusion was the cheapest setup observed.

1) Evidence so far: every run has been multiprofile. Weighted fusion clearly beats concat (0.537 vs 0.260). Avgpool clearly beats transformer aggregation (0.494 vs 0.328 with scVI). scGPT beats scVI (0.537 vs 0.494), and ViT-L edges out ResNet50 (0.537 vs 0.514). The best so far is config_025 (scGPT + ViT-L + avgpool + weighted, 0.537 accuracy, 0.518 F1). The biggest open question is the profile setting, since single-profile has never been tested. 2) This run keeps the strongest components (scGPT, ViT-L, weighted fusion) and switches to single-profile. It is the closest controlled comparison to config_025 and shows whether multiprofile aggregation is actually helping. 3) If single-profile matches or beats multiprofile, it opens a cheaper and possibly better branch for the remaining 3 experiments. If it loses, it confirms that multiprofile is worth its cost, and the remaining runs can test the PCA encoder or RNA-only variants. Expected cost is relatively low, likely below config_025's 2.94 GPU hours, because there is no multiprofile aggregation step.

1) Evidence: weighted fusion is clearly better than concat (0.537 vs 0.260 with scGPT/ViT-L). avgpool beats transformer aggregation (0.494 vs 0.328 with scVI). scGPT beats scVI (0.537 vs 0.494). ViT-L is slightly better than ResNet50. Single-profile scGPT/ViT-L/weighted (0.523) came close to the multiprofile best (0.537) at about 1/4 of the cost (0.67 vs 2.94 GPU hours). The main untested design choice is the pca_n2000 RNA encoder, which is often a strong baseline. 2) Test: config_008 checks pca_n2000 with the best known settings (ViT-L, weighted fusion) in the cheap single-profile setting. If PCA matches or beats scGPT, I can use a remaining experiment on its multiprofile avgpool weighted counterpart (config_036). If not, I can put the remaining budget into refining the scGPT branch.

1) Evidence: weighted fusion clearly beats concat (0.537 vs 0.260 for scGPT/ViT-L multiprofile avgpool). Avgpool clearly beats transformer aggregation (0.494 vs 0.327 for scVI). ViT-L beats ResNet50 (0.537 vs 0.514). Multiprofile avgpool gives a modest gain over single-profile for scGPT (0.537 vs 0.523). Among RNA encoders, PCA-2000 nearly matched scGPT in the single-profile setting (0.520 vs 0.523), while scVI was weaker. The main open question is whether PCA-2000 can match or beat scGPT once it is placed in the best known setup. 2) This experiment tests PCA-2000 with ViT-L, multiprofile avgpool and weighted fusion, keeping every other design choice at its best value. It isolates the RNA-encoder choice in the top-performing setup and could beat the current best of 0.537. 3) It is the most promising untested extension of the strongest evidence, and its result will guide the last two experiments. Expected cost is moderate, roughly 3–5 GPU hours, similar to other multiprofile avgpool weighted runs. That is higher than single-profile runs but justified by its higher expected accuracy.

1. Evidence: the multimodal, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted setup with the imagenet_vit_l encoder is the best family so far: pca 0.540 and scgpt 0.537. Concat fusion was much worse (0.26). Transformer aggregation was much worse (0.33 vs 0.49 with scvi). ViT-L beat ResNet50 (0.537 vs 0.514). The choice of RNA encoder mattered little between pca and scgpt, and the remaining untested multimodal variants (ResNet50, scvi, transformer, concat) all contain components that look worse. The main open question is whether the RNA branch helps at all, since no unimodal baseline has been tested.
2. This experiment: image-only, multiprofile, avgpool with the ViT-L encoder isolates the image branch inside the best-performing structure. Weighted fusion may already be leaning heavily on the image modality, so an image-only model could match or beat the multimodal ones by avoiding RNA noise.
3. Why now: it is the highest-information remaining option that still has a real chance of a new best, and it tells us whether the final experiment should refine multimodal or unimodal. Expected cost is moderate: likely lower than config_036 (7.0 GPU h) and roughly similar to or below config_025 (2.9 GPU h), because there is no RNA encoder or fusion step.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_036 (pca_n2000, ViT-L, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted) at 0.540 accuracy and 0.524 F1. The image-only ViT-L avgpool model (config_038) nearly matches it at 0.536. Avgpool clearly beats transformer aggregation and weighted fusion clearly beats concat, so those choices are settled. Swapping ViT-L for ResNet50 lowered accuracy with scGPT (0.514 vs 0.537), so config_030 (the ResNet50 version of the best setup) would likely land near 0.51. 2) Uncertainty: The RNA-only branch has never been tested. Because image-only nearly equals multimodal, it is unclear whether RNA contributes much under weighted fusion. Its standalone strength is the largest unexplored question. config_031 tests the RNA encoder that did best in multimodal runs (pca_n2000) with the best aggregation (multiprofile avgpool). 3) Why this last slot: Only the best accuracy counts, and the remaining multimodal variants are predictably at or below the current best. The higher-variance untested branch gives the best, though still uncertain, chance of exceeding 0.540, and RNA-only may well score lower. Expected cost is low to moderate, likely well below config_036's 7 GPU hours, since no image backbone features are processed.

1) Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been run, so there is no evidence yet about which design choices matter. My prior is that multimodal, multiprofile models are most likely to give the highest accuracy, but this has not been confirmed. 2) What it tests: config_024 is multimodal, multiprofile, scVI-200 RNA encoder, ResNet50 image encoder, avgpool aggregation and concat fusion. It is a strong but moderately priced baseline. Cheaper parts (avgpool, ResNet50, a compact 200-dimensional scVI representation, simple concat) let me check whether combining modalities across multiple profiles works before paying for transformer aggregation, ViT-L or scGPT. 3) Why now: A central, well-performing anchor is the best start under a 10-experiment budget. Later runs can change one factor at a time from it (aggregation, image encoder, RNA encoder, fusion) or compare against unimodal and single-profile variants. 1. Evidence: there is only one result so far. config_024 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI-200, ResNet50, avgpool, concat) reached 0.520 accuracy and 0.479 F1 for 7.27 GPU hours. What this tests: config_022 changes only the aggregation, from avgpool to a transformer, and keeps everything else fixed. Why it is the best next step: a single-factor comparison against the baseline gives a clean answer on a key design axis. 1. Evidence and uncertainty: Both completed runs use the multimodal, multiprofile setting with scvi_n200, resnet50 and concat fusion. They differ only in aggregation. Avgpool reached 0.520 accuracy and transformer reached 0.514. That gap is small, the transformer had higher F1 (0.498 vs 0.479), and it was cheaper (5.16 vs 7.27 GPU h). So aggregation looks roughly neutral so far. The bigger unknowns are the image encoder, RNA encoder and fusion type. 2. What this tests: config_036 keeps the cheaper transformer aggregation, scvi_n200 and concat fixed, and swaps only resnet50 for imagenet_vit_l. This isolates the effect of a stronger, larger image representation, which is plausibly the largest untested lever. 3. Why it is the best next use of budget: A clean single-factor comparison of the image encoder reduces uncertainty about a major design choice. It also has real upside for top accuracy. Later experiments can then test the RNA encoder (scgpt or pca) and weighted fusion on the better image backbone. Expected cost: moderately higher than config_022, perhaps around 6–8 GPU hours, because ViT-L features are larger.

1) Evidence: switching the image encoder from resnet50 to imagenet_vit_l gave a large jump, from about 0.51 to 0.715 accuracy (config_036), with F1 rising alongside it. With resnet50, the aggregation choice (avgpool vs transformer) made only a small difference. The transformer was cheaper and had better F1. The RNA encoder is the main design choice not yet explored: every run so far used scvi_n200. 2) Test: config_007 keeps the best setup (multiprofile, ViT-L, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) and swaps only the RNA encoder to scGPT. This isolates whether a foundation-model RNA embedding adds accuracy on top of the strong image features. 3) Why now: the RNA encoder could plausibly shift accuracy as much as the image encoder did. Settling it early tells the remaining 6 runs which RNA encoder to use for fusion and aggregation fine-tuning. Expected cost is similar to config_036 (about 5 GPU hours), possibly slightly higher due to the larger scGPT embeddings. That is moderate relative to the 17 GPU hours used so far.

1. Evidence: The image encoder is the dominant factor so far. imagenet_vit_l configs reached about 0.715–0.721 accuracy, while resnet50 configs reached about 0.51–0.52. The RNA encoder matters much less: scgpt (0.721) and scvi_n200 (0.715) are within noise. Fusion has never been varied, since every run used concat. 2. This experiment keeps the best configuration (config_007: scgpt + imagenet_vit_l + transformer, multiprofile) and changes only the fusion to weighted. That isolates the effect of the one remaining untested design choice on the strongest backbone. 3. A gain here would directly raise the best accuracy found. A loss would settle concat as the fusion choice and free the remaining budget for checking aggregation (avgpool) or an image-only vit_l baseline. 1) Evidence: the image encoder is the dominant factor so far. imagenet_vit_l with transformer aggregation and concat fusion reached about 0.715-0.721 accuracy, versus about 0.51-0.52 for resnet50. Concat fusion clearly beats weighted fusion (0.721 vs 0.537 with scgpt + ViT-L + transformer). scgpt and scvi_n200 perform about the same. The main open question within the strong ViT-L + concat region is aggregation: avgpool has only been tested with resnet50, where it was slightly ahead of transformer (0.520 vs 0.514) and within noise. 2) This experiment holds the best configuration (config_007: scgpt, ViT-L, concat) fixed and swaps transformer for avgpool. 1) Evidence: one combination clearly wins. ImageNet ViT-L with a transformer aggregator and concat fusion reached about 0.72 with both scGPT (0.721) and scVI (0.715). Each single change from that recipe dropped accuracy to about 0.51-0.54: switching to ResNet50, switching to avgpool aggregation, or switching to weighted fusion. Validation F1 follows the same pattern. The RNA encoder made little difference within the best recipe, so the image encoder and aggregator appear to drive performance. 2) This experiment completes the RNA-encoder comparison inside the winning recipe by testing the one untested option, pca_n2000. Weighted fusion, avgpool and ResNet50 variants are strongly indicated to underperform, so testing them would likely waste budget. An image-only ViT-L transformer run (config_043) remains a cheaper follow-up to check whether RNA contributes at all.

1) Evidence: the best results all share imagenet_vit_l with transformer aggregation and concat fusion. config_007 (scGPT) reached 0.721 and config_036 (scVI) reached 0.715. Swapping in resnet50, avgpool or weighted fusion consistently dropped accuracy to about 0.51-0.54. scGPT and scVI score almost the same, while PCA reaches 0.59, so the image branch looks like the main driver. It is still unclear whether the RNA branch adds anything beyond the image signal. 2) Test: an image-only run with the same strong backbone (ViT-L, multiprofile, transformer aggregation). If it falls clearly below, multimodal concat is confirmed and the last experiment can refine the RNA encoder or profile setting. 3) Why now: it stays within the best-performing region, so it has a real chance of matching the top result while resolving a key design question for the final experiment. 1) Evidence: Within multiprofile runs, ViT-L, transformer aggregation and concat fusion form the best combination. config_007 (scGPT) reached 0.721 and config_036 (scVI) reached 0.715. Swapping in avgpool (0.53) or weighted fusion (0.54) dropped accuracy sharply. PCA (0.59) and ResNet50 (about 0.52) were clearly worse. Image-only ViT-L scored 0.639, so adding RNA helps. The profile setting is the one major axis not yet tested: every run so far has been multiprofile. 2) This experiment keeps the winning RNA encoder, image encoder and fusion (scGPT + ViT-L + concat) and switches to singleprofile, which removes aggregation. This run explores the last untested key design choice at low risk and gives a basis for the final experiment. Expected cost is low, likely below the best multiprofile run (about 4 GPU hours), probably around 1–3 GPU hours, because no multiprofile aggregation is needed.

1) Evidence: The strong region is multiprofile + ViT-L + transformer + concat. scGPT reached 0.721 and scVI reached 0.715, while PCA reached 0.591. All three RNA encoders are now tested in that setup, so no untested near-copy of the best remains. Both alternatives to the best setup scored much lower with scGPT: avgpool fell to 0.532 and weighted fusion fell to 0.537. However, the weighted-fusion drop is a single data point and could depend on the encoder. 2) This experiment tests whether weighted fusion works better with the scVI ViT-L transformer setup, the second-best configuration. If the scGPT result was encoder-specific, this could beat 0.721. 3) With one run left, any choice is a long shot, but this is a one-factor change from a top configuration. The other one-step option, scVI with avgpool (config_018), changes a factor that hurt consistently and costs about 7 GPU hours. Image-only and RNA-only options are unlikely to beat multimodal. 1. Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been run, so I am relying on priors. For multimodal cellular profiling, combining RNA and image signals and pooling information across multiple profiles usually gives the highest accuracy. Strong pretrained image features (ViT-L) and a compact, well-regularized RNA latent space (scVI with 200 dimensions) are reasonable defaults. Learned weighted fusion and transformer aggregation tend to match or beat concatenation and average pooling. 2. What it tests: config_043 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI-n200, ViT-L, transformer, weighted) is my best prior guess for a top-performing setup. It sets a high-performing anchor that later runs can be compared against, one factor at a time. Likely follow-ups are avgpool vs. transformer (config_011), ResNet50 vs. ViT-L (config_010), and modality ablations to check whether the extra cost is justified. 3. Why now: Only the best accuracy within the budget counts, so securing a strong result early lowers risk and makes later cheaper ablations easy to interpret. Expected relative cost: high, among the most expensive options, because it combines multiprofile transformer aggregation, multimodal processing and ViT-L features. I accept that cost because this configuration is plausibly the best one.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: there is only one result so far. The full multimodal setup (multiprofile, scvi_n200 RNA encoder, ViT-L image encoder, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) reached 0.619 accuracy and 0.610 F1 at 3.6 GPU hours. We do not know which part of this expensive setup drives the score. The most important and most cost-relevant unknown is whether multiprofile aggregation helps at all. 2. What this tests: config_004 changes only the profile setting to singleprofile. It keeps the same RNA encoder, image encoder and fusion, so the comparison isolates the value of multiprofile aggregation. 3. Why it is the best next step: the answer determines where the remaining 8 experiments go. If single-profile comes close to 0.619, later searches over encoders and fusion can use cheap single-profile runs. If it drops clearly, we can focus on multiprofile variants such as aggregation type and RNA encoder with confidence. Expected cost is substantially lower than config_043, roughly 30-50% of its 3.6 GPU hours, since no multiprofile aggregation is needed.

1) Evidence: with the scVI-n200 + ViT-L weighted-fusion backbone held fixed, the multiprofile transformer reached 0.619 accuracy (F1 0.610). The single-profile version reached 0.573. That is a solid gain of about 4.6 points, but it cost about 7x more (3.60 vs 0.53 GPU h). Evidence: across three runs, multiprofile with transformer aggregation (config_043, 0.619 acc / 0.610 F1) clearly beats singleprofile (0.573) and avgpool aggregation (0.422). So transformer-based multiprofile aggregation is the strongest direction so far. Uncertainty: the RNA encoder, image encoder and fusion type have each been tested at only one value (scvi_n200, ViT-L, weighted). Test: config_005 keeps the best setup and changes only the RNA encoder, from scvi_n200 to scGPT, as a clean one-factor comparison. Why now: the RNA representation is plausibly the largest remaining lever on accuracy. Exploiting the best architecture while varying one key factor balances exploitation with reducing uncertainty, leaving five later runs to probe fusion (e.g., config_047) or a cheaper ResNet50 encoder (config_010). Expected cost: similar to or slightly above config_043, about 3.5–4.5 GPU hours, since it is still multiprofile multimodal with transformer aggregation and scGPT embeddings may be somewhat larger.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_043 (scVI + ViT-L, multiprofile, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) at 0.619 accuracy. Two design choices look settled. Transformer aggregation clearly beats avgpool (0.619 vs 0.422 with everything else the same). scVI beats scGPT (0.619 vs 0.520). Multiprofile with transformer also beats singleprofile (0.573). Fusion has not been varied at all, since every run so far used weighted fusion. 2) Test: config_047 changes only the fusion, from weighted to concat, on the best configuration. This cleanly tells us whether concat fusion helps the leading setup. 3) Why now: It exploits the strongest direction while closing the largest untested design gap. Changing just one factor makes the result easy to interpret. The answer tells us which fusion to use in later tests of PCA RNA features and the ResNet50 image encoder. Expected cost is similar to config_043, about 3.5–4 GPU hours, since it uses the same multiprofile transformer and ViT-L setup. That is moderately expensive, but justified because it is the most likely candidate to improve on the current best.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_043 (scVI + ViT-L, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion), at 0.619 accuracy and 0.610 F1. Since the RNA encoder has shown the largest single-swap effect apart from fusion and aggregation, which are now settled, this is the most likely route to a new best within the remaining budget. 1) Evidence: the best result so far is config_043 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI, ViT-L, transformer, weighted) at 0.619 accuracy / 0.610 F1. 1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_043 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI n200, ViT-L, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) at 0.619 accuracy and 0.610 F1. Test: config_027 keeps the strongest components (scVI n200 encoder and transformer multiprofile aggregation) but removes the image modality. 1) Evidence: The best result so far is the cheap RNA-only scVI multiprofile transformer (config_027, 0.629 acc, 0.40 GPU h). The best multimodal run (config_043, 0.619) scored slightly lower on accuracy, slightly higher on F1 (0.610 vs 0.599), and cost 9x more. So adding images has not clearly helped. Two design choices look settled: transformer aggregation beat avgpool by a wide margin, and weighted fusion beat concat by a wide margin. The RNA encoder is the main open lever. 1) Evidence: the best result so far is rna_only, multiprofile, scvi_n200 with a transformer (config_027, 0.629 acc), slightly ahead of its multimodal weighted counterpart (0.619). The image branch seems to add little. Several factors look clearly harmful: avgpool cost about 0.20 accuracy, scgpt about 0.10, pca about 0.10 to 0.20, and concat fusion was catastrophic. The mildest penalty seen was singleprofile versus multiprofile in the multimodal setting, about 0.046. 2) This experiment tests whether the strongest RNA-only setup (scvi_n200) works as well or better without multiprofile aggregation. Without the image branch and aggregation noise, a simpler model could match or exceed config_027. 3) Since this is the final experiment, the other candidates near the best are weak bets. scgpt RNA-only, scvi avgpool and image-only all have direct evidence of larger drops. It should also be the cheapest option, likely under 0.4 GPU hours, comparable to or below config_027.

1) No experiments have been run, so there is no evidence on any axis: modality, profile setting, RNA encoder, image encoder, aggregation or fusion. Priors from multimodal profiling suggest that combining RNA and image modalities, and aggregating over multiple profiles, both tend to improve accuracy. 2) config_004 tests that prior with a mid-range setup: multimodal, multiprofile, the compact scvi_n200 RNA encoder, the strong imagenet_vit_l image encoder, cheap avgpool aggregation and simple concat fusion. It avoids the costliest components (scgpt, transformer aggregation) while keeping the likely highest-value ones. 3) It is a strong anchor result early in the budget. Later experiments can then change one factor at a time: transformer vs. avgpool aggregation, scgpt or PCA vs. scVI, weighted vs. concat fusion, or unimodal and single-profile ablations. Expected cost is moderate to high: multiprofile multimodal training with ViT-L features costs more than unimodal or single-profile runs, but avgpool and the 200-dim scVI input keep it below the transformer or scgpt variants.

1) Evidence: there is only one result so far. The multimodal, multiprofile setup with scVI-200, ViT-L, avgpool and concat reached 0.635 validation accuracy and 0.618 F1, at 4.49 GPU hours. Nothing else has been measured yet. 2) Question: config_006 changes only the aggregation, from avgpool to a transformer, and keeps every other setting the same. This gives a clean test of whether learned attention across profiles beats mean pooling. Aggregation is a major design choice and likely has a large effect on accuracy in multiprofile settings. 3) Why now: of the single-factor changes available, this one has the best chance of improving on the current best. Whatever the result, it tells us which aggregation to carry forward into later RNA-encoder and fusion comparisons. Expected cost is moderately higher than config_004, roughly 1.2 to 1.5 times or about 5.5 to 7 GPU hours, because transformer aggregation adds overhead. 1) Evidence: Only two runs exist, and they differ only in aggregation. Avgpool (config_004: acc 0.635, F1 0.618) clearly beat transformer (config_006: acc 0.507, F1 0.455) with scVI + ViT-L + concat. Avgpool is the better aggregation for now, but the RNA encoder, image encoder and fusion choices are still untested. 2) This run keeps the best setup (multimodal, multiprofile, ViT-L, avgpool, concat) and swaps only the RNA encoder from scvi_n200 to scGPT. It tests whether a foundation-model RNA representation beats scVI. The RNA encoder is likely one of the most influential choices, with the largest possible gain over the current best. 3) A single-factor change from the best run gives a clean comparison.
