Expected cost is similar to config_004, about 4.5–5 GPU hours, and possibly slightly higher if scGPT embeddings are larger. This is a moderate cost, comparable to the runs so far.

1) Evidence: avgpool aggregation clearly beats transformer aggregation (0.635 vs 0.507 with scvi_n200 + ViT-L + concat). Swapping scvi_n200 for scgpt raised accuracy to 0.678, with F1 0.646, making scgpt + ViT-L + avgpool the best configuration so far. Fusion strategy is still completely untested: every run so far used concat. 2) This experiment keeps the best configuration fixed and changes only fusion from concat to weighted. That isolates whether learned modality weighting improves on simple concatenation. 3) It is the most direct extension of the current best, and it answers a design question that affects all later multimodal choices. Testing resnet50 instead would save some compute, but it seems less likely to beat ViT-L. Expected cost is relatively high, about 7 GPU hours, similar to config_016, because it uses scGPT, ViT-L and multiprofile aggregation. I accept that cost because this configuration has a strong chance of being the top performer.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_035 (scGPT + ViT-L + avgpool + weighted fusion), at 0.688 accuracy and 0.659 F1. Two trends are reasonably consistent. scGPT beat scVI under matched settings (0.678 vs 0.635). Avgpool clearly beat the transformer aggregator (0.635 vs 0.507). Weighted fusion edged out concat, and it trained faster. The image encoder has never been varied, since every run so far used ViT-L, so it is the largest unresolved design choice. 2. Test: This run keeps the best setup and swaps only the image encoder to ResNet50. That isolates whether a CNN image backbone helps or hurts relative to ViT-L. 3. Why now: This choice covers an untested dimension while keeping the strongest known RNA, aggregation and fusion choices, so it is both exploration and a real chance to beat the current best. The result also tells us which image encoder to use in the remaining runs, for example when trying PCA RNA features. Expected cost: ResNet50 features are smaller than ViT-L, so this should cost about the same as or less than config_035's 2.9 GPU hours, among the cheapest multimodal multiprofile runs.

1) Evidence: avgpool clearly beats transformer aggregation (0.635 vs 0.507 with scVI). ViT-L beats ResNet50 (0.688 vs 0.639 with scGPT and weighted fusion). Weighted fusion slightly beats concat for scGPT (0.688 vs 0.678), and F1 agrees. The best so far is config_035 (scGPT + ViT-L + avgpool + weighted, 0.688). The largest open question is the RNA encoder: scGPT beats scVI, but pca_n2000 has never been tested. 2) This run keeps the best-known setup fixed (multiprofile, ViT-L, avgpool, weighted fusion) and swaps only the RNA encoder to pca_n2000. That isolates whether a high-dimensional PCA representation can match or exceed scGPT. Simple PCA baselines are often competitive in single-cell tasks, so it has a real chance of beating 0.688. 3) It is the untested option most likely to set a new best while also settling an important design choice, and it avoids weaker directions such as transformer aggregation or swapping to ResNet. Expected cost is moderate, roughly 3–5 GPU hours, similar to the other ViT-L avgpool runs and well below the 7.18-hour config_016 run.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: the best result so far is config_035 (scGPT + ViT-L, avgpool, weighted fusion; acc 0.688, F1 0.659). Three choices look settled. scGPT clearly beats scVI and PCA, which collapsed to 0.21. ViT-L beats ResNet50 (0.688 vs 0.639). Weighted fusion slightly beats concat (0.688 vs 0.678). Transformer aggregation lost about 13 points against avgpool in the one direct comparison, so it looks unpromising. The one major design axis not yet tested is the profile setting: every run so far has been multiprofile. 2. What this tests: config_027 keeps the best components (scGPT, ViT-L, weighted fusion) but uses single-profile input. Why it is the best use of this slot: it reduces uncertainty about an untested dimension at low risk, since it keeps the strongest encoders and fusion. Evidence: the best result so far is config_035 (scGPT + ViT-L, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted fusion; acc 0.688, F1 0.659). Around it, scGPT beat scVI and PCA, ViT-L beat ResNet50, and weighted fusion slightly beat concat. The only design choice still uncertain near this optimum is aggregation. Our single transformer result (config_006, 0.507) used the weaker scVI encoder with concat fusion, so it is weak evidence that transformer aggregation hurts in general. Test: config_017 changes only the aggregation of the best configuration to transformer. This shows whether attention-based aggregation over profiles helps or hurts once paired with the strongest encoders and weighted fusion. Why now: it is the remaining single-factor change with a plausible chance of beating 0.688. Other options are unlikely to: scVI with weighted fusion was worse with concat, and the ResNet and PCA variants also underperformed. RNA-only scGPT is unlikely to win because the ViT-over-ResNet gain shows the image modality contributes. 1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_035 (0.688 acc, 0.659 F1), using scGPT, ViT-L, avgpool and weighted fusion. Three patterns are consistent. scGPT beats scVI (0.678 vs 0.635 under concat). Avgpool clearly beats transformer aggregation (about 0.13–0.15 lower with transformer). So they are unlikely to beat 0.688. For example, config_048 (scVI with weighted fusion) would probably land around 0.64–0.65. 2) Open question: The search has never tested a unimodal baseline. scGPT carries most of the signal, and the ViT-L vs ResNet50 gap shows the image branch matters, but RNA-only scGPT with multiprofile avgpool (config_029) has not been tried. It shows whether fusion truly adds accuracy or whether a simpler RNA-only model is competitive. 1. Evidence: the best result so far is config_035 (scGPT + ViT-L, multiprofile avgpool, weighted fusion) at 0.688 accuracy and 0.659 F1. Avgpool clearly beats transformer aggregation (about 0.13–0.15 better). ViT-L beats ResNet50 by about 0.05. Test: the only untested multimodal configuration that keeps all the winning choices except the RNA encoder is config_048 (scVI + ViT-L, avgpool, weighted). Why this is the best final experiment: it is the strongest remaining candidate built from the winning design choices. 1) No experiments have been run, so there is no evidence yet. Prior knowledge suggests that multimodal fusion and multiprofile aggregation usually help on cellular profiling tasks, but the size of each effect here is unknown. 2) config_014 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI-200 RNA, ResNet50 image, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) is a strong but moderately priced anchor. It uses the components most likely to work well while avoiding the most expensive ones (scGPT, ViT-L). Its result sets a baseline from which later runs can change one factor at a time: ablate to rna_only or image_only, swap avgpool for transformer aggregation, swap weighted for concat fusion, or upgrade the encoders. 3) Starting from a likely high-performing, mid-cost configuration makes the most of a 10-run budget. It probably yields a competitive score right away and gives a clean reference point for factor-wise comparisons. Expected cost is medium: multiprofile transformer aggregation and two modalities add cost, but the compact scVI and ResNet50 encoders keep it well below scGPT/ViT-L multiprofile configurations.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: there is only one result so far. config_014 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200 + resnet50, transformer, concat) reached 0.525 accuracy and 0.498 F1. That is a single point, so we do not yet know which design choices drive performance. The image encoder is one of the most important open questions, since a large pretrained ViT-L could give much richer morphology features than ResNet50. 2. What this tests: config_002 changes only the image encoder to imagenet_vit_l and keeps everything else the same. Any difference in accuracy can therefore be attributed to the image backbone. The result tells us which image encoder to carry forward in later multimodal configurations. 3. Why now: this is a clean single-factor comparison on a design axis that is likely high-impact. It reduces a key uncertainty and also has a reasonable chance of directly improving the best accuracy. Expected cost is moderately higher than config_014's 5.16 GPU hours, perhaps 1.3–2x, because ViT-L produces larger representations. That cost is justified because the image backbone is likely to matter for top accuracy. Cheaper axes such as avgpool aggregation and unimodal baselines can be explored next.

1) Evidence: The two runs differ only in the image encoder. Swapping ResNet50 for ImageNet ViT-L raised validation accuracy from 0.525 to 0.713, and F1 rose with it (0.498 to 0.695). This points to ViT-L as the stronger image backbone, though it rests on one pair of runs. ViT-L also cost slightly less (4.65 vs 5.16 GPU hours). The RNA encoder, aggregation and fusion choices are still untested. 2) Test: Keep the best setup (multimodal, multiprofile, ViT-L, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) and change only the RNA encoder from scVI to the pretrained foundation model scGPT. Changing one factor keeps the comparison clean. 3) Why now: The RNA encoder is likely the next most important design choice. A richer pretrained RNA representation could add accuracy on top of the strong image features. If it helps, later runs can tune aggregation and fusion around the new best. If it does not, scVI is confirmed and the remaining budget can go to cheaper avgpool or weighted-fusion variants. Expected cost: similar to config_002, about 4.5 to 5.5 GPU hours, possibly a bit more if scGPT embeddings are larger.

1) Evidence: the image encoder is the main driver so far. ImageNet ViT-L beat ResNet50 by about 0.19 accuracy (0.713 vs 0.525) with the same scVI encoder, transformer aggregation and concat fusion. scVI_n200 edged out scGPT (0.713 vs 0.688, with F1 agreeing), though that gap is modest. Fusion and aggregation are still completely untested. 2) This experiment holds the best setup fixed (scVI_n200 + ViT-L + multiprofile transformer) and changes only concat to weighted fusion. That isolates the effect of fusion on the strongest base configuration. 3) It exploits the clear direction while resolving an important open design choice in one step, and the result tells us which fusion to carry into later aggregation or RNA-encoder tests. Expected cost is similar to config_002 (about 4.5–5 GPU hours), since weighted fusion adds negligible compute over concat.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_002 (scVI + ViT-L + transformer + concat, 0.713 accuracy, 0.695 F1). ViT-L clearly beats ResNet50 (0.713 vs 0.525), and concat clearly beats weighted fusion (0.713 vs 0.535). scGPT comes close to scVI (0.688). Aggregation has never been varied, because every run so far used the transformer. 2. Test: config_025 keeps the winning setup (scVI, ViT-L, concat) and swaps transformer aggregation for avgpool. This isolates whether the transformer aggregator is needed, or whether simple pooling matches or beats it. 3. Why now: aggregation is the largest remaining untested design choice in the top region of the search space. The result tells us whether later experiments should stay with transformer or move to avgpool variants, such as PCA or scGPT RNA encoders with avgpool. Expected cost is moderate and likely lower than the transformer runs (about 3–4 GPU hours), because avgpool aggregation is lighter than a transformer.

1) Evidence: Within the multimodal multiprofile setting, the best result so far is config_002 (scvi_n200 + ViT-L + transformer + concat, 0.713 acc / 0.695 F1). Each single-factor change from it hurt performance. Switching to ResNet50 gave 0.525, weighted fusion gave 0.535, avgpool gave 0.260, and scGPT gave 0.688. So ViT-L, transformer aggregation and concat fusion look clearly preferred. 2) Test: The only untested RNA encoder in this winning setup is pca_n2000. config_046 is the one-factor swap that tests whether PCA features beat scVI. 3) Why now: The other components are well supported, so RNA encoder choice is the main open question with real upside. This makes config_046 the most likely way to improve on the current best. Expected cost is moderate, about 4–5 GPU hours, similar to the other ViT-L multimodal transformer runs. The 2000-dimensional PCA input may make it slightly more expensive than the scVI version.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_002 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI, ViT-L, transformer, concat) at 0.713 accuracy. Every one-factor change from it has scored worse: ResNet50 image encoder (0.525), weighted fusion (0.535), avgpool aggregation (0.260), and the scGPT and PCA RNA encoders (0.688, 0.632). All three RNA encoders have now been tried with ViT-L, transformer and concat, so that neighbourhood is exhausted. The main untested question is whether the RNA branch helps at all. RNA encoder choice shifts accuracy by about 8 points, but that does not show multimodal beats image-only, because a weak RNA representation could be adding noise. 2) Test: config_027 keeps the best image path (ViT-L with transformer multiprofile aggregation) and drops RNA. If it matches or beats 0.713, image-only becomes the best direction. If it falls clearly below, RNA fusion is confirmed as useful and the remaining two experiments can focus on the multimodal space, for example the single-profile variant config_018. 3) Why now: it removes a major uncertainty about model setting and has a realistic chance of a new best. Expected cost is moderate and likely slightly below the roughly 4–5 GPU hours of the multimodal multiprofile runs, since there is no RNA encoder or fusion step.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_002 (scVI + ViT-L, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) at 0.713 accuracy and 0.695 F1. Single-factor changes from it have all lowered accuracy. Swapping the RNA encoder to scGPT gave 0.688 and to PCA gave 0.632. Swapping the image encoder to ResNet50 gave 0.525. Switching fusion to weighted gave 0.535, and switching aggregation to avgpool gave 0.260. The image-only model reached 0.532, so RNA adds substantially. The main design choice still untested is single-profile versus multi-profile input. 2) Test: config_018 keeps the best encoders and concat fusion but uses single-profile input with no aggregation. This shows whether multi-profile aggregation is needed at all, or whether the transformer gains came from avoiding the poor avgpool aggregation. 3) Value: This is the one high-uncertainty factor whose answer could still beat config_002 or redirect the last experiment. Single-profile should also be the cheaper option, roughly 2–3 GPU hours against about 4.65 for config_002. With two experiments left, settling this now leaves one run to exploit the answer.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_002 (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l, multiprofile, transformer, concat) at 0.713 accuracy and 0.695 F1. Every single-factor change from it has been tested except one, and each did worse. Swapping the RNA encoder gave 0.688 (scgpt) and 0.632 (pca). Swapping the image encoder to resnet50 gave 0.525. Avgpool aggregation gave 0.260, weighted fusion gave 0.535, single-profile gave 0.527, and image-only gave 0.532. The one untested neighbour is the RNA-only version. 2. What this tests: config_047 (RNA-only, scvi_n200, multiprofile, transformer) measures how much of the multimodal gain comes from the RNA branch. Image-only reaches only 0.53, so RNA may carry most of the signal. If so, a cheap unimodal model could come close to or match the best. It also tells us whether the image branch is truly needed. 3. Why it is the best use of the slot: the remaining multimodal options pair at least one choice already shown to hurt (weighted fusion, avgpool, resnet50, pca or scgpt) and are unlikely to beat 0.713. This is the last unexplored direction adjacent to the best configuration. Expected cost is low, about 1–2 GPU hours, similar to the image-only run and roughly a third of a multimodal multiprofile run.

Evidence: the best result so far is config_002 (multimodal, scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l, transformer, concat) at 0.713 accuracy. The other design choices all scored clearly lower: avgpool aggregation 0.26, weighted fusion 0.54, resnet50 0.53, single-profile 0.53 and pca_n2000 0.63. The remaining multimodal transformer-concat options all use resnet50 or weighted fusion, so they are unlikely to beat 0.713 and each costs about 4-5 GPU hours. The surprise is that rna_only scvi with a transformer reached 0.678 at only 0.40 GPU hours, so most of the signal comes from the RNA side with multiprofile transformer aggregation. Test: config_051 swaps in scgpt for rna_only with transformer aggregation. scgpt was close to scvi in the multimodal setting (0.688 vs 0.713), so this checks whether scgpt alone gives a competitive or better RNA-only model. Why now: this is the last experiment, and no untested option has strong odds of beating 0.713. A cheap test with some upside is a better use than another 4-5 GPU hour multimodal run in a direction the data already disfavors. Expected cost is very low, about 0.4 GPU hours, roughly a tenth of the multimodal runs.

1) No experiments have been run, so there is no evidence about which modality, encoder, aggregation or fusion choice matters most. Prior expectations favor multimodal, multiprofile models that use strong pretrained encoders. 2) config_007 is a strong but not maximal anchor: multimodal, multiprofile, scVI (n200) RNA encoder, ImageNet ViT-L image encoder, avgpool aggregation, weighted fusion. Its result sets a high baseline. Later single-factor swaps from it can then isolate effects: transformer aggregation (config_005), concat fusion (config_034), other RNA encoders (config_001, config_016), ResNet50 (config_048), and unimodal or singleprofile ablations. 3) It is the best first experiment because it is likely to be near the top in accuracy while staying moderately priced. Avgpool aggregation and a compact 200-dimensional scVI embedding should be cheaper than transformer aggregation or scGPT-based variants. Expected relative cost: medium to high. Multimodal, multiprofile and ViT-L features add cost, but it should be cheaper than the transformer-aggregated multimodal configurations.

1) Evidence: there is only one result so far. The multimodal, multiprofile config_007 (scVI-200 + ViT-L, avgpool, weighted fusion) reached 0.635 accuracy and 0.618 F1 at 4.82 GPU hours. With a single data point, each design choice is still uncertain. 2) What this tests: config_005 changes only one factor, aggregation, from avgpool to transformer, with RNA encoder, image encoder and fusion held fixed. This gives a clean answer on whether learned attention over multiple profiles beats simple averaging. That choice is likely to have a large effect on multiprofile performance, and the answer carries over to every other multiprofile configuration. 3) Why now: it builds directly on the only known working configuration and has a reasonable chance of improving the best accuracy. It also settles a major axis of the search before encoder and fusion choices are explored. Expected cost is moderately higher than config_007, roughly 1.2–1.5 times its 4.82 GPU hours, because transformer aggregation adds compute. That is justified because aggregation is a high-impact choice and this configuration could plausibly become the best one.

1) Evidence: with the RNA encoder (scVI), image encoder (ViT-L) and fusion (weighted) held fixed, avgpool aggregation scored 0.635 accuracy and transformer scored 0.532. That is a large gap, and F1 agrees with it. Avgpool is the working base for now, though it is still a single comparison. The biggest open question is which RNA encoder works best, since only scVI has been tried. 2) This experiment keeps the best setup (multiprofile, ViT-L, avgpool, weighted fusion) and changes only the RNA encoder from scVI to scGPT. It is a clean one-factor test: it shows whether a pretrained foundation-model RNA representation beats scVI. 3) Changing the RNA encoder is likely to move accuracy more than changing the fusion method. It is also a direct exploit of the strongest configuration so far, which is a good use of an early slot. Expected cost is similar to config_007, roughly 4.5–5.5 GPU hours, and somewhat higher if scGPT embeddings are larger. PCA RNA, concat fusion and ResNet50 variants can be tested afterwards with the remaining budget.

1) Evidence: the best result so far is config_007 (scVI-n200 + ViT-L, avgpool, weighted fusion) at 0.635 accuracy. Two design choices already show large effects. Avgpool beat transformer aggregation (0.635 vs 0.532), and scVI beat scGPT (0.635 vs 0.422). Validation F1 follows the same pattern in both cases. Fusion type has not been tested at all, since every run so far used weighted fusion. 2) This experiment keeps the best configuration fixed and changes only weighted fusion to concat. Any difference can therefore be attributed to fusion type. 3) Fusion is the main unexplored design choice that applies across all multimodal configurations, so settling it early guides the remaining 6 experiments. Those later runs can then test pca_n2000 RNA encoding or ResNet50 images on the better fusion. Expected cost is similar to config_007, about 4.5–5 GPU hours. That is moderate and in line with the other ViT-L multiprofile runs.

1) Evidence: config_007 (scvi_n200, ViT-L, avgpool, weighted fusion) is the clear leader at 0.635 accuracy and 0.618 F1. Three single-factor changes from it all hurt. Transformer aggregation dropped accuracy to 0.532, scGPT dropped it to 0.422 and concat fusion dropped it to 0.421. So avgpool and weighted fusion look right. The RNA encoder had the largest effect (about 0.21 accuracy), and the third RNA option, pca_n2000, is still untested. 2) Test: config_016 keeps the winning setup and swaps only the RNA encoder to pca_n2000. This shows whether a simpler, higher-dimensional PCA representation can match or beat scVI. 3) Why now: the RNA encoder is the most influential dimension seen so far, so testing the remaining option on the best backbone has the highest chance of a new best. It also completes the RNA-encoder comparison before I test the image encoder (resnet50) or single-profile variants. Expected cost: similar to config_007, roughly 4.5–5 GPU hours (multiprofile, multimodal, ViT-L). It may be slightly more because the PCA input is larger. A cheaper resnet50 variant would mainly answer a cost question rather than an accuracy one.

1) Evidence: Four of five runs share the ViT-L image encoder, and they point consistently in one direction. Avgpool beat transformer aggregation (0.635 vs 0.532), weighted fusion beat concat (0.635 vs 0.421), and among RNA encoders pca_n2000 (0.721) did best, ahead of scvi_n200 (0.635) and scgpt (0.422). The best run so far is config_016 (pca_n2000 + ViT-L + avgpool + weighted, 0.721 accuracy, 0.681 F1). The image encoder is the main design choice we have not tested, since ResNet50 has never been tried. 2) This run keeps the best settings (pca_n2000, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted) and changes only the image encoder to ResNet50. That isolates whether the image backbone matters at the strongest RNA setting. 3) It is a direct one-variable extension of the current best, so it could beat it or show that ViT-L should stay fixed for the remaining three runs. Expected cost: a bit lower than config_016's 7.02 GPU hours, roughly 5–6, since ResNet50 has a smaller backbone than ViT-L but multiprofile multimodal training with PCA-2000 features is still required.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_016 (pca_n2000 + ViT-L, avgpool, weighted fusion) at 0.721 accuracy and 0.681 F1. Within multimodal multiprofile runs, three patterns hold. PCA beats scVI, which beats scGPT. Avgpool beats transformer aggregation and weighted fusion beats concat, though each of these comes from a single scVI comparison. ViT-L beats ResNet50 when paired with PCA. The large gains from changing the RNA encoder suggest RNA carries much of the signal. However, no unimodal baseline has been run, so we do not know whether the image branch helps or dilutes the PCA features. 2) This experiment runs the RNA-only version of the best setup (PCA, multiprofile, avgpool). It shows how much the image modality actually contributes. If RNA-only matches or beats 0.721, the remaining budget should go to RNA-centric variants. If it falls clearly short, image fusion is confirmed as useful, and the last runs can refine around config_016, for example single-profile or transformer variants with PCA and ViT-L. 3) It resolves the largest untested design choice, modality, at low cost. Dropping the ViT-L image branch should make it much cheaper than config_016's 7 GPU hours, likely about 2–4 GPU hours. It also has a realistic chance of becoming the new best.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_016 (pca_n2000 + imagenet_vit_l, multiprofile avgpool, weighted fusion), at 0.721 accuracy and 0.681 F1. The other design choices have been compared against close variants. pca_n2000 beat scvi_n200, which beat scgpt. vit_l beat resnet50 when paired with pca. Weighted fusion beat concat by about 0.21, and avgpool beat transformer by about 0.10, both measured with scvi. Multimodal beat RNA-only. One major axis, single-profile versus multiprofile, has never been tested. 2) Test: config_041 keeps every winning choice from config_016 (pca_n2000, vit_l, weighted fusion) and changes only the profile setting to single-profile. This cleanly shows whether multiprofile aggregation is actually needed, or whether single-profile inputs match or beat it. 3) Value and cost: Swapping to transformer aggregation or concat fusion was a clear loss in the scvi-based pairs, so retrying those with pca looks unpromising. The profile setting is the largest remaining uncertainty that could still raise the best score. Its result will also guide the final experiment: if single-profile is close or better, I would refine around it; if it is clearly worse, I would return to small variations near config_016. Expected cost is moderate and likely lower than config_016's 7 GPU hours, since it skips multiprofile aggregation (roughly 3-5 GPU hours).

1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_016 (pca_n2000 + ViT-L, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted fusion) at 0.721 accuracy and 0.681 F1. Swapping the RNA encoder to scvi or scgpt, or the image encoder to resnet50, all scored lower. Concat fusion clearly hurt in the one scvi comparison (0.421 vs 0.635), so config_040 looks unpromising. Transformer aggregation also lost with scvi (0.532 vs 0.635), but that is a single comparison, and the effect may depend on the RNA encoder. Rich 2000-dimensional PCA features may benefit from learned attention across profiles more than 200-dimensional scvi features did. 2. Test: config_042 keeps everything from the best configuration and changes only avgpool to transformer aggregation. This tells us whether aggregation is the remaining lever for the strongest encoder pair. 3. Why now: Only the best accuracy counts, and the next-best change, image-only (config_002), is unlikely to beat 0.72 because the multimodal model gains a lot over RNA-only. That makes the main untested design choice on the winning backbone the most plausible route to a higher score. If it underperforms, config_016 still stands as the best result. Expected cost is moderate, about 5-7 GPU hours, similar to config_016: transformer aggregation was actually cheaper than avgpool in the scvi pair (3.6 vs 4.8 GPU hours).

1. Evidence: the best result is config_016 (pca_n2000 + ViT-L, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted fusion) at 0.721 accuracy and 0.681 F1. Several single changes away from it did worse. Swapping ViT-L for ResNet50 gave 0.653. Using a single profile gave 0.632. Transformer aggregation gave 0.507. Weaker RNA encoders also did worse: scvi gave 0.635 and scgpt gave 0.422. The one design choice not yet tested on the best backbone is fusion type. Concat hurt scvi (0.635 to 0.421), but that is a single observation and the effect may depend on the encoder. 2. Test: config_040 keeps everything from config_016 and changes only weighted fusion to concat. This checks whether the stronger, higher-dimensional PCA features benefit from concat, and whether the concat penalty holds across encoders. 3. Why this is the best final experiment: with one run left, the realistic way to beat 0.721 is a one-factor change from the best configuration. The alternatives seem less likely to win. Image-only runs look weak given that scgpt+ViT with weighted fusion reached only 0.42, and transformer, ResNet50 and single-profile variants have already underperformed. The chance of beating 0.721 is modest given the scvi concat result, but it is the best remaining shot. Expected cost is about the same as config_016, roughly 7 GPU hours: mid-to-high for this study and cheaper than the ResNet50 multiprofile run.

1) No experiments have been run yet, so there is no evidence about modality, profile setting, encoder, aggregation or fusion. The prior is that multimodal, multiprofile models should do best, because they combine complementary RNA and image signals across several profiles. 2) This run sets a strong baseline using choices that are usually reliable: scVI (200-dimensional) RNA embeddings, ImageNet ViT-L image features, simple avgpool aggregation and concat fusion. Later runs can then vary one factor at a time against it: transformer vs. avgpool aggregation, weighted vs. concat fusion, the RNA encoder, or dropping a modality. 3) It is likely close to the top-performing region, so it supports exploitation, and it also works as a reference point for exploration. Expected cost is moderate to high: multimodal multiprofile with the large ViT-L features, but cheaper than the transformer-aggregation versions because avgpool is used.

1) Evidence and uncertainty: we have only one result. The multimodal, multiprofile config_029 (scVI-200 + ViT-L, avgpool, concat) reached 0.208 accuracy and 0.172 F1 at 4.49 GPU hours. One point says nothing yet about which design choices matter. 2) What this tests: config_023 keeps everything the same except the aggregation, which changes from avgpool to transformer. This is a clean single-variable test of how the multiple profiles are combined. Learned attention over profiles is a plausible large lever over simple mean pooling. 3) Why it is the best next step: it builds on the only known working setup while settling a key structural choice. That choice will then guide the later encoder, fusion and modality comparisons across the remaining 8 experiments. Expected cost is moderately higher than config_029 because transformer aggregation adds compute, roughly 5–6 GPU hours.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: The two completed runs differ only in aggregation. Transformer aggregation (config_023) reached 0.520 accuracy and 0.479 F1. Avgpool (config_029) reached 0.208 accuracy. This is strong evidence that transformer aggregation over multiple profiles matters most, so later runs should keep it. What we do not know is how much the image branch (ViT-L) adds on top of the scVI RNA representation. 2. What this tests: config_004 keeps the same scVI encoder, multiprofile setting and transformer aggregation, but drops the image modality. This isolates the image's contribution. If RNA-only comes close to 0.52, the remaining budget can focus on RNA encoders and transformer variants at lower cost. If it drops clearly, multimodal fusion is confirmed as important, and later runs can tune fusion and the image and RNA encoders within the multimodal transformer family. 3. Why this is the best next use: it settles a fundamental design question with a single controlled change. Expected cost is lower than the ~4.6 GPU-hour multimodal ViT-L runs, likely around 2–3 GPU hours, because there is no large image encoder to process.

1) Evidence: Transformer aggregation clearly beats avgpool (0.520 vs 0.208 for the same multimodal scVI + ViT-L concat setup). The cheap RNA-only scVI transformer model (0.532 accuracy, 0.516 F1, 0.40 GPU h) matches or slightly beats the multimodal concat version (0.520, 4.65 GPU h), so the image branch with concat fusion adds no measurable value so far. The RNA encoder is still completely unexplored, and it seems to drive most of the signal. 2) Test: config_039 keeps the best-known setup (RNA-only, multiprofile, transformer) and swaps scVI for scGPT embeddings. This isolates the effect of the RNA encoder. 3) Rationale: It probes an important untested design choice at very low cost (about 0.4-0.6 GPU h, roughly a tenth of a multimodal ViT-L run). The result will tell us which RNA encoder to carry into later, more expensive multimodal experiments, for example with weighted fusion.

1) Evidence: transformer aggregation clearly beats avgpool (0.520 vs 0.208 in the otherwise identical multimodal pair). The cheap RNA-only scVI transformer model (0.532 accuracy, 0.516 F1, 0.40 GPU h) currently matches or slightly beats the far costlier multimodal ViT-L version (0.520, 4.65 GPU h). So the RNA encoder looks like the main lever. scGPT does poorly (0.332), but pca_n2000 is untested. 2) This experiment holds the best cheap setup fixed (RNA-only, multiprofile, transformer) and swaps scVI for PCA-2000. That isolates the RNA encoder choice, which has the largest observed effect so far. 3) It should be cheap, about 0.4–0.6 GPU h, roughly 10x less than a multimodal run. If PCA beats scVI, it becomes the base for the remaining multimodal and fusion runs, such as the PCA multimodal transformer configs. If it does not, scVI is confirmed and the remaining budget can go to fusion type and image encoder choices (weighted fusion, ResNet50) with scVI.

Evidence: transformer aggregation clearly beats avgpool (0.520 vs 0.208 for the same multimodal setup). scVI is the strongest RNA encoder tested (0.532, versus 0.471 for PCA and 0.332 for scGPT). The current best is rna_only scVI with a transformer (0.532). The matching multimodal concat model, using ViT-L, scored slightly lower (0.520, F1 0.479 vs 0.516). This suggests that concat fusion fails to benefit from the image modality and may add noise. The key open question is whether weighted fusion lets the model down-weight or properly calibrate the image stream and push multimodal performance above RNA-only. This experiment changes only the fusion method relative to config_023 (scVI + ViT-L + transformer), so the comparison is clean. If weighted fusion helps, the remaining budget can exploit it, for example by trying the cheaper ResNet50 image encoder with weighted fusion. If it does not help, we can stop spending on expensive multimodal runs and refine RNA-only setups. Expected cost is high, about 4.5–5 GPU hours, similar to config_023. It is justified because it is the most likely route to beating the current best.

1) Evidence: transformer aggregation is critical, since avgpool reached 0.21 while transformer reached about 0.52 under the same multimodal setup. scVI is the strongest RNA encoder (0.532 vs 0.471 for PCA and 0.332 for scGPT). Adding ImageNet ViT-L images has not beaten RNA-only scVI (0.520 vs 0.532), though weighted fusion gave a slightly better F1 than concat (0.498 vs 0.479). Untested: whether a different image encoder makes the image branch useful. 2) Test: this keeps the best components (scVI, multiprofile, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) and swaps ViT-L for ResNet50. It checks whether ResNet50 image features add information on top of RNA and can beat the RNA-only best. 3) Why now: no other single change is as likely to beat 0.532, and it resolves the main open question, which image encoder to use. Expected cost: moderate, likely somewhat below the ViT-L multimodal runs (about 3–4 GPU hours) since ResNet50 features are smaller, but well above the RNA-only runs (about 0.4 GPU hours).

1) Evidence: the best result so far is config_044 (scVI + ResNet50, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) at 0.599 accuracy and 0.578 F1. Switching the image encoder from ViT-L to ResNet50 gave a gain of about 0.08. Transformer aggregation clearly beats avgpool (0.52 vs 0.21). scVI is the strongest RNA encoder tested (0.53 vs 0.47 for PCA and 0.33 for scGPT in RNA-only runs). With ViT-L, concat and weighted fusion gave the same accuracy (0.520 each), so fusion choice is unresolved and could matter for ResNet50. 2) Test: config_026 keeps every winning component (scVI, ResNet50, multiprofile, transformer) and changes only the fusion to concat. This is a clean single-variable check of whether concat can beat weighted fusion with ResNet50. 3) Why now: it is the most plausible untested configuration to exceed 0.599, since the alternatives swap in weaker components (PCA or scGPT encoders, avgpool, or dropping the RNA modality). It also leaves 2 experiments for follow-up. Expected cost is relatively high, similar to config_044 at about 6 GPU hours, because it is a multiprofile multimodal transformer run. That cost is justified because it is the likeliest candidate for the best result.

Evidence: the best result so far is config_026 (scVI + ResNet50 + transformer aggregation + concat fusion) at 0.706 accuracy and 0.667 F1. Two choices look settled. Transformer aggregation beats avgpool by a wide margin (0.52 vs 0.21 with ViT-L), and ResNet50 beats ViT-L in multimodal runs (0.60–0.71 vs 0.52). Concat beat weighted fusion with ResNet50, though that rests on one pair of runs. scGPT is clearly weak (0.33 RNA-only). The main open question near the optimum is the RNA encoder. PCA trailed scVI in the RNA-only setting (0.47 vs 0.53), but that gap is modest and has never been tested alongside the strong ResNet50 image features. The gap could shrink, or PCA's richer 2000-dim input could complement the image features under concat fusion. Test: config_027 keeps the winning backbone (ResNet50, transformer, concat) and changes only the RNA encoder to PCA. This is a clean one-factor comparison against the best configuration. Why now: it has the highest plausible chance of matching or beating 0.706. The alternatives look worse. Single-profile removes the aggregation step that has proven critical. Image-only drops the RNA modality, which likely contributes. Avgpool and scGPT variants are clearly inferior. Expected cost: high, about 5–6.5 GPU hours, similar to config_026 or slightly more because of the larger PCA input. This is justified because it is a credible candidate for the best configuration, and the result will tell us what to run with the final experiment.

Evidence: the best result so far is config_026 (scVI + ResNet50, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) at 0.706 accuracy and 0.667 F1. Several design choices look settled. Transformer aggregation strongly beats avgpool (0.52 vs 0.21). scVI is the best RNA encoder, and scGPT and PCA trail it. ResNet50 clearly beats ViT-L, because ViT-L multimodal runs only matched RNA-only (about 0.52), while adding ResNet50 lifted accuracy to 0.60-0.71. The open question is how much of the gain comes from ResNet50 image features alone, since no image-only run has been tested. Test: config_028 (image-only, ResNet50, transformer) isolates the image contribution under the best aggregation setting. If the image signal dominates, it could match or beat the multimodal result. If not, it confirms that fusion with scVI is needed and that config_026 is the final best. Why this run: other variants of the best configuration are poor bets. scGPT, PCA, avgpool and weighted fusion have each already underperformed, so no single-change variant has a strong expected upside. config_028 offers a plausible though modest chance of improvement while answering a key design question. Expected cost is moderate, roughly 3-5 GPU hours, cheaper than the 5-7 GPU hour multimodal ResNet50 runs because there is no RNA branch or fusion.

1) Evidence: config_014 (scGPT + ViT-L, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) is clearly best at 0.632 accuracy and 0.607 F1. Each one-factor change from it lost accuracy: avgpool aggregation 0.527, weighted fusion 0.260, ResNet50 image encoder 0.518, scVI RNA encoder 0.525, PCA RNA encoder 0.427 and RNA-only 0.523. The one design axis not yet tested is the profile setting, since every run so far used multiprofile. 2) This experiment keeps the winning encoders and concat fusion but uses single-profile input with no aggregation. It tests whether multiprofile aggregation is truly needed or whether single-profile multimodal input can match or beat 0.632. 3) This is the most informative remaining neighbor of the best configuration, and the answer decides where the last experiment goes. Single-profile models skip multiprofile aggregation, so I expect it to be cheaper than config_014, likely about 2-3 GPU hours versus 3.95.

1) Evidence: the best result so far is config_017 (singleprofile, scGPT + ViT-L, concat) at 0.688 accuracy / 0.659 F1, and it was also cheap (0.93 GPU h). Across experiments, ViT-L beat ResNet50, scGPT beat scVI and PCA, and concat clearly beat weighted fusion, which collapsed to 0.26. So most single-factor changes to config_017 (config_028, 041, 026) are expected to score lower. In the multiprofile setting, scGPT RNA-only (0.523) was well below multimodal (0.632), so images carry substantial signal. How well images do alone has never been tested. 2) This experiment runs the singleprofile ViT-L image-only model. It tests whether the image branch alone matches or beats the fused model, which would happen if the RNA branch adds noise in the singleprofile setting. 3) It is the one remaining neighbor of the best configuration with a plausible chance of beating it rather than predictably underperforming. It also settles which modality contributes what, which will guide the final experiment. Expected cost is very low, around 0.5–1 GPU hour (singleprofile, no RNA encoder, no aggregation), similar to or below config_017.

1) Evidence: The best result is image-only singleprofile ViT-L (0.715 acc, 0.687 F1). Adding scGPT RNA in singleprofile lowered accuracy slightly (0.688). Among multiprofile options, transformer aggregation clearly beat avgpool (0.632 vs 0.527). Concat clearly beat weighted fusion (0.632 vs 0.260). ViT-L clearly beat ResNet50 (0.632 vs 0.518). The multiprofile penalty seen so far was only measured with RNA fused in, so it may come partly from the RNA branch. 2) Test: This keeps the strongest modality and encoder (image-only, ViT-L) and adds the best aggregation (transformer). It checks whether multiprofile aggregation helps when RNA is removed. 3) Why now: Other candidates use components already shown to be weaker (ResNet50, weighted fusion, scVI or PCA RNA), so they are unlikely to beat 0.715. This is the only remaining option with a realistic chance of a new best. Expected cost is moderate: well above the 0.07 GPU-hour singleprofile run, but likely below the multimodal multiprofile runs (about 2–4 GPU hours).

1) Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been run, so there is no data yet on whether multimodal fusion, multiprofile aggregation, or the choice of encoder matters most. Prior expectation in cellular profiling is that combining RNA and image signals and aggregating over multiple profiles per sample help accuracy. 2) What it tests: config_023 is a strong anchor configuration: multimodal, multiprofile, transformer aggregation, scVI RNA embedding (compact, 200-dim), ViT-L image features and simple concat fusion. It shows how high the strongest architectural family can go. Later experiments can then compare against it to check whether removing modalities, swapping avgpool for transformer, or changing encoders or fusion moves accuracy. 3) Why now: Only the best accuracy counts, so starting with a likely-high configuration secures a strong incumbent early and gives a reference point for one-factor-at-a-time comparisons over the remaining 9 runs. scVI with 200 dimensions is cheaper than PCA-2000 or scGPT inputs, which limits cost somewhat. Expected relative cost is high (multiprofile transformer plus multimodal plus ViT-L features), but it is justified because this family is the most likely to contain the top performer.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: there is only one result so far. config_023 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI, ViT-L, transformer, concat) reached 0.540 accuracy and 0.524 F1 at 4.65 GPU hours. It is not yet known which of its design choices drive that performance, and the transformer aggregator is likely a major part of its cost. 2. What this tests: config_024 is the same configuration with transformer aggregation replaced by avgpool, so it isolates the aggregation choice. If avgpool performs about as well, the remaining searches over RNA encoders and fusion types can use the cheaper aggregator. If it performs clearly worse, the transformer is justified as the base for exploitation. 3. Why now and expected cost: this choice affects both accuracy and the cost of every later experiment, so settling it early makes the remaining 8 experiments more efficient. Expected cost is somewhat lower than config_023, roughly 3 to 4 GPU hours, because it keeps multiprofile multimodal inputs and ViT-L but uses a lighter aggregator.

1) Evidence: With the encoders and concat fusion held fixed, transformer aggregation beat avgpool by a wide margin (0.540 vs 0.332 accuracy, with F1 following the same pattern). So transformer aggregation is the best-supported direction so far. The RNA encoder is still an untested and likely important choice. 2) Test: config_029 changes only the RNA encoder, from scvi_n200 to scgpt, keeping multiprofile, imagenet_vit_l, transformer aggregation and concat fusion. This is a clean one-variable comparison that shows whether a foundation-model RNA embedding beats scVI. 3) Value: It exploits the strong transformer result while reducing uncertainty about a major design choice. That leaves budget for later fusion, image-encoder or modality-ablation tests on the winning backbone. Expected cost is about the same as config_023 (~4.5-5 GPU hours), possibly slightly higher if the scGPT embeddings are larger.

1) Evidence: with multimodal, multiprofile, ViT-L and concat held fixed, transformer aggregation clearly beat avgpool (0.540 vs 0.332, a gap of about 0.21). scVI also beat scGPT (0.540 vs 0.485), and F1 shows the same ordering. Fusion type has not been tested at all; every run so far used concat. 2) This experiment keeps the best configuration (config_023: scVI, ViT-L, transformer) and changes only fusion from concat to weighted. That isolates the effect of fusion on the strongest base, so the result is either a direct improvement or a clean answer for the remaining runs. 3) It is the best use of the budget because it exploits the strong aggregation and encoder evidence while resolving an important untested design axis in a single controlled comparison. The PCA RNA encoder and the ResNet50 image encoder can be tested on the best fusion choice afterward. Expected cost is similar to config_023, about 4.5–4.7 GPU hours, since weighted fusion adds negligible compute over concat.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_023 (scvi_n200, ViT-L, transformer, concat) at 0.540 accuracy. The other three runs each changed one component from it, and each change hurt. Avgpool dropped accuracy sharply to 0.332, so the transformer aggregator matters a lot. Weighted fusion fell to 0.435, so concat fusion is better. scGPT fell to 0.485, so scVI is the better RNA encoder. F1 follows accuracy in every case. 2) Uncertainty: The image encoder has never been varied, since all four runs used ViT-L. This experiment keeps the winning settings and swaps in ResNet50. It tells us whether the image backbone is a lever for improvement or whether ViT-L should stay fixed. 3) Why now: The image encoder is the largest untested design choice. Changing only that one factor from the best configuration gives a clean comparison. ResNet50 is a smaller backbone, so this run should be somewhat cheaper than the roughly 4.65 GPU hours of config_023, about 3.5 to 4.5 GPU hours. If it matches or beats ViT-L, we gain a cheaper strong option. If it loses, ViT-L is confirmed, and later runs can test the pca_n2000 RNA encoder (config_049).

1) Evidence and uncertainty: Each design axis has been tested with one-factor changes from the best run so far, config_023 (scvi_n200 + ViT-L + transformer + concat, 0.540 accuracy). Transformer aggregation clearly beats avgpool (0.540 vs 0.332). Concat beats weighted fusion (0.540 vs 0.435). scvi_n200 beats scgpt (0.540 vs 0.485). ViT-L is slightly ahead of ResNet50 (0.540 vs 0.518), and F1 shows the same ordering. The biggest remaining unknown is the pca_n2000 RNA encoder, which has never been tested. 2) What this tests: config_049 keeps the best-known setup and swaps in pca_n2000. The 4 remaining runs can then refine around the winner or check single-modality baselines. Expected cost is about the same as config_023 (~4–5 GPU hours), possibly a bit more because the PCA input is larger.

1) Evidence: The best result by far is config_049 (pca_n2000 + ViT-L, transformer, concat) at 0.725 accuracy and 0.685 F1. Swapping only the RNA encoder moved accuracy by about 0.19 (scVI 0.540, scGPT 0.485). Changing the image encoder moved it by only about 0.02 (ViT-L 0.540 vs ResNet50 0.518 with scVI). Transformer aggregation clearly beats avgpool (0.540 vs 0.332), and concat beats weighted fusion (0.540 vs 0.435). This suggests the RNA representation drives most of the performance. The open question is whether the image branch adds anything on top of PCA features. 2) Test: config_014 keeps the winning pca_n2000 + multiprofile transformer setup but removes the image modality. If it matches or beats 0.725, images add little or even add noise, and RNA-centric variants become the cheapest strong option. If it falls well short, multimodal fusion is confirmed as worthwhile. In that case the remaining experiments can go to multimodal pca_n2000 variants such as config_025 (ResNet50) or config_004 (single-profile). 3) Why now: with 3 experiments left, this resolves the most important remaining design question, which is how much the image modality contributes. It also has a realistic chance of producing a new best. Expected cost is low, likely about 2–3 GPU hours, well below the roughly 4–5 hours of the multimodal ViT-L runs, because no image encoder or fusion step needs to be processed.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_049 (pca_n2000 + ViT-L + transformer + concat) at 0.725 accuracy and 0.685 F1. It beats every scvi_n200 or scgpt variant by about 0.19 or more. Within the scvi runs, transformer aggregation clearly beat avgpool (0.540 vs 0.332) and concat clearly beat weighted fusion (0.540 vs 0.435). So the main open question is the image encoder: ResNet50 vs ViT-L gave 0.518 vs 0.540 with scvi, a gap small enough that it could reverse with pca_n2000. 2) Test: config_025 keeps every winning choice (pca_n2000, multiprofile, transformer, concat) and swaps only the encoder to ResNet50. This shows whether the strongest RNA encoder pairs better with ResNet50 features, and it is the only plausible single-factor change that could top 0.725. Weighted fusion (config_001) and avgpool (config_005) are each backed by a clear negative result, so they are poor bets. 3) Why now: with 2 experiments left, exploiting the best region by varying its only under-tested factor offers the best chance of a new maximum. Expected cost is relatively high, about 5 GPU hours, similar to config_011 (5.16 h) and slightly above the ViT-L runs. That cost is justified because this configuration is among the most likely to be the best performer.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_049 (pca_n2000 + imagenet_vit_l, multiprofile transformer, concat fusion) at 0.725 accuracy. The RNA encoder is the dominant factor: switching scvi to pca raised accuracy from about 0.54 to 0.72. The image encoder matters little (vit_l 0.725 vs resnet50 0.715). Transformer aggregation clearly beats avgpool (0.54 vs 0.33). Weighted fusion hurt in the one paired test (0.54 to 0.43), which makes config_001 unlikely to win. The profile setting has never been tested: every multimodal run used multiprofile. 2) Test: config_004 keeps the best encoders and concat fusion but uses single-profile input with no aggregation. This shows whether multiprofile aggregation is actually helping. The risky avgpool modules underperformed badly, so single-profile could plausibly do better than expected. 3) Why this experiment: It addresses the largest remaining uncertainty around the top configuration rather than re-testing a choice with negative evidence. The result also tells the final experiment whether to stay with multiprofile variants. Expected cost is low, likely about 1–2 GPU hours compared with about 4.8 for config_049, because there is no multiprofile aggregation.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_049 (pca_n2000 + imagenet_vit_l, multiprofile transformer, concat fusion) at 0.725 accuracy. Its ResNet50 counterpart is close behind at 0.715. PCA RNA features clearly beat scVI and scGPT. Transformer aggregation strongly beats avgpool. Singleprofile is cheaper but weaker (0.678). The one design choice not yet tested on the PCA backbone is fusion. The only evidence on weighted fusion is a single scVI comparison where it dropped accuracy by about 0.10, which is too little to rule it out for the stronger PCA representation. 2) Test: config_001 changes only the fusion method on the best configuration, from concat to weighted. This tells us whether weighted fusion helps once both modalities are strong. 3) Why this is the best final use: most other untested options swap in components already shown to be worse (avgpool, scVI/scGPT, singleprofile, unimodal). This is therefore the only nearby variant with a realistic chance of beating 0.725. If it fails, config_049 still stands as the best result. Expected cost is moderate, about 3.6–4.8 GPU hours, similar to or slightly cheaper than config_049 since the earlier weighted-fusion run was the cheapest multiprofile run.

1. Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been run yet. The main unknowns are whether multimodal fusion beats single modalities, whether multiprofile aggregation helps, and which encoders work best. In this domain, combining RNA and imaging with multiprofile aggregation is a reasonable prior for the highest accuracy. 2. What it tests: config_012 is a strong but moderately priced multimodal baseline. It uses multiprofile avgpool aggregation, the pretrained scGPT RNA encoder, a ResNet50 image encoder and simple concat fusion. Later runs can change one factor at a time from this anchor: ViT-L vs ResNet50, transformer vs avgpool, weighted vs concat fusion, or dropping a modality. 3. Why now: it starts in the region likely to hold the best configuration while avoiding the most expensive parts (ViT-L, transformer aggregation). That keeps GPU hours down and leaves 9 runs to exploit or ablate. Expected cost is medium: higher than single-modality or single-profile runs, but well below ViT-L or transformer multimodal configurations.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: there is only one result so far. The multimodal, multiprofile setup with scGPT, ResNet50, avgpool and concat reached 0.3275 accuracy and 0.288 F1, at 4.33 GPU hours. Every design axis is still largely unresolved. 2. What this tests: config_015 changes only the aggregation, from avgpool to transformer, and keeps everything else the same. This gives a clean answer on whether learned attention over multiple profiles beats simple mean pooling. That choice affects many of the remaining configurations. 3. Why it is the best next experiment: aggregation is likely one of the highest-impact choices in a multiprofile setting. A one-factor change against the known baseline gives interpretable evidence for steering later experiments, such as whether to pair transformer aggregation with ViT-L or other RNA encoders. Keeping ResNet50 limits the cost. Expected cost is moderately higher than the baseline because the transformer aggregator adds overhead, roughly 5 to 6 GPU hours. That should still be cheaper than switching to ViT-L.

Evidence: transformer aggregation roughly doubled accuracy over avgpool, with an identical scGPT/ResNet50/concat setup (0.635 vs 0.328 accuracy; F1 0.618 vs 0.288). That is a large, consistent gain, so transformer aggregation is the direction to build on. Uncertainty: the other main design choices (image encoder, RNA encoder, fusion) are still untested on top of it. The image backbone probably has the biggest remaining effect, since ImageNet ViT-L features are much richer than ResNet50. What this tests: config_007 changes only the image encoder from config_015 (ResNet50 to ViT-L) and keeps scGPT, transformer aggregation and concat fusion. Any difference can therefore be attributed to the image encoder. Why now: it exploits the strong transformer result while settling the most consequential open choice. The outcome will tell us which backbone to use when later experiments vary fusion (weighted) and the RNA encoder. Expected cost: somewhat above config_015's 9.06 GPU hours, roughly 10-13, because ViT-L adds larger representations to multiprofile transformer training. It is the most likely candidate to beat 0.635, which justifies the extra cost.

Evidence: Transformer aggregation clearly beats avgpool (0.635 vs 0.328 with scGPT+ResNet50+concat). With transformer aggregation, ResNet50 beats ViT-L (0.635 vs 0.530), and F1 agrees in both comparisons. The best setup so far is therefore scGPT + ResNet50 + transformer. Fusion is the remaining untested design choice: only concat has been tried. This experiment keeps the best configuration fixed and swaps concat for weighted fusion, isolating the fusion effect. It is a direct exploitation step around the current best, and the result decides which fusion to carry into the remaining experiments. Those can then test the RNA encoder (scVI, PCA). Expected cost is high, roughly 9 GPU hours, similar to config_015, since it uses multiprofile transformer aggregation with multimodal input. The cost is justified because this region holds the most likely best configuration.

1) Evidence: the best result so far is config_015 (scGPT + ResNet50, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) at 0.635 accuracy. Three of its design choices each look supported by a single one-factor comparison against it. Transformer beat avgpool by a wide margin (0.635 vs 0.328). ResNet50 beat ViT-L (vs 0.530). Concat beat weighted fusion (vs 0.527). The one major choice not yet varied is the RNA encoder, since every run so far used scGPT. 2) Test: this experiment keeps the best setup and swaps only the RNA encoder to scVI (200 dimensions). That isolates whether a compact probabilistic embedding can match or beat scGPT. 3) Why now: this is the most informative remaining one-factor change around the current best, and it could directly raise the top accuracy. If scVI does well, PCA-2000 (config_050) is a natural follow-up; if it does poorly, scGPT is confirmed. Expected cost is similar to or slightly below config_015 (about 7–9 GPU hours), because the smaller 200-dimensional RNA representation may train a bit faster. It should be cheaper than the weighted-fusion run (12.3 GPU hours).

Evidence: with multiprofile multimodal setups, transformer aggregation clearly beats avgpool (0.635 vs 0.328), and concat fusion beats weighted fusion (0.635 vs 0.527). ResNet50 beat ViT-L when paired with scGPT (0.635 vs 0.530). Among RNA encoders, scVI (0.650) slightly edges scGPT (0.635) and was much cheaper (5.16 vs 9.06 GPU h). The one untested RNA encoder in this best-performing template is PCA-2000. Test: config_050 keeps the winning template (ResNet50 + transformer + concat) and swaps in PCA-2000, which completes the RNA-encoder comparison. A simple linear embedding may perform competitively. Why now: this is the axis with the most remaining uncertainty and the most direct chance of beating 0.650. The other axes already have reasonably clear winners. Expected cost is moderate, roughly 5-9 GPU hours, similar to the scVI and scGPT transformer runs. That is acceptable because this is a plausible new best.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_050 (PCA_n2000 + ResNet50 + transformer + concat), at 0.721 accuracy and 0.681 F1. Swapping the RNA encoder changed results the most: PCA beat scVI (0.650) and scGPT (0.635). Transformer aggregation was far better than avgpool (0.635 vs 0.328), and weighted fusion was worse than concat (0.527 vs 0.635). So the RNA representation looks like the main driver, but no RNA-only run exists, and we do not know how much the image branch adds. 2. Test: config_013 (RNA-only, PCA_n2000, transformer) checks whether the ResNet50 image branch is really helping the PCA model, or whether a simpler RNA-only model matches or beats it. 3. Why now: With 3 experiments left, this result decides how to spend the last two. If RNA-only falls short, we focus the remaining runs on image-side changes to the PCA multimodal model, such as config_006 with ViT-L. If it matches or wins, it may itself be the best configuration, and future multimodal runs need strong justification. Expected cost is low: dropping the image branch should make it cheaper than config_050 (6.76 GPU hours), probably around 3–5 GPU hours.

Evidence: the best result so far is config_050 (pca_n2000 + resnet50 + transformer + concat, 0.721 acc, 0.681 F1). Transformer aggregation clearly beats avgpool (0.635 vs 0.328). Concat beat weighted fusion (0.635 vs 0.527). ResNet50 beat ViT-L (0.635 vs 0.530). Each of these comparisons is a single run, and all were made with the scGPT RNA encoder. The RNA encoder matters a lot (pca > scvi > scgpt), so the image-encoder ranking may change once the stronger PCA RNA features are used. Test: this run keeps the best recipe (pca_n2000, multiprofile, transformer, concat) and swaps only the image encoder to ViT-L. It checks whether the earlier ResNet50 advantage holds or reverses with PCA features, which is the main remaining uncertainty that could lift accuracy above 0.72. Why now: the other near-neighbour of the best config, weighted fusion (config_032), was both worse and the most expensive run so far (12.3 GPU h). In contrast, the ViT-L multiprofile transformer run cost only about 4 GPU h. Expected cost is low to moderate, roughly 4-7 GPU hours and likely below config_050's 6.76 h. With 2 runs left, the final experiment can then exploit the better image encoder.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_050 (PCA_n2000 + ResNet50 + transformer + concat, acc 0.721, F1 0.681). Its ViT-L counterpart reached 0.706. So the PCA RNA encoder with transformer aggregation over multiple profiles is clearly the strongest direction. Avgpool aggregation was very poor (0.33). Weighted fusion scored worse than concat in the scgpt/ResNet50 setting (0.527 vs 0.635), but that is a single comparison with a weaker RNA encoder. Whether fusion type interacts with the RNA encoder is still untested. 2) This experiment changes only the fusion method of the current best configuration, from concat to weighted. It checks whether weighted fusion can better balance the strong PCA RNA features against the ResNet50 image features. 3) This is the most direct remaining variant of the best configuration and the main open question about it. Singleprofile runs would be cheaper, but they drop the transformer aggregation that drives performance here, so they seem less likely to beat 0.72. Expected cost is relatively high, about 7–12 GPU hours. Weighted fusion took longer than concat before (12.3 vs 9.1 h for scgpt), and config_050 needed 6.8 h. The cost is justified because this is the most plausible path to a new best within the remaining budget.

1. Evidence: the clearest gains come from multiprofile transformer aggregation with concat fusion. Avgpool scored about 0.33 and weighted fusion about 0.52, both well below the concat-transformer runs. Within that family, pca_n2000 is the best RNA encoder (0.721 with resnet50, 0.706 with imagenet_vit_l), scvi_n200 is second (0.650) and scgpt is weakest. The remaining uncertainty is how scvi_n200 behaves with imagenet_vit_l, the only untested RNA × image pairing in this family. 2. Test: config_026 completes that grid and checks whether scvi pairs better with the ViT-L image encoder. The scgpt runs suggest ViT-L does not interact uniformly across RNA encoders, so a modest gain is possible. 3. Why this is the best final run: the other untested options belong to families that consistently underperformed (avgpool, weighted fusion) or are untested categories with no supporting evidence (single-profile, image-only). config_026 is the only remaining candidate with a plausible chance of matching or beating 0.721. Expected relative cost is low to moderate, roughly 4–5 GPU hours, since earlier ViT-L transformer runs (3.95 and 4.76 h) were cheaper than their resnet50 counterparts.

1. Evidence: No experiments have been run yet, so I am relying on priors. In multimodal cellular profiling, combining RNA with images and aggregating across multiple profiles usually gives the most information, and a transformer aggregator can model relationships between profiles better than average pooling. 2. What this tests: config_023 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI-200 RNA encoder, ResNet50 image encoder, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) sets a strong baseline for the most promising family of configurations. It uses mid-cost components: the compact scVI latent space and ResNet50 instead of the much heavier scGPT or ViT-L. Later runs can then change one factor at a time, such as encoder, aggregation, fusion or modality, against this anchor. 3. Why it is the best use of this experiment: it puts the first run in the likeliest high-accuracy region while avoiding the most expensive encoders. Expected cost is moderate to high relative to the other options: above single-profile or single-modality runs because of multiprofile, multimodal and transformer processing, but clearly below the ViT-L and scGPT multiprofile variants.

Evidence: there is only one result so far. config_023 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI-200, ResNet50, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) reached 0.494 validation accuracy and 0.453 F1. That is a moderate baseline, and no design choice has been compared yet. Test: config_035 changes only the image encoder, from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L, and keeps every other setting fixed. This isolates the effect of the image representation, which is likely one of the highest-impact choices for multimodal accuracy. Why now: a single-factor change gives a clean answer early. That answer then guides later choices of RNA encoder, aggregation and fusion. Swapping the RNA encoder or aggregation would also be informative, but the image backbone is the larger change in representational capacity, so it is the most likely route to a substantial gain. Expected cost: higher than config_023, roughly 1.5–2x its 5.16 GPU hours, because ViT-L features are larger. This is justified because it may become the best configuration, and it decides whether later experiments should be built on ViT-L.

1) Evidence: The two runs differ only in image encoder. Swapping ResNet50 for ImageNet ViT-L raised validation accuracy from 0.494 to 0.639, and F1 rose in step (0.453 to 0.620). That is a large and consistent gain, so ViT-L is the image backbone to build on. The RNA encoder, fusion method and aggregation have not been varied yet. Of these, the RNA encoder is probably the most important open question. 2) Test: This run keeps the best setup (multimodal, multiprofile, ViT-L, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) and changes only the RNA encoder, from scVI-200 to the pretrained scGPT. It shows whether a foundation-model RNA representation adds signal beyond scVI. 3) Why now: A clean one-factor change from the current best has a good chance of improving on it. The result will also guide later fusion and aggregation tests, which can use whichever RNA encoder wins. Expected cost: about the same as config_035 (~4.5–5.5 GPU hours), possibly slightly higher because scGPT embeddings are larger. Cheaper avgpool variants can be tested once the encoder choices are settled.

1. Evidence: All three runs used multiprofile, transformer aggregation and concat fusion. ImageNet ViT-L clearly beat ResNet50 (0.639 vs 0.494 with scVI). scVI beat scGPT (0.639 vs 0.573 with ViT-L). The best so far is config_035 (scVI + ViT-L + transformer + concat). Fusion strategy has never been varied, so it is the largest untested design choice near the current best. 2. Test: config_049 changes only concat to weighted fusion on the best setup. This cleanly isolates the effect of fusion. A gain would give a new best directly, and either result tells us which fusion to keep for later aggregation (avgpool vs transformer) and RNA-encoder (PCA) checks. 3. Why now: Changing one factor at a time around the leading configuration is the most informative and highest-upside use of the remaining six runs. Expected cost is similar to config_035, about 4.5–5 GPU hours, because weighted fusion adds little overhead over concat.

Swapping one component away from it lowered accuracy every time: ResNet50 dropped to 0.494, scGPT to 0.573 and weighted fusion to 0.527. Those three choices are fairly well supported, but each rests on a single comparison. Aggregation is still untested, because every run so far used the transformer. 2. Test: config_019 keeps the best setup and changes only the aggregation, from transformer to avgpool. This shows whether the transformer is actually adding value or whether simpler pooling does as well or better. 3. Why now: aggregation is the main design choice we know nothing about, and this one-change comparison against the best configuration gives a clean answer while still having a real chance of beating 0.639. Evidence: the best result so far is config_035 (scvi_n200 + ViT-L + transformer aggregation + concat fusion) at 0.639 accuracy and 0.620 F1. Single-factor changes from it all hurt. Swapping ViT-L for ResNet50 dropped accuracy to 0.494, transformer aggregation beat avgpool (0.537), and concat fusion beat weighted fusion (0.527). scGPT gave 0.573, below scVI. The main untested RNA choice is pca_n2000, which has never been tried. Test: config_043 keeps the winning setup (ViT-L, transformer, concat) and changes only the RNA encoder to pca_n2000. This finishes the RNA-encoder comparison inside the strongest setup. Why now: it is a clean one-factor test that could beat 0.639, since PCA features are sometimes competitive with learned encoders. With 4 experiments left, this is a better use of budget than lower-prior directions such as single-profile or ResNet variants.

1. Evidence: Six multimodal multiprofile runs show three consistent patterns. ViT-L beats ResNet50 (0.639 vs 0.494). Transformer aggregation beats avgpool (0.639 vs 0.537). Concat fusion beats weighted (0.639 vs 0.527). The RNA encoder matters less: pca_n2000 scored 0.653, scvi 0.639 and scGPT 0.573. The best so far is config_043 (pca_n2000, ViT-L, transformer, concat) at 0.653 accuracy and 0.628 F1. The main untested question is modality: we do not know whether RNA adds signal or partly adds noise on top of the strong ViT-L image features. 2. 1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_017 (scvi_n200 + resnet50 + transformer + concat, 0.725 acc). Three single changes from it all hurt. Swapping the image encoder to ViT-L dropped accuracy to 0.33. Swapping the RNA encoder to scGPT dropped it to 0.47. Switching fusion to weighted dropped it to 0.64. Concat fusion and ResNet50 look settled, and the RNA encoder is clearly a high-impact choice. The third RNA option, pca_n2000, has never been tested. 2) Test: config_012 keeps every component of the best config and changes only the RNA encoder to pca_n2000. This shows whether PCA features beat or match scVI, so the RNA-encoder dimension can be closed. 3) Why now: the RNA encoder has shown the largest effect among the testable components, so a better option here could raise the best accuracy, while a worse one confirms scVI. 1) Evidence: config_017 (scVI n200 + ResNet50 + transformer + concat) leads at 0.725 accuracy and 0.685 F1. One-factor changes from it all did worse. Swapping to the ViT-L image encoder dropped accuracy to 0.33. Swapping the RNA encoder to scGPT or PCA gave 0.47–0.51. Swapping concat for weighted fusion gave 0.64. These are single runs, but the gaps are large, so scVI, ResNet50 and concat look like the right choices. Aggregation is still untested: every run so far used the transformer. 2) This run keeps the best setup and changes only transformer to avgpool. 1) Evidence: the best result so far is config_017 (scVI + ResNet50, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) at 0.725 accuracy. Swapping in avgpool aggregation gave 0.713 with slightly higher F1, so aggregation matters little. Weighted fusion hurt (0.639). scVI clearly beats scGPT and PCA. ViT-L images collapsed accuracy to 0.33, so the image branch has a large effect, but we cannot yet tell whether ResNet50 images add signal or are only less harmful than ViT-L. 2) Test: config_005 is the RNA-only counterpart of config_017, using the same scVI encoder and transformer aggregation with no image branch. It measures how much the image modality adds. If it matches or beats 0.725, the remaining two runs should go to RNA-only variants. 1) Evidence: the scVI RNA encoder drives performance. Multimodal scVI+ResNet50 with transformer reached 0.725 accuracy (config_017), and RNA-only scVI with transformer nearly matched it at 0.721 (config_005) for only 0.40 GPU hours. So the image branch adds little at roughly 13x the cost. In the multimodal setting, avgpool aggregation gave slightly lower accuracy (0.713) but the best F1 (0.695), so the choice of aggregation is still unresolved. 2) This run tests avgpool aggregation in the cheap RNA-only scVI multiprofile setting, to see whether it can match or beat the current best accuracy. 3) It is the best use of the remaining budget because it is expected to be very cheap (about 0.4 GPU hours, far below the 5-9 hours of multimodal runs) and probes a plausible route to a new best. Its result will also show whether the last experiment should refine the RNA-only line or go back to multimodal variants.

1) Evidence: scVI-n200 is clearly the best RNA encoder (scGPT and PCA scored about 0.47 to 0.51), ResNet50 is far better than ViT-L (0.33), and concat beats weighted fusion with a transformer (0.725 vs 0.639). The best result, config_017 at 0.725, is barely above the RNA-only scVI transformer (0.721) at a fraction of the cost, so images add little in the multiprofile setting. Every completed run used multiprofile, so the profile setting is the largest untested design axis. 2) This run keeps the best components (scVI, ResNet50, concat) and switches to singleprofile, with no aggregation module. It tests whether per-profile modeling can match or beat multiprofile aggregation. It also shows whether the images contribute more when cells are not pooled. 3) Under-explored scVI+ResNet multiprofile variants remain, but they mostly recombine choices already shown to be weaker (avgpool, weighted fusion). This run is the most informative remaining test with a realistic chance of a new best. The caveat is that RNA results dropped sharply with avgpool, which hints that set-level modeling matters, so a drop here is plausible. Even a weaker result is useful: it would confirm multiprofile and point the final experiment back toward refining config_017. Expected cost is moderate, likely lower than the 5 to 7 GPU-hour multiprofile multimodal runs, since there is no multiprofile aggregation.

1. Evidence: scVI-n200 is clearly the strongest RNA encoder (scGPT reached 0.47 and PCA 0.51). ResNet50 is far better than ViT-L (ViT-L reached 0.33). Within the scVI+ResNet50 multiprofile family, transformer+concat is best (0.725), avgpool+concat is close (0.713, with the highest F1 of 0.695), and transformer+weighted is lower (0.639). 2. Question: config_027 (scVI+ResNet50, avgpool, weighted fusion) is the only untested cell in this top-performing family. It tests whether weighted fusion behaves differently under avgpool aggregation, where the setup already shows strong F1. 3. Why this one: on the final experiment, only a configuration near the current best has a realistic chance of beating 0.725. Options built on scGPT, PCA, ViT-L or singleprofile all have strong evidence of lower accuracy. Image-only and RNA-only alternatives also look unlikely to beat it, because RNA-only scVI already roughly matches the multimodal result. The chance of improving is modest, since weighted fusion underperformed with the transformer, but this is still the most plausible candidate left. Expected cost is relatively high, about 6–7.5 GPU hours, similar to config_047 and config_003.

1. Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been run yet. The two biggest open design choices are multimodal vs. single-modality and multiprofile aggregation vs. single profiles. Domain priors suggest that combining RNA and image data, and aggregating several profiles, should raise accuracy, but this is unconfirmed. 2. What this tests: config_034 sets a mid-cost anchor for the multimodal + multiprofile family. It uses compact components: a 200-dimensional scVI RNA embedding, a ResNet50 image encoder, simple average-pooling aggregation and concatenation fusion. If it scores well, later runs can test each upgrade in turn: a transformer aggregator, a ViT-L image encoder, scGPT embeddings, or weighted fusion. If it scores poorly, cheaper single-profile or single-modality baselines become the priority. 3. Why now: it sits in the likely-best region of the search space without paying for the most expensive components on the first try. 1. Evidence: there is only one result so far. config_034 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, avgpool, concat) reached 0.523 accuracy and 0.508 F1. That is one data point, so every design choice is still uncertain. 2. Test: config_020 changes only the aggregation from avgpool to transformer. This gives a clean one-variable comparison against the baseline. It shows whether learned attention over multiple profiles beats simple mean pooling, and the answer applies to every multiprofile configuration in the pool. 3. Why now: aggregation is a key design choice in multiprofile models, and a transformer is a plausible source of accuracy gains. Keeping the cheaper resnet50 encoder and the scvi_n200 encoder isolates the effect at moderate cost. Larger image-encoder swaps (ViT-L) and the single-profile check can follow once this is known. 1) Evidence so far: both runs use multimodal, multiprofile, scVI, ResNet50 and concat fusion. Avgpool (0.523 acc, 0.508 F1) slightly beat transformer aggregation (0.512 acc, 0.477 F1). The higher F1 supports avgpool as the better default, but the gap is small. Image encoder, RNA encoder and fusion are all still untested. 2) This run keeps the best configuration fixed and changes only the image encoder from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L.
