1) Evidence: ResNet50 clearly beats ImageNet ViT-L when everything else matches (0.523 vs 0.328). Avgpool is slightly ahead of transformer aggregation (0.523 vs 0.512, with a larger F1 gap). The current best is config_034 (scvi_n200 + ResNet50 + avgpool + concat). The RNA encoder is the biggest untested design choice, since every run so far used scvi_n200. 2) This experiment keeps the best known setup (ResNet50, avgpool, concat, multiprofile) and changes only the RNA encoder to scGPT. 1) Evidence so far: ResNet50 clearly beats ImageNet ViT-L (about 0.52-0.53 vs 0.33). Avgpool is slightly ahead of transformer aggregation (0.523 vs 0.512). scGPT is marginally the best RNA encoder: config_033 reached 0.532 accuracy and 0.516 F1, versus 0.523 for scVI. Evidence: switching fusion from concat to weighted gave a large jump, from 0.532 to 0.713 accuracy (F1 0.516 to 0.695), using scGPT, ResNet50 and avgpool (config_002). The other results point the same way. scGPT is at least as good as scVI, ResNet50 is far better than ViT-L, and avgpool vs transformer showed only a small gap under concat (0.523 vs 0.512 with scVI). Uncertainty: aggregation was only compared under the weaker concat fusion, so it may behave differently under weighted fusion. Test: config_029 keeps the best setup (scGPT, ResNet50, weighted) and changes only avgpool to transformer. This directly asks whether learned aggregation adds to the weighted-fusion gain. Why now: it is the most promising single-factor change around the current best, and the result will guide the remaining experiments. If it wins, I continue with transformer; if not, I return to avgpool and probe the RNA encoder or profile setting. Expected cost: moderate, about 4.5–5.5 GPU hours, in line with earlier multiprofile ResNet50 runs (transformer took 5.16 h before).

1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_002 (scGPT, ResNet50, avgpool, weighted fusion) at 0.713 accuracy and 0.695 F1. Switching from concat to weighted fusion raised accuracy by about 0.18 over the otherwise identical config_033 (0.532), so weighted fusion looks like the dominant design choice. Avgpool has beaten transformer aggregation in both comparisons; with weighted fusion the transformer collapsed to 0.227 and cost 12.3 GPU hours. ResNet50 clearly beat ViT-L (0.52 vs 0.33). Under concat, scVI and scGPT performed about the same (0.523 vs 0.532). The PCA_n2000 RNA encoder has never been tested. 2. Test: This run keeps the winning setup (multiprofile, ResNet50, avgpool, weighted fusion) and swaps in PCA_n2000. It checks whether the weighted-fusion gain carries over to a different RNA representation, and whether a simple high-dimensional PCA input can beat scGPT. 3. Why now: Running scVI with weighted fusion (config_032) would mostly confirm what we already expect, since scVI tracked scGPT closely under concat. PCA is the only untested RNA encoder in the best-performing setup, so it carries the most uncertainty and the best chance of beating 0.713. Expected cost is moderate, roughly 4–6 GPU hours, similar to config_002 and config_033, and far below the transformer runs.

1) Evidence: weighted fusion is the clearest win. It lifted scGPT+ResNet50+avgpool from 0.532 (config_033, concat) to 0.713 (config_002, best so far) and PCA reached 0.678 (config_035). The transformer aggregator collapsed under weighted fusion (0.227), and ViT-L performed poorly (0.328). The RNA encoder matters less: scVI and scGPT were close under concat (0.523 vs 0.532). One major axis is still completely untested: every run so far was multiprofile, so whether single-profile input is better or worse is unknown. 2) This test keeps the best settings (scGPT, ResNet50, weighted fusion) and switches to single-profile input with no aggregation. That isolates whether avgpool multiprofile aggregation is actually helping. Since the transformer aggregator hurt badly, aggregation may be adding noise. 3) It is the best use of the budget because scVI with weighted fusion (config_032) would likely land near 0.70 and probably not beat 0.713, whereas the profile setting is an unexplored dimension that could give a real jump. If single-profile is worse, I still have 2 runs to exploit the multiprofile branch. Expected cost is low, likely below config_002's 4.4 GPU hours (roughly 2–4 GPU hours), since there is no multiprofile aggregation.

1) Evidence: weighted fusion is the strongest design signal so far. With multiprofile, avgpool and resnet50, it lifted scGPT from 0.532 to 0.713 accuracy, the current best (config_002, F1 0.695). Weighted fusion also gave 0.678 with PCA, and 0.653 for the single-profile scGPT model. Transformer aggregation and the ViT-L image encoder have both performed poorly. The open uncertainty is the RNA encoder under weighted fusion: scVI is the only encoder not yet tested in the best setup. Under concat fusion, scVI (0.523) was nearly tied with scGPT (0.532). 2) Test: config_032 swaps scVI into the best configuration (multiprofile, resnet50, avgpool, weighted fusion). It completes the encoder comparison in the most promising region and is the untested option most likely to match or beat 0.713. 3) Budget: only two experiments remain, so exploiting the strongest direction is worth more than exploring weaker areas such as ViT-L or transformer variants. Expected cost is moderate, about 5–7 GPU hours, similar to the earlier scVI multiprofile avgpool run (7.27 h). That is more than config_002 but well below the transformer variants.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_002 (scGPT + ResNet50, multiprofile avgpool, weighted fusion) at 0.713 accuracy and 0.695 F1. Three choices look clearly harmful. Transformer aggregation dropped scGPT weighted to 0.227. ImageNet ViT-L dropped scVI concat from 0.52 to 0.33. scVI was weaker overall. Weighted fusion beat concat by a large margin for scGPT (0.713 vs 0.532), which suggests the model gains a lot by down-weighting the image branch, so scGPT RNA features may carry most of the signal. 2) This experiment: an RNA-only scGPT model with multiprofile avgpool keeps every element of the best setup except the image encoder. It tests whether the image branch adds signal or mostly adds noise. If image features mainly hurt, this could match or beat 0.713. 3) Why this is the best final pick: the main untested near-neighbours of config_002 swap in components with strong negative evidence (ViT-L or transformer aggregation), so they are unlikely to win. This is the plausible remaining candidate for a new best, and the best accuracy so far is kept whatever the outcome. 1. Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been run yet. The main open questions are whether multimodal input and multiprofile aggregation help, and how the RNA and image encoders compare. Prior expectation is that combining RNA with imaging and aggregating over multiple profiles should give the highest accuracy. 2. What this tests: config_011 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI-200 RNA, ResNet50 image, avgpool aggregation, concat fusion) sets an anchor in the region most likely to perform well, using the simplest aggregation and fusion choices. Later runs can change one factor at a time against it: transformer vs avgpool, weighted vs concat, ViT-L vs ResNet50, scGPT vs scVI, and unimodal or single-profile ablations. 3. 1. Evidence: there is only one result so far. config_011 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, avgpool, concat) reached 0.536 accuracy and 0.516 F1 at 7.27 GPU hours. One point cannot tell us which design choices matter. 2. What this tests: config_026 changes only the aggregation, from avgpool to transformer, and keeps everything else the same. This gives a clean comparison of whether learned attention over multiple profiles beats simple mean pooling. That choice is central to every multiprofile configuration, which make up most of the search space, so the answer will guide many later picks. 3. Why now: a one-factor change from the only known point is the most informative next step. It is more useful than jumping to a configuration that changes several factors at once. It also keeps the ResNet50 encoder, avoiding the larger cost of switching to ViT-L before we know whether aggregation matters. 1) Evidence: with everything else fixed (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, concat), transformer aggregation (config_026) beat avgpool (config_011) by a wide margin: 0.721 vs 0.536 accuracy and 0.681 vs 0.516 F1. It was also cheaper (5.16 vs 7.27 GPU h). Transformer aggregation is therefore the current best basis, but no other design choice has been tested yet. 2) This experiment keeps config_026 and changes only the image encoder, from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L. It isolates whether a stronger, larger image representation improves multimodal accuracy. The image backbone is likely one of the most influential remaining choices. 3) This is a one-factor extension of the strongest result, so it exploits that result while resolving a major uncertainty that will guide the later RNA-encoder and fusion tests. 1. Evidence: Transformer aggregation clearly beats avgpool. config_026 reached 0.721 accuracy versus 0.536 for config_011, and F1 shows the same pattern. ResNet50 also beat ViT-L under transformer aggregation (0.721 vs 0.632). Fusion strategy and RNA encoder are still completely untested. 2. Test: config_041 changes only the fusion method of the best configuration so far (concat to weighted), keeping scvi_n200, ResNet50 and transformer aggregation. Why now: It exploits the best region while resolving one untested design choice with a single-variable change. If weighted fusion helps, later runs can try it with other RNA encoders such as scgpt or pca_n2000. If it does not, concat stays the default. 1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_026 (scvi_n200 + resnet50 + transformer + concat, acc 0.721, F1 0.681). Each single-factor change from it lowered performance. 1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_026 (scVI-200 + ResNet50 + transformer aggregation + concat fusion), with 0.721 accuracy and 0.681 F1. Each one-factor change from it scored worse. 1) Evidence: config_026 (scvi_n200 + resnet50 + transformer aggregation + concat, multiprofile) is clearly best at 0.721 accuracy and 0.681 F1. 1. Evidence: config_026 (scVI + ResNet50, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) leads at 0.721 accuracy and 0.681 F1. Every single-factor change tested so far has done worse: avgpool 0.536, weighted fusion 0.512, ViT-L 0.632, scGPT 0.639, PCA 0.332, and single-profile 0.535. Test: config_013 (image-only, ResNet50, multiprofile, transformer) shows whether the RNA branch actually helps the fused model or adds noise. Why now: the other untested options combine components that already underperformed, such as scGPT + ViT-L or weighted fusion, so they are unlikely to beat config_026. Evidence: config_026 (scVI + ResNet50, multiprofile, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) is clearly the best so far at 0.721 accuracy and 0.681 F1. Each one-factor change from it hurt. Weighted fusion dropped accuracy by about 0.21 and avgpool by about 0.18. The other two changes cost less: scGPT lost about 0.08 and ViT-L about 0.09. PCA was far worse. Single-modality and single-profile models trail well behind. Every untested configuration changes at least one setting of the winner. So the only way to beat 0.721 is a positive interaction among the mildest changes. What this tests: config_025 is the only untested configuration that keeps the two strongest design choices, transformer aggregation and concat fusion. It pairs the two least-harmful encoder swaps, scGPT and ViT-L, which are both large pretrained foundation embeddings and might complement each other in ways neither does alongside scVI or ResNet. Why it is the best final use: options with weighted fusion, avgpool, PCA or single profiles have strong evidence against them, so they have little chance of beating the current best. Config_025 is a long shot, but it has the highest chance of improving on 0.721, and if it fails, config_026 still stands as the result. Expected cost is high, roughly 8–10 GPU hours, similar to config_009 (scGPT, 9.06 h), since it is multimodal, multiprofile and uses large representations. This is the last experiment, so the extra cost is acceptable.

1) Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been run yet, so every design choice is uncertain. Prior knowledge suggests multimodal, multiprofile models are the most likely top performers in cellular profiling, but the encoder and aggregation choices are open questions. 2) What this tests: config_042 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200 RNA, resnet50 image, avgpool, concat) is a strong but relatively cheap anchor. It checks whether multimodal multiprofile modeling performs well, using the compact scVI encoder, the lighter ResNet50 image encoder, and simple avgpool aggregation with concat fusion. 3) Why now: Running this first gives a solid reference point. Later experiments can then change one factor at a time: ViT-L vs. ResNet50, transformer vs. avgpool, weighted vs. concat fusion, and unimodal ablations. 1. Evidence and uncertainty: only one experiment is done. The multimodal multiprofile baseline (scVI-200 RNA, ResNet50 image, avgpool, concat) reached 0.525 accuracy and 0.498 F1. Every design axis is still uncertain, and the image encoder is one of the choices most likely to move accuracy. 2. What this tests: config_001 changes only the image encoder, from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L, and keeps everything else the same. Any accuracy or F1 difference can therefore be attributed to image representation quality. 3. Why it is the best next use of the budget: a stronger pretrained ViT-L is a plausible large gain. If it wins, it becomes the backbone for later tests of aggregation (transformer vs. avgpool), fusion (weighted vs. concat) and RNA encoder. If it loses, we can keep the cheaper ResNet50 for the rest of the search. Expected cost is moderately higher than the 7.27 GPU-hour baseline, perhaps 1.2–1.5x, because ViT-L features are larger. That is justified because this is a high-impact design choice tested cleanly.

Evidence: with everything else held fixed (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, avgpool, concat), swapping ResNet50 for ImageNet ViT-L raised validation accuracy from 0.525 to 0.586 and F1 from 0.498 to 0.574. ViT-L was also cheaper (4.49 vs 7.27 GPU hours), so it is the clear image-encoder choice for now. The remaining major untested choices are aggregation, RNA encoder and fusion. Of these, aggregation is the most likely to give a large gain in a multiprofile setting, because a transformer can learn interactions across profiles that average pooling discards. What it tests: config_029 changes only avgpool to transformer on the current best configuration. That gives a clean single-factor answer on whether learned aggregation helps, which will guide the later RNA-encoder and fusion experiments. Why now: it exploits the strongest direction found so far while settling a key design choice. Expected cost is moderately higher than config_001, roughly 1.3–1.8x or about 6–8 GPU hours, because the transformer aggregator adds compute. That cost is justified by the expected accuracy gain, and it should still be comparable to or below the ResNet50 run.

1) Evidence: the best result so far is config_001 (scVI + ViT-L, avgpool, concat) at 0.586 accuracy and 0.574 F1. Swapping ViT-L for ResNet50 lowered accuracy to 0.525 and cost more GPU hours. Swapping avgpool for a transformer aggregator collapsed accuracy to 0.224. So ViT-L with avgpool is the strongest backbone so far, and the transformer aggregator looks unreliable. The fusion method (concat vs. weighted) is still completely untested. 2) This experiment keeps the winning config_001 setup and changes only concat to weighted fusion. That isolates whether learned modality weighting improves on simple concatenation. 3) It is a low-risk, single-variable step from the current best, so the result is easy to interpret and feeds directly into later choices about the RNA encoder (scGPT or PCA). Expected cost is about the same as config_001 (~4.5 GPU hours), which is among the cheaper multimodal runs.

Evidence: the best result so far is config_001 (scVI + ViT-L + avgpool + concat) at 0.586 accuracy and 0.574 F1. One-at-a-time changes from it all hurt. Swapping in ResNet50 gave 0.525, transformer aggregation gave 0.224 and weighted fusion gave 0.411. So ViT-L, avgpool and concat look like the right choices for now. The RNA encoder is the main design choice not yet tested, since every run so far used scVI. This experiment keeps the best image, aggregation and fusion settings and swaps scVI for scGPT. It isolates whether a foundation-model RNA embedding beats scVI. It is the best use of the next slot because it is a direct exploitation step from the current best while resolving the largest remaining uncertainty. If scGPT helps, later runs can build on it; if not, PCA-2000 (config_043) is the natural follow-up. Expected cost is similar to config_001, about 4.5–5.5 GPU hours, possibly slightly more if scGPT embeddings are larger. That is much cheaper than the ResNet50 multiprofile runs.

1. Evidence: The RNA encoder has had the largest effect so far. Swapping scvi_n200 for scgpt raised accuracy from 0.586 to 0.713, with F1 rising from 0.574 to 0.695. In the same setup, the transformer aggregator and weighted fusion each caused large drops, so avgpool with concat fusion and the ViT-L image encoder looks like the best backbone. The image encoder also matters (ViT-L 0.586 vs ResNet50 0.525), which makes an image-free RNA-only run unlikely to win. The main open question is the third RNA encoder, pca_n2000, which has never been tested. 2. This experiment keeps the best backbone fixed (multiprofile, ViT-L, avgpool, concat) and swaps in pca_n2000. That gives a clean three-way comparison of RNA encoders and checks whether a simple 2000-dimensional PCA input can match or beat scgpt. 3. It explores the design choice with the most leverage, while the remaining budget can still exploit whichever encoder wins, for example by testing single-profile or RNA-only variants. Expected cost is moderate, around 4.5–6 GPU hours, similar to the scvi ViT-L run and probably cheaper than the 7.2-hour scgpt run.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_010 (scGPT + ViT-L, avgpool, concat) at 0.713 accuracy and 0.695 F1. Changing the RNA encoder caused the largest gain: scGPT beat scVI by about 0.13 and PCA by about 0.19 with everything else fixed. Concat clearly beat weighted fusion, and avgpool clearly beat transformer aggregation. ViT-L beat ResNet50 in the one comparison we have. The main open question is whether the image branch helps at all, since we have no unimodal baseline. 2. Test: config_002 is RNA-only scGPT with multiprofile avgpool, which is config_010 with the image branch removed. If it matches or beats 0.713, image features are adding noise, and the remaining budget should go to RNA-focused variants. If it scores clearly lower, fusion is confirmed as useful, and the last runs can refine the best multimodal setup, for example single-profile or scGPT with ResNet50. 3. Why now: Of the remaining design choices, modality is the one most likely to change where we search next, and this run has a real chance of producing a new best. Dropping the ViT-L branch should make it noticeably cheaper than config_010's 7.18 GPU hours. I estimate roughly 3–5 GPU hours, among the cheapest options available.

Evidence: the best result so far is config_010 (scGPT + ViT-L, avgpool, concat) at 0.713 accuracy and 0.695 F1. The other tested axes point the same way. Avgpool beat transformer aggregation (0.586 vs 0.224). Concat beat weighted fusion (0.586 vs 0.411). ViT-L beat ResNet50 (0.586 vs 0.525). scGPT beat both scVI and PCA. So the untested scGPT variants that change aggregation, fusion or image encoder (024, 025, 027, 030, 048, 050) are expected to do worse than config_010. Uncertainty: the profile setting has never been tested, since every multimodal run so far was multiprofile. This experiment: config_044 keeps the winning settings (scGPT + ViT-L + concat) and uses single-profile input, so it directly tests whether multiprofile aggregation is needed. If it matches or beats config_010, it may set a new best at lower cost. If it falls short, we confirm multiprofile and can use the last experiment for a different refinement. Why now: of the remaining options, this one has a real chance of beating 0.713 while also resolving an open design choice. Expected cost: lower than config_010's 7.18 GPU hours, roughly 3–5 GPU hours, because there is no multi-profile aggregation.

1. Evidence: the best result so far is config_010 (scGPT + ViT-L, multiprofile, avgpool, concat; acc 0.713, F1 0.695). scGPT clearly beats scVI and PCA as the RNA encoder, and multiprofile clearly beats single-profile. In the scVI series, each single change from the best setup hurt accuracy: transformer aggregation dropped it by about 0.36, weighted fusion by about 0.18, and ResNet50 instead of ViT-L by only about 0.06. 2. This experiment swaps only the image encoder of the best configuration, keeping scGPT, multiprofile, avgpool and concat. The gap between image encoders was the smallest seen, so it is the one-step change most likely to interact differently with the stronger scGPT features. It will show whether the ViT-L advantage holds when paired with scGPT. 3. With two experiments left, this is the neighbour of the best configuration with the best chance of matching or beating it. Weighted fusion and transformer aggregation both showed large, consistent drops, and image-only or single-profile options are unlikely to exceed 0.713. Expected cost is relatively high, roughly 7 to 8 GPU hours, similar to config_010 and config_042. Even so, it is the most promising candidate for improving the best accuracy.

1. Evidence: the clear best result is config_010 (scGPT + ViT-L, avgpool, concat) at 0.713 accuracy and 0.695 F1. scGPT is the strongest RNA encoder, ViT-L is the strongest image encoder, and multiprofile avgpool beats singleprofile (0.523). The only untested one-step variants of config_010 change the aggregation or the fusion. With scVI, transformer aggregation collapsed accuracy to 0.22. Weighted fusion also lowered it (0.586 to 0.411), but less severely, and that drop may depend on the encoder. Image-only and RNA-only options look unlikely to beat a multimodal 0.71. 2. Test: whether weighted fusion helps when the RNA embedding is the richer scGPT representation, which could balance the modalities better than concat. 3. Rationale: this is the last experiment, and only the best accuracy counts. A close neighbour of the best configuration is the only realistic chance of exceeding 0.713, and the weighted-fusion variant is the less risky neighbour. Expected cost is about 7 GPU hours, similar to config_010 and on the higher side.

1) Evidence: no experiments have been completed, so there is no data yet. The general prior is that combining RNA and image data (multimodal) and pooling several profiles per sample (multiprofile) should do best. Stronger pretrained encoders (scGPT for RNA, ImageNet ViT-L for images) should help, and learned weighted fusion should be at least as good as plain concatenation. 2) Test: this run sets a strong anchor using multimodal + multiprofile + scGPT + ViT-L + weighted fusion. It uses the simpler avgpool aggregation, which isolates the value of the strong encoders and fusion before adding a transformer aggregator. 3) Why now: starting with a likely top performer locks in a high best-so-far accuracy early. Later experiments can then compare against it with one change at a time: avgpool vs transformer (config_019), weaker or cheaper encoders (pca_n2000, resnet50) and single-modality ablations. Expected cost is relatively high, because it is multimodal, multiprofile and uses ViT-L features. It should still be cheaper than the transformer-aggregation version, which is a reasonable trade-off for a strong first anchor.

1) Evidence and uncertainty: we have only one result. The multimodal, multiprofile config (scGPT + ViT-L, avgpool, weighted fusion) reached 0.530 accuracy and 0.515 F1. That gives a baseline but says nothing yet about which design choices matter. 2) What this tests: config_019 is identical except that avgpool is replaced by transformer aggregation. This one-variable change isolates whether learned attention across a cell's multiple profiles beats simple mean pooling. Aggregation is likely one of the highest-impact choices for multiprofile models, and the answer applies to many of the remaining configs. 3) Why it is the best next use of the budget: it exploits the only known working setup while settling a key design question. If it helps, later experiments can vary the RNA encoder, image encoder and fusion under transformer aggregation. If it does not, we stay with the cheaper avgpool and explore elsewhere. Expected cost is moderately higher than the 2.94 GPU-hour baseline, roughly 1.2–1.5x, because of the extra transformer aggregator. That is justified because it is a plausible candidate for the best accuracy.

1. Evidence: the two completed runs (scGPT + ViT-L, multiprofile, weighted fusion) differ only in aggregation and score almost the same (0.5305 vs 0.5318 accuracy, with similar F1). Aggregation is therefore not a strong lever here, while the RNA encoder, image encoder and fusion choices are still untested. 2. Test: this run keeps the slightly better transformer/weighted/ViT-L setup and swaps the scGPT RNA encoder for scVI (n200). It isolates whether the RNA representation, a likely high-impact factor, can lift accuracy above about 0.53. 3. Why now: changing a single important factor against the current best gives a clean comparison and reduces the biggest remaining uncertainty early in the budget. If scVI helps, later runs can explore fusion and image-encoder variants around it. Expected cost is about the same as previous runs, roughly 2.9 GPU hours for multimodal multiprofile with ViT-L. The scVI encoder is lighter than scGPT, so it may be marginally cheaper.

1) Evidence: All three completed runs used multiprofile, multimodal, ImageNet ViT-L and weighted fusion. Accuracies sit within about 0.005 (0.527 to 0.532), so aggregation (transformer vs. avgpool) and RNA encoder (scGPT vs. scVI) look like minor factors. scGPT with transformer aggregation (config_019) is currently best at 0.532, but the margin is too small to call decisive. Fusion type has never been varied, which leaves it as the largest open design question. 2) Test: config_030 changes only fusion, from weighted to concat, on the current best setup. This cleanly isolates the effect of fusion. 3) Why now: A single-variable change from the best configuration both exploits that configuration and resolves a major unexplored axis. The result will tell us whether later runs should use concat or weighted fusion, before spending budget on other axes such as image encoder or PCA RNA. Expected cost is similar to config_019, about 2.9 GPU hours, since the architecture is otherwise identical and concat fusion is no more expensive than weighted.

1. Evidence: All four tests used the imagenet_vit_l image encoder with multiprofile multimodal inputs. Weighted fusion beat concat (0.532 vs 0.518, and a much larger F1 gap). Transformer and avgpool aggregation were nearly tied (0.532 vs 0.530). scGPT edged out scVI (0.532 vs 0.527). The image encoder is a major design choice that is still completely untested. 2. Test: config_034 keeps the best setup (config_019: scGPT, transformer, weighted, multiprofile) and changes only the image encoder to resnet50. This gives a clean single-factor answer on whether ViT-L is needed or a CNN works as well or better. 3. Why now: Changing aggregation or RNA encoder again would likely yield only small gains. The image encoder question could shift the whole remaining search, either toward cheaper resnet50 configurations or by confirming ViT-L for exploitation. Expected cost is moderate, likely somewhat below the ViT-L runs at roughly 2-2.5 GPU hours, because resnet50 features are smaller.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: The image encoder is by far the strongest factor so far. Switching from ViT-L to ResNet50 raised validation accuracy from about 0.53 to 0.706, and F1 rose from 0.516 to 0.667. Under ViT-L, the aggregation choice (avgpool vs transformer) made almost no difference, and weighted fusion beat concat. The RNA encoder was only compared between scGPT and scVI, which were close. PCA_n2000 has never been tested, so whether a different RNA representation adds value on top of the stronger ResNet50 features is an open question. 2. What this tests: config_021 keeps everything from the best configuration (multiprofile, ResNet50, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) and swaps only the RNA encoder to PCA_n2000. That isolates an untested RNA representation within the winning setup. 3. Why it is the best next step: it exploits the ResNet50 result while reducing uncertainty about the one design axis still unexplored, and it either finds a better configuration or confirms scGPT for the remaining 4 experiments. Expected cost is high, similar to config_034 at roughly 10–12 GPU hours. That is justified because ResNet50 multimodal is the only region likely to produce the best accuracy, and PCA features are not expected to add cost over scGPT.

1) Evidence: The only strong result is config_034 (scGPT + ResNet50 + transformer + weighted) at 0.706 accuracy. Every ImageNet ViT-L variant plateaued at about 0.52-0.53. ResNet50 does not help on its own: with PCA RNA (config_021) it reached only 0.52. So the gain seems to come from scGPT combined with ResNet50. Among the ViT runs, weighted fusion beat concat, scGPT slightly beat scVI, and avgpool vs transformer aggregation made almost no difference (0.530 vs 0.532). 2) Test: config_047 keeps the winning scGPT + ResNet50 + weighted combination and swaps transformer aggregation for avgpool. This isolates whether aggregation matters in the high-performing regime. Transformer aggregation did not matter for ViT, so avgpool has a real chance of matching or beating 0.706. 3) Why now: it exploits the strongest direction while answering a remaining design question. Avgpool should cost less than transformer aggregation, so I expect it to be somewhat cheaper than config_034's 12.31 GPU hours, while still multiprofile and multimodal and far above the ViT runs. That leaves budget for testing scVI with ResNet50 (config_037) or other refinements later.

1) Evidence: ResNet50 with transformer aggregation and weighted fusion is the clear winner so far. config_034 (scGPT) reached 0.706 accuracy and 0.667 F1, well above every ViT-L run (about 0.52-0.53). The RNA encoder matters strongly in the ResNet50 setting: PCA dropped the same architecture to 0.520 (config_021). The ViT runs suggest scVI is close to scGPT (0.527 vs 0.532). Concat fusion hurt with ViT, and avgpool fell below transformer with ResNet50 (0.586 vs 0.706). 2) Test: this swaps only the RNA encoder to scVI in the best architecture. It checks whether scVI can match or beat scGPT where the encoder choice clearly matters, which is the most plausible remaining route past 0.706. 3) Why now: it is a one-change extension of the best result, unlike concat (already shown worse) or riskier image-only runs. Expected cost is high, similar to or somewhat below config_034's 12.3 GPU hours, judging by scVI ViT runs that were only slightly more expensive than scGPT. That cost is justified because this configuration is the most likely new best.

1. Evidence: config_034 (scGPT + ResNet50 + transformer + weighted) is clearly best at 0.706 accuracy and 0.667 F1. Swapping out any one of its components hurt badly: avgpool gave 0.586, and replacing scGPT with PCA or scVI gave 0.520 and 0.422. Fusion type is the only design choice not yet tested on this strong backbone. The single concat-vs-weighted comparison (ViT-L, 0.518 vs 0.532) is small, comes from a much weaker setting and may not transfer, given the strong encoder interactions seen with ResNet50. 2. This experiment tests whether concat fusion can match or beat weighted fusion on the best-known backbone, with everything else held fixed. 3. Why it is the best use of the slot: it is the most direct remaining neighbor of the leader and the most plausible way to exceed 0.706. Single-profile, image-only and RNA-only variants all remove parts the evidence suggests are essential (transformer aggregation over profiles, and the scGPT-ResNet50 pairing). Expected cost is high, about 12-14 GPU hours (similar to or slightly above config_034, since concat ran costlier than weighted with ViT-L). That cost is justified because this region is where the best accuracy is found.

Evidence: scGPT + ResNet50 is by far the strongest pairing. The best result is config_049 (transformer, concat) at 0.713 accuracy and 0.695 F1, followed by config_034 (transformer, weighted) at 0.706. With ResNet50, swapping scGPT for PCA or scVI dropped accuracy to 0.42-0.52, so the other RNA encoders are not worth trying. Within scGPT + ResNet50, avgpool with weighted fusion (config_047) reached 0.586. Question: the one untested cell of the aggregation x fusion grid in this family is avgpool with concat. Concat beat weighted under transformer aggregation, especially on F1. This run tests whether concat also lifts the avgpool variant and whether that variant can match the transformer result. Why this run: with one experiment left, an untested near neighbour of the best family has a better chance of approaching the 0.713 best than more distant options. Those include image-only, single-profile, or scVI/PCA configurations, which existing evidence suggests are weaker. I don't expect this run to clearly beat 0.713, because avgpool lagged transformer by about 0.12 under weighted fusion. Expected cost is moderate, about 4-6 GPU hours, cheaper than the 9-12 hour transformer ResNet50 runs.

1) Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been run yet, so I am relying on priors. Combining RNA and imaging, and aggregating over multiple profiles, usually beats a single modality or a single profile. Which encoder, aggregation and fusion choices work best is still unknown. 2) What this tests: it sets a strong first anchor. It is multimodal and multiprofile, uses the compact scVI (200-dim) RNA latent, the ImageNet ViT-L image encoder, transformer aggregation and simple concat fusion. Later runs can ablate one factor at a time from this point: avgpool vs transformer, scGPT or PCA vs scVI, ResNet50 vs ViT-L, weighted vs concat, and unimodal baselines. 3) Why now: with 10 runs, starting near the likely high-accuracy region gives a competitive result early, so later runs can either exploit it or show whether cheaper variants match it. Expected relative cost is high, roughly among the most expensive options, because it combines multiprofile transformer aggregation with ViT-L features. The low-dimensional scVI input keeps it somewhat cheaper than the PCA-2000 or scGPT versions.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: there is only one result so far. config_011 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI, ViT-L, transformer, concat) reached 0.512 accuracy and 0.477 F1 at 4.65 GPU hours. We do not yet know whether the expensive ViT-L image branch adds any accuracy. 2. What this tests: config_036 removes the image branch and keeps everything else the same (scVI encoder, multiprofile, transformer aggregation). This directly measures how much the image modality contributes. If RNA-only matches or beats 0.512, the remaining budget can go to cheaper RNA-centric variants such as other RNA encoders and aggregation choices. If it falls clearly short, image information matters and later experiments should focus on multimodal settings, such as fusion type and image encoder. 3. Why it is the best next step: modality is the highest-level design choice, and a clean one-factor ablation of it reduces the most uncertainty per experiment. Dropping the ViT-L branch should make this run substantially cheaper than config_011, likely well under half its cost.

Evidence: RNA-only multiprofile transformer with scVI (config_036) reached 0.619 accuracy and 0.610 F1 for only 0.40 GPU h. Multimodal concat with ViT-L (config_011) did much worse, at 0.512 accuracy for 4.65 GPU h. That suggests the image branch or concat fusion adds noise, though one run is not conclusive. The biggest open question in the strong, cheap RNA-only line is the RNA encoder. config_009 keeps the winning multiprofile transformer setup and swaps scVI for scGPT. This isolates whether a foundation-model RNA embedding beats scVI. The result will also tell us which RNA encoder to carry into later multimodal runs, for example with weighted fusion. Expected cost is low: likely about 0.4 to 0.8 GPU h, slightly above config_036 because scGPT embeddings are larger, and far below any multimodal ViT-L run. This makes it an efficient experiment that can both improve the best score and reduce uncertainty.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is RNA-only scVI with a multiprofile transformer (0.619 acc, 0.610 F1), and it was cheap at 0.40 GPU h. Swapping in scGPT dropped accuracy to 0.328, so the choice of RNA encoder matters a lot. Adding ImageNet ViT-L images with concat fusion lowered accuracy to 0.512 and cost 4.65 GPU h. The third RNA encoder, pca_n2000, is still untested, which is the largest open question about a design choice that clearly drives performance. 2. Test: config_040 keeps the winning setup (RNA-only, multiprofile, transformer aggregation) and only swaps the encoder to PCA-2000. This isolates whether PCA can beat scVI. The answer also tells us which RNA encoder to carry into any later multimodal or aggregation experiments. 3. Why now: Expected cost is low, about 0.4–0.6 GPU h, similar to the earlier RNA-only runs and far below multimodal ViT-L runs. It could plausibly produce a new best, and it narrows the search cheaply before more expensive multimodal configurations are tried.

1) Evidence: The RNA encoder matters most so far. pca_n2000 (0.713 acc, 0.695 F1) clearly beats scvi_n200 (0.619) and scgpt (0.328) under the same rna_only, multiprofile, transformer setup. The one multimodal run (scvi + ViT-L, concat) scored 0.512, well below scvi rna_only at 0.619. That suggests naive concatenation of image features may hurt, but it is a single run and fusion type has not been tested. 2) This experiment pairs the best RNA encoder (pca_n2000) with resnet50 under transformer aggregation and weighted fusion. It tests whether weighted fusion can down-weight noisy image features so that image information adds to the strong PCA baseline rather than degrading it. 3) Why now: Whether multimodal fusion can beat rna_only is the largest remaining question, and it determines whether to spend the remaining budget on multimodal or rna_only variants. Using resnet50 instead of ViT-L gives an informative multimodal test at moderate cost. I expect it to cost roughly 2-3 GPU hours: more than the ~1 h rna_only runs but well under the 4.65 h ViT-L run. If it fails, cheap rna_only follow-ups remain, such as config_015 (PCA with avgpool) and config_016 (PCA single-profile).

Evidence: RNA-only models clearly lead. The best is pca_n2000 with multiprofile transformer aggregation (0.713 acc, 0.695 F1), ahead of scvi_n200 (0.619) and scgpt (0.328). Both multimodal runs scored lower (0.48-0.51) and cost far more (4.6-6.6 GPU h each), so adding images has not helped so far. The main open question is aggregation, because every run used a transformer. This experiment keeps the best encoder and profile setting (pca_n2000, multiprofile, RNA-only) and swaps the transformer for avgpool. That tells us whether simpler pooling matches or beats the transformer, which matters for all remaining choices. With 4 experiments left, it is a low-risk way to improve on or confirm the current best. Expected cost is low, about 0.5-1 GPU h, likely below config_040's 0.99 GPU h and far below any multimodal run.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is RNA-only pca_n2000 with multiprofile transformer aggregation (0.713 accuracy, 0.695 F1). PCA clearly beats scVI (0.619) and scGPT (0.328) as the RNA encoder. Transformer aggregation beats avgpool for PCA (0.713 vs 0.678). Both multimodal runs were much worse than their RNA-only counterparts (0.51 and 0.48) and cost the most (4.7 to 6.6 GPU hours), so adding image features currently looks harmful. 2) Open question: the profile setting has not been tested at all, since every run so far was multiprofile. This experiment keeps the best RNA encoder (pca_n2000) and switches to singleprofile. It shows whether multiprofile aggregation actually adds value or whether a simpler per-profile model is as good or better. 3) Why now: this is the main untested design axis within the strongest branch of the search. It is also likely the cheapest option, well under 1 GPU hour, because it has no aggregation module and no image branch. The answer will tell me whether to spend the last two experiments on refining multiprofile RNA-only or on singleprofile variants. Expected cost: low, roughly 0.3 to 0.8 GPU hours.

1) Evidence: the best result so far is config_040 (RNA-only, pca_n2000, transformer, 0.713 accuracy, 0.695 F1). For RNA encoders, pca_n2000 beats scvi_n200 (0.619), which beats scgpt (0.328). Transformer aggregation beats avgpool (0.678), and multiprofile beats singleprofile (0.519). The untested RNA-only options use weaker encoders or single profiles, so none of them is likely to beat 0.713. The only realistic route to a higher score is adding images to the winning RNA setup. The two multimodal runs so far both scored poorly, but each confounds several factors. config_008 paired pca_n2000 with resnet50 and weighted fusion. config_011 paired the weaker scvi_n200 encoder with ViT-L and concat. The combination of the best RNA encoder, ViT-L and concat fusion has not been tested. 2) Test: config_005 (pca_n2000 + imagenet_vit_l, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) checks whether the stronger image encoder and simpler fusion can add useful information to the best RNA pipeline. If it does not, that confirms RNA-only is the ceiling. 3) Why now: this is the only remaining direction with a plausible chance of exceeding 0.713, and it leaves one experiment to follow up (for example, weighted fusion in config_034) or stop. Expected cost is high, about 5–7 GPU hours, similar to config_011 and config_008 and well above the 1 GPU hour of the RNA-only runs. That cost is justified because the cheaper untested options are unlikely to beat the current best.

1) Evidence: the best result so far is RNA-only, multiprofile, pca_n2000 with transformer aggregation (0.713 accuracy, 0.695 F1). Every multimodal run scored between 0.48 and 0.53 and cost 4.6 to 6.6 GPU hours, so adding images has consistently hurt. Among RNA encoders, pca_n2000 beat scvi_n200 (0.619), which beat scgpt (0.328). Multiprofile clearly beat singleprofile (0.519). 2) Test: config_050 is RNA-only, multiprofile, scvi_n200 with avgpool aggregation. It checks whether the transformer-over-avgpool advantage seen with PCA (0.713 vs 0.678) also holds for the second-best encoder. This tells us whether aggregation interacts with encoder choice. 3) Why this run: with one experiment left after this one, the expensive multimodal options are unlikely to beat 0.713 given four consistent failures. The only untested RNA-only multiprofile options are config_050 and config_051 (scgpt, avgpool). I chose config_050 because scvi_n200 was far stronger than scgpt. Even so, I do not expect it to exceed 0.713 (scvi with the transformer only reached 0.619), so its main value is the aggregation check rather than a new best. It is cheap at about 0.4 to 0.6 GPU hours, roughly a tenth of a multimodal run, which keeps total GPU hours low while 0.713 remains our best result.

1) Evidence: the best result is RNA-only, multiprofile, PCA-2000 with a transformer aggregator (config_040, 0.713 acc / 0.695 F1). Every multimodal run scored between 0.48 and 0.53, whatever the fusion or image encoder, so adding images consistently hurts by about 0.18. That gap is unlikely to close by switching to weighted fusion or avgpool, since avgpool was worse than the transformer even for RNA-only. scGPT was clearly weak (0.33). Single-profile setups trail multiprofile by about 0.19 for PCA (0.519 vs 0.713). 2) Test: this run checks whether the single-profile penalty also holds for scVI. It completes the profile-setting comparison across RNA encoders and confirms that multiprofile aggregation is the key design choice. 3) Rationale: no remaining configuration has a realistic chance of beating 0.713. An expensive multimodal run (about 5–7 GPU hours) would very likely land near 0.5 and waste compute. This single-profile RNA-only run is the cheapest option, expected at about 0.05 GPU hours (similar to config_016's 0.04), so the budget ends with minimal extra GPU time. config_040 is expected to remain the best configuration.

1) No experiments have been run, so there is no evidence yet. Priors suggest that combining RNA and image data, aggregating over multiple profiles and using a learned transformer aggregator should give the highest accuracy, but this is untested. 2) config_007 tests that design: multimodal, multiprofile, transformer aggregation and weighted fusion. It pairs them with a compact scVI (200-dim) RNA encoder and a ResNet50 image encoder. That makes it a strong anchor for later comparisons: single-profile vs multiprofile, RNA-only vs multimodal, avgpool vs transformer, concat vs weighted, and scGPT/PCA vs scVI and ViT-L vs ResNet50. 3) It is a likely high performer and a good base for one-factor-at-a-time comparisons. It avoids the cost of ViT-L features until we know whether a larger image encoder is needed. Expected relative cost is moderate to high: multiprofile transformer aggregation over two modalities costs more than single-profile or unimodal runs. It should still be clearly cheaper than the equivalent ViT-L configurations (e.g., config_034).

Evidence: there is only one result so far. config_007 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI + ResNet50, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) reached 0.688 accuracy and 0.659 F1 at 6.22 GPU hours. 1. Evidence: The two experiments differ only in aggregation. With scVI + ResNet50 + weighted fusion, transformer reached 0.688 accuracy while avgpool reached 0.427. Test: This experiment keeps the best setup (multiprofile, ResNet50, transformer, weighted fusion) and swaps only the RNA encoder from scVI to scGPT. Why now: It builds on the best result so far while reducing uncertainty in a dimension that could plausibly raise accuracy. 1) Evidence: config_007 (scVI + ResNet50, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) is the clear leader at 0.688 acc / 0.659 F1. 1) Evidence: config_007 (scvi_n200 + resnet50 + transformer + weighted fusion) is clearly best at 0.688 accuracy and 0.659 F1. Each single-factor change away from it hurt badly. 1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_007 (scVI + ResNet50 + transformer + weighted fusion, 0.688 accuracy, 0.659 F1). One-factor comparisons point consistently the same way. 1. Evidence: Within multiprofile multimodal models, config_007 (scvi_n200 + resnet50 + transformer + weighted, 0.688 accuracy) is best. 1) Evidence: config_007 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI, ResNet50, transformer, weighted fusion; 0.688 acc, 0.659 F1) is the best so far. Single-factor changes from it all scored lower. Avgpool (0.427), scGPT (0.332), ViT-L (0.421) and single-profile (0.525) were much worse. Concat (0.650) and PCA (0.629) were only slightly worse. 1) Evidence: the best result so far is config_007 (scVI + ResNet50 + transformer + weighted, 0.688 accuracy, 0.659 F1). Every single-factor change from it lowered accuracy. Swapping the RNA encoder to scGPT gave 0.33 and to PCA gave 0.63. Swapping the image encoder to ViT-L gave 0.42. Combinations of two already-worse changes, such as config_033 (PCA + concat), are unlikely to beat 0.688. 3) It reuses the proven ResNet50 + transformer components and has some chance of improving on the best result. Expected cost is low to moderate: it drops the RNA branch, so it should be cheaper than the roughly 6 GPU-hour multimodal transformer runs.

1) Evidence: the best result so far is config_007 (scvi_n200 + resnet50 + transformer + weighted, val acc 0.688, F1 0.659). The transformer aggregation, resnet50 and multimodal setting are each clearly important. Avgpool dropped accuracy to 0.43, imagenet_vit_l to 0.42, scGPT to 0.33, and single-profile to 0.53. Within this strong region, pca_n2000 with weighted fusion scored 0.629, and concat fusion with scvi scored 0.650. The one untested combination in this backbone is pca_n2000 with concat fusion. 2) Test: whether pca_n2000 pairs better with concat fusion than with weighted fusion, which would mean the two factors interact. This matters because the higher-dimensional PCA input might benefit from direct concatenation. 3) Why this choice: it is the last experiment and only the best accuracy counts, so I am spending it on the one untested option inside the clearly dominant resnet50 + transformer region. Every alternative changes a factor that has already shown large drops. Admittedly, the additive evidence suggests it will likely land around 0.60-0.65, and config_007 will probably remain the final best. 1) Evidence: no experiments have been run yet, so we have no data on modality, profile setting, encoders, aggregation or fusion. Domain priors suggest that combining RNA and image modalities and aggregating several profiles per sample usually improve accuracy. 2) What it tests: config_019 is a strong, mid-complexity anchor (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200 RNA encoder, resnet50 image encoder, simple avgpool aggregation, concat fusion). It checks whether the multimodal multiprofile direction is as promising as expected. It uses the simplest and cheapest component choices, so later runs can vary one factor at a time: a ViT-L image encoder, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion, or a different RNA encoder like scGPT or PCA. It also lets us ablate down to single-modality or single-profile variants to confirm each component helps. 3) Why now: a likely high-performing but not maximally expensive starting point gives a solid incumbent early and a clean reference for factor-wise comparisons within the 10-run budget. Multiprofile aggregation and two modalities add cost over single-modality or single-profile runs, but resnet50 and avgpool keep it well below ViT-L and transformer variants.

1) Evidence: there is only one result so far. config_019 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI RNA encoder, ResNet50 images, avgpool, concat) reached 0.411 accuracy and 0.378 F1 for 7.27 GPU hours. One run cannot tell us which design choices drive performance, and the image encoder is one of the biggest open questions. 2) Test: config_008 changes only the image encoder, from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L, and keeps everything else fixed. That makes it a clean comparison of how much a stronger image representation helps inside the same multimodal, multiprofile setup. 3) Why now: the image backbone is likely to have a large effect on accuracy. If ViT-L clearly wins, it becomes the base for later tests of transformer aggregation, weighted fusion and alternative RNA encoders. If it does not, we can stay with the cheaper ResNet50 for the rest of the budget. Expected cost is higher than config_019, roughly 1.5–2x (about 11–15 GPU hours), because ViT-L is a larger model. That cost is justified because this choice could plausibly hold the best configuration.

1) Evidence: The two runs differ only in the image encoder. Swapping ResNet50 for ImageNet ViT-L, with the same multimodal, multiprofile, scVI, avgpool and concat setup, raised validation accuracy from 0.411 to 0.514 and F1 from 0.378 to 0.498. It also cut cost from 7.27 to 4.49 GPU hours, so ViT-L is the clear image encoder to build on. The biggest untested design choice in this strong setting is the aggregation method: transformer versus avgpool. 2) Test: config_025 keeps the best config_008 setup and changes only avgpool to transformer aggregation. This isolates whether learned attention over multiple profiles adds accuracy over simple pooling. 3) Why now: This one-variable extension of the current best is the most likely to beat it, and the result will decide aggregation for all later multiprofile runs. RNA encoder and fusion type can be tested afterwards. Expected cost is moderate, somewhat above config_008's 4.49 GPU hours because of the transformer aggregator, likely about 5 to 6 GPU hours, and still below the ResNet50 run.

1) Evidence: with scVI RNA features and concat fusion held fixed, the ViT-L image encoder beat ResNet50 (0.514 vs 0.411). Switching ViT-L from avgpool to transformer aggregation gave a large further gain (0.678 accuracy, F1 0.646, config_025). The image encoder and aggregation choices look settled. The RNA encoder is completely unexplored: every run so far used scvi_n200. 2) This experiment keeps the best setup (multiprofile, ViT-L, transformer, concat) and swaps only scvi_n200 for scGPT. That isolates whether a richer foundation-model RNA embedding adds signal on top of the strongest pipeline. 3) Of the remaining single-factor choices, RNA encoder is plausibly larger in effect than fusion type (concat vs weighted), so it is the most informative next step. If it wins, it becomes the new base for testing fusion; if not, scVI is confirmed and the remaining budget can go to fusion or pca_n2000. Expected cost is similar to or slightly above config_025 (about 4.7–5.5 GPU hours), because scGPT embeddings are somewhat larger than scVI's 200 dimensions.

1) Evidence: Transformer aggregation gave the largest gain so far, from 0.514 (avgpool, config_008) to 0.678 (config_025, scvi_n200 + ViT-L + transformer + concat). ViT-L clearly beat ResNet50. scVI clearly beat scGPT under the transformer setup (0.678 vs 0.540). Fusion is the main design choice not yet tested: every run so far used concat. 2) Test: config_041 keeps the best setup and changes only concat to weighted fusion. This cleanly shows whether learned modality weighting adds accuracy and F1 on top of the current best, and which fusion to use for the remaining runs, such as later testing pca_n2000 as the RNA encoder. 3) Why now: it exploits the strongest direction while answering an open, important question with a single change. Expected cost is similar to config_025, about 4.5–5 GPU hours, since weighted fusion adds little overhead. That makes it a moderate-cost, high-value next step.

1. Evidence: Multiprofile multimodal runs with a ViT-L image encoder and transformer aggregation are the strongest so far. config_025 (scVI RNA encoder, concat fusion) is best at 0.678 accuracy and 0.646 F1. Changing one component of config_025 hurt each time: scGPT dropped to 0.540, weighted fusion to 0.591, avgpool aggregation to 0.514, and ResNet50 avgpool reached only 0.411. The RNA encoder clearly matters, and the third option, PCA with 2000 components, is still untested. 2. Test: config_030 keeps the best setup (ViT-L, transformer, concat) and swaps scVI for PCA-2000. This shows whether a simpler, higher-dimensional RNA representation can beat scVI. 3. Why now: Swapping the RNA encoder has produced the largest swings seen so far, so this is the most likely single change to raise the best accuracy. It is also a direct exploit of the top configuration. Expected cost is similar to config_025, roughly 4–5 GPU hours, possibly slightly more from the larger PCA input. That is well below the ResNet50 runs.

1) Evidence: config_025 (scvi_n200 + ViT-L, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) is clearly best at 0.678 accuracy and 0.646 F1. Each single-factor change from it lowered accuracy: scGPT gave 0.540, PCA gave 0.520, weighted fusion gave 0.591, and avgpool aggregation gave 0.514. ResNet50 was also worse than ViT-L under avgpool (0.411 vs 0.514). The local neighborhood around config_025 is now well mapped. The main open question is how much the RNA branch actually contributes. The RNA encoder choice swung accuracy by about 0.15, which could mean scVI adds a lot or that weaker RNA embeddings add noise. 2) This experiment: config_024 is the image-only version of the winning recipe (multiprofile ViT-L with transformer aggregation). It directly tests whether RNA fusion helps. If it scores near or above 0.678, the remaining budget should go to image-centric variants. If it scores well below, multimodal scVI fusion is confirmed as essential and later runs should refine around config_025. 3) Why now: the remaining multimodal neighbors (e.g., ResNet50 with transformer) are unlikely to win given the ResNet result. This ablation resolves the largest structural uncertainty and also has some chance of matching the current best. Expected cost: lower than the multimodal runs, roughly 3–4 GPU hours, since there is no RNA encoder or fusion step.

1) Evidence: config_025 (scvi_n200 + ViT-L, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) is clearly best at 0.678 accuracy and 0.646 F1. Most single-factor changes from it hurt. Switching to scGPT or PCA RNA encoders dropped accuracy to 0.52–0.54. Weighted fusion dropped it to 0.59. ResNet50 was much weaker than ViT-L under avgpool (0.41 vs 0.51). Image-only with transformer reached only 0.507, so the scVI RNA branch carries much of the signal. The main open question near the optimum is whether the image branch truly helps on top of scVI, or whether scVI alone with transformer aggregation is as good or better. 2) This experiment runs RNA-only, scvi_n200, multiprofile, transformer aggregation. That isolates the RNA contribution and shows whether the ~0.17 gain over image-only comes from fusion or mainly from scVI. If it matches or beats 0.678, it is a cheaper and possibly better optimum. If it falls short, that confirms multimodal fusion and points the last experiment at remaining multimodal neighbours such as config_023 or config_006. 3) It is the most informative untested neighbour of the best configuration. The ResNet50 variant is unlikely to win given the prior ResNet result. Expected cost is low, about 1–2 GPU hours, similar to the image-only run and well below the ~4.6 h multimodal runs.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is RNA-only scVI with transformer aggregation over multiple profiles (config_010, acc 0.715, F1 0.687). It beats every multimodal run, and adding images consistently lowered accuracy. Within multimodal runs, scVI clearly beat scGPT and PCA, and transformer aggregation clearly beat avgpool. So the RNA encoder and aggregation choices look settled. The profile setting has never been tested: every experiment so far was multiprofile. 2. Test: config_004 is RNA-only scVI with a single profile. It isolates whether multiprofile aggregation is actually needed for the strongest modality, or whether the simpler single-profile model matches or beats 0.715. 3. Why now: the other RNA-only options (scGPT or PCA encoders, avgpool aggregation) change choices that already lost clearly, so they are unlikely to beat config_010. Profile setting is the one major design axis with zero evidence, so this run reduces the most uncertainty. It also leaves the last experiment free to exploit whichever profile setting wins. Expected cost is the lowest of any option, below config_010's 0.40 GPU hours, since there is no aggregation and no image branch.

Evidence: the best result so far is RNA-only multiprofile scVI with transformer aggregation (config_010, 0.715 acc / 0.687 F1). That beats every multimodal variant, including the best one (config_025, 0.678). So image fusion has not helped. Transformer aggregation clearly beats avgpool (0.678 vs 0.514), which makes config_009 unlikely to win. ResNet50 underperformed ViT-L, so config_023 is unlikely to win either. The remaining open question is whether another RNA encoder can beat scVI in the RNA-only transformer setting. In multimodal runs scGPT and PCA trailed scVI, but those runs included the image branch, which may have masked RNA-encoder differences. Between the two, scGPT edged out PCA (0.540 vs 0.520 acc; 0.524 vs 0.479 F1). This final experiment tests RNA-only multiprofile scGPT with transformer aggregation, the most plausible untested route to exceeding 0.715. The chance of beating config_010 is modest, but it is the best remaining shot. Expected cost is very low (about 0.4–0.6 GPU hours, comparable to config_010), far cheaper than any multimodal option.

1) No experiments have been run, so there is no evidence about any design choice yet. Priors suggest that combining both modalities and aggregating over multiple profiles should give the highest accuracy for cellular profiling. 2) Config_013 tests that prior directly: it is multimodal and multiprofile, uses transformer aggregation and concat fusion, and pairs a compact RNA encoder (scVI, 200 dimensions) with a mid-sized image encoder (ResNet50). It gives a strong anchor result. Later experiments can then change one factor at a time: the image encoder (ViT-L), the RNA encoder (PCA or scGPT), the aggregation method (avgpool) and the fusion method (weighted). Simpler baselines such as single-modality or single-profile runs can be checked later if needed. 3) Starting near the expected best region, but with cheaper components than scGPT or ViT-L, balances getting a high result early against compute cost. Expected relative cost is medium. Multiprofile transformer aggregation and multimodal processing add training time, but the small scVI and ResNet50 representations keep it below the ViT-L and scGPT variants.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: We have one result so far. config_013 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI RNA encoder, ResNet50 images, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) reached 0.427 accuracy and 0.417 F1. One run says nothing yet about which design choices matter most. The image encoder is plausibly a major lever, since ImageNet ViT-L gives much richer image features than ResNet50. 2. What this tests: config_003 changes only the image encoder (ResNet50 to ViT-L) and keeps everything else the same. Any difference can therefore be attributed to the image backbone. This settles a key design choice that splits about half of the remaining search space. 3. Why it is the best next step: The image encoder is likely the largest source of accuracy gain, and testing it now tells us which backbone to carry into later RNA-encoder, aggregation and fusion comparisons. Expected cost is moderately higher than config_013, roughly 1.3–1.6x (about 7–8 GPU hours), because ViT-L embeddings are larger. That cost is justified because it may well be the stronger backbone. If ViT-L shows no gain, we can switch to cheaper ResNet50 variants for the rest of the search.

1) Evidence: with the scVI RNA encoder, multiprofile transformer aggregation and concat fusion held fixed, the ViT-L image encoder beat ResNet50 by a clear margin (acc 0.485 vs 0.427, F1 0.464 vs 0.417). ViT-L was also slightly cheaper (4.65 vs 5.16 GPU h). So ViT-L should be the image backbone going forward. The RNA encoder choice is still completely untested, and it is likely a major driver of accuracy. 2) This experiment keeps the best setup (ViT-L, multiprofile, transformer, concat) and swaps scVI for scGPT. It isolates the effect of a pretrained foundation-model RNA embedding against scVI. 3) Choosing the RNA encoder is the biggest open design question. Settling it early lets the remaining 7 experiments fine-tune fusion (weighted vs concat) and aggregation (avgpool vs transformer) around the best encoder pair. 1. Evidence: The RNA encoder is the largest lever so far. Swapping scVI for scGPT, with ViT-L, transformer aggregation and concat fusion, raised accuracy from 0.485 to 0.632, and F1 rose in step (0.464 to 0.607). ViT-L also beat ResNet50 under scVI. The main uncertainty is fusion: every run so far used concat, so weighted fusion is completely untested. 2. Test: config_019 keeps the best setup (multimodal, multiprofile, scGPT, ViT-L, transformer) and changes only concat to weighted fusion. This cleanly measures whether weighting the modalities improves on the current best, which matters because scGPT RNA features may deserve more weight than the image features. 3. Why now: It exploits the strongest region found so far while resolving a design choice that has had no exploration. Any gain directly raises the best accuracy, and the result guides the remaining 6 runs. Those runs can then test pca_n2000 RNA (config_007/029) and avgpool aggregation. Expected cost is similar to config_001, about 4 GPU hours, since weighted fusion adds negligible overhead to the multiprofile transformer pipeline.

1) Evidence: scGPT with ViT-L, transformer aggregation and concat fusion (config_001) is clearly best at 0.632 accuracy and 0.607 F1. scGPT beat scVI by about 0.15 under the same setup. ViT-L beat ResNet50 for scVI. Weighted fusion did worse than concat (0.591). Aggregation has never been varied: every run so far used a transformer, so it is the largest untested design choice around the best setup. 2) This experiment keeps the best RNA encoder, image encoder and fusion fixed and swaps transformer aggregation for avgpool. That isolates whether the transformer aggregator is needed or whether simpler pooling matches or beats it. 3) Of the untested choices, this one is most likely to produce a new best, and it settles a choice that decides how the remaining 5 experiments should be spent. 1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_001 (scGPT + ViT-L + transformer + concat, 0.632 accuracy, 0.607 F1). Within that setup, weighted fusion (0.591) and avgpool aggregation (0.523) both did worse. Switching the RNA encoder from scVI to scGPT gave the largest gain seen (+0.15). That makes the RNA encoder the most influential choice. Its third option, pca_n2000, has not been tested in any context. 2) Test: config_007 keeps the best context (multiprofile, ViT-L, transformer, concat) and swaps scGPT for PCA-2000. This shows whether PCA features beat or match scGPT. If PCA wins, the best result improves directly. If it loses, scGPT is confirmed and the remaining 3 experiments can target other questions, such as single-profile or RNA-only variants. 3) Why now: This experiment completes the most impactful design axis in the most promising context, so it is the best balance of exploration and exploitation. 1) Evidence: The RNA encoder matters most so far. With ViT-L, transformer aggregation and concat fusion, scGPT scored 0.632, against 0.514 for PCA and 0.485 for scVI. Transformer aggregation beat avgpool (0.632 vs 0.523), and concat beat weighted fusion (0.632 vs 0.591). ViT-L beat ResNet50 in the scVI pairing (0.485 vs 0.427), so a ResNet50 swap is unlikely to win. The open question is whether the image branch adds signal at all, since no unimodal run has been done. 2) Test: config_017 keeps the best settings (scGPT, multiprofile, transformer aggregation) but drops images. This isolates how much the image modality contributes. If it matches or beats 0.632, the image branch is noise and the best model is simpler. If it falls well short, multimodal fusion is confirmed and the last runs can focus on refining around config_001. 3) Why now: It is both a real chance at a new best and a direct test of an untested design choice, at low cost. Removing the ViT-L image pathway should make it cheaper than config_001's 3.95 GPU hours, likely around 2–3.

Evidence: the RNA-only model (scGPT, multiprofile, transformer, config_017) is the best result so far at 0.721 accuracy and 0.681 F1. It was also the cheapest run at 0.51 GPU hours. Every multimodal variant did worse (at most 0.632), which suggests the image branch adds noise. Within multimodal runs, scGPT clearly beat scVI and PCA as the RNA encoder, and transformer aggregation beat avgpool by about 0.11. So swapping the encoder or switching to avgpool is unlikely to beat 0.721. Uncertainty: the profile setting has never been tested, since every run so far used multiprofile. This experiment tests whether single-profile scGPT RNA-only can match or beat multiprofile aggregation. That is the main untested design choice left in the most promising model family. Budget: with 2 experiments remaining after this one, the result tells us whether to refine further around multiprofile RNA-only or around single-profile RNA-only. Expected cost: very low, likely below config_017's 0.51 GPU hours because there is no aggregation step and no image processing. It should be among the cheapest options available.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_017 (RNA-only, multiprofile, scGPT, transformer) at 0.721 accuracy and 0.681 F1. Adding images has hurt in every multimodal run, with a best of 0.632. scGPT is clearly the strongest RNA encoder, ahead of PCA (0.514) and scVI (0.485) in matched multimodal comparisons. Multiprofile beats singleprofile for scGPT RNA-only (0.721 vs 0.650). 2) Question: Aggregation is the only design choice for the leading configuration not yet tested in the RNA-only setting. Avgpool did worse than the transformer in the multimodal setting (0.523 vs 0.632). However, a simpler pooling head could behave differently, and possibly overfit less, on a lower-dimensional RNA-only input. config_032 tests scGPT RNA-only multiprofile with avgpool. 3) Why this experiment: The other plausible candidates, scVI or PCA RNA-only multiprofile, swap in encoders that were consistently much weaker than scGPT. They are unlikely to beat 0.721. This run keeps the strongest components and varies the one remaining open choice, so it offers the best chance of improving on the current best with 2 experiments left. 1. Evidence: The best result so far is RNA-only, multiprofile, scGPT with transformer aggregation (config_017, acc 0.721, F1 0.681). Adding the image branch consistently lowered accuracy (best multimodal 0.632). Transformer aggregation clearly beat avgpool, both in the multimodal runs and in the RNA-only runs. Among RNA encoders in the multimodal setting, scGPT led, PCA-2000 came second (0.514) and scVI came last (0.485). No other scGPT RNA-only configuration remains untested. 2. Test: config_008 keeps the winning RNA-only + multiprofile + transformer recipe and swaps in PCA-2000, the second-best encoder. It checks whether the encoder ranking seen in multimodal runs also holds without image noise. It is the most plausible remaining path to beating 0.721, because image-only and multimodal options have shown no sign of exceeding RNA-only. 3. Why now: As the final experiment, it is the logical exploitation of the strongest design pattern found. It is also very cheap: RNA-only multiprofile runs cost about 0.4–0.5 GPU hours, roughly a tenth of a multimodal run, so the low cost justifies the modest chance of a gain.

1) Evidence: no experiments have been run, so every design choice is uncertain. Priors from multimodal cellular profiling suggest three things: combining RNA and image modalities usually beats either one alone, aggregating multiple profiles usually beats single profiles, and stronger image encoders (ViT-L) and compact learned RNA embeddings (scVI) often do well. 2) Test: config_013 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI-200, ViT-L, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) sets a strong 'everything likely-good' anchor. Later experiments can then ablate one factor at a time from this anchor (avgpool vs transformer, resnet50 vs ViT-L, scGPT/PCA vs scVI, weighted vs concat, unimodal baselines) to see which components actually matter and which can be swapped for cheaper options. 3) Why now: only the best accuracy counts, so getting a likely top performer early protects the result and gives a reference for judging cheaper variants. 1. Evidence: there is only one result so far. A one-factor change gives a clean comparison against the current best, and the answer guides many later multiprofile picks (encoder and fusion variants). 1. Evidence: Singleprofile multimodal (config_002: scVI + ViT-L, concat) is clearly the best result at 0.678 accuracy and 0.646 F1, and it cost only 0.62 GPU hours. 1. Evidence: Single-profile multimodal with scVI and ViT-L using concat fusion (config_002) is clearly the best so far, at 0.678 accuracy and 0.646 F1, for only 0.62 GPU hours. 1) There is no history yet, so all design choices are uncertain. Evidence: there is only one result so far. The full multimodal, multiprofile model (scVI + ViT-L, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) reached 0.527 accuracy and 0.510 F1 at 3.6 GPU hours. Evidence: with scVI + ViT-L + weighted fusion, the single-profile model (0.540 acc, 0.524 F1, 0.53 GPU h) slightly beat the multi-profile transformer (0.527 acc, 3.60 GPU h) at about one-seventh the cost. 1. Evidence: the best result so far is the cheap singleprofile scvi_n200 + ViT-L model with weighted fusion (config_027, acc 0.540, F1 0.524, 0.53 GPU h). The multiprofile transformer version (config_024) scored lower (0.527) and cost about 7x more. Swapping scvi for scgpt also hurt (0.525, with lower F1). 1. Evidence: weighted fusion clearly beats concat (0.540 vs 0.422 with the same other settings). Singleprofile scvi_n200 + ViT-L + weighted (config_027, 0.540) is the current best. The multiprofile transformer version scored slightly lower (0.527) at about 7x the cost. scvi_n200 edges out scgpt (0.540 vs 0.525, with higher F1), but the third RNA encoder, pca_n2000, is untested. 2. Test: config_008 keeps the best cheap setup (singleprofile, ViT-L, weighted fusion) and swaps in pca_n2000. 1. Evidence: Weighted fusion is clearly better than concat (0.540 vs 0.422 with scvi_n200 and ViT-L). With weighted fusion, the RNA encoders differ only slightly (scvi 0.540 > pca 0.535 > scgpt 0.525), so scvi_n200 + ViT-L + weighted is the strongest base. Multiprofile has been tried only once, with transformer aggregation (0.527 accuracy, 3.6 GPU h). That run underperformed singleprofile and was about 7x more expensive. One run is too little to rule out multiprofile: the transformer aggregator may simply be overfitting or hard to optimise, while avgpool is a simpler, more robust way to aggregate profiles. 2. Test: config_019 keeps the best components (scvi_n200, ViT-L, weighted fusion) and swaps only the aggregator to avgpool. This isolates whether multiprofile aggregation can beat the 0.540 singleprofile result. 3. Why now: Aggregation is the main remaining design choice that could give a substantial accuracy gain, whereas the RNA encoder looks nearly saturated. Resolving it now leaves 3 runs to exploit the answer, for example trying pca_n2000 with avgpool or testing a ResNet50 image encoder cheaply in singleprofile. Expected cost is moderate to high, likely about 2-3 GPU h. That is cheaper than the transformer variant because avgpool avoids attention over profiles, but well above the ~0.6 GPU h singleprofile runs.

1. Evidence: weighted fusion clearly beats concat (about 0.54 vs 0.42). Singleprofile matches or beats multiprofile (0.540 vs 0.527 for transformer and 0.520 for avgpool) while costing 5 to 9 times fewer GPU hours. Among RNA encoders, scvi_n200 (0.540) and pca_n2000 (0.535) are about equal and both ahead of scgpt (0.525). The image encoder has never been varied, because every run so far used imagenet_vit_l. 2. This experiment keeps the best configuration (config_027: singleprofile, scvi_n200, weighted fusion) and swaps the image encoder to resnet50. It isolates the last untested major design choice. 3. Possible outcomes: if resnet50 matches or beats ViT-L, it could become the new best. If it is worse, it confirms ViT-L and points the remaining two experiments toward exploiting the singleprofile ViT-L weighted configurations. Expected cost is low, about 0.5 GPU hours, similar to or below config_027, since resnet50 features are smaller than ViT-L. That makes it a cheap, informative test compared with the 3.6 to 4.8 GPU-hour multiprofile runs.

Evidence: switching the image encoder from ViT-L to ResNet50 in the best single-profile scVI + weighted-fusion setup gave the largest gain so far (0.540 to 0.629 accuracy, F1 0.599). Other choices barely mattered. RNA encoders differed only slightly with ViT-L (scVI 0.540, PCA 0.535, scGPT 0.525). Multiprofile aggregation did not help (0.520 to 0.527) and cost 6 to 9 times more GPU hours. Concat fusion clearly hurt (0.422). Open question: is the gain driven entirely by ResNet50 image features, with RNA adding little or even noise? This test: the single-profile, image-only ResNet50 model (config_028) isolates the image contribution. If it matches or beats 0.629, the last experiment should go to image-only variants. If it falls short, RNA fusion is confirmed useful and the last run can refine the RNA encoder or try a ResNet50 multiprofile model. Why now: swapping the RNA encoder is unlikely to beat scVI, and multiprofile runs are costly with no demonstrated benefit. This answers a key design question and could itself produce the best model. Expected cost: lowest of the options, probably about 0.4 to 0.5 GPU hours, slightly below the 0.59 h of config_029 since there is no RNA branch.

Evidence: Switching the image encoder from ViT-L to ResNet50 gave the largest gain so far. config_029 (scVI + ResNet50, single-profile, weighted fusion) reached 0.629 accuracy and 0.599 F1, against about 0.54 for the ViT-L versions. Weighted fusion clearly beat concat (0.540 vs 0.422). Multiprofile aggregation did not help with ViT-L (transformer 0.527, avgpool 0.520, vs 0.540 single-profile) and cost 6–9 times more GPU hours. Among RNA encoders, scVI (0.540) and PCA (0.535) were close, with scGPT lower (0.525). The remaining open question is whether another RNA encoder paired with ResNet50 can beat scVI. 2. Test: config_042 keeps the winning recipe (ResNet50, single-profile, weighted fusion) and swaps in PCA-2000. PCA was nearly tied with scVI under ViT-L. This tells us whether the ResNet50 gain carries over across RNA encoders and could give a new best. 3. Why now: This is a low-risk extension of the best configuration that could plausibly top 0.629. 1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_003 (singleprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, concat) at 0.715 accuracy and 0.687 F1. Every single change away from it hurt. This experiment keeps the best components (pca_n2000, resnet50, concat) and changes only avgpool to transformer aggregation in the multiprofile setting. It tests whether attention-based pooling over profiles can recover and exceed singleprofile performance. 3. 1) Evidence: the best results so far are unimodal multiprofile models with avgpool: RNA-only scVI at 0.635 and image-only ViT-L at 0.632. Multimodal fusion has not beaten either. Weighted fusion beats concat, and transformer aggregation helped weighted fusion but slightly hurt RNA-only. scGPT was weaker than scVI.
