1. Evidence: The single-modality baselines are strong and similar: scVI RNA-only reaches 0.635 and ViT image-only reaches 0.632 (multiprofile, avgpool). Every multimodal run tested so far has done worse than either baseline: concat 0.33, weighted 0.54, transformer+weighted 0.59. These failures all used multiprofile aggregation. For RNA-only, single-profile (0.619) was close to multiprofile (0.635), so aggregation is not obviously needed. 2. Question: This run uses the best encoder pair (scVI + ViT-L) with the better fusion method (weighted) in the single-profile setting, with no aggregation. It tests whether the multimodal shortfall comes from fusion itself or from how fusion interacts with multiprofile aggregation. 3. Why now: This is the largest unresolved question in the study. If single-profile multimodal beats about 0.635, there is a clear new direction to exploit. If it also falls short, that points to fusion as the bottleneck, and remaining runs should go to single-modality refinements. Filling in config_038 (transformer+concat) would only refine a fusion method that already looks weak.

1) Evidence and uncertainty: the best result so far is config_035 (singleprofile, scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l, weighted fusion), with 0.678 accuracy and 0.646 F1. 1. Evidence: Only one experiment is complete. config_030 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200 + resnet50, avgpool, concat) reached 0.422 accuracy and 0.405 F1. 1) Evidence: with the scVI-n200 encoder, multiprofile setting and avgpool aggregation, adding ResNet50 image features through concat fusion dropped accuracy sharply, from 0.650 (RNA-only) to 0.422. Evidence: with scVI + ResNet50 + avgpool, concat fusion did poorly (0.422 acc), while weighted fusion reached 0.653 acc / 0.628 F1. 1) Evidence so far: with scVI RNA features, ResNet50 image features and multiprofile input, weighted fusion clearly beat concat (0.653 vs 0.422 accuracy). 1) Evidence and uncertainty: Every run so far has used the scvi_n200 RNA encoder. Within that setting, three patterns are fairly consistent. Weighted fusion strongly beats concat (0.653 vs 0.422). 1. Evidence: the best multimodal run, config_031 (scVI + ResNet50, avgpool, weighted fusion, 0.653 accuracy), barely beats RNA-only scVI with avgpool, config_005 (0.650). 1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best multimodal result (config_031, scVI + ResNet50, avgpool, weighted fusion; 0.653 acc / 0.628 F1) is essentially tied with RNA-only scVI (config_005; 0.650 / 0.628). 1. Evidence: The best multimodal run (config_031, scVI + ResNet50, avgpool, weighted fusion, 0.653 acc / 0.628 F1) is essentially tied with RNA-only scVI (config_005, 0.650 / 0.628). 1) No experiments have been run yet, so we know nothing about any design choice: modality, single vs. multi-profile, encoders, aggregation or fusion. 2) config_030 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI-200, ResNet50, avgpool, concat) is a central reference point. Each design choice can be isolated later by changing one factor at a time: RNA-only (config_005), image-only (config_011), single-profile (config_028), transformer aggregation (config_032), weighted fusion (config_031), or a different encoder (config_018, config_036, config_042). 3) A plausible, mid-complexity configuration used as this hub makes every later experiment a clean one-factor comparison. 1. Evidence: only one result exists. The multimodal model (scVI RNA, ResNet50 images, avgpool, concat) reached 0.435 accuracy and 0.423 F1. With a single point, we cannot tell how much of that comes from the image branch versus the RNA representation. 2. Evidence: the multimodal scVI+ResNet50 avgpool concat model (0.435 acc, 0.423 F1) far outperforms the matched RNA-only model (0.208 acc). That gap suggests most of the signal may come from the image modality. What is still unknown is whether fusion adds anything beyond images alone. Image-only ResNet50 with multiprofile avgpool completes a clean modality ablation, since every other setting matches the two runs already done. If it scores close to 0.435, the image encoder is the main driver, and the next budget should go to image encoders and aggregation rather than RNA encoders or fusion type. If it scores clearly lower, RNA contributes complementary signal, and further searching over multimodal fusion and RNA encoders is justified. This single run decides where in the large multimodal grid the remaining budget is best spent.

1. Evidence: Image features carry most of the signal. Image-only reached 0.421 accuracy, while RNA-only (scVI) reached only 0.208. Multimodal concat improved slightly on image-only, to 0.435 accuracy and 0.423 F1. This suggests RNA adds a small amount and the image representation is the main performance lever. Only ResNet50 has been tested, so the image encoder choice is the largest open question. 2. Test: This run changes one factor from the current best (config_030), swapping ResNet50 for ImageNet ViT-L. scVI, multiprofile, avgpool and concat stay fixed, so any difference can be attributed to the image encoder. 3. Why now: Because images dominate performance, the encoder choice is likely to matter most. This experiment both reduces uncertainty about an important design choice and could plausibly beat the current best. Aggregation, fusion and the RNA encoder are better tested after the image backbone is settled.

1. Evidence: The image encoder is the dominant factor so far. Swapping ResNet50 for ImageNet ViT-L in the same multimodal scVI/avgpool/concat setup raised accuracy from 0.435 to 0.725, with F1 rising in step from 0.423 to 0.685. RNA alone is weak (0.208), and adding it to ResNet50 gave only a small gain over image-only (0.435 vs 0.421). Aggregation has never been varied; every multiprofile run used avgpool. 2. Test: config_038 keeps the best configuration fixed and changes only avgpool to transformer aggregation. This isolates whether learned attention over multiple profiles beats simple averaging when the image features are strong. 3. Why now: Aggregation is a major untested design axis. Testing it on the strongest backbone is both informative and likely to perform well. Fusion type, RNA encoder choice and an image-only ViT-L ablation can follow once we know the better aggregator.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_036 (scVI + ViT-L, avgpool, concat) at 0.725 accuracy and 0.685 F1. That is a large jump over the ResNet50 multimodal run (0.435). But RNA-only scVI is weak (0.208), and with ResNet50, adding RNA barely beat image-only (0.435 vs 0.421). So it is unclear whether the gain comes from multimodal fusion or almost entirely from the ViT-L image encoder. 2) Test: Image-only ViT-L with avgpool differs from config_036 only by removing RNA. This isolates the RNA contribution when the image encoder is strong. 3) Why now: The answer decides how to spend the remaining budget. If ViT-L alone matches 0.725, RNA encoder and fusion choices matter little, and we should focus on image-side and aggregation choices. If it falls clearly short, RNA adds value, and exploring alternative RNA encoders (scGPT, PCA) and weighted fusion around config_036 becomes the priority. It is also a plausible high performer in its own right.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_036 (multimodal, scVI + ImageNet ViT-L, avgpool, concat) at 0.725 accuracy and 0.685 F1. Evidence: the best result so far is config_036 (scVI + ViT-L, avgpool, concat) at 0.725 accuracy and 0.685 F1. Why now: it is both a sensible exploitation step (scGPT is a pretrained foundation encoder that might improve on 0.725) and the best way to reduce uncertainty about a design axis with no data yet. Evidence: the best result so far is config_036 (scVI + ViT-L, avgpool, concat; acc 0.725, F1 0.685). Single-factor changes from it all hurt badly: transformer aggregation (0.332), weighted fusion (0.494) and the scGPT encoder (0.227). 1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_036 (scVI + ViT-L + avgpool + concat, acc 0.725, F1 0.685). Single-factor changes from it have each been tested and all lowered performance. What this tests: config_030 is a mid-range multimodal anchor using simple, commonly strong components: scvi_n200 for RNA, resnet50 for images, multiprofile avgpool aggregation and concat fusion. 1. Evidence: Only one experiment exists, config_030 (multimodal, scVI + ResNet50, avgpool, concat). It reached 0.527 accuracy and 0.510 F1. What this tests: config_005 changes a single factor from that baseline by removing the image branch, keeping the same scVI encoder, multiprofile setting and avgpool aggregation. 1. Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been run, so we have no data on whether multimodal fusion, multi-profile aggregation, or any encoder choice matters. 2. What this tests: config_030 is a mid-complexity multimodal anchor. It uses scVI RNA features (a compact, widely used representation), a ResNet50 image encoder, multi-profile average-pool aggregation and concat fusion. That gives a clean single-factor test of whether learned attention across profiles beats simple pooling. 3) It exploits the strongest direction found so far while settling a major unexplored design axis. Aggregation applies across many remaining configurations, so the result guides later choices of encoder and modality.

1) Evidence: Weighted fusion clearly beats concat (0.678 vs 0.427 with scVI + ViT-L + avgpool). Avgpool beat transformer aggregation in the one comparison we have. The best multimodal run (0.678) is only modestly above scVI RNA-only (0.650), so RNA features appear to carry most of the signal. All four runs so far used scVI, which leaves the RNA encoder choice completely untested. 2) This run keeps the best setup fixed (multiprofile, ViT-L, avgpool, weighted fusion) and swaps scVI for scGPT. It tests whether a foundation-model RNA encoder improves on scVI. 3) Because RNA seems to be the dominant modality, the RNA encoder is likely the highest-leverage unexplored choice. Changing only that one factor in the strongest setup could raise performance directly and gives a clean comparison for later decisions (scVI vs scGPT, and whether PCA is worth testing).

1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is config_037 (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, weighted fusion) at 0.678 accuracy and 0.646 F1. Earlier runs suggest three patterns. Weighted fusion beats concat (0.678 vs 0.427), avgpool beats transformer aggregation (0.678 vs 0.518), and scvi_n200 beats scGPT (0.678 vs 0.537). What this tests: config_031 keeps the best settings and swaps only the image encoder to resnet50. This isolates whether the image backbone matters. Why this is the best next run: it varies one factor away from the current best, so it stays close to good performance while resolving the largest remaining blind spot. Testing the pca_n2000 RNA encoder or single-profile inputs matters too, but the image encoder is the one entire design axis with no evidence at all.

1) Evidence: Every experiment so far used multiprofile. Within that setting, several one-factor comparisons favour scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + avgpool + weighted fusion (config_037, 0.678 acc / 0.646 F1). Swapping in transformer aggregation, concat fusion, scGPT or ResNet50 each lowered performance, sometimes sharply. Weighted fusion beats RNA-only only modestly (0.678 vs 0.650), and the profile-setting dimension has never been tested. 2) This experiment keeps the best encoders and weighted fusion but switches to singleprofile (no aggregation). 1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is config_037 (scVI + ViT-L, avgpool, weighted fusion) at 0.678 accuracy and 0.646 F1. Each one-factor change from it has hurt performance. 1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_037 (scVI + ViT-L, avgpool, weighted fusion) at 0.678 accuracy and 0.646 F1. RNA-only scVI with avgpool (config_005) reaches 0.650, so adding images helps only modestly. The image modality has never been tested alone, so we do not know how much ViT-L features contribute by themselves. The collapse under concat fusion (0.427) and with ResNet50 (0.208) suggests image features may be weak or noisy, and that weighted fusion helps by down-weighting them. 2) This experiment tests image-only ViT-L with multiprofile avgpool, which mirrors the best setup. 1) Evidence: Image-only ViT-L with multiprofile avgpool (config_014, 0.713 acc / 0.695 F1) is the current best. The best multimodal run (config_037, weighted fusion, 0.678) does not beat it. In multimodal runs, switching to singleprofile dropped accuracy to 0.520 and transformer aggregation dropped it to 0.518. It differs from config_014 only in the profile setting, so it directly measures how much multiprofile aggregation contributes for the leading image representation. It also checks whether the single-profile penalty seen in multimodal holds without RNA. 3) Why now: profile setting is a top-level design choice that determines whether later aggregation and fusion refinements are worthwhile. A clean ablation on the best-performing branch reduces more uncertainty than exploiting a transformer variant (already weakly negative) or ResNet50 (strongly negative at 0.208).

1) Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been run, so every design choice is open: modality, encoders, single vs. multi-profile input, aggregation, and fusion. 2) What it tests: config_018 is a central, simple configuration: multimodal input, multiple profiles, PCA RNA features, ResNet50 image features, average-pool aggregation and concatenation fusion. It uses the simplest option on each axis while including the two most likely sources of gain, combining modalities and using multiple profiles. That makes it a clean reference point. Later runs can change one factor at a time from it: drop to RNA-only or image-only (config_002, config_011), switch to single-profile (config_016), or swap in a transformer aggregator, weighted fusion, or a pretrained encoder (scGPT, ViT-L). 3) Why it is the best use of the budget: With no data yet, a mid-complexity baseline that is likely to be competitive gives both a reasonable performance bar and an anchor for one-factor-at-a-time comparisons. Starting with the most complex or least likely configuration would reveal less about which design choices matter.

1) Evidence/uncertainty: Only one experiment has been run (config_018: multimodal, multiprofile, PCA RNA, ResNet50, avgpool, concat; accuracy 0.411, F1 0.378). We know nothing yet about which design choices drive performance, so the most useful next step is a controlled single-factor change from this baseline. 2) What it tests: config_024 keeps every setting fixed except the image encoder, swapping ResNet50 for ImageNet ViT-L. This isolates whether a larger, stronger image representation improves multimodal performance. 3) Why it is the best use of the budget: Representation quality is often a dominant factor, and the image-encoder choice affects many downstream configurations (aggregation, fusion and RNA-encoder variants all pair with one of the two image encoders). Resolving it early should prune about half the search space. Aggregation (config_020) and modality ablations (e.g., config_002) are natural follow-ups once the stronger encoder is known.

1. Evidence: Only two experiments are done. They differ only in the image encoder, and ImageNet ViT-L clearly beats ResNet50 (accuracy 0.591 vs 0.411; F1 0.573 vs 0.378). That gap is large enough to anchor further search on ViT-L. Aggregation, fusion and RNA encoder remain completely untested. 2. Test: config_026 keeps the best setup (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA, ViT-L, concat) and swaps avgpool for transformer aggregation. This is a single-factor change, so it isolates whether learned attention over multiple profiles beats simple averaging. 3. Why now: Aggregation is a core design choice for multiprofile models and could have a large effect. Changing one factor from the current best both reduces uncertainty and has a realistic chance of improving on 0.591. Fusion type and RNA encoder (scVI, scGPT) are natural next ablations once the aggregation question is settled.

1) Evidence: Two design choices have some support. Swapping ResNet50 for ImageNet ViT-L, holding everything else fixed, raised accuracy from 0.41 to 0.59, a large and consistent gain in both accuracy and F1. Avgpool beat transformer aggregation (0.59 vs 0.52), though that rests on a single comparison. The RNA encoder has never been varied, since all three runs used pca_n2000, so it is the largest untested design axis with three levels. 2) Test: this keeps the current best setup (ViT-L, multiprofile, avgpool, concat) and changes only the RNA encoder from PCA to the pretrained scGPT model. That cleanly shows whether a pretrained RNA representation helps the way the pretrained image encoder did. 3) Why now: it varies one factor from the best configuration, so the result is easy to interpret. 1) Evidence so far: with multiprofile, multimodal PCA RNA, ViT-L beat ResNet50 by a wide margin (0.591 vs 0.411 accuracy). Avgpool beat transformer aggregation (0.591 vs 0.523). PCA beat scGPT, which dropped accuracy sharply to 0.224. All four runs used concat fusion, so fusion is the one design axis with no evidence at all. 2) config_025 keeps the current best setup (PCA n2000, ViT-L, avgpool, multiprofile) and changes only concat to weighted fusion. This gives a clean single-factor test of whether fusion matters. Weighted fusion could also let the model down-weight a weaker RNA branch, which the scGPT collapse suggests may be important. 3) It is the best use of the next experiment because it reduces uncertainty on a completely untested axis while staying near the top-performing region. That gives a real chance of a new best result, and the answer tells us which fusion to use in later RNA encoder (scVI) and modality-ablation comparisons.

1) Evidence: The current best is config_025 (pca_n2000 + ViT-L + avgpool + weighted, acc 0.706, F1 0.667). Three design choices have each been tested once. Weighted fusion beat concat by about 0.12 accuracy. ViT-L beat ResNet50 by about 0.18. Avgpool beat transformer by about 0.07 under concat. The RNA encoder is the least resolved choice. scGPT did very poorly (0.224) in one concat run, and scvi_n200 has never been tested, so a major design choice is completely unexplored. 2) Test: Swapping PCA for scvi_n200 while keeping every other setting from the best configuration isolates the RNA encoder's effect in the strongest known context. A strong result could give a new best. A weak result would support PCA as the right RNA representation and narrow the search. 3) Value: This targets the largest remaining uncertainty while staying in a high-performing region, so it combines exploration and exploitation. Alternatives such as transformer + weighted (config_027) or single-profile variants refine choices that already have some evidence.

1) Evidence and uncertainty: The six experiments so far point the same way on three axes. PCA_n2000 clearly beats scVI and scGPT (about 0.59–0.71 vs about 0.21–0.22). ViT-L clearly beats ResNet50 (0.59 vs 0.41). Avgpool beat transformer under concat (0.59 vs 0.52). Weighted fusion beat concat (0.706 vs 0.591, with F1 also higher). The best result is config_025 (PCA + ViT-L, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted). Every run so far has used multiprofile, so the profile setting, a major design axis, is completely untested. 2) What this tests: config_023 keeps the best components (PCA + ViT-L + weighted fusion) and switches to singleprofile. This is a clean one-variable comparison with config_025 that shows whether combining multiple profiles is responsible for the gains. 3) Why it is the best use of the budget: Rechecking transformer aggregation (config_027) is less informative, because it already did worse once. Spending runs on weak RNA encoders is unlikely to help. Testing profile setting resolves the largest remaining blind spot. It could also reveal a better configuration or confirm multiprofile as the right base for further work.

1) Evidence: every run so far is multimodal, so the model-setting choice (RNA-only vs image-only vs multimodal) has never been tested. Within multimodal runs, pca_n2000 with imagenet_vit_l, avgpool and weighted fusion leads at 0.706 accuracy (F1 0.667). Swapping only the RNA encoder to scVI or scGPT collapsed accuracy to about 0.21–0.22, even with the strong ViT-L image encoder. That suggests the RNA branch carries most of the signal, but we don't know how much the image modality actually adds. 2) This experiment: config_002 is the RNA-only counterpart of the best setup (pca_n2000, multiprofile, avgpool). It directly measures the RNA modality's contribution. If it approaches 0.7, imaging adds little and further fusion tuning is low-value. If it falls well short, multimodal fusion is justified and later work should target fusion and aggregation, for example config_027. 3) Why now: the earlier comparisons (encoder, fusion, aggregation) already point one way, while the most basic design choice has no evidence at all. Resolving it gives the largest reduction in uncertainty per experiment and anchors how to read all later results.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_025 (PCA RNA, ViT-L image encoder, avgpool aggregation, weighted fusion), at 0.706 accuracy and 0.667 F1. RNA-only with PCA reached only 0.471, and swapping in scVI or scGPT RNA encoders dropped multimodal accuracy to about 0.21. This suggests most of the predictive signal may come from the ViT-L image features, and that a poor RNA encoder can actively hurt fusion. We have never measured an image-only ViT-L baseline, so we cannot tell how much PCA RNA actually adds. 2) This experiment: The image-only ViT-L multiprofile avgpool model is the matching ablation for the current best setup. If it scores near 0.70, RNA adds little and remaining budget should go to image-side choices. If it scores clearly lower, the multimodal gain is real, and testing fusion and aggregation variants (for example config_027 or config_019) becomes the priority. 3) Why now: This one run settles whether multimodality is worth pursuing, which shapes how the rest of the limited budget should be spent. Variants like transformer aggregation already looked weaker under concat fusion, so another small tweak would tell us less.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_025 (PCA RNA, ViT-L image, avgpool, weighted fusion) at 0.706 accuracy and 0.667 F1. Weighted fusion beat concat by about 0.12 accuracy in the matched comparison (config_025 vs config_024). PCA is clearly the strongest RNA encoder, since scVI and scGPT both scored below 0.23. Transformer aggregation has been tested only once, and only with concat fusion, where it underperformed avgpool (0.523 vs 0.591). 2. What this tests: config_027 keeps PCA and ViT-L, uses weighted fusion and switches to transformer aggregation. This shows whether transformer aggregation's weakness holds generally or depends on fusion, for example whether learned modality weighting stabilizes a more expressive aggregator. 3. Why now: Aggregation is the main design choice still uncertain within the best-performing region. This experiment improves our understanding and is also a credible candidate to beat config_025. The alternatives are lower value: more scVI or scGPT runs look unpromising, and ResNet50 variants are weak.

1) Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been run, so nothing is known yet about which design choices matter: modality, single- vs multi-profile, encoder type, aggregation, or fusion. 2) What this tests: config_030 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI RNA encoder, ResNet50 image encoder, avgpool aggregation, concat fusion) is a central anchor point. Every factor sits at a moderate, simple setting. It combines both modalities and multiple profiles, which are the configurations most likely to perform well. It uses simple avgpool and concat rather than transformer aggregation or weighted fusion. Its encoders are mid-complexity choices. Later experiments can each change one factor from this anchor, such as swapping to rna_only or image_only, singleprofile, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion, or other encoders, so that each factor's effect can be attributed cleanly. 3) Why now: With a limited budget, a reasonably strong and interpretable baseline is the best first step. It should produce competitive accuracy and gives a reference point for efficient one-factor-at-a-time ablations. Starting at an extreme corner, such as a single-modality model or the most complex transformer/weighted setup, would be harder to interpret.

1) Evidence: only one experiment has been run (config_030: multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200 + resnet50, avgpool, concat; val acc 0.635, F1 0.618). With no comparison point, we cannot yet tell which design choices drive this result. The biggest open question is whether the image modality adds value over RNA alone. 2) Test: config_005 changes exactly one factor. It keeps the scvi_n200 encoder, multiprofile setting and avgpool aggregation, but removes the image branch. This is a clean ablation of modality. If accuracy drops clearly, imaging contributes and the remaining budget should go to multimodal choices such as image encoder, fusion and aggregation. If accuracy is similar or higher, the RNA encoder and aggregation choices matter more, and many multimodal configurations become lower priority. 3) Why now: modality is the highest-level design decision and determines how much of the search space deserves budget. Answering it with a controlled single-factor comparison reduces uncertainty more than a local tweak such as changing fusion or aggregation, whose effect would be hard to interpret without knowing whether imaging helps at all.

1. Evidence: Adding ResNet50 image features with concat fusion (config_030, acc 0.635, F1 0.618) did clearly worse than the RNA-only model with the same scVI encoder and avgpool aggregation (config_005, acc 0.713, F1 0.695). So naive concatenation appears to hurt. The open question is whether the image modality is inherently unhelpful or whether concat lets weak or noisy image features dilute the stronger RNA signal. 2. Test: config_031 is identical to config_030 except it uses weighted fusion. This single-factor change isolates fusion strategy. If weighted fusion recovers or exceeds RNA-only performance, fusion design is the bottleneck. If it stays well below RNA-only, ResNet50 image features likely add little value. 3. Why now: whether and how to fuse modalities shapes the entire multimodal half of the search space. A controlled comparison here tells us early whether to keep investing in multimodal configurations, and with which fusion type, before spending budget on encoder or aggregation variants.

Adding ResNet50 images lowered performance under both fusions, though weighted fusion (0.688) hurt less than concat (0.635). So far all three runs used avgpool aggregation, so the effect of aggregation is completely unknown even though it applies to every multiprofile configuration. Its result will show whether later multimodal and alternative-encoder runs should use transformer aggregation. That is a better use of one run than swapping the image encoder or RNA encoder first.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is RNA-only with scvi_n200 and avgpool (0.713 accuracy, 0.695 F1). Adding resnet50 images lowered performance, with concat hurting more (0.635) than weighted fusion (0.688). Transformer aggregation was much worse than avgpool (0.494). Every run so far used scvi_n200, so the choice of RNA encoder is completely untested, even though RNA is clearly the strongest signal. 2. Test: config_008 changes only the encoder, swapping scvi_n200 for the scGPT foundation-model embedding while keeping the best known setup (RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool). Why now: The RNA encoder affects every RNA-only and multimodal configuration in the remaining space, so this one experiment informs about two-thirds of the candidates. 1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is RNA-only scVI with multiprofile avgpool (0.713 accuracy, 0.695 F1), with scGPT close behind (0.706). Transformer aggregation collapsed to 0.494. Adding ResNet50 images lowered performance under both concat (0.635) and weighted fusion (0.688). Every completed run used multiprofile, so the profile-setting axis is untested. What this tests: config_004 changes only the profile setting relative to the current best (scVI, RNA-only, single-profile). Why it is the best next use of budget: This axis affects roughly half of the remaining search space, including every singleprofile multimodal config. 1) Evidence and uncertainty: Multiprofile with avgpool is clearly the strongest setup. The best result is RNA-only scvi_n200 avgpool (0.713 accuracy, 0.695 F1), with scgpt close behind (0.706). Adding ResNet50 images lowered performance with both concat (0.635) and weighted fusion (0.688). Weighted fusion recovered most of the loss, which suggests the image features were adding noise. This isolates whether a stronger image representation can make the multimodal model match or beat the RNA-only baseline. 3) Why it is the best next experiment: Whether images help at all is the most important open design question. 1. Evidence: The best results so far come from RNA-only models with multiprofile avgpool aggregation (scvi_n200 at 0.713 accuracy, scgpt at 0.706). Adding images has lowered accuracy in every run: resnet50 weighted fusion reached 0.688, concat 0.635, and ViT-L weighted 0.520. We have never tested images alone, so we cannot tell why fusion hurts. The image features may carry little signal, or the fusion step may be failing to use useful features. 2. Test: An image-only run with resnet50 and multiprofile avgpool, the strongest image setup seen so far, measures how much the image modality predicts on its own. 3. Why now: Most of the remaining options (over half) are multimodal, so this answer has high value. If image-only accuracy is near chance, we can drop most multimodal variants and focus the budget on RNA encoders and aggregation. If it is reasonably strong, that points to fusion design as the problem, and further multimodal tests (for example, scgpt with weighted fusion) become worth the budget.

1) Evidence: Multiprofile avgpool aggregation is clearly the strongest pattern so far. RNA-only scvi_n200 reached 0.713 accuracy and scGPT reached 0.706. Transformer aggregation (0.494) and singleprofile (0.260) were much worse. Adding images has not beaten RNA-only: the best multimodal run, resnet50 with weighted fusion, reached 0.688, and image-only resnet50 reached only 0.485. The main remaining uncertainty is the RNA encoder, because pca_n2000 has never been tested. 2) This experiment tests pca_n2000 in the best-performing template (RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool). Since that template is fixed, any change can be attributed to the encoder alone. 3) This is a good use of the budget because it closes the largest untested gap with a single run and could produce a new best. 1. Evidence: Multiprofile avgpool is clearly the strongest design. The top results are RNA-only scVI (0.713) and RNA-only scGPT (0.706). With the scVI/resnet50 pairing, weighted fusion beat concat (0.688 vs 0.635). Even so, the best multimodal run is still below RNA-only, so whether adding images helps at all is unresolved. Transformer aggregation and ViT-L both performed poorly in their single tests, so they are less promising for now. 2. Test: config_043 uses the best-known multimodal recipe (resnet50, avgpool, weighted fusion) with scGPT instead of scVI. Value: This changes one factor in the best multimodal setup, so the result is easy to interpret. 1. Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been run, so we have no evidence about which modality, encoder, profile setting, aggregation or fusion matters for this task. 2. What this tests: config_018 is a central, simple anchor point. It uses multimodal input, multiprofile with avgpool aggregation, concat fusion, and the simplest encoders (pca_n2000 and resnet50). It shows whether a basic multimodal, multi-profile model works well without adding the extra complexity of transformer aggregation, weighted fusion or pretrained foundation encoders. Later experiments can change one factor at a time from this baseline: single vs. multi profile (config_016), unimodal ablations (config_002, config_011), avgpool vs. transformer (config_020), concat vs. weighted (config_019), and stronger encoders (config_030, config_024, config_042). 3. Why it is the best first use of budget: Starting at the extremes, such as an unimodal single-profile model or the most complex scGPT/ViT/transformer setup, would give a less useful reference. 1. Evidence: Only one experiment has been run. config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA RNA, ResNet50, avgpool, concat) gave a baseline of 0.520 accuracy and 0.479 F1. Why now: Aggregation applies to every multiprofile configuration, unimodal and multimodal, so the answer narrows a large part of the search space. 1) Evidence: with everything else fixed (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000 + resnet50, concat), transformer aggregation beat avgpool by about 10 points in both accuracy (0.619 vs 0.520) and F1 (0.610 vs 0.479). That is a large, consistent gap, so it is reasonable to keep transformer aggregation as the working baseline, though it rests on a single pair of runs. This isolates whether a foundation-model RNA representation adds value beyond PCA. 3) Why now: the encoder axis has the most options and plausibly the largest effect. 1. Evidence: Two single-factor comparisons point the same way. Transformer aggregation beat avgpool by about 0.10 accuracy and 0.13 F1 (config_020 vs config_018). scGPT beat PCA by about 0.11 accuracy and 0.07 F1 (config_044 vs config_020). Test: config_050 keeps the current best setup (scGPT, multiprofile, transformer, concat) and changes only the image encoder from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L. Why now: It explores a major uncertain factor while staying in the most promising region, so it could also improve on the current best. Evidence: Four experiments, all using concat fusion, point to transformer aggregation (+0.10 accuracy over avgpool with PCA/ResNet50), scGPT RNA embeddings (+0.11 over PCA) and ResNet50 over ViT-L (+0.05 with scGPT/transformer). The best so far is config_044 at 0.725 accuracy and 0.685 F1. Fusion strategy has never been varied, so it is the largest remaining uncertainty among the multimodal design choices. What it tests: config_045 keeps the best configuration fixed and switches only concat to weighted fusion. This gives a clean one-factor test of whether fusion matters. Why now: it explores an untested axis while staying in the most promising region, so it may also improve on the best result. If weighted fusion helps, later runs can extend it to other settings. If it does not, concat can be fixed and the budget moved to unimodal baselines, such as scGPT RNA-only with transformer aggregation, to measure what the images contribute.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_044 (scGPT + ResNet50 + transformer + concat, accuracy 0.725, F1 0.685). Single-variable comparisons favor transformer over avgpool aggregation (+0.10 with PCA), scGPT over PCA (+0.11), ResNet50 over ViT-L (+0.05), and concat over weighted fusion (+0.14). The scVI_n200 RNA encoder has never been tested, so its effect is the largest open uncertainty about the RNA encoder, which has so far been the factor with the biggest impact. 2) Test: config_032 swaps only the RNA encoder to scVI and keeps the best-known ResNet50, transformer and concat settings. This gives a clean comparison against config_044 (scGPT) and config_020 (PCA), completing the RNA-encoder comparison under the strongest settings. 3) Value: It covers an untested option of a high-impact design choice and still has a reasonable chance of matching or beating the current best. 1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_044 (scGPT + ResNet50, transformer aggregation, concat fusion), at 0.725 accuracy and 0.685 F1. The history points to several robust patterns. The RNA encoder matters most: scGPT beats PCA (0.619), which beats scVI (0.427). Transformer aggregation beats avgpool (0.620 vs 0.520 with PCA). Concat fusion beats weighted (0.725 vs 0.586). ResNet50 beats ViT-L (0.725 vs 0.678). The key untested question is whether the image modality adds anything at all. Every run so far has been multimodal, and the large swings from changing the RNA encoder suggest RNA may carry most of the signal. 2. Test: config_009 is the RNA-only version of the best setup (scGPT, multiprofile, transformer). It directly measures the image branch's contribution. If it matches or beats 0.725, multimodality is not helping, and the remaining budget should shift toward RNA-side choices. If it falls clearly below, the image branch is earning its place, and further image or fusion tuning is justified. 3. Why now: This one ablation resolves the most basic open design decision (modality setting), which affects how the rest of the budget is spent. It also has a realistic chance of matching the current best, so it serves both exploration and exploitation.

1) Evidence: The other design choices have each been compared at least once, all within the multiprofile setting. Transformer aggregation clearly beat avgpool (0.62 vs 0.52 with PCA). scGPT was the best RNA encoder (0.72, vs 0.62 for PCA and 0.43 for scVI). ResNet50 beat ViT-L (0.72 vs 0.68). Concat fusion beat weighted fusion (0.72 vs 0.59). Multimodal far exceeded RNA-only (0.72 vs 0.33). Profile setting has never been varied, so whether multiprofile modeling is needed is the largest open question about a core design choice. 2) Test: config_040 takes the current best stack (scGPT + ResNet50 + concat) and switches it to the single-profile setting. Comparing it with config_044 isolates the effect of multiprofile modeling with transformer aggregation. 3) Why now: This contrast fills the one untested dimension, anchored to the strongest configuration so far. A large drop would confirm multiprofile as essential and justify focusing the remaining budget on refining multiprofile variants. A comparable or better result would open the cheaper single-profile branch (configs 016, 022, 028, 046, etc.) for further search.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_044 (scGPT + ResNet50, transformer, concat; 0.725 accuracy, 0.685 F1). 1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_044 (scGPT + ResNet50 + transformer + concat, 0.725 accuracy, 0.685 F1). 1. Evidence: No experiments have been run yet, so there is no evidence about which design choices matter: modality, single vs. multi-profile, RNA encoder, image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. 2. What this tests: config_030 is a central anchor. 1. Evidence: there is only one result so far, the multimodal multiprofile scVI + ResNet50 avgpool concat model (config_030) at 0.540 accuracy and 0.524 F1. Test: config_005 removes only the image modality and keeps the same RNA encoder (scVI), multiprofile setting and avgpool aggregation. 1. Evidence: with the same scVI RNA encoder and multiprofile avgpool setup, adding ResNet50 images with concat fusion (config_030, acc 0.540, F1 0.524) did much worse than RNA-only (config_005, acc 0.688, F1 0.659). Test: config_031 changes only one factor, concat to weighted fusion, keeping everything else identical to config_030. If weighted fusion recovers to or beats RNA-only accuracy, the fusion mechanism caused the drop and multimodal search stays promising. If it stays near 0.54, images (at least ResNet50) are likely hurting. That would point the search toward RNA-only variants or a different image encoder. 3. Why now: fusion type appears in half of the multimodal space, so resolving it early tells us whether the many remaining multimodal configurations are worth the budget. 1. Evidence: RNA-only with scVI and avgpool (config_005) reached 0.688 accuracy and 0.659 F1. Adding ResNet50 image features with the same RNA encoder and aggregation dropped performance sharply, to about 0.53 accuracy. This held for both concat and weighted fusion, so the drop is consistent across fusion types. The key uncertainty is why. Either the image modality is generally unhelpful or noisy for this task, or the ResNet50 image encoder specifically gives poor features that swamp the RNA signal. 2. Test: config_036 keeps everything identical to config_030 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI, avgpool, concat) and swaps only ResNet50 for ImageNet ViT-L. This is a clean one-factor comparison of the image encoder. If ViT-L closes the gap or beats RNA-only, the multimodal branch is still worth pursuing with ViT-L. If it also falls well below 0.688, image fusion looks generally harmful and we can focus the remaining budget on RNA-only choices like encoder and aggregation. 3. Why now: the multimodal configurations make up most of the remaining search space. Learning whether any image encoder can help is the single most budget-relevant question, and it will decide how much of that space deserves further exploration.

1) Evidence: RNA-only scVI with avgpool (config_005, 0.688 acc / 0.659 F1) clearly beats every multimodal run (0.41-0.54), all of which used avgpool. Adding images, especially ViT-L, appears to hurt, and concat versus weighted fusion made little difference. Evidence: the best result so far is RNA-only scVI with multiprofile avgpool (0.688 accuracy, 0.659 F1). Every multimodal variant scored lower, especially with ViT-L (0.41). 1) Evidence: The best result so far is RNA-only, multiprofile, scVI with avgpool (0.688 accuracy, 0.659 F1). 1) Evidence: The best result so far is RNA-only, multiprofile, scVI with avgpool (0.688 accuracy, 0.659 F1). 1) Evidence and uncertainty: RNA-only with multiprofile avgpool is the strongest setting so far. scVI scored 0.688 accuracy (F1 0.659) and PCA 0.653. Adding images consistently hurt: scVI+ResNet50 scored 0.54 (concat) and 0.53 (weighted), and scVI+ViT-L scored 0.41. However, no image-only model has been run. So we cannot tell whether the image features carry little signal, or whether the fusion setup is the problem (for example, image noise drowning out the RNA signal). 2) What this tests: an image-only ResNet50 model, using the best-performing multiprofile avgpool setting, directly measures how much predictive signal the image branch carries. If it scores near chance, the remaining budget should focus on RNA-only refinements. 1. Evidence: Unimodal models do well. The best result is RNA-only scVI with avgpool (0.688 accuracy). RNA-only PCA (0.653) and image-only ResNet50 (0.639) also perform well, all with avgpool. Multimodal scVI+ResNet50 with avgpool scored well below both of its own unimodal parts, with concat (0.540) and weighted fusion (0.525) about equally poor. Adding ViT-L as the image encoder was worse still (0.411). The key open question is why fusion fails: is it specific to the scVI pairing, or is the multimodal pipeline itself the problem? 2. Test: config_018 keeps everything else from config_030 (ResNet50, multiprofile, avgpool, concat) and swaps the RNA encoder to PCA, the second-strongest RNA representation. If it reaches or beats the unimodal baselines, the fusion failure is specific to the scVI pairing and multimodal search with PCA is worth pursuing. If it also underperforms, the evidence points to a general fusion or optimization problem, and remaining budget should go to unimodal refinement. 3. Why now: Multimodal configurations make up most of the remaining search space. This controlled one-factor comparison tells us whether to keep exploring that space, so it is worth more than a small exploit on unimodal models.

1) No experiments have been run yet, so there is no evidence about which design choices matter: modality, single vs. multi-profile, RNA encoder, image encoder, aggregation or fusion. 2) This multimodal, multi-profile configuration (scVI RNA, ImageNet ViT-L image, avgpool aggregation, concat fusion) serves as a central anchor. Evidence: only one experiment has been run (config_036: multimodal, multiprofile, scVI + ViT-L, avgpool, concat). It reached 0.427 accuracy and 0.417 F1, so there is no baseline to tell whether this is good or which component drives it. Test: config_005 keeps the same RNA encoder (scVI), multiprofile setting and avgpool aggregation, but drops the image modality. Comparing the two isolates how much the ViT-L image branch and concat fusion add over RNA alone. Why now: whether multimodality is worth it is the highest-level design question in this search space. The answer decides whether to spend the remaining budget on fusion, image-encoder and aggregation variants of multimodal models, or to focus on cheaper unimodal ones. A controlled one-factor ablation reduces more uncertainty than a local tweak such as switching to transformer aggregation or weighted fusion.

1) Evidence: Adding ViT-L image features with concat fusion (config_036, acc 0.427, F1 0.417) performed far worse than the matched RNA-only model (config_005, acc 0.721, F1 0.681). Both use scVI encoding, multiprofile input and avgpool. This gap is too large to be noise. Either the image features hurt, or naive concatenation lets noisy or high-dimensional image features overwhelm the RNA signal. 2) Test: config_037 is identical to config_036 except it uses weighted fusion, so it isolates the fusion choice. If it recovers to near or above 0.72, the fusion method was the problem and multimodal models are worth exploring further. 1. Evidence: RNA-only (scVI, avgpool) reached 0.72 accuracy and 0.68 F1. Both multimodal runs that added the ImageNet ViT-L image encoder fell to about 0.42–0.43, and concat versus weighted fusion made almost no difference. So the drop is not about the fusion choice. It comes either from this particular image encoder or from adding images at all. 2. Test: config_030 keeps everything identical to config_036 (scVI, multiprofile, avgpool, concat) and changes only the image encoder to ResNet50. Why now: most of the remaining configurations are multimodal, so learning whether that whole branch is salvageable saves the most budget. Exploiting the RNA-only branch (aggregation or RNA encoder) can follow once this question is settled.

Evidence: RNA-only scVI with avgpool (config_005) is clearly best at 0.721 accuracy and 0.681 F1. All three multimodal variants sharing that RNA encoder and aggregation scored far lower (0.42-0.54), so adding image features seems to hurt in this setup. ResNet50 beat ViT-L, and concat and weighted fusion were about the same. Every experiment so far used avgpool, so it is unknown whether transformer aggregation over multiple profiles helps. What this tests: config_006 is identical to the best configuration except that it uses transformer aggregation instead of avgpool. Any difference in accuracy or F1 can therefore be attributed to aggregation alone. Why it is the best use of the budget: it builds on the strongest direction (RNA-only scVI) while answering an open design question that affects every multiprofile configuration. The result will guide later choices among RNA encoders (scGPT, PCA) and whether to revisit multimodal configurations with transformer aggregation.

1) Evidence: RNA-only scVI with avgpool is clearly the best so far (0.721 accuracy, 0.681 F1). Every multimodal variant has been much worse (0.42–0.54), with ViT-L worse than ResNet50. Transformer aggregation also hurt RNA-only (0.535 vs 0.721). Together these point to the RNA branch with simple pooling as the strongest direction. However, scVI is the only RNA encoder tested, so the RNA encoder, possibly the most important remaining design choice, is still unexplored. 2) Test: config_008 swaps scVI for the scGPT foundation-model embeddings while keeping everything else fixed (RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool). This isolates the effect of the RNA representation. 3) Why now: the experiment both exploits the best-performing setup and resolves a major uncertainty. If scGPT beats scVI, it could raise the ceiling and should be carried into any later multimodal or aggregation tests. If it does not, the evidence that scVI is the right encoder gets stronger. Other options, such as PCA or single-profile baselines, are useful but less likely to beat the current best.

1. Evidence: The best result by a wide margin is RNA-only scVI with avgpool multiprofile aggregation (config_005, acc 0.721, F1 0.681). Every variant tested so far performs worse. Adding images drops accuracy to 0.42–0.54, transformer aggregation gives 0.535, and swapping to scGPT gives 0.542. However, the profile setting has never been varied. All six runs were multiprofile, so we do not know whether pooling multiple profiles helps at all. 2. Test: config_004 keeps the best RNA encoder (scVI) and RNA-only setting but uses singleprofile. Why now: It resolves the largest untested design axis while staying anchored to the best-known setup, so it has both exploratory value and a real chance of matching or beating the current best. The answer also guides the remaining budget: it tells us whether to keep exploring multiprofile variants (e.g., the PCA encoder) or shift to singleprofile configurations.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is RNA-only, multiprofile, scVI with avgpool (0.721 accuracy, 0.681 F1). Every multimodal run has scored lower, by roughly 0.18 to 0.30, and transformer aggregation underperformed avgpool for scVI. Among RNA encoders in this RNA-only multiprofile avgpool setting, scGPT reached only 0.542 accuracy with weaker F1, and pca_n2000 has never been tested in any configuration. Why now: it exploits the strongest direction found so far while closing the encoder gap, which also bears on every multimodal configuration that uses PCA. 1) Evidence: The best result so far is RNA-only scVI with avgpool on multiprofile data (config_005: accuracy 0.721, F1 0.681). Adding images to that same setup lowered accuracy, to 0.537 with ResNet50 and to about 0.42 with ViT-L. Fusion type made little difference (concat 0.427 vs weighted 0.421). The image modality has never been tested on its own, so it is unclear why multimodal runs underperform. Either the image features carry little label information, or the fusion setup is diluting a strong RNA signal. 2) Test: Image-only ResNet50 with avgpool on multiprofile data uses the same profile and aggregation settings as the best runs, with ResNet50 as the stronger image encoder in fusion. It directly measures how much the images alone can predict. 3) Why now: About half of the remaining space is multimodal. A low image-only score would justify deprioritizing those configurations and spending the budget on RNA-only refinements around config_005. A reasonable score would mean fusion is the bottleneck and alternative fusion or aggregation designs deserve testing. Either outcome cuts uncertainty across many remaining configurations, which is more useful than a small local tweak.

1) Evidence: The best results so far are unimodal. RNA-only scVI with avgpool reached 0.721 accuracy, and image-only ResNet50 with avgpool reached 0.688. Every multimodal run did worse than either. Multimodal ResNet50 with concat reached 0.537, and both multimodal ViT-L runs sat near 0.42–0.43. Switching ViT-L fusion between concat and weighted changed little. That makes the image encoder look like a bigger factor than the fusion method. However, ViT-L has never been tested on its own, so we cannot tell whether it is weak in itself or only weak when fused. 2) Test: config_014 runs image-only ViT-L with multiprofile avgpool, which matches config_011 except for the image encoder. It is a clean ResNet50 vs ViT-L comparison. It will show whether the poor multimodal ViT-L results come from weak ViT-L features or from a fusion problem that would also affect ResNet50. 3) Value: The result tells us whether to drop ViT-L across the many remaining multimodal configs. It also tells us whether multimodal underperformance is a fusion problem worth investigating further. It also has a real chance of being competitive with the current best image-only result. That makes it a better use of the budget than another fusion tweak, which earlier evidence suggests matters little.

1) No experiments have been run, so there is no evidence yet about which design choices matter: modality (RNA, image, or multimodal), profile setting (single vs. multi), encoder type, aggregation, or fusion. 2) config_018 is a central reference point: multimodal, multiprofile with avgpool aggregation and concat fusion, using the simplest encoders (PCA for RNA, ResNet50 for images). 1) Evidence: there is only one result so far. config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000 + resnet50, avgpool, concat) reached 0.518 accuracy and 0.484 F1. With a single point, we cannot yet tell which design choices matter. 2) Test: config_020 changes only the aggregation from avgpool to a transformer and keeps everything else fixed. This gives a clean one-factor comparison of how the multiple profiles are combined. Learned aggregation is likely one of the larger levers in multiprofile setups, and it is also the more expensive option, so it matters to know early whether it is worth the cost. 3) Why now: a controlled ablation against the existing baseline gives an interpretable result whichever way it goes. Whichever aggregation wins can then be carried forward into later tests of the image encoder (ViT-L), the RNA encoder (scVI or scGPT) and the fusion method. 1) Evidence: Only two runs exist, both multimodal multiprofile with pca_n2000, resnet50 and concat fusion. The transformer aggregation (config_020) beat avgpool (config_018) by about 2.2 points in accuracy and about 4 points in F1. That is moderate, consistent evidence for transformer aggregation. The encoders and fusion type are still completely untested. 2) This experiment keeps the best setup fixed and swaps only the image encoder from resnet50 to imagenet_vit_l. Changing one factor gives a clean read on whether a larger pretrained image backbone improves the multimodal model. 3) The encoder choice likely matters more than the fusion type, and the image encoder is a major unexplored axis. The result will guide whether later RNA encoder (scVI or scGPT) and fusion comparisons should use ViT-L or ResNet50.

Evidence: all three runs use the pca_n2000 RNA encoder with concat fusion. Within that setup, two single-factor changes each improved results. Switching aggregation from avgpool to transformer gave about +0.022 accuracy (0.518 to 0.540, with ResNet50). Switching the image encoder from ResNet50 to ViT-L gave about +0.059 (0.540 to 0.599, with transformer). The F1 changes track the accuracy changes. Each comparison rests on a single run, so these are early signals only. The RNA encoder is a major design choice and remains completely untested. Experiment: config_050 keeps the current best setup (multiprofile, ViT-L, transformer, concat) and changes only the RNA encoder to scGPT, a pretrained foundation model. This isolates whether the RNA representation matters as much as the image backbone did. Why now: it builds on the strongest configuration found so far, so it also has a good chance of a new best. It also resolves uncertainty about a three-level factor that strongly shapes the remaining search space. That is a more valuable use of one run than testing fusion type, which has only two options and probably a smaller effect.

1) Evidence: Three one-factor changes have each helped. Transformer aggregation beat avgpool by about 2 points (0.540 vs 0.518). ViT-L beat ResNet50 by about 6 points (0.599 vs 0.540). scGPT beat PCA by about 12 points (0.721 vs 0.599), and F1 moved the same way each time. The best configuration so far is config_050 (scGPT, ViT-L, transformer, concat). Fusion is the one major design choice not yet tested: every run so far used concat. 2) Test: config_051 keeps config_050's settings and changes only concat to weighted fusion. This gives a clean estimate of the fusion effect at the strongest setting found so far. 3) Why now: It closes the biggest remaining uncertainty among the multimodal design choices. It also has a reasonable chance of becoming the new best result. Unimodal ablations such as scGPT RNA-only would show how much the image modality contributes, but they are unlikely to beat the current best, so they can come later.

Evidence: switching the RNA encoder from PCA to scGPT gave the largest gain so far (0.599 to 0.721 accuracy, with F1 rising alongside). Image encoder and aggregation choices gave smaller gains of about 0.02 to 0.06, and weighted fusion clearly hurt (0.525). This suggests RNA representation quality may dominate performance, but we do not yet know how much the image branch actually contributes. Test: config_009 is RNA-only with scGPT and transformer aggregation over multiple profiles. It is a direct single-factor ablation of the current best config_050, removing the image modality and fusion while keeping everything else the same. Why now: if it matches or beats 0.72, the remaining budget should shift toward RNA-side choices (encoder, aggregation, single vs. multiprofile) rather than image or fusion variants. If it falls well short, it confirms that multimodal concat adds value and justifies exploiting nearby multimodal variants such as config_038 (scVI) or config_048 (avgpool). Either outcome resolves a high-level design question that steers all later experiments.

1) Evidence: the best result so far is config_050 (scGPT + ViT-L + transformer + concat, 0.721 acc / 0.681 F1). Single swaps suggest ViT-L beats ResNet50, transformer beats avgpool, and concat beats weighted fusion. scGPT beat PCA by about 12 points in the same setting, so the RNA encoder looks like a high-impact choice. However, scVI_n200, one of only three RNA encoders, has never been tested. 2) This experiment keeps the best known settings (ViT-L, transformer, concat) and swaps only the RNA encoder to scVI_n200. The result will show whether scGPT's advantage is specific to scGPT or whether a compact learned latent space is just as good or better. 3) The RNA encoder has shown the largest effect of any choice, and one of its three options is completely unexplored. This controlled test is therefore the best use of one experiment: it reduces uncertainty about an important design choice and could also produce a new best configuration.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_050 (scGPT + ImageNet ViT-L, multiprofile, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) at 0.721 accuracy and 0.681 F1. Several choices already have support. 1) Evidence: no experiments have been run, so we have no information about which modality, encoder, aggregation or fusion choice matters. 2) Test: config_030 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI RNA encoder, ResNet50 image encoder, avgpool aggregation, concat fusion) sets a reference point near the middle of the design space. 1. Evidence: only one run exists. config_030 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI, ResNet50, avgpool, concat) reached 0.520 accuracy and 0.498 F1. 1. Evidence: Adding ResNet50 image features with concat fusion cut validation accuracy from 0.688 (RNA-only, scVI, avgpool) to 0.520, with F1 falling similarly. That is a large drop. Evidence: RNA-only scVI with avgpool reached 0.688 accuracy (F1 0.659). If it also falls well below RNA-only, that is strong evidence the image modality adds noise, and the budget should shift toward RNA-only refinements such as transformer aggregation and the scGPT and PCA encoders. 1. Evidence: The best result so far is RNA-only scVI with multiprofile avgpool (0.688 acc, 0.659 F1). Adding images consistently lowered performance. The avgpool result (0.532) suggests aggregation choice matters a lot, so a single-profile baseline is needed to read that effect correctly. 3) Why now: further tweaks to fusion or encoders are unlikely to beat config_032 given the current evidence. 1) No experiments have been run yet, so we have no evidence on any design choice: modality (RNA, image, or multimodal), single- vs multi-profile input, encoder type, aggregation, or fusion. 2) config_018 is a simple, central multimodal anchor. It uses basic encoders (PCA RNA, ResNet50 image), simple avgpool aggregation and concat fusion, and sits on the multimodal/multiprofile branch that likely has the highest ceiling. Its result sets a baseline from which single-factor changes can be tested next: removing a modality (config_002, config_011), switching to single-profile (config_016), swapping encoders (scVI/scGPT, ViT-L), and trying transformer aggregation or weighted fusion. 3) Under a limited budget, a mid-complexity anchor pays off both ways. It is a reasonable chance at strong performance, and it serves as the shared reference point that makes later one-factor comparisons interpretable. A unimodal or most-complex starting point would leave more confounded factors.

1. Evidence: Only one experiment has been run. config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000 + resnet50, avgpool, concat) reached 0.535 accuracy and 0.519 F1. With one data point, we cannot tell how much each component contributes. 2. What this tests: config_002 is a controlled ablation that changes one thing. It keeps the same RNA encoder, multiprofile setting and avgpool aggregation, but removes the image branch. This directly measures whether adding resnet50 images to concat fusion helps beyond RNA alone. 3. Why now: Modality is the most basic design choice in the space. If RNA-only matches config_018, the image encoder and fusion choices probably matter little, and later budget should go to RNA encoders (scvi, scgpt) and aggregation. If RNA-only is clearly worse, multimodal is confirmed as a real benefit, and later experiments can focus on image encoder (vit_l), aggregation and fusion. Either result cleanly prunes a large part of the search space.

1. Evidence: Two experiments share the same RNA encoder (pca_n2000), multiprofile setting and avgpool aggregation. Adding ResNet50 image features with concat fusion lowered validation accuracy from 0.639 (RNA-only) to 0.535, and F1 fell similarly (0.620 to 0.519). The open question is why. Either concatenation lets weaker or noisier image features dilute the RNA signal, or the image modality simply adds no useful information here. 2. Test: config_019 changes only one thing, swapping concat for weighted fusion. If accuracy recovers to or above the RNA-only baseline, fusion strategy is the bottleneck and the multimodal half of the search space stays worth exploring. If it stays near 0.535, image features are likely harmful in general, and the search should shift toward RNA-only variants such as other RNA encoders or transformer aggregation. 3. Why now: Fusion choice affects about half of the remaining configurations. A clean one-variable comparison with the existing multimodal run is the most efficient way to decide whether multimodal models deserve more of the limited budget.

1) Evidence: RNA-only (PCA, multiprofile, avgpool) is the best result so far at 0.639 accuracy and 0.620 F1. Both multimodal runs with ResNet50 did worse (0.535 and 0.512) under either fusion. So RNA appears to be the main source of signal, and these ResNet50 image features have not helped. The RNA encoder, which may matter a lot, has only been tested with PCA. 2) This run keeps the best setup (RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool) and swaps PCA for scGPT. It tests whether a pretrained foundation-model RNA embedding beats PCA. 3) Since RNA carries most of the signal, the RNA encoder is the design choice most likely to move accuracy, and the result will guide which encoder to use in later multimodal runs. This is a better use of the budget than more fusion or aggregation variants built on the weak image branch.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is RNA-only PCA with multiprofile avgpool (0.639 acc, 0.620 F1). Adding ResNet50 images lowered performance under both concat (0.535) and weighted fusion (0.512), and scGPT was much weaker than PCA (0.435). Every multiprofile run so far used avgpool, so we do not know whether the aggregation method matters. 2. Test: config_003 changes only avgpool to transformer on the strongest baseline. This isolates the effect of aggregation and gives a clean, single-factor comparison. 3. Why now: Aggregation affects every multiprofile configuration, including all the remaining multimodal and image variants. Resolving it on the best-performing branch is both a reasonable exploitation step and a large reduction in uncertainty for future choices. 1) Evidence: The best result so far is RNA-only with PCA-2000, multiprofile and avgpool (acc 0.639, F1 0.620). The RNA encoder matters a lot: scGPT in the same setting scored about 0.20 lower. 1) Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is RNA-only PCA with avgpool on multiprofile input (0.639 accuracy, 0.620 F1). Swapping in other RNA encoders (scVI 0.494, scGPT 0.435), using transformer aggregation (0.537) or adding ResNet50 images (0.535 and 0.512) all did worse. Evidence: pca_n2000 is clearly the strongest RNA encoder. It beats scVI and scGPT, and multiprofile avgpool (0.639) is the best result so far. Adding ResNet50 images lowered accuracy with both concat (0.535) and weighted fusion (0.512). The open question is why: is the image modality uninformative, or is ResNet50 a poor image encoder for this task? The other image encoder, imagenet_vit_l, has never been tested in any setting. This experiment keeps everything from the best multimodal setup (pca_n2000, multiprofile, avgpool, concat, which beat weighted) and swaps only the image encoder. That isolates whether image-encoder choice drives the multimodal penalty. If ViT-L closes or reverses the gap with RNA-only, the multimodal ViT-L configurations become worth exploring. If it does not, the image modality likely adds little, and the remaining budget can go to the RNA-only side. Either outcome resolves a major uncertainty, and the run also has a realistic chance of producing a new best, so it serves both exploration and exploitation.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_024 (PCA + ViT-L, avgpool, concat; acc 0.688, F1 0.659). It beats RNA-only PCA avgpool (0.639). By contrast, PCA + ResNet50 multimodal runs scored below RNA-only (0.512-0.535), so the gain depends strongly on which image encoder is used. Two patterns look consistent but rest on only one or two comparisons each: avgpool beat transformer aggregation for RNA-only, and concat beat weighted fusion with ResNet50. No image-only model has been tested, so it is unclear whether ViT-L image features carry most of the signal by themselves or whether the gain comes from combining them with RNA. 2) Test: Image-only ViT-L with multiprofile avgpool isolates the image branch under the best-performing aggregation. If it scores near 0.69, the image representation is the main driver, and RNA adds little at the current fusion settings. If it scores clearly lower, the two modalities are complementary, and further fusion and aggregation tuning on PCA + ViT-L (e.g., config_025 or config_026) is well justified. 3) Why now: This single run settles the attribution question behind the main design choice, whether to invest in multimodal fusion or in image encoders. That makes it more informative under the limited budget than a small fusion or aggregation tweak to config_024, which the current trends suggest is unlikely to give a large improvement.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is image-only ViT-L with multiprofile avgpool (0.725 acc, 0.685 F1). Adding PCA RNA via concat lowered it to 0.688, and ResNet50-based multimodal runs were much weaker (0.51 to 0.54). This points to the ViT-L image branch as the main source of performance. Aggregation is still uncertain: transformer aggregation underperformed avgpool once, for PCA RNA (0.537 vs 0.639). That is a single experiment on a different modality, so it may not transfer to image features. 2) Test: Swapping avgpool for transformer aggregation on the leading image-only ViT-L configuration isolates whether learned multi-profile aggregation helps the strongest branch. 3) Why now: This exploits the most promising direction while settling a key design choice. If transformer aggregation helps, it could raise the best accuracy and would change which multimodal variants (e.g. config_026 and config_027) are worth running. If it hurts, it confirms that avgpool generalizes across modalities, and later experiments can focus on fusion and RNA-encoder choices.

1. Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been run yet, so nothing is known about which design choices matter: modality, single vs. multiprofile, RNA encoder, image encoder, aggregation or fusion. 2. What this tests: config_036 is a central anchor point. Why it is the best next step: Because the configuration sits in the middle of the design space, later runs can each change one factor from it. 1. Evidence: Only one experiment is complete. The multimodal model (scVI RNA + ViT-L image, multiprofile avgpool, concat fusion) reached 0.332 accuracy and 0.315 F1. With no comparison point, we cannot yet tell whether the image branch adds anything. That is the most basic open question in the design space, and it affects how the rest of the budget should be spent. 2. Test: config_005 keeps the RNA encoder, profile setting and aggregation the same and removes only the image modality. If RNA-only matches the multimodal model, later experiments should focus on RNA encoders and aggregation. If it falls clearly short, image encoders and fusion strategies deserve more of the budget. 1. Evidence: with the same scVI-n200 encoder, multiprofile setting and avgpool aggregation, RNA-only reached 0.653 accuracy and 0.628 F1. Adding ImageNet ViT-L image features with concat fusion dropped this to 0.332 accuracy and 0.315 F1. It is unclear whether the image modality is unhelpful or whether concat fusion is the problem, for example high-dimensional ViT features swamping the RNA signal. 2. Test: config_037 is identical to config_036 except it uses weighted fusion, so it isolates the fusion choice. If weighted fusion recovers or beats RNA-only performance, concat was the bottleneck and multimodal search remains promising. If it stays low, the image features themselves are likely the issue. 3. Value: fusion type affects every multimodal configuration, which is most of the remaining space. One controlled comparison here will guide many later choices more than testing another RNA encoder or aggregation would.

1. Evidence: RNA-only scVI with avgpool (config_005) reached 0.653 accuracy. Adding ImageNet ViT-L image features with the same RNA encoder and aggregation sharply reduced accuracy, to 0.332 with concat fusion and 0.494 with weighted fusion. F1 followed the same pattern. Weighted fusion was clearly better than concat, which suggests the model does better when it can down-weight the image branch. The open question is whether image data hurts in general or whether the ViT-L features are the problem. 2. Test: config_031 keeps everything the same as config_037 (multiprofile, scVI, avgpool, weighted fusion) and changes only the image encoder to ResNet50. This isolates the image-encoder effect within the better fusion strategy. 3. Why now: whether to keep pursuing multimodal models at all is the most consequential design decision, and it should be resolved before spending more budget on smaller choices like aggregation or RNA encoder. If ResNet50 multimodal approaches or beats RNA-only, the image branch is worth keeping with a better encoder. If it also underperforms, that is strong evidence to focus remaining experiments on RNA-only refinements such as transformer aggregation or scGPT.

1) Evidence: RNA-only with scvi_n200 and avgpool is clearly the best result so far (acc 0.653, F1 0.628). All three multimodal runs scored much lower (0.33–0.52), so adding image features appears to hurt in the current setup, especially with concat fusion. The answer also guides later choices, since the aggregation result can carry over to other RNA encoders and to any revisited multimodal setups. Comparing RNA encoders (scGPT, PCA) is the natural follow-up.

1. Evidence: RNA-only models with scvi_n200 clearly lead (0.653 with avgpool, 0.678 with transformer). Every multimodal run scored much lower (0.33 to 0.52), so adding images has hurt so far. Transformer aggregation gave a small but consistent gain in both accuracy and F1. The biggest untested design choice is the RNA encoder, since only scvi_n200 has been tried. 2. Test: config_009 keeps the strongest setup (RNA-only, multiprofile, transformer) and swaps in scGPT. This isolates whether a pretrained foundation-model encoder beats scVI. 3. Why now: it explores a key unknown while staying in the best-performing region. If scGPT wins, it sets a new best and changes which encoder later multimodal runs should use. 1. Evidence and uncertainty: RNA-only models are clearly strongest so far (scVI with transformer 0.678 and with avgpool 0.653). All multimodal runs used avgpool and did much worse (0.33-0.52). Weighted fusion beat concat by a wide margin, and resnet50 with weighted fusion (config_031, 0.520) was the best multimodal run. For RNA-only, transformer aggregation beat avgpool. So it is unclear whether multimodal models are poor because adding images hurts, or because avgpool handles multiple profiles badly. 2. What this tests: config_033 keeps everything from the best multimodal run (scVI, resnet50, weighted fusion) and changes only the aggregation to transformer. That isolates whether transformer aggregation can recover multimodal performance toward or above the RNA-only level. 3. Why this is the best use of the budget: the result decides whether the remaining multimodal transformer configurations are worth exploring. 1. Evidence: RNA-only models clearly lead, at 0.64-0.68 accuracy, while every multimodal run is far lower, at 0.33-0.52. Adding images currently hurts, so further multimodal tuning is low-value for now. Within RNA-only, transformer aggregation beat avgpool for scVI (0.678 vs 0.653, supported by F1). scVI also beat scGPT under transformer (0.678 vs 0.639). The pca_n2000 encoder has never been tested, so the RNA encoder choice, a major design decision, is still only partly mapped. 2. Test: config_003 keeps the best-performing setup (RNA-only, multiprofile, transformer) and swaps in pca_n2000. This isolates the encoder effect against config_006 and config_009 and checks whether a simple high-dimensional PCA baseline matches or beats the learned embeddings. 3. Why now: it exploits the strongest known direction while resolving the largest remaining uncertainty that could change the best configuration. 1. Evidence and uncertainty: RNA-only models clearly lead. The best is scvi_n200 with transformer aggregation (0.678 accuracy, 0.646 F1), and scvi_n200 has beaten both scgpt and pca_n2000. All four multimodal runs fell far below RNA-only (0.33–0.52), so adding images currently hurts. However, every run so far has used the multiprofile setting, so we have no evidence on whether aggregating multiple profiles helps at all. 2. What this tests: config_004 is the singleprofile counterpart of the best RNA-only setup, keeping the scvi_n200 encoder fixed. It directly measures how much the multiprofile setting, and with it the aggregation step, contributes. Comparing it with config_005 (avgpool) and config_006 (transformer) separates the effect of using multiple profiles from the effect of the aggregation method. 3. Why it is the best use of budget: profile setting is a top-level design choice that applies to every model family, and it is completely unexplored. One run in the strongest region of the search space resolves this uncertainty. That is more useful than further multimodal variants, which consistently underperform, or than small encoder swaps.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: RNA-only models are clearly strongest. The best is scvi_n200 with transformer aggregation (0.678 accuracy, 0.646 F1), followed by scvi avgpool (0.653). Every multimodal run underperforms these, from 0.33 to 0.52 accuracy. However, no image-only model has been tested, so we do not know why fusion hurts. The image features might carry little signal on their own. Alternatively, the fusion step might be dragging down a usable image signal. 2. What this tests: config_011 runs the image-only branch with resnet50, multiprofile and avgpool. This is the image encoder and aggregation used in the best multimodal run so far (config_031, 0.52), so the comparison is direct. It measures how much signal the image modality has by itself. 3. Why now: this closes the largest unexplored axis (image-only) with one controlled run. 1. Evidence: No experiments have been run, so nothing is known yet about any design choice: modality, single- vs multi-profile, RNA encoder, image encoder, aggregation or fusion. 2. What it tests: config_030 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI RNA encoder, ResNet50 image encoder, avgpool aggregation, concat fusion) is a central, moderately complex anchor. It uses both modalities and multiple profiles, which are plausible sources of gain. It pairs mid-range encoders (scVI rather than PCA or scGPT, ResNet50 rather than ViT-L) with the simplest options for aggregation and fusion. Its result sets a strong reference point. Later one-factor-at-a-time changes can then measure the effect of each choice: single-profile, unimodal ablations, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion, or swapping encoders. 3. Why now: Starting from a central, likely competitive configuration balances exploitation, since it has a reasonable chance of good accuracy and F1, with exploration, since it gives a clean baseline for the most informative follow-up ablations under a limited budget.

1. Evidence: we have only one result so far. config_030 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI-200 + ResNet50, avgpool, concat) reached 0.520 accuracy and 0.479 F1. With a single data point, we cannot yet tell which design choices drive performance. The most basic open question is whether the image branch adds anything beyond RNA. 2. Test: config_005 keeps everything else identical (scVI-200, multiprofile, avgpool) and removes only the image modality, so it is a clean one-factor ablation. If RNA-only performs about as well as config_030, image features from ResNet50 add little. In that case the search should focus on RNA encoders and aggregation rather than image encoders and fusion. If accuracy drops clearly, that supports multimodal fusion and justifies spending budget on image encoder and fusion variants. 3. Why now: this choice decides how the remaining budget is spent across the largest group of configurations (the multimodal ones). 1. Evidence: Adding ResNet50 image features to the scVI RNA model (config_030, acc 0.520) did not beat RNA-only scVI with avgpool (config_005, acc 0.520), and F1 was actually lower (0.479 vs 0.498). So the image modality has shown no value so far. It is unclear whether imaging is uninformative or ResNet50 is a weak image encoder. 2. Test: config_036 keeps everything in config_030 fixed (multiprofile, scVI, avgpool, concat) and swaps only ResNet50 for ImageNet ViT-L. This is a one-variable change that isolates the effect of the image encoder within the multimodal setting. 3. Why now: Whether multimodality is worth pursuing is the most important open design decision, because roughly 36 of the remaining configurations are multimodal.
