1) Evidence: holding everything else fixed (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool, concat), swapping ResNet50 for ImageNet ViT-L raised validation accuracy from 0.520 to 0.688, with F1 rising from 0.479 to 0.659. The ResNet50 multimodal model only matched RNA-only (0.520 accuracy). So the image encoder looks like the dominant factor, but we don't know how much RNA adds once ViT-L features are present. 2) Test: config_014 is image-only ViT-L with the same multiprofile avgpool setup. It is a clean ablation of the best run with the RNA branch removed. If it scores near 0.69, RNA adds little, and remaining budget should go to image-side and aggregation choices rather than RNA encoders (pca, scGPT) or fusion. If it scores clearly lower, multimodal fusion is synergistic, and RNA encoder and fusion variants with ViT-L become worth exploring. 3) Why now: the RNA encoder and fusion options make up much of the remaining space. A single controlled ablation tells us whether those dimensions deserve budget, which reduces uncertainty more efficiently than an incremental variant of the current best.

Evidence: the image encoder is the dominant factor so far. With scVI RNA, avgpool and concat fusion, swapping ResNet50 for ViT-L raised accuracy from 0.520 to 0.688, and F1 rose with it. The ViT-L multimodal model also beat ViT-L image-only (0.586), so adding RNA helps when paired with a strong image encoder. Aggregation, fusion type and RNA encoder are all still untested, and aggregation has only been tried as avgpool. Test: config_038 keeps the best setup (scVI, ViT-L, multiprofile, concat) and changes only aggregation to transformer. This cleanly isolates whether learned multiprofile aggregation beats mean pooling. Why now: it builds on the strongest result while resolving a major structural choice that affects every multiprofile configuration. Aggregation is likely a larger lever than concat versus weighted fusion. Fusion and RNA encoder can then be tested on whichever aggregation wins.

1) Evidence: imagenet_vit_l clearly beats resnet50 in multimodal concat (0.688 vs 0.520). Multimodal beats either single modality (0.688 vs 0.586 image-only and 0.520 RNA-only). Transformer aggregation slightly beats avgpool (0.715 vs 0.688, with F1 agreeing). That isolates the effect of the fusion strategy without confounding it with other factors. 3) It is the best use of the next experiment because it builds on the strongest region found so far while answering a design question we have no data on. If weighted fusion helps, it may also be the next best configuration. If it does not, we can fix concat and spend later runs on the RNA encoder question (scgpt or pca vs scvi).

Evidence so far: ViT-L clearly beats ResNet50 as the image encoder (0.688 vs 0.520 multimodal). Transformer aggregation modestly improved on avgpool (0.715 vs 0.688, with F1 agreeing). Evidence: every experiment so far used multiprofile inputs. Within that setting, the ViT-L image encoder clearly beats ResNet50 (0.69 vs 0.52 under avgpool/concat). Transformer aggregation modestly beats avgpool (0.715 vs 0.688). Concat fusion strongly beats weighted fusion, though that rests on a single run. scGPT and scVI perform about the same (0.721 vs 0.715), so the RNA encoder looks like a minor factor. The biggest untested design choice is the profile setting: singleprofile has never been tried, so we do not know whether multiprofile aggregation is needed at all. Test: config_046 keeps the current best setup (scGPT, ViT-L, concat) and changes only the profile setting to singleprofile, giving a clean comparison with config_050. Why now: it resolves uncertainty about a whole axis that applies to many remaining configurations. If singleprofile matches or beats multiprofile, that is an important finding. If it does much worse, it confirms multiprofile with transformer aggregation as the direction to refine, so the result is informative either way.

1) Evidence: The strongest pattern so far is multiprofile + imagenet_vit_l + transformer aggregation + concat fusion. Two RNA encoders in that setting score almost the same: scGPT at 0.721 accuracy (config_050) and scVI at 0.715 (config_038). The other design choices look better settled. ViT-L clearly beat ResNet50 (0.688 vs 0.520). Transformer beat avgpool (0.715 vs 0.688). Multimodal beat image-only (0.688 vs 0.586). Single-profile and weighted fusion each scored poorly. The PCA RNA encoder, however, has not been tested in any configuration. 2) Test: Run pca_n2000 in the best-known setting (config_026). This completes the RNA encoder comparison where it matters most. It shows whether pretrained or learned RNA representations (scVI, scGPT) beat a simple linear baseline. If PCA comes out close or better, that would suggest the RNA encoder choice barely matters. 3) Why now: The other design axes already have reasonably clear directional evidence, so the encoder question is the largest remaining gap. It is also a direct extension of the top configuration, so it has a realistic chance of matching or beating the current best. That combines exploitation with closing a key uncertainty in one experiment.

Evidence: multiprofile clearly beats singleprofile (0.42 vs about 0.72). ViT-L clearly beats ResNet50 (0.69 vs 0.52 under scVI with avgpool). Transformer aggregation modestly beats avgpool (0.715 vs 0.688), and scGPT and scVI are nearly tied at the top (0.721 vs 0.715). Fusion is the least resolved choice. Weighted fusion was tested only once (config_039) and collapsed to 0.43, below even single-modality baselines. That points to an unstable or poorly fit run rather than a reliable fusion effect, but one run cannot tell us which. This experiment changes only the fusion method on the current best setup (scGPT, ViT-L, transformer, multiprofile). If weighted fails again, concat is confirmed and the remaining budget can go to fine-tuning near the optimum. If it works with scGPT, the earlier failure was specific to scVI, and weighted fusion becomes a candidate to beat 0.72. A single run settles the most uncertain choice and also stays next to the best configuration, so it is the best use of the next experiment.

This gives a clean one-factor ablation of the image contribution. 3) Why now: this result decides where the remaining budget should go. 1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_031 (scVI + ResNet50, avgpool, weighted fusion; 0.715 accuracy, 0.687 F1). Several patterns are fairly consistent. 1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_031 (scVI + ResNet50, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted fusion; accuracy 0.715, F1 0.687). 1. Evidence: The multimodal scVI + ResNet50 + avgpool + concat setup (config_030, acc 0.715, F1 0.687) far exceeds RNA-only (0.421) and image-only (0.260). 1) Evidence: the best result so far is config_030 (scVI + ResNet50 + avgpool + concat + multiprofile) at 0.715 accuracy and 0.687 F1. Single-factor changes from it have mostly hurt. Evidence: the multimodal multiprofile setup with resnet50 and concat fusion is clearly the strongest region. scvi_n200 with avgpool reached 0.715 (F1 0.687), and the transformer variant was nearly tied at 0.706. pca_n2000 with avgpool was competitive at 0.678. Evidence: the best result so far is config_018 (PCA-2000 + ResNet50 + avgpool + concat, acc 0.688, F1 0.659). Single-factor changes from it all hurt. If it hurts again, avgpool is confirmed and later experiments can focus on whether RNA adds value.

1) Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been run, so we have no information about any design choice. That includes the most important one: whether multimodal fusion beats a single modality, and whether pooling over multiple profiles helps. 2) What this tests: config_018 is a multimodal, multiprofile model built from the simplest, cheapest component in each slot: PCA RNA features, ResNet50 image features, average pooling and concatenation fusion. It gives a central anchor point for the search. Later experiments can then change one factor at a time against it, such as dropping a modality, switching to single-profile, using transformer aggregation, weighted fusion, or stronger encoders (scVI/scGPT, ViT-L). 3) Why it is the best first use of the budget: Starting in the middle of the design space lets each later run isolate one factor's effect, which is more efficient than starting at an extreme like an RNA-only, single-profile model. Using plain components avoids confounding early conclusions with sensitivity to complex architectures, while still offering a reasonable chance of strong accuracy.

1. Evidence: Only one experiment exists. The multimodal, multiprofile configuration (PCA RNA, ResNet50 image, avgpool, concat) reached 0.525 accuracy and 0.498 F1. With a single point, we cannot tell which component drives this result, or whether the image branch helps at all. 2. Test: config_002 keeps every other setting the same (PCA, multiprofile, avgpool) but removes the image modality. This is a clean one-factor ablation of the most consequential choice, multimodal versus RNA-only. 3. Why now: Whether to use multimodal models decides which half of the search space is worth exploring. Answering this first is more informative than adjusting aggregation, fusion or encoders within a direction we have not yet validated. If RNA-only matches or beats the multimodal result, later budget should go to RNA encoders and aggregation. Evidence: the multimodal PCA+ResNet50 avgpool concat model (0.525 accuracy, 0.498 F1) beats the matched RNA-only model (0.435, 0.423) by about 9 points. That is a sizeable margin, so the image modality appears to add real signal, and further search should focus on the multimodal space. Uncertainty: the choice of image encoder (ResNet50 vs ImageNet ViT-L) is untested, and it splits the multimodal space in half. Test: config_024 changes only the image encoder relative to the current best, keeping PCA, multiprofile, avgpool and concat fixed. Any difference in accuracy or F1 can therefore be attributed to the encoder alone. Why now: this controlled one-factor comparison resolves a high-impact choice that will guide many later experiments. It also has a reasonable chance of improving on the current best. Aggregation, fusion and RNA-encoder choices can be tested next on whichever image backbone wins.

1) Evidence: multimodal fusion beats RNA-only by about 9 accuracy points (0.525 vs 0.435), so multimodality clearly matters. The two image encoders perform almost the same (ResNet50 0.525 vs ViT-L 0.518, with F1 consistent), so that choice looks minor. Aggregation, fusion type and RNA encoder are still completely untested, and every run so far used avgpool. 2) This run keeps the best configuration (config_018: multimodal, multiprofile, PCA, ResNet50, concat) fixed and changes only avgpool to transformer. 1) Evidence: Transformer aggregation gave a large gain over avgpool in the resnet50/pca_n2000/concat setup (accuracy 0.650 vs 0.525, F1 0.628 vs 0.498). 1) Evidence: Transformer aggregation gave the largest gain so far, raising accuracy from 0.525 to 0.650 with pca/resnet50/concat. Swapping pca for scGPT raised it further to 0.706 (best). ResNet50 and ViT-L were nearly tied under avgpool (0.525 vs 0.518), so the image encoder looks like a minor factor. 1) Evidence so far: transformer aggregation clearly beats avgpool (0.650 vs 0.525 with PCA+ResNet50). Concat clearly beats weighted fusion (0.706 vs 0.328 in the scGPT setting). The RNA encoder matters: switching from PCA to scGPT gave +0.056 accuracy and +0.040 F1, and scGPT+ResNet50+transformer+concat is the best so far at 0.706. The two image encoders looked similar under avgpool (0.525 vs 0.518). Filling the untested scVI option therefore reduces more uncertainty than testing ViT-L under the transformer setting. It also stays in a strong region of the space, so it could still produce a competitive result.

1) Evidence: Transformer aggregation clearly beats avgpool (0.650 vs 0.525 with PCA+ResNet50). scGPT is the strongest RNA encoder so far (0.706 vs 0.650 for PCA and 0.494 for scVI). Concat fusion far outperforms weighted fusion (0.706 vs 0.328). The remaining open question is the image encoder. ViT-L and ResNet50 were compared only under avgpool with PCA, where they came out nearly tied (0.518 vs 0.525 accuracy, with F1 slightly favoring ResNet50), so the evidence is weak. 2) This run keeps the best-known settings fixed (scGPT, transformer aggregation, concat fusion, multiprofile) and changes only the image encoder to ViT-L. It shows whether the image backbone matters once a strong aggregator and RNA encoder are in place, since a stronger aggregator may exploit richer ViT features differently. 3) It is a single-variable test in the most promising region. It could directly improve on the current best of 0.706, and if it does not, it confirms ResNet50 as the image choice. Either way it resolves the least-tested major design decision with one experiment.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_044 (scGPT + ResNet50 + transformer + concat, acc 0.706, F1 0.667). Transformer aggregation clearly beats avgpool (PCA: 0.525 to 0.650). ResNet50 has beaten ViT-L in both paired comparisons. Fusion is the main open question. Weighted fusion has been tried only once (config_045), where it collapsed to 0.328 accuracy and 0.288 F1. That one result could mean weighted fusion is inherently poor, or it could be a failure specific to scGPT, such as an optimization problem. 2) This experiment: config_021 is the strong PCA + ResNet50 + transformer setting (config_020, concat, 0.650), with only the fusion changed to weighted. That makes it a clean paired test of whether weighted fusion fails across RNA encoders. If it collapses again, weighted fusion can be dropped. If it matches or beats concat, the scGPT result was a specific failure, and weighted fusion should be revisited for the best setup. 3) Why now: weighted fusion configurations make up roughly half of the remaining multimodal options. Settling this question, which so far rests on a single run, prunes or reopens the largest share of the search space for one experiment. That is better value than a small exploitative tweak to the current best.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: Several design choices now have consistent evidence. Transformer aggregation beats avgpool (0.650 vs 0.525 with PCA+ResNet50). Concat fusion beats weighted in both pairs tested, and weighted fusion collapsed with scGPT (0.328 vs 0.706). ResNet50 beats ViT-L under both PCA and scGPT. scGPT+ResNet50+transformer+concat (config_044) is the clear best at 0.706 accuracy and 0.667 F1. The profile setting is a major design axis that has never been varied: every run so far used multiprofile. 2. What this tests: config_040 keeps the best encoder pair (scGPT RNA, ResNet50 image) and concat fusion but switches to singleprofile, which has no aggregation. Comparing it with config_044 shows how much of the top result comes from using multiple profiles plus learned transformer aggregation, rather than from the encoders alone. 3. Why it is the best use of the budget: Further tuning of fusion or image encoder around the best config adds little information, since those axes already show consistent direction. A single-axis ablation of a completely untested factor, anchored to the best known configuration, reduces the largest remaining uncertainty. It also clarifies whether multiprofile is essential or whether simpler singleprofile models are competitive.

1. Evidence: No experiments have been run, so there is no evidence yet about which modality, RNA encoder, image encoder, aggregation or fusion choice matters. 2. What it tests: config_030 is a central anchor. Why it is the best use of the budget: Every later experiment can change one factor from this anchor. 1. Evidence and uncertainty: We have only one result so far. The multimodal setup (scVI-200 RNA, ResNet50 image, avgpool, concat) reached 0.411 accuracy and 0.378 F1. With a single data point, we cannot yet tell whether the image branch adds anything beyond the RNA representation. 2. 1. Evidence: With the same scVI RNA encoder and avgpool aggregation, the multimodal ResNet50 concat model (config_030, acc 0.411, F1 0.378) did much worse than RNA-only (config_005, acc 0.579, F1 0.563). If weighted fusion recovers or beats RNA-only accuracy, fusion is the bottleneck and multimodal search is still worth pursuing. If it stays near 0.41, the image branch is the likelier cause, which points next to the image encoder (ViT-L) or to RNA-only refinements. 3. Value: Fusion applies to every multimodal configuration, which is about two-thirds of the remaining space. A clean one-variable comparison against an existing baseline is therefore the most informative use of the next experiment under a limited budget.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is RNA-only scVI with avgpool (acc 0.579, F1 0.563). Adding ResNet50 images lowered performance with both concat (0.411) and weighted fusion (0.535). So the current image branch does not help, and RNA carries most of the signal. Aggregation is a key open question: every run so far used avgpool, so we know nothing about the transformer option. 2. Test: config_006 keeps the best setup (RNA-only, multiprofile, scVI) and changes only avgpool to transformer. This isolates whether learned attention over a cell's profiles beats simple averaging. 3. Why now: Aggregation affects every multiprofile configuration in the search space, both RNA-only and multimodal. This makes it a high-leverage choice to resolve. The change also builds directly on the strongest result, so it could improve the best score. 1) Evidence so far: the best result is RNA-only with scVI, multiprofile and avgpool (0.579 acc, 0.563 F1). Adding ResNet50 images lowered accuracy with both fusion types (0.411 with concat, 0.535 with weighted). Transformer aggregation also underperformed avgpool (0.427). 1. Evidence and uncertainty: RNA-only with avgpool is the strongest result so far (scGPT 0.591, scVI 0.579). Adding ResNet50 images to scVI lowered accuracy, to 0.535 with weighted fusion and 0.411 with concat. Weighted fusion is clearly the better of the two. What we cannot tell yet is whether images are unhelpful in general or whether the ResNet50 features are the problem. ImageNet ViT-L has not been tested at all. 2. What this tests: config_037 keeps everything from config_031 the same (scVI, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted fusion) and only swaps ResNet50 for ViT-L. That gives a controlled test of the image encoder. 3. Why this is the best next experiment: the result decides how much of the remaining budget should go to multimodal configurations. If ViT-L fusion matches or beats RNA-only, multimodal remains worth pursuing and scGPT with ViT-L is the logical next step. 1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_037 (scVI + ViT-L, avgpool, weighted fusion) at 0.713 accuracy. It clearly beats the matched ResNet50 version (config_031, 0.535) and RNA-only avgpool (about 0.58 to 0.59). Weighted fusion also beat concat for ResNet50. The open question is that no image-only model has been run, so we cannot tell whether the ViT-L gain comes from combining modalities or mostly from the image encoder. 2) Test: Image-only ViT-L with multiprofile avgpool isolates the image contribution under the same aggregation as config_037. If it reaches about 0.70, the RNA branch adds little, and future runs should focus on image encoder and aggregation choices. If it is much lower, the fusion benefit is confirmed, and swapping RNA encoders (e.g., scGPT in config_049) becomes the logical next step. 3) Why now: The scGPT vs. scVI gap in RNA-only runs is small (0.591 vs. 0.579) and likely within noise. Establishing the missing image-only baseline therefore resolves a larger uncertainty about which modality drives performance, and it guides how to spend the remaining budget.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_037 (scVI + ViT-L, avgpool, weighted fusion) at 0.713 accuracy and 0.695 F1. It beats both the image-only ViT-L model (0.650) and the RNA-only models (~0.58), so fusion adds real value. With ResNet50, weighted fusion clearly beat concat (0.535 vs 0.411). Transformer aggregation hurt RNA-only performance (0.427 vs 0.579). Among RNA encoders tested alone, scGPT edged out scVI (0.591 vs 0.579), but that gap is small. 2) Question: config_049 keeps the best-performing setup and changes only the RNA encoder from scVI to scGPT. Evidence: the best result so far is config_037 (scVI + ViT-L, multiprofile avgpool, weighted fusion; 0.713 accuracy, 0.695 F1). It beats ViT-L image-only (0.650) and scVI RNA-only (0.579), so fusing the two modalities appears to help. Weighted fusion also beat concat with ResNet50 (0.535 vs 0.411), and the transformer aggregator hurt in the one RNA-only test (0.427 vs 0.579). 1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is config_037 (scVI + ViT-L, avgpool, weighted fusion) at 0.713 accuracy and 0.695 F1. 1) No experiments have been run, so we have no evidence on any design factor: modality, profile setting, RNA encoder, image encoder, aggregation or fusion. 2) Config_036 is a mid-complexity anchor: multimodal, multiprofile with avgpool aggregation, scVI RNA embeddings, ViT-L image features and concat fusion. 1) Evidence: only one experiment exists so far. Config_036 (multimodal, scVI RNA, ViT-L image, avgpool, concat) reached 0.591 accuracy and 0.573 F1. With no point of comparison, we cannot tell how much the image modality adds. 2) Test: config_005 keeps everything the same (scVI, multiprofile, avgpool) but removes the image encoder. Test: config_014 is the image-only counterpart, with ViT-L, multiprofile and avgpool, so it isolates the image contribution. Evidence: adding ImageNet ViT-L image features through concat fusion (config_036, acc 0.514, F1 0.498) did slightly worse than the matched RNA-only scVI avgpool model (config_005, acc 0.532, F1 0.517). With only two runs, this gap is small and may be noise. It could mean the image modality adds little, or that naive concatenation lets noisy image features dilute the RNA signal. Test: config_037 changes only one factor from config_036, switching concat to weighted fusion while keeping scVI, ViT-L, multiprofile and avgpool fixed. It cleanly tests whether the fusion strategy explains the multimodal shortfall. Why now: whether multimodal can match or beat RNA-only is the central question in this search, and fusion type affects about half of the remaining multimodal configurations. If weighted fusion closes or reverses the gap, multimodal weighted configurations become worth exploiting. If not, the budget should shift toward RNA-only variants such as aggregation and encoder choices.

1) Evidence and uncertainty: all three completed runs share scVI-200 RNA, multiprofile and avgpool aggregation. RNA-only scored best (0.532 acc / 0.517 F1). Adding ImageNet ViT-L did not help (0.514–0.520 acc, ~0.498 F1). The concat vs weighted fusion gap is too small to interpret. Aggregation method has never been varied, yet it affects every multiprofile configuration. 2) What this tests: switching from avgpool to a transformer aggregator in the current best setting (RNA-only, scVI). Changing only this one factor shows whether learned set aggregation over multiple profiles beats simple pooling. 3) Why it is the best next run: it isolates a high-impact, unexplored design choice without confounding from the image branch, which so far has added noise rather than signal. It also has a reasonable chance of improving on the current best. Its result will tell us which aggregation to use when later varying the RNA encoder (scGPT, PCA) or revisiting multimodal fusion.

1. Evidence: Aggregation is the dominant factor so far. RNA-only scVI with transformer aggregation reached 0.721 accuracy and 0.681 F1. With avgpool it reached only 0.532 accuracy, and both multimodal avgpool runs were similar at 0.514 and 0.520. Under avgpool, adding ViT-L images gave no gain over RNA-only. The weighted and concat fusion results were nearly tied, with identical F1. The key uncertainty is whether imaging adds value once the stronger transformer aggregation is used, since avgpool may simply have masked cross-profile structure. 2. Test: config_039 keeps everything else fixed (scVI, ViT-L, multiprofile) and changes only the aggregation to transformer, using weighted fusion. This gives a clean comparison against both config_037 (avgpool) and config_006 (RNA-only transformer). It tests whether the transformer gain carries over to the multimodal setting and whether images help on top of it. 3. Why now: This exploits the strongest finding so far while resolving the most important open question, multimodal versus RNA-only under the best aggregation. That answer decides where the remaining budget should go: image encoder and fusion choices if images help, or RNA encoder comparisons such as PCA and scGPT if they do not. Weighted fusion is chosen over concat because of its slight accuracy edge in the avgpool pair.

1. Evidence: transformer aggregation gave the best result so far (RNA-only scVI, 0.721 accuracy vs 0.532 with avgpool). But multimodal transformer with weighted fusion (config_039) collapsed to 0.208. With avgpool, concat and weighted fusion performed about the same (0.514 vs 0.520), and both were slightly below RNA-only. It is unclear whether the collapse comes from weighted fusion interacting with the transformer, or from the ViT-L image features hurting transformer-based models in general. 2. Test: config_038 keeps every setting from config_039 except fusion, switching weighted to concat. This isolates fusion under transformer aggregation. If it recovers to about 0.72 or higher, weighted fusion caused the failure and multimodal transformers stay viable, possibly beating RNA-only. If it also collapses, the image modality is likely the problem, and RNA-only refinements (e.g., trying other RNA encoders) should come next. 3. Value: this one controlled comparison settles whether multimodal plus transformer is a promising direction worth the remaining budget. It also tests the configuration most likely to exceed the current best.

1. Evidence: The clearest signal so far is that transformer aggregation strongly helps the RNA-only scVI model (0.721 accuracy vs 0.532 with avgpool, with F1 rising in step). Adding ImageNet ViT-L images hurt in every multimodal run, and badly with the transformer (0.21–0.33). The RNA encoder is still a major untested choice, since every experiment so far used scvi_n200. 2. Test: This keeps the best-performing setup (RNA-only, multiprofile, transformer) and swaps scVI for scGPT. It shows whether the transformer gain carries over to a foundation-model RNA embedding and whether that embedding beats scVI. 3. Why now: It builds directly on the strongest result while closing a large gap in what we know. Its answer also decides which RNA encoder later multimodal experiments should use. More multimodal ViT-L runs look unpromising for now, and the image-side diagnosis (image-only or ResNet50) can follow once the best RNA backbone is settled.

1) Evidence: Transformer aggregation is the clearest positive factor so far. RNA-only scVI with transformer reached 0.721 accuracy and 0.681 F1, versus 0.532 with avgpool. The RNA encoder also matters a lot: scGPT with transformer reached only 0.427. Adding ImageNet ViT-L images hurt in every case, and badly with transformer (0.21–0.33). PCA_n2000, the third RNA encoder, has never been tested. 2) This experiment: It keeps the strongest known setup (RNA-only, multiprofile, transformer) and swaps scVI for PCA_n2000. That directly tests whether scVI is the best RNA representation or whether a higher-dimensional linear embedding does as well or better. 3) Why now: It combines exploitation (a logical extension of the best-performing setup, with a real chance of a new top score) and exploration (it fills the main remaining gap in the RNA-encoder comparison). That comparison will determine which encoder to carry into any later multimodal tests, such as a ResNet50 fusion check. Investigating the image branch next would be riskier given its consistently poor results.

Evidence: the best result so far is RNA-only scVI with transformer aggregation (0.721 accuracy, 0.681 F1). Adding ImageNet ViT-L images with transformer aggregation made it much worse (0.328 with concat, 0.208 with weighted). With avgpool, ViT-L multimodal runs were also slightly below RNA-only (0.514 and 0.520 vs 0.532). Every multimodal run so far used the ViT-L encoder, so we cannot yet tell whether adding images hurts in general or whether this particular image encoder is the problem. Test: config_032 keeps the best RNA setup (scVI, multiprofile, transformer, simple concat fusion) and only swaps the image encoder to ResNet50. If it matches or beats 0.72, images can help and ViT-L was the issue. If it also collapses, images likely hurt with transformer aggregation in this setup, and the remaining budget should go to RNA-only refinements and baselines. Why now: it settles the most important open question, whether the multimodal branch is worth pursuing, and it also has a real chance of producing a new best configuration.

Evidence: the best result so far is config_032 (scVI + ResNet50, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) at 0.725 accuracy and 0.685 F1. That is only marginally above RNA-only scVI with transformer aggregation (0.721 accuracy). Transformer aggregation clearly beats avgpool for scVI. ViT-L images hurt badly under transformer aggregation, so the image encoder strongly affects how well fusion works. The fusion choice is still unresolved: with ViT-L, weighted fusion was slightly better under avgpool but much worse under transformer. Fusion has never been tested with ResNet50, and that is where it matters most. Test: config_033 changes only concat to weighted inside the best-performing setup. This isolates whether weighted fusion can draw more benefit from ResNet50 images or whether it repeats the collapse seen with ViT-L. Why now: it is a single-variable change in the most promising region, so it has a real chance of becoming the new best. It also settles the fusion choice for the leading direction before budget is spent on less promising encoders such as scGPT or PCA.

1) No experiments have been run yet, so there is no evidence about which design choices matter. 2) This configuration is a central anchor point: multimodal fusion, multiple profiles, a mid-complexity RNA encoder (scvi_n200), a standard image encoder (resnet50), simple aggregation (avgpool) and the simplest fusion (concat). Each key factor is one step away from it: removing a modality (config_005 or config_011), going to a single profile (config_028), using transformer aggregation (config_032), using weighted fusion (config_031), or swapping encoders (config_018, config_036, config_042). 3) Starting from this reasonably strong, low-complexity point should give competitive performance immediately. It also sets up efficient one-factor-at-a-time comparisons, so the next experiments can quickly show which choices drive accuracy under the limited budget.

1. Evidence: only one experiment has run. The multimodal, multiprofile setup (scVI-200 RNA, ResNet50 image, avgpool, concat) reached 0.523 accuracy and 0.508 F1. With no comparison point, we cannot tell which component drives this result, or whether the image branch adds anything. 2. What this tests: config_005 is the matched RNA-only version, with the same scVI-200 encoder, multiprofile setting and avgpool aggregation, and only the image modality removed. The accuracy and F1 difference against config_030 estimates how much the ResNet50 image features contribute. 3. Why now: whether to fuse modalities at all is the highest-level design choice, and it determines whether later budget should go to tuning image encoders and fusion or to RNA encoders and aggregation. A single-factor ablation against the existing baseline gives a clean, interpretable answer and reduces uncertainty about that choice.

1) Evidence: Multimodal scVI+ResNet50 (avgpool, concat) beat RNA-only scVI by only ~0.6 points in accuracy (0.523 vs 0.518), though F1 rose more (0.508 vs 0.484). The image branch may add a little, but with ResNet50 the benefit is uncertain and could be noise. 2) Test: config_036 keeps everything else fixed and swaps ResNet50 for ImageNet ViT-L. This isolates whether a stronger image encoder makes the multimodal gain larger. 3) Why now: The image encoder decides whether the image modality is worth pursuing across the rest of the multimodal space, so a controlled single-factor change is the most informative next step. If ViT-L gives a clear gain, I can exploit it with aggregation and fusion variants. If it does not, I will shift budget toward RNA encoder and aggregation choices.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is scVI+ResNet50 with avgpool and concat fusion (0.523 accuracy, 0.508 F1). It is only slightly above RNA-only scVI (0.518 accuracy), although its F1 is clearly higher (0.508 vs 0.484). Swapping in ViT-L under concat fusion dropped accuracy sharply to 0.328. This suggests concat fusion lets a poorly matched image representation hurt performance. It also means it is unclear whether images add real value. Fusion strategy has not been tested at all. 2. Test: This experiment changes only the fusion method, from concat to weighted, on the current best setup. It shows whether learned modality weighting improves the gain from adding images. 3. Why now: It is a controlled one-factor comparison that both exploits the strongest configuration and settles an important design question. If weighted fusion helps here, it is a strong reason to retry weighted fusion with ViT-L or with transformer aggregation. If it does not help, concat stays the default and the search can move on to aggregation and RNA encoder choices.

1. Evidence: with scvi_n200 and avgpool fixed, the best result so far is resnet50 with concat fusion (0.523 accuracy, 0.508 F1). It is only marginally ahead of RNA-only (0.518), although its F1 is clearly higher. Swapping in ViT-L (0.328) or weighted fusion (0.422) hurt substantially, so those directions look less promising for now. Aggregation is a major design axis that has not been tested at all, since every completed run used avgpool. 2. Test: this run keeps the current best configuration and changes only avgpool to transformer aggregation. It shows whether a learned aggregation over multiple profiles improves on simple pooling, and whether it widens the small multimodal advantage over RNA-only. 3. Why now: it is a single-variable extension of the strongest configuration, so the result is easy to interpret. It also tests an important open design choice while having a reasonable chance of producing a new best. RNA encoder alternatives (PCA, scGPT) remain good follow-ups once the aggregation choice is clarified.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: All five runs so far used the scvi_n200 RNA encoder. The best result is multimodal resnet50 with avgpool and concat (0.523 acc / 0.508 F1). RNA-only scvi is nearly as good (0.518), which suggests the RNA representation drives most of the performance. Switching to the ViT-L image encoder (0.328) or weighted fusion (0.422) clearly hurt. Transformer aggregation was roughly neutral (0.512). The RNA encoder is the biggest untested design choice. 2. What this tests: config_042 changes only the RNA encoder, from scvi to scgpt, while keeping the best known setup (multiprofile, resnet50, avgpool, concat). This gives a clean one-factor comparison against config_030 and shows whether a foundation-model RNA embedding beats scvi. 3. Why it is the best next experiment: Since RNA appears to be the dominant signal, the RNA encoder probably has the largest remaining effect on accuracy. Running it in the strongest known setup balances exploiting the current best with exploring an important unexplored axis.

1. Evidence: All six completed runs used the multiprofile setting. The best result so far is scGPT + ResNet50 with concat fusion at 0.532 accuracy and 0.516 F1, slightly ahead of scVI + ResNet50 at 0.523. Concat beat weighted fusion. Avgpool was slightly better than transformer aggregation. ResNet50 clearly beat ViT-L. The profile setting is the one major design choice with no evidence at all. 2. Test: config_040 keeps the best-performing encoders and concat fusion but switches to singleprofile, which uses no aggregation. This isolates whether pooling multiple profiles actually helps. 3. Why now: This one run opens a completely unexplored dimension while staying in the strongest region of the space. It either confirms multiprofile as a design decision or reveals that a simpler setting does as well or better, which would redirect the remaining budget.

1. Evidence: The best result so far, config_040 (scGPT + ResNet50, concat, singleprofile, 0.591 accuracy / 0.573 F1), beats its multiprofile counterpart config_042 (0.532 / 0.516). That gap is much larger than the other differences seen so far. It is the only paired comparison of profile setting, though, and it uses only the scGPT encoder. Other findings are fairly consistent: ResNet50 beats ViT-L, concat beats weighted fusion, avgpool is about equal to transformer aggregation, and scGPT is roughly equal to scVI under multiprofile (0.532 vs 0.523). 2. Test: config_028 is the singleprofile version of config_030 (scVI + ResNet50, concat). This gives a second paired test of singleprofile versus multiprofile. It shows whether the advantage holds across RNA encoders or depends on scGPT. 3. Why now: Profile setting looks like the most influential design choice. Replicating it before committing the remaining budget to singleprofile variants (fusion, encoder or modality ablations) reduces the risk of overinterpreting one comparison. If the gain holds, the search can focus on singleprofile configurations; if it does not, attention returns to the encoder choice.

Evidence: the best result so far is config_040 (scGPT + ResNet50, single-profile, concat) at 0.591 accuracy and 0.573 F1. With scVI, the single-profile version did much worse (0.411), so scGPT seems to drive the gain. It is still unclear how much the image branch contributes. RNA-only scVI multi-profile (0.518) nearly matched its multimodal counterpart (0.523), which suggests images add little. Test: scGPT RNA-only single-profile isolates the RNA encoder's contribution in the best-performing setting and shows whether multimodal fusion adds value beyond scGPT. Why now: this answers a central design question (is multimodality worth it, or is the RNA encoder doing the work?). That answer decides whether the remaining budget should go to fusion and image variants or to RNA-only refinements. It is more informative than small tweaks such as weighted fusion or ViT-L, both of which have underperformed so far.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is config_040 (scGPT + ResNet50, singleprofile, concat fusion) at 0.591 accuracy and 0.573 F1. scGPT is consistently stronger than scVI, and ResNet50 beats ViT-L. Fusion type is still uncertain. Weighted fusion has been tested only once, in the scVI multiprofile setting, where it dropped accuracy from 0.523 to 0.422. That single result cannot settle the question, especially because other factors already interact strongly: singleprofile helped scGPT but hurt scVI. 2. What this tests: config_041 differs from the best configuration only in using weighted instead of concat fusion. This isolates the fusion choice in the most promising region of the search space and checks whether the earlier weighted-fusion penalty holds generally or was specific to scVI. 3. Why it is the best next use of budget: Fusion type splits roughly half of the remaining multimodal configurations, so clarifying it narrows the space efficiently. The experiment also keeps a realistic chance of beating the current best, so it combines exploitation with reducing a key uncertainty.

1. Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been run, so every design factor is uncertain: modality, single- vs multi-profile, RNA encoder, image encoder, aggregation and fusion. 2. What this tests: config_018 is a central, low-complexity anchor. It is multimodal and multiprofile, using the simplest components on each axis: PCA RNA features, a ResNet50 image encoder, avgpool aggregation and concat fusion. Its result sets a reference point. Later single-factor changes can then be compared against it: rna_only (config_002), image_only (config_011), singleprofile (config_016), transformer aggregation (config_020), weighted fusion (config_019), and swapping in scVI/scGPT or ViT-L encoders. 3. Why it is the best use of the first run: Starting from a simple, plausibly strong configuration gives a useful baseline. Each next experiment can then be a clean ablation that isolates one design choice. Starting at either extreme (the simplest unimodal model or the most complex one) would make those attributions harder to read.

1. Evidence: We have one result so far. config_018 (multimodal, PCA-2000 RNA + ResNet50 image, avgpool, concat) reached 0.678 accuracy and 0.646 F1. With a single point, we cannot tell which parts of the design are driving that performance. 2. Test: config_002 keeps everything the same (multiprofile, PCA-2000, avgpool) but removes the image branch. This is a controlled one-factor ablation. It shows whether the image modality adds real value over RNA alone, or whether RNA carries most of the signal. 3. Why now: Whether to use both modalities is the most basic design choice in this search space. The answer decides whether the remaining budget goes to the multimodal region (image encoder, fusion type) or to RNA-only options (RNA encoder, aggregation). Settling this first makes every later experiment better targeted than tuning a secondary factor such as aggregation or fusion would.

Evidence: with pca_n2000, multiprofile and avgpool held fixed, the multimodal concat model (0.678 acc, 0.646 F1) beat the RNA-only model (0.619 acc, 0.610 F1) by about 6 points. We do not yet know whether this gain comes from combining the two modalities or simply from the image features being strong by themselves. Test: config_011 is the image-only counterpart (resnet50, multiprofile, avgpool). It changes only the modality and completes the three-way comparison. Why now: if image-only matches or beats multimodal, the search should focus on image encoders such as ViT-L and aggregation, and RNA encoder variants matter less. If it falls clearly below multimodal, the modalities are complementary, and fusion and RNA encoder choices deserve more of the budget. Settling which modality drives performance makes every later choice more efficient, so it is worth more than a small one-factor tweak to the current best configuration.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: multimodal concat fusion (config_018, acc 0.678, F1 0.646) beats RNA-only (0.619) and image-only (0.421). So fusion helps, but the ResNet50 image branch is weak on its own. None of the other design axes have been tested yet: image encoder, RNA encoder, aggregation and fusion type. 2. What this tests: config_024 keeps everything from the best run fixed (multiprofile, pca_n2000, avgpool, concat) and swaps only the image encoder to imagenet_vit_l. This isolates whether a stronger image representation lifts the weak modality and the fused model. 3. Why it is the best use of the budget: the image branch is clearly the bottleneck and has the most room to improve. A one-factor change from the current best is cleanly interpretable and could also beat the best so far. The result will decide whether later experiments on aggregation, fusion and RNA encoder should use ViT-L or ResNet50.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is multimodal ResNet50 + PCA with avgpool and concat fusion (config_018, acc 0.678). It beats RNA-only (0.619) and image-only (0.421), so image features add value. However, swapping in ViT-L under concat collapsed accuracy to 0.328, well below RNA-only. That suggests concat fusion may let a weak or high-dimensional image embedding overwhelm the RNA signal. Fusion strategy is therefore a key unresolved design choice. 2. Test: config_019 keeps the best configuration fixed and changes only concat to weighted fusion. This isolates the fusion effect on the strongest backbone. It shows whether learned modality weighting improves on or matches concat, and whether weighting could plausibly rescue the ViT-L setting. 3. Why now: It exploits the current best direction while answering a high-leverage question. The outcome determines which fusion to carry forward into later aggregation (transformer) and RNA-encoder (scVI, scGPT) comparisons, so the remaining budget is spent more efficiently.

1) Evidence: In the multimodal multiprofile setting, the best result so far is config_018 (pca_n2000 + resnet50 + avgpool + concat), with 0.678 accuracy and 0.646 F1. Three design choices already have direct comparisons: multimodal beats RNA-only and image-only, concat beats weighted fusion (0.678 vs 0.540), and resnet50 beats imagenet_vit_l (0.678 vs 0.328). Aggregation is untested: every multiprofile run so far used avgpool. 2) Test: config_020 changes only avgpool to transformer, keeping the best configuration otherwise identical. This gives a clean single-factor test of whether learned attention over multiple profiles helps or hurts. 3) Why now: Aggregation is a central design choice for multiprofile modeling and is fully uncertain. It can be checked without confounding by the factors already compared. The run may also beat the current best. If it does not, the result still indicates whether to keep avgpool when later testing the untried RNA encoders (scvi, scgpt).

1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_018 (multimodal, PCA RNA, ResNet50, avgpool, concat; acc 0.678, F1 0.646). One-factor changes from it all hurt: weighted fusion fell to 0.540, transformer aggregation to 0.332, and ViT-L images to 0.328. RNA-only (0.619) is much stronger than image-only (0.421), so RNA carries most of the signal. The RNA encoder has only been tested as PCA, which leaves the main source of signal unexplored. 2. Test: Swap only the RNA encoder from PCA to scVI while keeping every other setting from config_018. This isolates the effect of the RNA representation within the best-known multimodal setup. 3. Why now: Fusion, aggregation and image encoder each already have a one-factor comparison against the best config. The RNA encoder is the most important untested choice and could lift performance beyond config_018. It also tells us whether learned RNA embeddings are worth more of the budget, such as scGPT variants, or whether PCA should stay fixed. Profile setting (single vs. multi) can follow.

1. Evidence: The best configuration so far is config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA-2000 + ResNet50, avgpool, concat) at 0.678 accuracy and 0.646 F1. One-factor changes around it all performed worse. Weighted fusion dropped to 0.540, transformer aggregation to 0.332, ViT-L to 0.328 and scVI to 0.536. Profile setting is the one major design axis that has never been varied: every run so far used multiprofile. 2. Test: config_016 keeps config_018's encoders and concat fusion but uses a single profile. This directly measures whether multiprofile avgpool aggregation adds value over single-profile inputs. 3. Why now: Profile setting is a structural choice affecting half the search space, and we have no evidence on it yet. Testing it against the best configuration is a clean ablation that removes a large uncertainty. It also has a reasonable chance of matching or beating the current best, since the transformer aggregation result shows that aggregation choices can hurt badly. Trying the scGPT encoder is a good follow-up afterwards.

1) Evidence: config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA, ResNet50, avgpool, concat) is the clear best at 0.678 accuracy and 0.646 F1. Single-factor changes from it have each hurt performance: ViT-L image encoder (0.328), weighted fusion (0.540), transformer aggregation (0.332), scVI RNA encoder (0.536) and single-profile (0.507). These one-off results suggest each of those choices is worse here. The scGPT RNA encoder is the only major design option never tested in any setting. Since RNA is the strongest modality (RNA-only 0.619 vs image-only 0.421), the RNA encoder is likely a high-impact choice. 2) config_042 swaps PCA for scGPT and keeps every other setting from the best configuration. This cleanly tests whether a pretrained foundation-model RNA embedding beats PCA within the best-known pipeline. 3) It is the best use of the next experiment because it resolves the largest remaining uncertainty on a high-leverage factor. It also has a real chance of producing a new best, unlike re-testing options that have already underperformed.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_042 (multiprofile, scGPT, ResNet50, avgpool, concat) at 0.715 accuracy and 0.687 F1. Each competing choice was worse in the tested combinations: weighted fusion, transformer aggregation, the ViT-L image encoder and single-profile input. With PCA features, adding images to RNA raised accuracy from 0.619 to 0.678, but image-only reached just 0.421. The main open question is how much of config_042's gain comes from scGPT alone and how much from fusing it with images. 2) Test: config_008 runs scGPT RNA-only under the same multiprofile avgpool setup. Comparing it with config_042 measures the image contribution on top of scGPT. Comparing it with config_002 measures the scGPT versus PCA gain without image effects. 3) Why now: This one run clarifies two core design decisions, the RNA encoder and whether multimodality helps. That tells us whether later experiments should focus on improving the RNA representation or the fusion and image path. Other candidates, such as weighted fusion or transformer aggregation with scGPT, are likely to underperform given the consistent negative evidence for those choices.

1. No experiments have been run yet, so we have no evidence about which design choices matter: modality, single vs. multiprofile input, RNA encoder, image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. 2. config_030 is a central anchor point: multimodal with multiprofile input, scVI RNA embeddings, a ResNet50 image encoder, avgpool aggregation and concat fusion. Each choice is a moderate, commonly reasonable default, so the result gives a credible early estimate of achievable performance. 3. Most later configurations differ from it by one factor, such as the RNA or image encoder, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion, single-profile input, or a unimodal ablation. 1. Evidence: there is only one result so far. config_030 (multimodal, scVI + ResNet50, avgpool, concat) reached 0.525 accuracy and 0.498 F1. With no baseline, we cannot tell how much each modality contributes. 2. Test: config_005 changes only one factor by removing the image branch, keeping the scVI encoder, multiprofile setting and avgpool aggregation. This isolates whether imaging adds value over RNA alone. If RNA-only scores close to 0.525, the image encoder and fusion choices matter less, and later experiments should focus on RNA encoders and aggregation. If it scores clearly lower, multimodal fusion is justified, and testing image encoders (e.g., ViT-L) and fusion types becomes the priority. 3. Why now: the modality question sits at the top of the design hierarchy and determines which other axes are worth searching. 1) Evidence: adding ResNet50 image features through concat fusion (config_030, acc 0.525, F1 0.498) performed far worse than the matched RNA-only model (config_005, acc 0.725, F1 0.685). Encoder, profile setting and aggregation were the same, so the drop comes from adding the image modality. It is unclear whether the image features are simply uninformative or whether naive concatenation lets them swamp the stronger RNA signal. 2) config_031 changes only the fusion from concat to weighted. If weighted fusion recovers near-RNA-only performance or beats it, the failure was mainly a fusion problem and multimodal models remain worth exploring. If it stays poor, the ResNet50 image features probably add noise, and later budget can shift toward RNA-side choices (encoder, transformer aggregation) or a different image encoder. 3) This single-variable comparison resolves a key decision point: whether the large multimodal region of the search space, which is most of the remaining configurations, deserves more budget. That makes it the best use of the next experiment.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is RNA-only scVI with multiprofile avgpool (acc 0.725, F1 0.685). Adding ResNet50 images lowered performance with both concat (0.525) and weighted fusion (0.471). Transformer aggregation also hurt RNA-only (0.536). So the strongest current pipeline is RNA-only with avgpool. One RNA encoder has been tested, which leaves RNA representation as the largest unexplored design choice. 2) Test: config_008 swaps scVI for scGPT and holds everything else fixed (RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool). 1. Evidence: The best result so far is RNA-only scVI with avgpool (config_005, acc 0.725, F1 0.685). Adding ResNet50 images to that same setup sharply lowered performance, to 0.525 with concat and 0.471 with weighted fusion. So the ResNet50 image features may be poor or noisy, but no other image encoder has been tested, and we cannot yet tell whether the image modality or this specific encoder is the problem. 2. Compared directly with config_030, this isolates the effect of the image encoder. 3. 1. Evidence: The best result so far is RNA-only multiprofile scVI with avgpool (0.725 acc, 0.685 F1). Every multimodal variant has underperformed it: ResNet50 concat reached 0.525, ResNet50 weighted 0.471 and ViT-L concat 0.586. ViT-L does appear to be the better image encoder. No image-only model has been tested yet, so we cannot tell whether the image features are weakly informative or whether fusion is failing to combine two useful signals. 2. Test: Image-only multiprofile ViT-L with avgpool directly measures how much predictive signal the stronger image encoder carries. It uses the same profile setting and aggregation as the best RNA and multimodal runs, so the comparison is controlled. 3. Value: If image-only accuracy is near chance, the remaining budget should go to the RNA-only branch, such as PCA or scGPT combined with other aggregation and profile settings. If it is reasonably strong, the multimodal shortfall points to a fusion problem, which justifies testing more fusion and aggregation variants with ViT-L. Either outcome resolves the biggest open question for the remaining search.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is RNA-only scVI with multiprofile avgpool (0.725 acc, 0.685 F1). Every multimodal run used scVI and underperformed it, and the best of them, ViT-L concat at 0.586, is still well below. Since all fusion evidence comes from one RNA encoder, it is unclear whether image fusion hurts in general or only fails to add to an already strong scVI representation. 2. Test: config_024 changes only the RNA encoder of the best multimodal setup (ViT-L, multiprofile, avgpool, concat) to PCA. PCA RNA-only scored 0.629, so this gives a clean comparison. If fusion beats PCA alone, image features can help weaker RNA representations and the choice of RNA encoder matters for fusion. If it falls below PCA alone, fusion is consistently harmful and the budget should go to RNA-only refinements. 3. Value: Whether to keep exploring the large multimodal part of the space is the biggest remaining open question. This single experiment addresses it while holding the best-known aggregation and fusion choices fixed. Alternatives look less informative: transformer aggregation and weighted fusion both already showed clear drops, and the advantage of multiprofile is supported by a roughly 0.1 accuracy gap.

1. Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been run, so there is no evidence yet on any design factor (modality, single vs. multi profile, RNA encoder, image encoder, aggregation, fusion). 2. What this tests: config_036 is a central anchor point. It is multimodal and multiprofile, using the mid-complexity scVI RNA encoder, the ImageNet ViT-L image encoder, simple avgpool aggregation and simple concat fusion. Later experiments can then change one factor at a time from this point: switch to rna_only or image_only to test the value of each modality, switch to singleprofile to test the value of multiple profiles, try transformer aggregation or weighted fusion, or swap the encoders. 3. Why it is the best use of budget: starting from a mid-level configuration rather than a trivial baseline or the most complex option makes every follow-up a clean, interpretable ablation. 1) Evidence so far: only one result exists. The multimodal scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l model with avgpool and concat fusion reached 0.535 accuracy and 0.519 F1. With a single data point, we cannot tell which component drives this performance, or whether the image branch helps at all. 2) This experiment is a one-factor ablation. config_005 keeps the same RNA encoder (scvi_n200), multiprofile setting and avgpool aggregation, but removes the image modality. 1) Evidence: with the same scvi_n200 encoder and avgpool aggregation, adding ViT-L image features through concat fusion (config_036, 0.535 acc / 0.519 F1) did about 10 points worse than RNA-only (config_005, 0.635 / 0.618). This tests whether learned modality weighting can down-weight weak image features and recover or beat RNA-only performance. 3) This one-variable comparison bears directly on a key design question: does multimodality help at all under a better fusion scheme? The answer decides whether the remaining budget should go to multimodal weighted-fusion variants or to RNA-only refinements such as aggregation and encoder choice.

1) Evidence: RNA-only scVI with multiprofile avgpool is the best result so far (acc 0.635, F1 0.618). Both ViT-L multimodal variants did worse (about 0.52–0.54), whether fusion was concat or weighted. So adding ViT-L image features through avgpool has not helped yet. Why now: it exploits the best-performing branch and resolves a major open design question with a clean single-factor comparison. 1. Evidence: RNA-only scVI with avgpool is the best result so far (0.635 accuracy / 0.618 F1). Adding ViT-L image features lowered accuracy to about 0.52–0.54, with both concat and weighted fusion, so the fusion method does not explain the drop. Aggregation (avgpool 0.635 vs transformer 0.632) and RNA encoder (scVI 0.635 vs scGPT 0.599) have each been tested once. Test: config_030 keeps the best RNA setup (scVI, multiprofile, avgpool, concat) and changes only the image encoder to ResNet50.
