1) Evidence: RNA-only models clearly lead. scVI multiprofile reached 0.635 accuracy with avgpool and 0.632 with transformer. Adding images consistently hurt: about 0.52-0.54 with ViT-L and 0.42 with ResNet50. Fusion type and aggregation made only small differences. The RNA encoder did matter, with scVI at 0.635 versus scGPT at 0.599 accuracy and consistent F1. The third RNA encoder, PCA (pca_n2000), has not been tested at all. 2) This experiment runs PCA RNA-only in the best-known setup (multiprofile, avgpool). It shows whether a simple linear embedding matches or beats scVI. 3) The encoder is the design choice with the most demonstrated effect and the largest untested option, so this has both high information value and real upside. The result also tells us which RNA encoder to carry into later tests of single versus multiprofile, or any further multimodal attempts.

1. Evidence: every completed run used multiprofile. The best result so far is RNA-only scVI with avgpool (config_005, 0.635 acc / 0.618 F1). Transformer aggregation was about the same (0.632), and scVI beat scGPT and PCA. Adding images has consistently lowered performance (0.42–0.54), so the RNA-only scVI branch is the strongest direction. Profile setting is a major design choice we have no evidence on. 2. Test: config_004 is the singleprofile counterpart of the current best. Encoder and modality stay the same, so the comparison isolates whether multiprofile aggregation helps. 3. Why this one: it closes the largest untested gap with a clean one-variable comparison. It also stays close to the best region found so far, so it has a reasonable chance of matching or beating it. The result will tell us whether later experiments, including multimodal ones, should use single or multiple profiles.

Evidence: RNA-only scVI with multiprofile avgpool is the best result so far (0.635 accuracy, 0.618 F1). Every multimodal run has been worse. ViT-L concat scored 0.535, ViT-L weighted 0.523 and ResNet50 concat 0.421, so adding images currently hurts. No image-only model has been tested, so we cannot tell whether the image features are weak on their own or whether the fusion step is failing. Test: config_014 is image-only with ViT-L, multiprofile and avgpool, matching the setup of the best runs. It measures the image modality by itself, using the stronger of the two image encoders seen in multimodal runs. Why now: if image-only accuracy is near chance or far below RNA-only, further multimodal trials look unpromising and the budget should go to RNA-only variants such as scGPT or PCA with transformer aggregation. If it is reasonably strong, fusion is the bottleneck and transformer aggregation or other fusion variants deserve testing. This one run informs roughly 36 untested multimodal configurations.

Evidence: image-only ViT-L with avgpool is the best result so far (0.688 acc / 0.659 F1). It beats every RNA-only run (best 0.635) and every multimodal run (0.42–0.54), so the current fusion setups appear to hurt performance. Multiprofile clearly beats singleprofile (scVI 0.635 vs 0.411). The aggregation choice is still uncertain: for scVI RNA-only, transformer (0.632) and avgpool (0.635) were about equal, and it has never been tested on the image branch, which carries the strongest signal. Test: this run swaps only the aggregation (avgpool to transformer) on the best image-only setup. It shows whether learned attention over profiles helps image features even though it was neutral for RNA. Why now: it builds directly on the strongest direction while isolating one key design choice. Either outcome is useful. A gain gives a new best, and the result tells us which aggregation to carry into later multimodal or ResNet50 comparisons.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: No experiments have been run, so every design choice is open. These are modality (RNA, image, or both), single vs. multi-profile, RNA encoder, image encoder, aggregation and fusion. 2. What this tests: config_030 is a central anchor. It is multimodal and multiprofile, using the scVI RNA encoder, the ResNet50 image encoder, average pooling and concatenation fusion. These are mid-complexity, commonly robust choices, so it is a reasonable bet for decent accuracy. It also sits one change away from many other configs: RNA-only (005), image-only (011), single-profile (028), transformer aggregation (032), weighted fusion (031), and other encoders (018, 036, 042). 3. Why it is the best use of the budget: Starting from this anchor lets each later experiment act as a single-factor ablation. Each result then shows how much one design decision matters, which uses the limited budget efficiently. A minimal baseline like config_001 would be less likely to perform well and less useful as a reference point.

1. Evidence: Only one experiment has been run, config_030 (multimodal, scVI RNA encoder, ResNet50 image encoder, avgpool aggregation, concat fusion). It reached 0.542 accuracy and 0.483 F1. With no comparison point, we cannot tell whether the image branch helps, hurts, or does nothing. 2. What this tests: config_005 keeps the same RNA encoder, multiprofile setting and avgpool aggregation but drops the image branch. That isolates the contribution of imaging. If accuracy drops clearly, multimodality is worth pursuing, and later runs can tune image encoder, fusion and aggregation. If accuracy is similar or higher, RNA carries most of the signal, and the budget should shift toward RNA encoders and aggregation. 3. Why now: whether to use images at all is the highest-level design choice and affects most of the remaining search space. A clean one-factor ablation answers it efficiently before spending budget on finer multimodal settings.

1. Evidence: Adding ResNet50 image features with concat fusion (config_030, acc 0.542, F1 0.483) did worse than the matched RNA-only scVI avgpool model (config_005, acc 0.586, F1 0.574). The drop is sizable, but it comes from a single comparison. It is unclear whether the image modality itself is unhelpful or whether naive concatenation lets noisy image features dilute the stronger RNA signal. 2. Test: config_031 changes only the fusion method from concat to weighted. Everything else stays identical to config_030, so this is a clean one-factor test of whether learned modality weighting recovers or exceeds RNA-only performance. 3. Value: Fusion strategy determines whether the large multimodal half of the search space is worth exploring. If weighted fusion matches or beats RNA-only, multimodal configurations stay promising. If it still underperforms, we can shift the budget toward RNA-only encoder and aggregation choices.

Evidence: all three runs use scvi_n200, multiprofile and avgpool. RNA-only (0.586 acc, 0.574 F1) beats both multimodal variants. Weighted fusion (0.573) clearly beats concat (0.542), which suggests the resnet50 image features add noise that weighted fusion partly suppresses. So RNA is the main signal, and aggregation has not been varied at all. Question: does transformer aggregation over multiple profiles beat avgpool? This run changes only that one variable from the current best configuration, so the comparison is clean. Why now: aggregation applies to every multiprofile configuration, RNA-only or multimodal, so the answer narrows a large part of the remaining space. It is both exploitation (extending the best setup) and exploration (an untested axis). Image encoder and RNA encoder questions are best tested once the better aggregation is known.

1) Evidence so far, all with scVI and multiprofile: transformer aggregation beat avgpool in RNA-only runs (0.619 vs 0.586 accuracy). Weighted fusion beat concat in multimodal avgpool runs (0.573 vs 0.542), with a larger F1 gain (0.573 vs 0.483). Multimodal models have not yet matched RNA-only, so whether adding ResNet50 image features helps at all is still unresolved. Each finding rests on a single pair of runs, so neither is certain. 2) config_033 (scVI, ResNet50, transformer, weighted) differs from the tested config_031 only in aggregation. It therefore checks whether the transformer gain carries over to the multimodal setting. It also gives a direct comparison against the best RNA-only result (config_006, 0.619) on whether images add value. 3) This is the best use of the next experiment because it builds on both observed trends and is a plausible candidate for the best result so far. It also answers the most important open design question, whether to pursue multimodal models at all, before spending budget on encoder swaps such as scGPT or ViT-L.

1) Evidence: the best result so far is RNA-only scVI with transformer aggregation (acc 0.619, F1 0.610). It beats RNA-only avgpool (0.586), so transformer aggregation looks helpful for RNA. Adding ResNet50 images has not helped: concat 0.542, weighted 0.573. The multimodal transformer+weighted run collapsed (0.227), which looks more like training instability than a real signal. Every run so far used scVI, so the choice of RNA encoder is completely untested. 2) This experiment holds the best-performing setup fixed (RNA-only, multiprofile, transformer) and swaps scVI for scGPT. It isolates whether the RNA representation is a key lever and whether a foundation-model embedding can beat scVI. 3) It is the best use of budget because it exploits the strongest direction while closing a major gap. If scGPT wins, it may become the new best and guide later multimodal runs. If it loses, scVI is confirmed as the default and future runs can focus on image or fusion questions.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is RNA-only with scVI and transformer aggregation (config_006, acc 0.619, F1 0.610). The RNA encoder matters a lot: scGPT with the same setup dropped to 0.328. None of the multimodal resnet50 runs has beaten the RNA-only baseline. The pca_n2000 encoder has not been tested at all. 2. Test: config_003 changes only the RNA encoder relative to config_006, swapping scVI for PCA while keeping RNA-only, multiprofile and transformer aggregation. This cleanly shows whether PCA features match or beat scVI, completing the encoder comparison within the strongest pipeline. 3. Why now: the RNA encoder looks like the highest-impact factor, and every multimodal variant is built on it. This run has a real chance of a new best while also resolving which RNA backbone to carry into later fusion experiments. That makes it more informative per experiment than more fusion tuning on a backbone that may not be the best choice.

Evidence: RNA-only transformer aggregation is the strongest direction, with pca_n2000 best at 0.713 and scvi at 0.619. Every multimodal run (scvi plus resnet50) did worse than its matching RNA-only baseline. The transformer plus weighted multimodal run collapsed to 0.227. No image-only model has been tested, so we cannot tell whether resnet50 image features carry useful signal or mostly add noise and instability. Test: config_012 runs resnet50 image-only with multiprofile transformer aggregation. This matches the encoder and aggregation used in the failed multimodal runs, so its result can be attributed cleanly to the image modality. Why now: whether images help is the largest open design question, since it affects about two-thirds of the remaining configurations. A weak result would justify focusing the budget on RNA-only and pca-based variants. A decent result would make pca plus image fusion (such as config_020) a worthwhile next step and point to the fusion method as the cause of the earlier failures.

1) Evidence: The strongest single components are pca_n2000 for RNA (0.713 accuracy with transformer, far above scvi at 0.619 and scgpt at 0.328), resnet50 for images (0.635 image-only), and transformer aggregation (better than avgpool in the scvi RNA-only pair). Multimodal fusion has not yet beaten the best unimodal baselines. All multimodal runs so far used scvi. With scvi and avgpool, weighted fusion (0.573) edged concat (0.542). Transformer with weighted fusion collapsed to 0.227, which may be an instability specific to that pairing. 2) This run combines the best RNA encoder, the best tested image encoder and transformer aggregation, using concat fusion. It tests whether adding images on top of pca_n2000 improves on the 0.713 RNA-only result. Using concat also checks whether the transformer collapse was tied to weighted fusion. 3) This is the highest expected-value experiment that also answers the central open question: does multimodality help when the strongest RNA representation is used? If the result is at or below 0.713, a transformer-weighted variant (config_021) or a ViT image encoder are the natural follow-ups.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best run so far is RNA-only PCA with a transformer (config_003, 0.713 accuracy). Transformer aggregation beat avgpool where both were tested (scVI RNA-only, 0.619 vs 0.586). Image-only ResNet50 with a transformer was also competitive (0.635). Every multimodal run has underperformed its unimodal counterparts, and the transformer-based fusions were the worst (0.42 and 0.23). We do not know whether this is a fusion problem or a weak-image-feature problem, because imagenet_vit_l is completely untested. That encoder choice covers more than a third of the remaining configurations. 2. What this tests: config_015 changes only the image encoder relative to config_012 (image-only ResNet50, transformer, multiprofile). The comparison therefore directly measures whether ViT-L gives stronger image features. 3. Why it is the best next experiment: It resolves a major untested design dimension cleanly, without fusion instability confounding the result. A strong ViT result would point to ViT-based multimodal follow-ups with PCA RNA. A weak result would let us deprioritize that whole branch and focus on RNA-centric or fusion fixes.

1. Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been run yet, so we have no evidence on any design choice. The biggest unknowns are whether multimodal fusion helps, whether multiprofile aggregation helps, and which encoders work best. 2. What this tests: config_036 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI RNA encoder, ViT-L image encoder, avgpool aggregation, concat fusion) is a central anchor. It uses the simplest aggregation and fusion options, a standard compact RNA representation, and a likely strong pretrained image encoder. Its score sets a reference point for later one-factor-at-a-time comparisons. Swapping single components (RNA-only or image-only, single-profile, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion, other encoders) will then show directly how much each design choice matters. 3. Why it is the best next experiment: With a limited budget, a central multimodal configuration with plausibly good performance is more useful as a first run than an extreme baseline. It is likely to perform reasonably well while also maximizing how informative the following ablations will be.

1) Evidence: only one experiment has been run. The multimodal scVI + ViT-L config with avgpool and concat (config_036) reached 0.208 accuracy and 0.172 F1. On its own, this result cannot tell us whether combining modalities helps or whether one modality drives most of the performance. 2) Test: config_005 is a one-factor ablation of config_036. It keeps the scVI encoder, multiprofile setting and avgpool aggregation, but drops the image branch (RNA-only). Comparing the two directly estimates how much the ViT-L image features and concat fusion add over RNA alone. 3) Why now: whether to use multimodal models at all is the most consequential open design choice. It decides whether later experiments should focus on fusion and image encoders or on RNA encoders and aggregation. A controlled single-variable comparison against the only known baseline is the most informative use of the next experiment, ahead of tuning secondary settings such as aggregation or fusion type.

Evidence: adding ViT-L image features with concat fusion (config_036, acc 0.208, F1 0.172) roughly halved performance compared with the otherwise identical RNA-only model (config_005, acc 0.435, F1 0.423). It is unclear whether this drop means the image modality is uninformative or harmful, or whether naive concatenation is the problem. For example, the high-dimensional ViT-L features may swamp the scVI embedding. Test: config_037 changes only the fusion (concat to weighted) and keeps the RNA encoder, image encoder, multiprofile setting and avgpool aggregation fixed. If accuracy recovers to near or above the RNA-only level, the fusion method was the bottleneck and multimodal search remains promising. If it stays low, the image features are likely the issue, and the budget should shift toward RNA-only variants or image-only checks. Why now: this single-variable comparison resolves the largest open uncertainty, whether multimodal fusion is viable at all. That answer determines how to spend the remaining budget across roughly 36 multimodal configurations.

1. Evidence: Fusion choice matters a lot. With scVI + ViT-L + avgpool, weighted fusion (0.527 accuracy, 0.510 F1) far outperformed concat (0.208 accuracy) and beat RNA-only (0.435 accuracy). Weighted fusion therefore looks like the right way to add the image modality. Aggregation is still completely untested: every run so far used avgpool. 2. Test: config_039 keeps the best setup (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI, ViT-L, weighted) and changes only avgpool to transformer. This isolates whether learned attention over multiple profiles adds to the strong weighted-fusion result. 3. Why now: it builds directly on the best configuration while resolving an important open design choice in one clean comparison. That makes it both a likely high performer and an informative experiment for the limited budget. Encoder swaps (ResNet50, PCA, scGPT) can follow once the best aggregation is known.

1) Evidence: with scVI and ViT-L fixed, weighted fusion clearly beat concat (0.527 vs 0.208). Avgpool also beat transformer aggregation under weighted fusion (0.527 vs 0.421). The best multimodal model also beat the RNA-only scVI baseline (0.435), and F1 follows the same pattern. Fusion and aggregation therefore look fairly settled, but the RNA encoder has not been varied at all. 2) This experiment keeps the best recipe (multiprofile, ViT-L, avgpool, weighted fusion) and swaps only the RNA encoder from scVI to scGPT. That isolates whether a foundation-model RNA embedding beats scVI. 3) The RNA encoder is a major untested axis, and RNA alone already carries strong signal. A one-variable change on the best configuration can either find a better model or confirm scVI, which narrows a large part of the remaining search space within the limited budget.

1) Evidence so far: weighted fusion clearly beat concat (0.527 vs 0.208). Avgpool beat transformer aggregation (0.527 vs 0.421). scGPT and scVI RNA encoders performed about the same (0.537 vs 0.527), and multimodal weighted fusion beat RNA-only (0.435). The image encoder has never been varied, since every multimodal run used imagenet_vit_l. 2) This run keeps the current best setup (scGPT, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted fusion) and swaps only the image encoder to resnet50, so any change can be attributed to the encoder. 3) The image encoder is the largest remaining untested design choice. A single-factor change from the best configuration either confirms vit_l or reveals a better encoder, which makes it the most informative use of the next run.

1. Evidence: Weighted fusion clearly beat concat (0.527 vs 0.208 with scvi_n200 + ViT-L), and avgpool beat transformer aggregation in the one comparison so far. The current best is scgpt + resnet50 + avgpool + weighted at 0.653 accuracy and 0.628 F1, well above scgpt + ViT-L at 0.537. However, the resnet50 advantage comes from a single comparison within scgpt, so it could be a scgpt-specific interaction rather than a general image-encoder effect. 2. Test: config_031 keeps the winning recipe (multiprofile, avgpool, weighted) and swaps scgpt for scvi_n200 with resnet50. It completes a 2x2 design (scvi or scgpt by ViT-L or resnet50) under fixed aggregation and fusion. This shows whether resnet50 reliably beats ViT-L. It also gives a cleaner estimate of whether scgpt beats scvi_n200, which looked only slightly better with ViT-L (0.537 vs 0.527). 3. Why now: Confirming a major design factor across two RNA encoders reduces the risk of overfitting to one result. It also keeps the experiment within the most promising region, so it may perform well too. That makes it a better use of budget than less-supported transformer or concat variants.

Evidence: the best result so far is config_043 (scGPT + ResNet50, avgpool, weighted fusion), at 0.653 accuracy and 0.628 F1. It beats every other tested combination by more than 0.1. Weighted fusion clearly beats concat (0.527 vs 0.208), and transformer aggregation was worse than avgpool in the one comparison we have (0.421 vs 0.527). The encoder results show an interaction: ResNet50 worked well with scGPT but poorly with scVI. The biggest remaining uncertainty is profile setting, since all seven experiments used multiprofile. This experiment keeps the best encoders and fusion fixed and switches to singleprofile, which tests whether aggregating multiple profiles is actually needed. It is the best use of the budget because it answers a major design question that has never been tested, while staying close to the leading region. If singleprofile matches or beats 0.653, the search space shifts substantially. If it drops, we can confidently fix multiprofile and spend the remaining budget on refining aggregation and encoders.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_043 (scGPT + ResNet50, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted fusion), with 0.653 accuracy and 0.628 F1. Multiprofile beat singleprofile in this setting (0.653 vs 0.532). Weighted fusion clearly beat concat. The only aggregation comparison used the weaker scVI + ViT-L pairing, where the transformer did worse than avgpool (0.421 vs 0.527). Encoder results also show strong interactions: ResNet50 helped with scGPT but not with scVI. So that single transformer result may not carry over to the best encoder pair. 2. What this tests: config_045 changes only the aggregation (transformer instead of avgpool) on the current best configuration. It shows whether the transformer penalty holds generally or whether learned set aggregation helps once the representations are stronger. 3. Why now: Aggregation is the main design choice still uncertain in the leading region. A gain would mean a new best, and a loss would firmly settle on avgpool. Either way the budget then goes to other questions, such as the scGPT RNA-only baseline or the PCA encoder.

1) Evidence: the best result so far is scGPT + ResNet50 + avgpool + weighted fusion (0.653 accuracy, 0.628 F1). Other trends are fairly consistent. Avgpool beat transformer aggregation in both paired comparisons. Weighted fusion beat concat by a large margin in the one paired test. scGPT beat scVI with both image encoders. The main open question is the pca_n2000 RNA encoder, which has never been tested. 2) This experiment keeps the best-performing settings (multiprofile, ResNet50, avgpool, weighted) and swaps only the RNA encoder to pca_n2000. That isolates whether scGPT's advantage reflects pretrained representation quality or whether a simple high-dimensional PCA baseline is competitive or better. 3) It is the best next use of budget because it explores a completely untested level of an important design factor. Placing it in the strongest known context also gives it a realistic chance of matching or beating the current best, so it balances exploration and exploitation better than repeating already-supported comparisons.

1) No experiments have been run yet, so there is no evidence about any of the design choices: modality, single vs. multi-profile, RNA encoder, image encoder, aggregation or fusion. 2) config_030 is a central anchor point: multimodal, multiprofile with simple avgpool aggregation, simple concat fusion, the mid-sized scVI RNA encoder and the standard ResNet50 image encoder. It gives a realistic reference score for the full pipeline without using the most complex options. 3) It is the best first use of the budget because every other design question is one change away from it. Each later experiment can isolate a single factor: RNA-only (config_005), image-only (config_011), singleprofile (config_028), transformer aggregation (config_032), weighted fusion (config_031), ViT-L image encoder (config_036), or PCA/scGPT RNA encoders (config_018/config_042). Starting from a trivial unimodal baseline instead would make later multimodal comparisons less direct.

1. Evidence: Only one experiment exists. config_030 (multimodal, scVI-200 + ResNet50, multiprofile avgpool, concat fusion) reached 0.411 accuracy and 0.378 F1. With no comparison point, we cannot tell whether the image branch helps, hurts or does nothing. 2. Test: config_005 keeps the same RNA encoder (scVI-200), multiprofile setting and avgpool aggregation, but drops the image modality. It is a clean single-factor change, so the result directly estimates how much the ResNet50 image features add over RNA alone. 3. Why now: Whether the study should center on multimodal models is the most consequential and most uncertain design choice. It determines whether later experiments should go to image encoders and fusion methods or to RNA encoders and aggregation. A matched ablation resolves this with one run and gives a reference point for interpreting all later experiments.

1. Evidence: Adding ResNet50 image features with concat fusion (config_030, acc 0.411, F1 0.378) performed clearly worse than the matched RNA-only model (config_005, acc 0.485, F1 0.464). Both used scVI and avgpool. So the current evidence says this way of adding images hurts. It cannot yet tell us whether the image modality is unhelpful or whether naive concatenation lets weak image features swamp the RNA signal. 2. Test: config_031 changes only the fusion, from concat to weighted, and keeps every other setting the same. If weighted fusion recovers or beats RNA-only performance, the problem was the fusion method and multimodal models are still worth pursuing. If it stays well below RNA-only, that is stronger evidence that ResNet50 images add little. In that case the budget should shift toward RNA-only variants (encoder, aggregation) or a different image encoder. 3. Why now: Whether multimodal fusion is viable decides how the large multimodal part of the search space gets explored. A clean one-factor comparison resolves this efficiently, and it has a plausible chance of improving on the current best.

1) Evidence: with scvi_n200, resnet50, multiprofile and avgpool held fixed, weighted fusion (0.579 acc / 0.563 F1) clearly beat concat (0.411 / 0.378) and RNA-only (0.485 / 0.464). Accuracy and F1 agree, so weighted fusion looks like a real advantage. Aggregation is a major design axis that has not been tested at all: every run so far used avgpool. 2) This experiment changes one variable from the current best (config_031), swapping avgpool for transformer aggregation. It shows whether learned set-level aggregation across profiles adds value on top of weighted fusion. 3) It exploits the strongest direction found so far while answering a key open question cleanly. The result will tell us which aggregator to carry forward before we spend budget on image-encoder (ViT-L) or RNA-encoder (scGPT) variations.

1. Evidence: Weighted fusion clearly beats concat under the same setup (0.579 vs 0.411 accuracy, with F1 following). Avgpool beats transformer aggregation with weighted fusion (0.579 vs 0.520). The best setup so far, config_031 (scvi_n200, resnet50, avgpool, weighted), also beats RNA-only (0.485), so adding images helps when fusion is weighted. The main untested choice is the image encoder: every multimodal run used resnet50, so the effect of imagenet_vit_l is unknown. 2. Test: config_037 keeps config_031's settings and swaps only the image encoder to imagenet_vit_l. Any change can therefore be attributed to the encoder. 3. Why now: this exploits the strongest known setup while resolving a major open design choice. It also has a real chance of raising the best score. Changing the RNA encoder (scGPT or PCA) is a natural follow-up once the image backbone question is settled.

1. Evidence: Weighted fusion clearly beats concat (0.579 vs 0.411 accuracy), and F1 agrees. Avgpool beats transformer aggregation (0.579 vs 0.520). ResNet50 beats ViT-L (0.579 vs 0.536). The best multimodal run also beats RNA-only (0.485). However, every run so far used scVI as the RNA encoder. That makes the RNA encoder the largest unexplored design choice. 2. Test: This run keeps the best-known settings (multiprofile, ResNet50, avgpool, weighted fusion) and swaps scVI for scGPT. Any difference can then be attributed to the RNA encoder alone, telling us whether a pretrained foundation-model RNA representation helps in the strongest pipeline. 3. Why now: The other settings already have reasonable evidence, while the RNA encoder is completely untested and could shift the best result substantially. Evidence: the best result so far is config_031 (scVI + ResNet50 + avgpool + weighted fusion, 0.579 accuracy, 0.563 F1). One-factor changes from it were all worse: transformer aggregation (0.520), ViT-L image encoder (0.536), scGPT RNA encoder (0.518) and concat fusion (0.411). Weighted fusion therefore looks important, and the other choices near the best point are partly mapped. The profile setting, however, has never been varied: every run is multiprofile. Test: config_029 keeps config_031 exactly but uses a single profile, isolating whether multiprofile aggregation actually helps. Why now: this is a major untested design axis and a clean controlled comparison against the current best. It tells us whether to keep investing in multiprofile variants or whether simpler single-profile models are competitive. 1. Evidence: config_031 is the best result so far (multiprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, avgpool, weighted fusion; acc 0.579, F1 0.563). Every single-factor change from it has scored lower. Concat fusion gave 0.411, transformer aggregation 0.520, ViT-L image encoder 0.536, scGPT RNA encoder 0.518 and single-profile input 0.471. The one design axis never tested is the pca_n2000 RNA encoder. 2. This experiment keeps the best settings and swaps only the RNA encoder to pca_n2000. It finishes the one-factor check around the current best. It shows whether the simple PCA representation matches or beats scvi_n200, given that the more complex scGPT encoder did worse. 3. It fills the largest remaining gap with a controlled comparison. It also has a realistic chance of producing a new best result. That makes it better value than further probing settings that already performed poorly.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_019 (PCA-2000 RNA, ResNet50, avgpool, weighted fusion; acc 0.619, F1 0.610). Switching the RNA encoder to PCA from scVI improved accuracy by about 0.04. Weighted fusion clearly beats concat (0.579 vs 0.411). Avgpool beat transformer aggregation, and ResNet50 beat ViT-L, but each of those conclusions rests on a single comparison made with the scVI encoder. The image-encoder gap (0.579 vs 0.536) is moderate and could interact with the RNA representation. 2. Test: config_025 keeps the best setup and changes only the image encoder to ViT-L. This shows whether ResNet50's advantage holds on the strongest RNA encoder or was specific to scVI. 3. Why now: it is a single-factor change around the current best, so it is likely to perform competitively while settling an image-encoder choice that currently rests on weak, single-comparison evidence. If ViT-L wins, it opens a new branch to exploit. If it loses, ResNet50 is confirmed and later budget can go to the aggregation question (config_021).

1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is config_019 (PCA-2000 + ResNet50, avgpool, weighted fusion; 0.619 accuracy, 0.610 F1). It beats the matched scVI run, config_031 (0.579). Weighted fusion clearly beats concat (0.579 vs 0.411). Avgpool beat transformer once (0.579 vs 0.520), but that is a single comparison. With scVI, adding images to the RNA-only baseline raised accuracy from 0.485 to 0.579. We do not yet know whether PCA's edge comes from PCA being a better RNA representation or from it fusing better with images. 2. What this tests: config_002 is RNA-only, multiprofile, PCA-2000, avgpool. It is the missing unimodal baseline for the best encoder. Comparing it with config_005 (scVI RNA-only) isolates the RNA-encoder effect without images. Comparing it with config_019 measures how much the image branch adds for PCA. 3. Why now: This single run settles where the current best performance comes from, which is the key uncertainty for later choices. That includes whether a transformer aggregation variant of the best setup (config_021) is worth testing. If PCA alone is strong, later experiments should focus on PCA-based setups. If it is not, the gain comes from fusion, and the search should focus on the image and fusion components instead.

1. There is no evidence yet, so every design choice is open: modality, single- vs multi-profile, RNA encoder, image encoder, aggregation and fusion. 2. This experiment sets a central anchor point. It is a multimodal, multiprofile model with mid-complexity choices: the compact learned scVI RNA embedding, the strong pretrained ViT-L image encoder, simple avgpool aggregation and plain concat fusion. It sits in the region most likely to perform well, and it is not an extreme on any axis. 3. Under a limited budget, a central anchor lets later experiments change one factor at a time and attribute the effect. Examples are dropping a modality (config_005 or config_014), switching to singleprofile (config_034), or changing to transformer aggregation (config_038), weighted fusion (config_037), scgpt or pca RNA encoders, or resnet50. Starting from the simplest baseline would give less information per experiment.

1. Evidence: only one experiment exists, config_036 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI, ViT-L, avgpool, concat), which reached 0.227 accuracy and 0.191 F1. With a single data point, we have no evidence yet about which design choices matter. 2. What this tests: config_038 changes only the aggregation, from avgpool to transformer, and keeps everything else fixed. That isolates how multiple profiles are combined, a major architectural choice that could plausibly give large gains by modeling interactions between profiles. 3. Why this is the best use of the budget: a clean single-factor comparison against the existing baseline lets us attribute any change directly to aggregation. It also has real upside for the primary accuracy objective. Modality ablations (RNA-only or image-only) and fusion changes are natural follow-ups once aggregation is settled.

1. Evidence: With scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + concat held fixed, transformer aggregation (0.485 acc, 0.464 F1) far outperformed avgpool (0.227 acc, 0.191 F1). Both accuracy and F1 agree, so transformer aggregation looks like a strong design choice for multiprofile models. Fusion strategy, however, is still completely untested. 2. Test: config_039 keeps the best setup and changes only one thing, concat to weighted fusion. Any difference can therefore be attributed to fusion alone. 3. Why now: it exploits the strongest direction found so far and has a realistic chance of beating the best result. It also resolves an open multimodal design choice that applies to every other encoder pairing, which makes it a good use of a limited budget. Swapping the encoders or running unimodal ablations next, with transformer and the better fusion fixed, would then be well grounded.

1) Evidence: All three runs used scvi_n200 RNA and imagenet_vit_l images. Transformer aggregation beat avgpool by a wide margin (0.485 vs 0.227 accuracy, with F1 agreeing). Concat fusion beat weighted fusion (0.485 vs 0.332). Both gaps are large enough to treat transformer + concat as the working backbone. The RNA encoder has not been varied at all, and it has three options, so it is the largest unexplored design axis. 2) Test: config_050 keeps everything from the best run (config_038: multiprofile, vit_l, transformer, concat) and swaps only scvi_n200 for scGPT. Any change in accuracy or F1 can therefore be attributed to the RNA encoder alone. 3) Why now: it varies one factor at a time from the current best, so it is both exploitation and exploration. A pretrained foundation encoder like scGPT has a plausible chance of beating the best result. Even if it does not, the outcome tells us whether RNA representation matters before we spend budget on the image-encoder swap or unimodal ablations.

1) Evidence: Transformer aggregation clearly beat avgpool (0.485 vs 0.227). Concat beat weighted fusion (0.485 vs 0.332). Switching the RNA encoder from scVI to scGPT gave the best result so far (0.632 accuracy, 0.607 F1). Every run so far used imagenet_vit_l, so the image encoder is the one major design choice with no evidence at all. 2) This experiment keeps the best setup fixed (scGPT, multiprofile, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) and swaps the image encoder to resnet50. That isolates the effect of the image encoder in the most promising context. 3) It is the best use of the next run because it fills the largest untested gap in the design space and could also find a better configuration. A large drop would confirm ViT-L as the image encoder to keep. A similar or higher score would show the image encoder matters little or that resnet50 is better, which would shape the remaining budget. Either result is informative.

Evidence: Transformer aggregation clearly beats avgpool (0.48 vs 0.23 with scVI/ViT-L). scGPT strongly outperforms scVI (0.63 vs 0.48). ResNet50 beats ViT-L when paired with scGPT (0.715 vs 0.63, with F1 agreeing). Weighted fusion underperformed concat once, but that is a single comparison. The key unresolved question is whether the image modality adds anything at all, since every run so far is multimodal and RNA encoder quality appears to drive most of the gains. Test: config_009 (scGPT, RNA-only, multiprofile, transformer) is a direct unimodal ablation of the current best, config_044. If it nears 0.715, images contribute little and the remaining budget should focus on RNA and aggregation choices. If it falls well below, the multimodal gain is confirmed and later runs can refine the image side and fusion (e.g., config_045). Why now: this one run answers the most consequential open design question and guides the rest of the search, which is worth more than another small fusion tweak on the current best.

Evidence: transformer aggregation clearly beats avgpool (0.485 vs 0.227), and scGPT beats scVI. ResNet50 beats ViT-L as the image encoder with scGPT. However, the best multimodal run (config_044, scGPT+ResNet50+transformer+concat, 0.715 accuracy, 0.687 F1) only matches RNA-only scGPT (0.721 accuracy, 0.681 F1). So it is unclear whether the image modality adds value under concat fusion. Fusion has been compared only once, in a weak setting (scVI+ViT-L), where weighted fusion was worse. That single result may not hold for stronger encoders. Test: config_045 keeps the best multimodal setup and switches to weighted fusion. Weighted fusion can down-weight a weaker image branch, so this checks whether better fusion lets multimodal surpass RNA-only. It also checks whether the concat-over-weighted conclusion holds outside the scVI/ViT-L case. Why now: it targets the top-performing region while resolving the design choice that is both highly uncertain and most relevant to the main question of whether multimodal fusion beats RNA-only.

Evidence: scGPT is clearly the strongest RNA encoder, at 0.63-0.72 accuracy versus 0.23-0.48 for scVI. Transformer aggregation beat avgpool by a wide margin in the only comparison (0.485 vs 0.227). Concat beat weighted fusion in all three paired tests. RNA-only scGPT with transformer aggregation (0.721 acc, 0.681 F1) roughly matches the best multimodal run (0.715 acc, 0.687 F1). That suggests the RNA profile carries most of the signal. However, every completed run so far used multiprofile, so the profile-setting dimension is completely untested. Test: config_007 runs scGPT RNA-only in singleprofile mode. Compared directly against config_009, it measures how much multiprofile modelling with transformer aggregation contributes beyond a single-profile scGPT baseline. Why now: this is the largest remaining blind spot in the design space, and it uses the strongest known encoder. If singleprofile is competitive, a whole cheaper branch of configurations becomes worth exploring. If it is clearly worse, it confirms that multiprofile plus transformer aggregation is the key choice, and the remaining budget can focus there.

1) Evidence: concat beats weighted fusion in all three paired comparisons. Transformer beats avgpool aggregation, though only in one pair. scGPT is clearly the strongest RNA encoder. However, the best multimodal run (scGPT + ResNet50, transformer, concat: 0.715 acc / 0.687 F1) only matches the RNA-only scGPT transformer baseline (0.721 acc / 0.681 F1). The key open question is whether the image modality carries useful signal at all, and no image-only run exists yet. 2) This experiment runs ResNet50 image-only with multiprofile transformer aggregation. That is the image counterpart of the best RNA-only setup and uses the better-performing image encoder. It measures how much predictive signal images provide on their own. 3) It is the best use of budget because the answer decides where to spend the remaining runs. If image-only performance is weak, further multimodal fusion tuning is unlikely to pay off, and effort should shift to RNA-side and aggregation choices. If it is reasonably strong, the lack of multimodal gain points to a fusion problem, which justifies exploring fusion and aggregation variants with scGPT + ResNet50.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: Several design choices look consistent. Transformer aggregation beats avgpool (0.485 vs 0.227). Concat fusion beats weighted fusion in both matched pairs. Multiprofile beats singleprofile for scGPT RNA-only (0.721 vs 0.650). scGPT beats scVI. The best result so far is scGPT RNA-only with a transformer (0.721 acc). It is essentially tied with the scGPT+ResNet50 concat multimodal model (0.715 acc, slightly higher F1), so adding images has not yet clearly helped. The largest unexplored design choice is the RNA encoder: pca_n2000 has never been tested in any setting. 2. What this tests: config_003 applies pca_n2000 in the strongest known RNA-only setup (multiprofile, transformer). This isolates the effect of the encoder with no confound from fusion or the image encoder. It will show whether a simple high-dimensional PCA representation can match or beat scGPT. 3. Why it is the best next experiment: Repeating minor variants of the scGPT path would add little information. A whole level of the encoder factor is still unknown, and this run fills that gap at low risk. If PCA is competitive, pca_n2000+ResNet50 transformer concat (config_020) becomes the logical follow-up. If it is weak, scGPT is confirmed as the RNA encoder, and the remaining budget can focus on whether multimodal fusion adds value.

1) Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been run, so every design choice is open: modality, single vs. multi-profile input, RNA encoder, image encoder, aggregation and fusion. The most important open question is whether combining modalities beats either one alone. 2) What this tests: config_018 is a central, simple multimodal baseline. It uses the classic encoders (PCA RNA, ResNet50 image), multi-profile input with the simplest aggregation (avgpool), and the simplest fusion (concat). The other factors are kept simple, so the result gives a reference point for overall performance in the multimodal region. Later runs can each change one factor from this anchor: image-only (config_011), RNA-only (config_002), single-profile (config_016), transformer aggregation (config_020), weighted fusion (config_019), and swapping in scVI/scGPT or ViT-L. 3) Why it is the best use of the budget: Starting at a reference point with many one-factor neighbors lets each later experiment act as a clean ablation, which helps learn which choices matter. Multimodal, multi-profile inputs are also plausibly high-performing for cellular profiling, though this is an untested prior, so the run serves both exploration and possible early exploitation.

1) Evidence and uncertainty: there is only one result so far. The multimodal, multiprofile model (PCA RNA + ResNet50, avgpool, concat) reached 0.532 accuracy and 0.517 F1. With nothing to compare against, we cannot tell whether the image modality adds anything over RNA alone, and that is the most basic design question in the search. 2) What this tests: config_002 changes only one factor from config_018. It drops the image branch and keeps the PCA RNA encoder, multiprofile setting and avgpool aggregation. The gap between the two runs directly estimates how much ResNet50 images contribute under concat fusion. 3) Why it is the best next use of budget: if RNA-only performs about as well, later experiments should focus on RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT) and aggregation rather than on image encoders and fusion. If multimodal clearly wins, it justifies spending budget on image-encoder and fusion variants. Either way, this controlled ablation should cut uncertainty about where to search more than a jump to another multimodal variant would.

1) Evidence so far: multimodal PCA+ResNet50 with avgpool and concat reached 0.532 accuracy and 0.517 F1. RNA-only PCA with avgpool reached 0.514 accuracy and 0.498 F1. Adding images therefore gave only a small gain (about 0.02 accuracy and F1), so RNA appears to carry most of the signal. The RNA encoder is still completely untested beyond PCA. 2) This experiment changes one factor from the current best: it swaps PCA for the pretrained scGPT encoder and keeps ResNet50, multiprofile avgpool and concat fusion. Any difference can then be attributed to the RNA representation. 3) Because RNA dominates performance, the RNA encoder is likely the highest-leverage design choice left to resolve. A foundation-model encoder could plausibly bring a large improvement, so this run both answers a key uncertainty and exploits the strongest configuration so far. Aggregation, fusion and image-encoder variants are better tested once the RNA encoder question is settled.

1) Evidence so far: the best result is multimodal PCA+ResNet50 with avgpool and concat (config_018, acc 0.532, F1 0.517). It only modestly beats RNA-only PCA with avgpool (0.514). scGPT as the RNA encoder performed far worse (0.260), so PCA is the RNA encoder to build on. Aggregation has only ever been tested as avgpool, so how to combine multiple profiles is a major open question. 2) Config_020 keeps the best configuration fixed and changes only the aggregation, from avgpool to transformer. This gives a clean single-variable test of whether learned attention over profiles beats mean pooling. 3) Aggregation applies to every multiprofile configuration, so the answer will shape the rest of the search. Since this experiment starts from the current best setup, it is also a plausible route to a higher score. The image encoder (ViT-L), fusion type and scVI remain to be tested after this.

Evidence: PCA RNA plus ResNet50 multimodal beats RNA-only with avgpool (0.532 vs 0.514), so the image modality may help slightly. Transformer aggregation gave a clear gain over avgpool (0.591 vs 0.532 accuracy, with F1 agreeing). scGPT performed poorly in the one run that used it. The image encoder has never been varied, and the RNA result shows encoder choice can matter a great deal. This experiment keeps the best configuration (config_020: PCA, transformer, concat) and changes only ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L. That isolates the effect of the image encoder within the strongest setup found so far. Why now: image encoder is a major untested design choice, and this test both explores it and exploits the promising transformer direction. Fusion type (concat vs weighted) is likely a smaller effect and can be tested next on whichever image encoder wins.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_020 (PCA + ResNet50 + transformer aggregation + concat fusion, acc 0.591, F1 0.573). Transformer aggregation beat avgpool by about 0.06 under concat fusion. PCA clearly beat scGPT, and ResNet50 beat ViT-L under transformer aggregation. The fusion choice is the biggest open question: weighted fusion has never been tested, so its effect is completely unknown. 2. Test: config_021 changes only the fusion method on the best configuration, from concat to weighted. This isolates the effect of fusion. 3. Why now: it directly exploits the strongest configuration while closing the largest untested gap in the design space. Either result is useful. It may set a new best, or it will confirm concat and let later experiments focus on the RNA encoder (for example scVI on this setup) or on modality ablations.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_020 (PCA-2000 RNA, ResNet50, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) at 0.591 accuracy and 0.573 F1. The other variants of that setup all did worse. Switching to avgpool gave 0.532, to ViT-L gave 0.520, and to weighted fusion gave 0.542 with a lower F1. The RNA encoder is the least settled choice. scGPT was much worse than PCA under avgpool (0.260 vs 0.532), and scVI-200 has never been tested. 2. What this tests: config_032 keeps the best setup and changes only the RNA encoder from PCA-2000 to scVI-200. That isolates whether a learned, compact latent space can match or beat PCA when paired with the strongest aggregation, image encoder and fusion settings. 3. Why now: The RNA encoder is a high-impact factor, given how badly scGPT did. Testing scVI in the most promising setup either finds a better model or confirms PCA as the RNA encoder, which would let later runs focus on profile setting and the unimodal baselines. Both outcomes are useful under a limited budget.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_020 (PCA + ResNet50 + transformer + concat, 0.591 acc / 0.573 F1). The only modality comparison uses avgpool. There, multimodal (0.532) beat RNA-only (0.514) by just about 2 points. Switching to transformer aggregation added about 6 points for multimodal. So it is unclear whether the gain comes from the image modality or from transformer aggregation over profiles. 2. Test: RNA-only with PCA and transformer aggregation is a direct counterpart to config_020 that removes the image branch. If it scores near 0.59, the image modality adds little and the transformer drives performance. If it stays near 0.51–0.53, fusing images matters specifically when combined with transformer aggregation. 3. Why now: The modality question underlies every later choice, including fusion type, image encoder and whether to keep exploring multimodal configurations. Answering it with one cheap, controlled experiment reduces uncertainty more than another small tweak around the current best.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_020 (PCA + ResNet50, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) at 0.591 accuracy and 0.573 F1. The evidence is fairly consistent on three choices. Transformer beats avgpool in both the multimodal and RNA-only settings. PCA beats scVI and scGPT as the RNA encoder. Concat beats weighted fusion. The big untested question is the profile setting: every completed run used multiprofile. 2. Test: config_016 is the singleprofile version of the best encoder and fusion choices (PCA + ResNet50, concat). It shows how much multiprofile aggregation adds over single profiles. That tells us whether the transformer and avgpool gains are real benefits of aggregating multiple profiles, or whether singleprofile is a competitive or even better option. 3. Why now: it settles a high-level design choice that has never been sampled, at low cost and with a clear contrast to the known best model. That is more informative than another small fusion or encoder variation, where the evidence already points in one direction.

1) Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is config_016 (multimodal, singleprofile, PCA + ResNet50, concat; 0.619 accuracy, 0.610 F1). It beats every multiprofile run, including the best transformer variant (0.591). But singleprofile has been tested only once, so the gain could come from the singleprofile setting itself or from how the image and RNA features combine under it. In multiprofile, adding images helped somewhat (0.591 vs 0.540 RNA-only with transformer; 0.532 vs 0.514 with avgpool). We do not yet know whether that holds in singleprofile. 2) What this tests: config_001 is the RNA-only singleprofile counterpart to config_016. It gives two controlled comparisons at once. Against config_016, it isolates the image modality's contribution in singleprofile. Against config_002 and config_003 (RNA-only multiprofile), it checks whether the singleprofile advantage appears in a second model setting rather than resting on one run. 3) Why now: Before spending budget refining fusion, image encoder or RNA encoder within singleprofile (e.g., config_017, config_022, config_028), it is more efficient to confirm that singleprofile is genuinely better. We also need to know whether multimodality is the key driver. This single, cheap ablation addresses the two most important open design questions at the same time.

1. Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been run, so every design choice is open: modality, single- vs multi-profile, RNA encoder, image encoder, aggregation and fusion. 2. What this tests: config_030 is a central anchor in the multimodal region. It uses scVI (n200), a widely used mid-complexity RNA encoder, together with the standard ResNet50 image encoder, multiprofile input with simple avgpool aggregation, and plain concat fusion. It is a reasonable prior guess for a strong configuration, and each of its components can be changed one at a time in later runs. Those one-factor comparisons would cover RNA encoder (PCA vs scGPT), image encoder (ViT-L), aggregation (transformer), fusion (weighted), profile setting (single) and modality (the rna_only and image_only counterparts). 3. Why it is the best use of the next experiment: Under a limited budget, an anchor near the likely optimum gives a useful performance baseline and lets later runs be read as controlled ablations, instead of starting from an extreme corner of the space.

1) Evidence: only one experiment is complete. config_030 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI, ResNet50, avgpool, concat) reached 0.427 accuracy and 0.417 F1. That gives a baseline but says nothing yet about which design choices matter. 2) Test: config_036 changes one factor, the image encoder, from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L, and keeps everything else fixed. Any change in accuracy or F1 can therefore be attributed to the image encoder. 3) Why now: the image encoder splits the multimodal search space in half, so learning its effect early guides many later choices. ViT-L is also a plausible upgrade, so this run combines a clean comparison with a real chance of beating the baseline. Modality ablations and aggregation or fusion variants can follow once the encoder question is clearer.

Evidence: in an otherwise identical setup (scVI RNA, multiprofile, avgpool, concat), swapping ResNet50 for ViT-L dropped accuracy from 0.427 to 0.260, with F1 falling similarly. So the image branch strongly affects performance and can clearly hurt it. We do not yet know whether ResNet50 features add anything beyond RNA, or whether 0.427 mostly comes from the RNA side. Test: config_005 is the RNA-only counterpart of config_030, with the same scVI encoder, multiprofile setting and avgpool aggregation. It isolates the image modality's contribution. Value: this baseline decides how to spend the remaining budget. If RNA-only matches or beats config_030, multimodal fusion and image encoder choices matter less, and the search should shift toward RNA encoders and aggregation. If it falls clearly below, ResNet50-based multimodal setups are confirmed as the direction to exploit, and the next steps would test transformer aggregation (config_032) and weighted fusion (config_031).

1) Evidence: RNA-only scVI with avgpool reached 0.653 accuracy. Adding images with concat fusion dropped this sharply, to 0.427 with ResNet50 and 0.260 with ViT-L. Image features as currently fused appear to add noise that overwhelms the RNA signal. It is unclear whether this harm comes from multimodality itself or from naive concat fusion. 2) config_031 keeps everything identical to config_030 (scVI, ResNet50, multiprofile, avgpool) and only switches concat to weighted fusion. This isolates the fusion choice. If weighted fusion can down-weight the weak image branch, accuracy and F1 should recover toward or beyond the RNA-only baseline. If not, multimodality is likely harmful here. 3) Most remaining configurations are multimodal, so this single controlled comparison decides whether that large region deserves further budget. If it does not, the search can focus on RNA-only variants such as aggregation (config_006) and encoder choice (scGPT, PCA).

1. Evidence: Fusion choice clearly matters. With scVI + ResNet50 + avgpool, weighted fusion reached 0.721 accuracy (F1 0.681), while concat reached only 0.427. Weighted fusion is also the only setup that beats RNA-only (0.653), so it appears to be what makes the image modality useful. Aggregation is still completely untested, since every run so far used avgpool. 2. Test: config_033 keeps the best setup (scVI, ResNet50, multiprofile, weighted fusion) and changes only avgpool to transformer. Any difference can therefore be attributed to aggregation. 3. Why now: this extends the strongest result found so far while also answering an open question about a major design choice. Testing weighted fusion with ViT-L or other RNA encoders would be useful, but those rank behind it because ViT-L has so far performed poorly.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: Fusion is the strongest signal so far. With scVI + ResNet50 + avgpool, weighted fusion reached 0.721 accuracy versus 0.427 for concat, and F1 followed the same pattern. Avgpool beat transformer aggregation under weighted fusion (0.721 vs 0.573). RNA-only scVI already reaches 0.653, so RNA carries most of the predictive signal. Yet every experiment so far has used scVI, so the RNA encoder choice is completely untested. 2. What this tests: config_043 keeps the best pipeline (ResNet50, avgpool, weighted fusion) and swaps scVI for scGPT. This isolates the effect of the RNA encoder within the current best setup. 3. Why this is the best next experiment: since RNA drives most of the performance, the RNA encoder is likely a high-impact choice that remains unexplored. This run could produce a new best result, and if it does not, it still tells us whether scVI should stay fixed. That is more valuable than testing ViT-L under weighted fusion, because the image modality appears to contribute less.

Evidence: weighted fusion clearly beats concat. With scVI, ResNet50 and avgpool, accuracy rose from 0.427 with concat (config_030) to 0.721 with weighted (config_031), the best result so far, with F1 0.681. ImageNet ViT-L has been tried only once, with concat (config_036, 0.260). So we cannot tell whether ViT-L is a weak image encoder or whether it simply suffered from concat fusion. Question: config_037 changes only the image encoder relative to the best configuration (scVI, ViT-L, avgpool, weighted). It tests whether the image-encoder choice matters once fusion is done well. Why now: the image encoder is the most confounded of the important design axes. If ViT-L with weighted fusion matches or beats ResNet50, half the remaining multimodal space becomes promising again. If it stays clearly worse, we can confidently drop ViT-L configurations and focus the rest of the budget on the RNA encoder (e.g., PCA) and profile-setting questions around the current best.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is config_031 (scVI + ResNet50, multiprofile avgpool, weighted fusion), with 0.721 accuracy and 0.681 F1. Some design choices already look settled. Weighted fusion beat concat by a wide margin in both direct comparisons. Avgpool beat transformer aggregation, and scVI beat scGPT, though each of those rests on a single comparison. The profile setting is the largest open question. Every experiment so far has been multiprofile, so we have no evidence on whether pooling multiple profiles helps compared with a single profile. 2. What this tests: config_029 keeps the strongest known components (scVI, ResNet50, weighted fusion) and switches only to singleprofile. It is therefore a clean single-factor test of whether multiprofile aggregation actually adds value. 3. Why now: This is a major structural design axis with zero data. Resolving it is more informative than further refining encoders or aggregation within the multiprofile setting. Because it uses the best known components, it also keeps a reasonable chance of a competitive result.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_031 (scVI + ResNet50 + avgpool + weighted fusion, 0.721 acc / 0.681 F1). Weighted fusion has beaten concat in both paired comparisons, by a large margin. Avgpool beat transformer aggregation in the one test we have. ResNet50 has clearly beaten ViT-L. Among RNA encoders, scVI beat scGPT (0.721 vs 0.632), but the third encoder, PCA (n=2000), has never been tested in any setting, so the RNA encoder choice is the largest remaining uncertainty. 2. Test: config_019 keeps the best-known setup (ResNet50, avgpool, weighted fusion, multiprofile) and swaps only the RNA encoder to PCA. This isolates whether scVI's advantage holds against a simple high-dimensional baseline, or whether PCA does as well or better. 3. Why now: This one-factor change fills the only untested level of a key design choice while staying in the high-performing region, so it can both inform the search and possibly improve on the best result. It is more informative than another small refinement of a factor we already have evidence on.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is the scVI + ResNet50 + avgpool + weighted multimodal setup (0.721 accuracy, 0.681 F1). It beats RNA-only scVI with avgpool (0.653 accuracy, 0.628 F1), which suggests images add value. Some design choices already look fairly settled: weighted fusion beat concat in both image-encoder pairs, ResNet50 beat ViT-L, scVI beat scGPT and PCA, and avgpool beat transformer in one test. The big open question is that no image-only baseline has been run, so we don't know how informative ResNet50 image features are on their own. 2. Test: Image-only, multiprofile, ResNet50 with avgpool shows how much predictive signal the image branch carries alone. That tells us whether the ~7-point multimodal gain comes from strong, complementary image information or only a modest boost. It also helps explain why concat fusion collapsed (0.43), possibly because a weak image modality was drowning out the RNA signal. 3. Why now: The remaining scVI + ResNet50 variants (singleprofile concat, transformer concat) combine choices that have already performed worse, so they are unlikely to beat 0.72 and would teach us little. This baseline fills a key gap in understanding the modality contributions, which will guide how much of the remaining budget to spend on image-side choices versus RNA-side and fusion refinements.

1) Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been run, so we know nothing about which design choices matter. The open questions are whether multimodal fusion beats a single modality, whether multiprofile aggregation helps, and which encoders work best. 2) What this tests: config_018 is a central reference point in the design space. It is multimodal (PCA RNA + ResNet50 image), multiprofile with avgpool aggregation, and uses simple concat fusion. Its encoders and fusion are the simplest options, so it gives a strong but low-complexity baseline that contrasts with many neighbors through one-factor changes: unimodal variants (config_002, config_011), singleprofile (config_016), transformer aggregation (config_020), weighted fusion (config_019), and other encoders (config_030, config_042, config_024). 3) Why it is the best first use of the budget: starting from the middle of the space rather than an extreme corner gives a likely-competitive result. It also makes the following one-factor comparisons as informative as possible for estimating the main effects of modality, profile setting, aggregation, fusion and encoder choice.

1. Evidence: Only one run exists (config_018: multimodal, multiprofile, PCA + ResNet50, avgpool, concat; accuracy 0.520, F1 0.479). With one data point, we cannot yet tell which design choices drive performance. 2. Test: config_020 changes only the aggregation, from avgpool to a transformer, and keeps everything else fixed. This isolates whether learned attention across profiles beats simple averaging. That is a central design question for the multiprofile setting, and the answer carries over to every other encoder and fusion combination. 3. Why now: As a one-factor change, any difference in accuracy or F1 can be attributed to aggregation, which gives a clean answer. It also has a real chance of improving on the current best, so it balances learning with progress. Ablations of modality (e.g., config_002) and comparisons of encoders (scVI, scGPT, ViT-L) are natural next steps once the aggregation choice is clearer.

Evidence: in the only controlled comparison so far (pca_n2000 + resnet50 + concat, multiprofile), transformer aggregation beat avgpool by about 0.20 in accuracy (0.721 vs 0.520), and F1 moved the same way (0.681 vs 0.479). That gap is large enough to treat transformer aggregation as the working default. The other factors (image encoder, RNA encoder and fusion) are still untested. What this tests: config_026 keeps the best configuration fixed and changes only the image encoder from resnet50 to imagenet_vit_l. This isolates whether a stronger pretrained image backbone improves on the current best. Why now: changing one factor at a time gives clean attribution. The image encoder probably affects representation quality more than the fusion rule, so this experiment could both find a better configuration and settle which backbone to use in later RNA-encoder and fusion comparisons.

1) Evidence: Three runs so far. Transformer aggregation clearly beat avgpool with PCA+ResNet50+concat (0.721 vs 0.520 accuracy, with F1 agreeing). ResNet50 clearly beat ViT-L under transformer aggregation (0.721 vs 0.507). Every run used the PCA RNA encoder, so the RNA encoder choice, with three options, is completely unexplored. Fusion type is also untested, but it has only two options and probably a smaller effect. 2) Test: Keep the best setup (multiprofile, ResNet50, transformer, concat) and swap only the RNA encoder from PCA to the scGPT foundation-model embedding. This isolates whether a pretrained RNA representation improves on PCA. 3) Value: It exploits the strongest known setup while removing the largest remaining uncertainty. scGPT differs most from PCA, so the result is the most informative about whether the RNA encoder matters. Either outcome tells us whether later budget should go to RNA encoders (including scVI) or to fusion tuning.

1. Evidence: config_020 (pca_n2000 + resnet50 + transformer + concat) is clearly best at 0.721 accuracy and 0.681 F1. Each single-factor change from it dropped performance to about 0.51–0.53: avgpool aggregation, the ViT-L image encoder and the scGPT RNA encoder. So transformer aggregation, resnet50 and pca_n2000 each appear to matter. Fusion is the one design axis never varied; every run so far used concat. 2. Test: config_021 changes only fusion (concat to weighted) on the best configuration. This isolates whether weighted fusion helps, hurts or makes no difference. 3. Why now: it is both exploitative, since it may beat 0.721, and informative, since it closes the largest gap in our understanding of the design space with a clean one-factor comparison. That is a better use of one run than trying scVI or unimodal ablations first.

1. Evidence: config_020 (PCA, ResNet50, transformer, concat) is clearly best at 0.721 accuracy and 0.681 F1. Every single-factor change from it so far has dropped performance to about 0.51–0.54, with F1 falling in step. Those changes were avgpool aggregation, the ViT-L image encoder, the scGPT RNA encoder and weighted fusion. So these design choices interact strongly, and the full set of 020 settings appears to matter. The main RNA-encoder option not yet tested in this context is scVI. 2. Test: config_032 changes only the RNA encoder in the winning configuration, swapping PCA for scVI. It shows whether PCA is uniquely suited here or whether a compact learned embedding can match or beat it. 3. Why now: this completes the one-factor-at-a-time view around the current best on the remaining open encoder choice. It also has a realistic chance of improving on 020, so it serves both learning and optimization. Modality ablations such as RNA-only or image-only would help explain the result but are less likely to produce a better model, so they can come later.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: All six experiments so far are multimodal. The best is config_020 (PCA_n2000 + ResNet50 + transformer + concat) at 0.721 accuracy and 0.681 F1. Every single-factor change from it fell to 0.51-0.58: avgpool instead of transformer, ViT-L instead of ResNet50, scGPT or scVI instead of PCA, and weighted instead of concat fusion. Because config_020 sits well above all its neighbours, it could be a real optimum or partly noise. We also have no unimodal baselines, so we cannot tell how much the image branch contributes. 2. What this tests: config_003 is RNA-only with the same PCA_n2000 encoder, multiprofile setting and transformer aggregation as the best run. Comparing it with config_020 isolates whether adding ResNet50 image features actually improves results. If RNA-only scores close to 0.72, the RNA representation and transformer aggregation drive performance, and further image-encoder or fusion tuning is low priority. If it scores well below, multimodal fusion is confirmed as important. 3. Why it is the best next experiment: Testing more neighbours of config_020 would mostly confirm that those changes hurt. Whether multimodality is worth it is the most important untested design question, and answering it with one matched ablation will guide how the remaining budget is spent.

1. Evidence: config_020 (pca_n2000 + resnet50 + transformer + concat) is the clear leader at 0.721 accuracy and 0.681 F1. Every single-factor change from it dropped performance to about 0.51–0.58: avgpool aggregation, the ViT-L image encoder, scGPT or scVI RNA encoders, and weighted fusion. The RNA-only version with the same pca + transformer setup reached only 0.514. So the 0.72 result is either a real synergy or partly an outlier, and we have no image-only baseline to tell which. 2. Test: config_012 runs resnet50 + transformer on images alone (image_only, multiprofile). If it scores near 0.72, the image pathway drives performance and RNA adds little. If it scores near 0.5, the multimodal combination is responsible for the gain. 3. Why now: modality contribution is the most important unresolved design question. The answer decides whether the remaining budget should go to refining RNA encoders and fusion, or to the image and aggregation side.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_020 (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA RNA, ResNet50, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) at 0.721 accuracy and 0.681 F1. Single-factor changes from it all scored lower, mostly by large margins: avgpool aggregation 0.520, ViT-L image encoder 0.507, scGPT RNA 0.525, weighted fusion 0.537 and scVI RNA 0.579. Image-only ResNet50 with transformer aggregation reached 0.678, so adding RNA gives a modest gain over images alone. The one design dimension still completely untested is the profile setting: every completed experiment used multiprofile. 2. Test: config_016 is identical to config_020 except that it uses singleprofile, with no aggregation. It cleanly measures how much multiprofile input with transformer aggregation contributes over a single profile. The large avgpool-versus-transformer gap suggests the aggregation step matters a lot, but we cannot yet tell whether multiprofile helps or whether avgpool simply hurts. 3. Why now: This is a one-factor-away ablation of the current best on the only unexplored major axis. It closes the largest remaining uncertainty in the design space at the cost of a single experiment, which suits the limited budget. If singleprofile turns out competitive, the singleprofile branch becomes worth exploring; if not, multiprofile with transformer aggregation is confirmed as the core design choice.

Evidence: the two strongest results are close. config_020 (multiprofile, transformer, concat, pca_n2000 + resnet50) reached 0.721 accuracy, and config_016 (singleprofile, concat, pca_n2000 + resnet50) reached 0.715 accuracy with a slightly higher F1. In the multiprofile transformer setting, single changes to the RNA encoder, image encoder, fusion or aggregation caused large and somewhat erratic drops (0.51-0.58). That makes the transformer regime look sensitive, so each of those comparisons is weak evidence. The RNA encoder effect rests on one comparison: scvi_n200 scored 0.579 versus 0.721 for pca. Across RNA encoders, scvi_n200 has been the stronger alternative to pca. Test: config_028 swaps pca_n2000 for scvi_n200 in the simpler, near-best singleprofile concat + resnet50 setup. This checks whether the RNA encoder ranking holds outside the sensitive transformer setting, with everything else matched to config_016. Why now: it is a one-variable comparison against a strong baseline and has a realistic chance of beating the current best. It also clarifies whether scvi's earlier deficit reflects the encoder itself or an interaction with transformer aggregation. That makes it more informative per experiment than further changes in the unstable multiprofile regime or weak RNA-only and ViT runs.

1) Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been run, so nothing is known about which design choices matter: modality, single vs. multi-profile input, encoder type, aggregation method, or fusion method. 2) What this tests: config_018 is a central reference point. It is multimodal (PCA RNA + ResNet50 image), uses multiple profiles, and pairs the simplest aggregation (avgpool) with the simplest fusion (concat). Each later experiment can change one factor from this point: drop a modality (vs. config_002/011), switch to a single profile (vs. config_016), swap in a stronger encoder (scGPT, scVI, ViT-L), or try transformer aggregation or weighted fusion. 3) Why it is the best use of the budget: An anchor near the middle of the design space makes later single-factor comparisons cleaner than starting at an extreme. It is also a reasonable bet for good performance, since combining modalities and profiles is plausibly helpful. Using the cheaper, simpler components first means later gains from more complex components can be attributed to them rather than confounded.

1. Evidence: Only one experiment has been run. The multimodal, multiprofile model (PCA + ResNet50, avgpool, concat; config_018) reached 0.532 accuracy and 0.517 F1. With a single data point, we cannot tell which parts of the design drive this result. The most basic open question is whether adding the image modality helps at all. 2. Test: config_002 keeps the same RNA encoder (PCA), the same multiprofile setting and the same avgpool aggregation, but drops the image branch. This makes it a clean one-factor ablation of the image modality. If RNA-only matches or beats 0.532, the image branch adds little and later experiments should focus on RNA encoders and aggregation. If it falls clearly short, multimodal fusion is justified, and swapping in a stronger image encoder (ViT-L) or changing fusion becomes the logical next step. 3. Why now: Whether to use both modalities determines the structure of most of the remaining search space. Answering it early, with a controlled comparison, reduces the most uncertainty per experiment before we spend budget tuning finer choices.

1. Evidence: The multimodal concat model with PCA RNA, ResNet50 and avgpool (0.532 accuracy, 0.517 F1) only slightly beats the matched RNA-only model (0.520, 0.498). The image branch therefore adds a small, uncertain gain, and with one run each we cannot tell whether images are weakly informative or the ResNet50 features are just a weak representation. 2. Test: config_024 keeps everything identical to the best run (PCA RNA, multiprofile, avgpool, concat) and swaps only the image encoder to ImageNet ViT-L. Comparing the two isolates the effect of image encoder quality on multimodal performance. 3. Why now: Image encoder is a major, untested design axis, and this one-factor change is both informative and a plausible improvement. A clear gain would show that image features matter and point the search toward stronger image backbones. No gain would suggest RNA dominates, so later experiments should focus on the RNA encoder (scVI or scGPT) and aggregation choices.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is multimodal PCA + ResNet50 with avgpool and concat fusion (acc 0.532, F1 0.517). It is only slightly above RNA-only PCA (0.520 / 0.498), so the image branch adds a little at best. Swapping in ViT-L under concat dropped accuracy to 0.224, well below RNA-only. That suggests naive concatenation lets a poor image representation degrade the model. Fusion type is therefore a key open design choice, and it has not been tested yet. 2) This experiment keeps the best configuration fixed and changes only concat to weighted fusion. It cleanly isolates the effect of fusion. Weighted fusion may let the model balance RNA and image contributions, turning the marginal image gain into a clearer one. 3) It is the best use of the next run because it both exploits the leading configuration and resolves an important uncertainty with a single-variable change. If weighted fusion helps, it supports testing weighted fusion on the ViT-L arm (config_025) and on other RNA encoders. If it does not, the search can turn to aggregation (transformer) or the RNA encoder instead.

1) Evidence: Weighted fusion is the clearest signal so far. config_019 (weighted, 0.721 acc / 0.681 F1) beat config_018 (concat, 0.532 / 0.517), and it was the only multimodal run that clearly beat RNA-only (0.520). With concat fusion, ResNet50 did far better than ViT-L (0.532 vs 0.224). Aggregation is completely untested: every run so far used avgpool. 2) Test: config_021 keeps the best setup (PCA RNA, ResNet50, multiprofile, weighted fusion) and changes only avgpool to transformer. This isolates the effect of aggregation and is a natural extension of the strongest result. 3) Why now: aggregation affects most of the remaining multimodal and unimodal configurations, so settling it early is worth more than refining smaller choices. Running it on the current best base means one result both reduces uncertainty and could become the new best. Testing ViT-L or other RNA encoders can come after the aggregation choice is clearer.
