1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is config_019 (PCA + ResNet50 + avgpool + weighted fusion, acc 0.721, F1 0.681). Weighted fusion clearly beat concat at fixed settings (0.721 vs 0.532), and transformer aggregation came in lower (0.629). The RNA encoder is the largest untested design axis: every run so far used pca_n2000, and RNA-only PCA already reached 0.520. 2. What this tests: config_031 keeps the best-performing setup (ResNet50, avgpool, weighted fusion) and swaps only the RNA encoder to scVI. This isolates whether a learned, lower-dimensional RNA representation improves or hurts the strongest multimodal model. 3. Why it is the best next experiment: it exploits the most promising configuration while reducing uncertainty about a major untested choice. The result will also show whether scVI or scGPT variants deserve more of the limited budget. Testing whether weighted fusion rescues ViT-L (config_025) is a lower priority, because ViT-L performed very poorly (0.224) and weighted fusion may simply down-weight it.

1) Evidence: Weighted fusion clearly beats concat. With the PCA, ResNet50 and avgpool backbone, accuracy was 0.721 versus 0.532, and F1 agreed. Avgpool beat transformer aggregation (0.721 vs 0.629). Among RNA encoders, PCA beat scVI (0.721 vs 0.579). The ViT-L image encoder did badly, but it was only tested with concat. The biggest open question is the scGPT RNA encoder, which has never been tried in any setting. 2) This run keeps the best-known setup (multiprofile, ResNet50, avgpool, weighted fusion) and swaps in scGPT. That isolates whether a pretrained foundation-model RNA encoder beats PCA. 3) This is the best use of the budget for two reasons. It explores the only RNA encoder with no data at all. It also stays in the most promising region, so it could produce a new best result. Checking whether ViT-L recovers with weighted fusion seems less promising, given how far behind it was (0.224).

1) Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is config_019 (PCA-2000 + ResNet50, avgpool, weighted fusion), with 0.721 accuracy and 0.681 F1. Weighted fusion clearly beat concat (0.53). PCA beat scVI (0.58) and scGPT (0.52). Avgpool beat transformer aggregation (0.63). However, every experiment so far has used multiprofile. Whether aggregating multiple profiles helps at all is a major design choice that remains completely untested. 2) What this tests: config_017 matches the best configuration exactly, except that it uses singleprofile. This isolates the value of multiprofile aggregation in the strongest known setting. 3) Why it is the best next experiment: It resolves uncertainty about an entire untested dimension with one clean controlled comparison. The outcome will show whether later budget should go to the multiprofile or the singleprofile branch. It also has a reasonable chance of matching or beating the current best, so it is exploratory but not wasteful.

1. Evidence: Weighted fusion clearly beats concat with PCA+ResNet50 (0.721 vs 0.532 accuracy, with F1 agreeing). PCA_n2000 is the best RNA encoder tested so far. Single-profile and multi-profile perform about the same (0.725 vs 0.721). The image encoder remains unresolved: ImageNet ViT-L was only tried with concat fusion, where it collapsed (0.224). That failure may reflect the poor fusion method rather than the encoder. 2. Test: config_025 swaps ViT-L into the best-known multi-profile setup (PCA, avgpool, weighted fusion). This directly tests whether ViT-L's poor result was caused by concat fusion or by the encoder itself, changing only the image encoder relative to config_019. 3. Value: The image encoder choice governs about half of the remaining search space. If ViT-L stays poor under weighted fusion, all ViT-L configurations can be deprioritized and the budget focused on ResNet50 refinements. If it recovers or beats ResNet50, it opens a promising new direction. This controlled comparison is worth more than a small exploitative tweak to the current best.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: weighted fusion with PCA and ResNet50 is the clear winner so far, at 0.725 accuracy single-profile (config_017) and 0.721 multi-profile (config_019). Concat fusion did consistently worse, and RNA-only reached only 0.520 (config_002). The two profile settings score about the same. What remains unknown is how much of the ~0.72 comes from the image branch alone. 2. What this tests: the image-only ResNet50 single-profile baseline measures that directly. If it scores near 0.72, the RNA branch adds little, and comparing RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT) is low value. If it scores well below 0.72, multimodal fusion is confirmed as the key design choice, and later experiments should refine the RNA encoder and fusion within the weighted, single-profile setup. 3. Why now: it is a single cheap baseline that settles the most basic design question, which modality carries the signal. That steers how the rest of the limited budget is spent better than another small variation near the current best.

1) No experiments have been run, so there is no evidence yet on whether multimodal fusion, multiprofile aggregation, or the choice of encoder matters. 2) config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA RNA + ResNet50, avgpool, concat) is a central anchor built from the simplest choice in every dimension. Its result will be a reference point for one-factor-at-a-time comparisons later: it can be paired with unimodal runs (config_002, config_011), single-profile runs (config_016), stronger encoders (scGPT, ViT-L), transformer aggregation, and weighted fusion. 3) With a limited budget, a simple baseline that touches every major design axis (both modalities, multiple profiles) gives the most reusable reference for later ablations. It still has a reasonable chance of performing well, rather than spending the first run on a narrow unimodal setup or the most complex combination.

1) Evidence: there is only one result so far. The multimodal, multiprofile pipeline (PCA RNA + ResNet50, avgpool, concat) reached 0.632 accuracy and 0.607 F1. With no comparison point, we cannot tell how much of that comes from RNA and how much from imaging. 2) Test: this runs the exact RNA-only counterpart, keeping the same PCA encoder, multiprofile setting and avgpool aggregation. It isolates one factor: whether adding the ResNet50 image branch helps at all. 3) Why now: modality is the most basic design choice, and its answer shapes the rest of the search. If RNA alone nearly matches 0.632, the image branch adds little, and the budget is better spent on RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT) and aggregation. If accuracy drops clearly, imaging carries signal, and improving the image encoder (ViT-L) and fusion becomes the priority. A single controlled ablation gives more direction per experiment than an unanchored encoder swap.

1. Evidence: Only two runs exist. With pca_n2000 RNA and avgpool aggregation held fixed, adding resnet50 images with concat fusion raised accuracy from 0.507 to 0.632, and F1 rose similarly. Image information therefore appears to drive most of the gain. Which image encoder works best is still completely untested, and it is likely a high-impact choice. 2. Test: config_024 changes only the image encoder (resnet50 to imagenet_vit_l) and keeps everything else in the best configuration fixed. Any difference can be attributed cleanly to the image encoder. 3. Why now: This both exploits and explores. It builds on the strongest result so far, which could raise the top score, while settling a major design choice. Aggregation, fusion and RNA encoder likely matter less given the current evidence, so testing them can wait. An image-only control is also useful, but it would not improve the best result and can be run later.

1) Evidence so far: the ResNet50 + PCA multimodal model with avgpool and concat fusion reached 0.632 accuracy and 0.607 F1. That is well above RNA-only (0.507) and the ViT-L multimodal variant (0.512). This points to ResNet50 as the stronger image encoder and suggests image information adds value. Aggregation is still untested: every run so far used avgpool, so we do not know whether learned set aggregation helps on multiprofile inputs. 2) This experiment keeps the best configuration fixed and changes only avgpool to transformer aggregation. Any difference can then be attributed to aggregation alone. 3) This exploits the most promising backbone while resolving a structural choice that affects many of the remaining configurations. The result tells us whether later RNA-encoder and fusion comparisons should use avgpool or transformer aggregation, which is a better use of the budget than broader, less controlled exploration.

1) Evidence so far: multimodal beats RNA-only by about 12 accuracy points, so the image modality clearly adds value. ResNet50 beats ViT-L by about 12 points, a strong and consistent signal. Transformer aggregation is modestly better than avgpool (0.653 vs 0.632 accuracy, with F1 agreeing), but that rests on a single comparison. All runs so far used the pca_n2000 RNA encoder and concat fusion, so the RNA encoder choice is completely unexplored and could matter a lot. 2) This run keeps the best-known setup (ResNet50, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) and swaps the RNA encoder to the pretrained scGPT. That isolates the RNA encoder effect against our strongest baseline, config_020. 3) The RNA encoder is the largest remaining source of uncertainty, and the large gap between RNA-only and multimodal suggests the RNA representation may be a bottleneck. Fusion type (weighted vs concat) is likely a smaller effect and can be tested afterward. Running this in the current best context also gives a realistic chance of beating 0.653, so it serves both exploration and exploitation.

Evidence so far: ResNet50 clearly beats ViT-L (0.63 vs 0.51 with PCA/avgpool/concat), so image encoder choice matters a lot. Transformer aggregation gives a modest gain over avgpool (0.653 vs 0.632). scGPT beats PCA under the best setting (0.688 vs 0.653), with F1 agreeing. Fusion is completely untested, because every multimodal run used concat. This experiment keeps the best configuration (config_044: scGPT, ResNet50, transformer, multiprofile) and changes only fusion to weighted. That isolates the effect of the one design dimension we know nothing about. It is the best use of the next run because it reduces uncertainty about a whole axis that applies to every multimodal configuration. It also has a reasonable chance of becoming the new best result, so it serves both exploration and exploitation. Testing scVI or more ViT variants would add less new information.

1. Evidence: ResNet50 clearly beat ViT-L in the matched comparison (0.632 vs 0.512 accuracy). Transformer aggregation modestly beat avgpool (0.653 vs 0.632). scGPT improved on PCA (0.688 vs 0.653), and weighted fusion added a further gain (0.721, F1 0.681). The scVI RNA encoder is still completely untested, so the RNA encoder choice is only partly resolved. 2. Test: config_033 keeps the current best setup (multiprofile, ResNet50, transformer, weighted fusion) and swaps only scGPT for scVI. This isolates whether scGPT is truly the best RNA encoder or whether the compact scVI embedding matches or beats it. 3. Why now: it exploits the strongest known pipeline, so it has a real chance of improving the best result. It also resolves the largest remaining unexplored axis in a single controlled comparison. That is a better use of budget than refining fusion with PCA, or revisiting ViT-L, which has already performed poorly.

Evidence: every multimodal run so far is multiprofile. The best result is scGPT + ResNet50 + transformer + weighted fusion (config_045, 0.721 accuracy, 0.681 F1). Encoder and fusion choices have had some testing: scGPT beat PCA and scVI, ResNet50 beat ViT-L, the transformer beat avgpool, and weighted beat concat. The profile setting has never been varied, so we cannot tell whether multiprofile aggregation is actually needed. This experiment keeps the best configuration and changes only to singleprofile. If accuracy drops clearly, multiprofile is a key ingredient and the remaining budget can focus on refining it. If accuracy stays similar, a simpler model works as well and the earlier aggregation gains need re-reading. It is the best next use of the budget because it tests a completely unexplored, high-level design choice in the strongest setting, and it could still be competitive in performance.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_045 (scGPT + ResNet50, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion; acc 0.721, F1 0.681). The ImageNet ViT-L image encoder has been tested only once, in a weak setting (PCA RNA, avgpool, concat; 0.512 vs 0.632 for ResNet50 in the same setup). That single run is weak grounds for dropping an entire image-encoder branch. The encoder may interact with the stronger scGPT RNA encoder, the transformer aggregation or the weighted fusion. 2) Test: config_051 keeps every component of the current best configuration and swaps only ResNet50 for ViT-L. Its result directly isolates the image-encoder effect in the most relevant context. 3) Why now: The image encoder is the least-resolved major design axis. Fusion, aggregation and RNA encoder each already have at least one comparison. This run either confirms ResNet50, letting us prune all remaining ViT-L configurations, or gives a new best if ViT-L benefits from weighted fusion. That makes it both informative and a reasonable bet for exploitation.

Evidence: the best results come from scGPT with transformer aggregation and weighted fusion (0.721 with ResNet50, 0.715 with ViT-L). The image encoder seems to matter little in this region. The only test of aggregation (transformer 0.653 vs avgpool 0.632) used PCA with concat fusion, so we don't know if transformer aggregation still matters with the stronger scGPT encoder and weighted fusion. This experiment changes only the aggregation (avgpool instead of transformer), keeping scGPT, ResNet50 and weighted fusion. It shows whether transformer aggregation is needed in the top-performing region or whether a simpler pooling performs as well. That clarifies a key design choice next to the current best, so it is both exploratory and relevant to exploitation. This is a better use of the limited budget than another fusion or encoder swap, where the evidence is already more consistent.

1. Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been run, so we have no information about any design axis: modality, single vs. multiprofile, RNA encoder, image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. 2. What this tests: config_018 is a central, simple reference point. It is multimodal, uses multiprofile inputs with avgpool aggregation, pairs the simplest encoders (PCA for RNA, ResNet50 for images), and fuses by concatenation. Its result sets a baseline that later one-factor changes can be compared against. Each of those comparisons isolates a single question: unimodal vs. multimodal (config_002 or config_011), singleprofile vs. multiprofile (config_016), avgpool vs. transformer (config_020), concat vs. weighted fusion (config_019), and simple vs. pretrained encoders (configs 030/042 for RNA, config_024 for images). 3. Why it is the best first use of budget: Starting from a low-complexity anchor near the middle of the design space makes later comparisons easy to interpret. Its expected performance is also reasonable, since it uses both modalities and multiple profiles. Starting at an extreme, such as the most complex scGPT + ViT-L transformer setup, would confound several factors at once and give less diagnostic value.

1) Evidence/uncertainty: There is only one result so far. The multimodal, multiprofile model (PCA-2000 RNA, ResNet50, avgpool, concat) reached 0.421 accuracy and 0.412 F1. With a single data point, we cannot tell how much each modality contributes to that score. 2) What this tests: config_002 keeps the same RNA encoder, profile setting and aggregation but removes the image branch. This is a clean one-factor ablation of the image modality. If RNA-only matches or beats 0.421, images add little at this stage. The search should then focus on RNA encoders such as scVI or scGPT and on aggregation. If RNA-only drops clearly, multimodal fusion is valuable, and testing image encoders and fusion choices becomes a priority. 3) Why this is the best next use of budget: whether to use multimodal models at all is the most basic design choice. Settling it first decides where later experiments should go across most of the remaining configurations. A controlled ablation also gives more interpretable information than changing several factors at once.

1) Evidence: Adding ResNet50 images to PCA RNA with concat fusion (config_018) cut validation accuracy from 0.540 to 0.421, and F1 dropped similarly (0.524 to 0.412). Two explanations remain: the image features add noise, or concat fusion lets a weak modality swamp the RNA signal. 2) Test: config_019 changes only the fusion method (concat to weighted) and keeps the RNA encoder, image encoder and avgpool aggregation fixed. If weighted fusion recovers to RNA-only accuracy or beats it, fusion was the problem and multimodal models are still worth pursuing. If it stays near 0.42, the ResNet50 image features themselves are probably harmful. 3) Why now: most of the remaining configurations are multimodal and split on fusion type. Settling whether weighted fusion avoids the multimodal penalty therefore decides whether to spend the budget on multimodal models or on RNA-only encoder and aggregation choices.

1. Evidence: The only RNA-only run (config_002, PCA, multiprofile, avgpool) is clearly best, at 0.540 accuracy and 0.524 F1. Adding ResNet50 images under the same settings hurt substantially: 0.421 with concat fusion and 0.327 with weighted fusion. So the RNA branch currently carries the signal. However, only one RNA encoder (PCA) has been tested, so the effect of the RNA representation is unknown. 2. Test: config_008 changes only the RNA encoder, from PCA to scGPT embeddings, and keeps rna_only, multiprofile and avgpool fixed. This cleanly measures whether a foundation-model RNA representation improves on PCA. 3. Why now: It exploits the strongest direction (RNA-only) while resolving a major untested design axis that every multimodal configuration also depends on. Its result will guide later choices of RNA encoder for both unimodal and fused models, which is more informative than tuning fusion or image settings that have so far only hurt.

1) Evidence: RNA-only models are the strongest so far. scGPT reached 0.573 accuracy and 0.573 F1, versus 0.540 accuracy for PCA. Adding resnet50 images through concat or weighted fusion clearly hurt performance (0.42 and 0.33 accuracy). Every run so far used avgpool aggregation, so the aggregation choice is completely unexplored. 2) This experiment changes only the aggregation of the current best setup (scGPT RNA-only, multiprofile), from avgpool to transformer. That isolates whether learned attention over multiple profiles improves on simple mean pooling. 3) Aggregation is a major design axis that affects every multiprofile branch, including later multimodal runs, so this result informs many remaining configurations. It also builds directly on the best-performing setup, giving both new information and a good chance of a new best score. The image-encoder question (resnet50 vs ViT-L) is better tested after the RNA-side design is settled.

1. Evidence: RNA-only models are clearly strongest so far, with scGPT plus avgpool at 0.573 accuracy and 0.573 F1. Adding ResNet50 image features to PCA RNA hurt performance badly. Accuracy fell from 0.540 to 0.421 with concat fusion and to 0.328 with weighted fusion. No image-only model has been tested yet, so we cannot tell whether the image modality has little signal or whether ResNet50 features specifically are weak or noisy. 2. Test: an image-only ImageNet ViT-L model under the same multiprofile avgpool setting measures how much predictive signal a stronger image encoder carries on its own. 3. Why this is the best next experiment: the result decides whether the large multimodal half of the search space is worth exploring. If ViT-L image-only performs well, scGPT plus ViT-L multimodal configs become promising. If it performs poorly, the remaining budget should go to RNA-side choices such as scVI encoders and single- versus multi-profile settings. This answers an uncertainty that affects many remaining configurations, rather than making a small exploitation step.

Evidence: the only multimodal runs so far paired pca_n2000 with resnet50, and both scored below RNA-only pca_n2000 (0.421 concat and 0.328 weighted, vs 0.540). Concat beat weighted. The strongest unimodal results are scGPT RNA-only with avgpool (0.573 acc, 0.573 F1) and ViT-L image-only with avgpool (0.532). This makes it unclear whether multimodal fusion is inherently harmful here or whether the earlier failures came from weaker encoders (pca and resnet50; resnet50 image-only is untested). This experiment fuses the two best encoders, scGPT and ViT-L, keeping avgpool aggregation and concat fusion, the better choices observed so far. If it beats 0.573, fusion adds value with strong encoders, which is the most promising direction. If it still falls below RNA-only scGPT, that is stronger evidence that fusion hurts in this setup, and remaining budget should go to unimodal refinement. It combines exploiting the best known components with resolving the most important open question: whether multimodal is worth pursuing.

Evidence: the best result so far is config_048 (scGPT + ViT-L, avgpool, concat) at 0.688 accuracy and 0.659 F1. It clearly beats both unimodal baselines (scGPT RNA-only 0.573, ViT-L image-only 0.532), so the scGPT/ViT-L/avgpool/concat setup is a strong base. Single results suggest weighted fusion (0.33 vs 0.42 concat with PCA/ResNet) and transformer aggregation (0.54 vs 0.57 avgpool with scGPT RNA-only) both hurt, though each rests on one comparison. The largest open question is the RNA encoder: scVI has never been tested in any setting, and we only know scGPT slightly beats PCA in RNA-only runs (0.573 vs 0.540). Test: config_036 keeps the winning setup (ViT-L, avgpool, concat) and swaps only scGPT for scVI. This isolates whether scVI can match or beat scGPT in the strongest multimodal context. Why now: it explores a completely unexamined encoder while staying inside the most promising region of the search space, so it could plausibly set a new best result. It is also more informative than re-testing fusion or aggregation options that already look weaker.

1) Evidence: the best result so far is config_048 (scGPT + ViT-L, avgpool, concat), at 0.688 accuracy and 0.659 F1. Fusion and aggregation already have some signal. Concat beat weighted for PCA+ResNet50 (0.42 vs 0.33). Avgpool beat transformer for scGPT RNA-only (0.57 vs 0.54, with a larger gap in F1). Profile setting has no signal at all: all eight experiments used multiprofile. 2) This run keeps the best encoder pair and concat fusion and switches only to singleprofile. It isolates whether aggregating multiple profiles actually drives the strong multimodal result, or whether a single profile does as well or better. 3) Profile setting is the largest untested design dimension and affects about half of the search space, so one controlled comparison on the strongest configuration gives the most information per experiment. It also stays near the current best, so it may still produce a competitive result.

1. Evidence: the best result so far is config_048 (scGPT + ViT-L, multiprofile, avgpool, concat), at 0.688 accuracy and 0.659 F1. It clearly beats both unimodal baselines (scGPT RNA-only 0.573, ViT-L image-only 0.532) and its single-profile counterpart (0.599). Multiprofile, scGPT and ViT-L therefore look like the right choices. Fusion strategy is still poorly understood. The only weighted-vs-concat comparison used the weak PCA + ResNet50 backbone (0.421 concat vs 0.328 weighted), and that single, low-performing pair may not transfer to stronger encoders. 2. This experiment changes only the fusion method on the best configuration, so it is a controlled test of whether weighted fusion helps or hurts when both modalities are informative. 3. Fusion is a core design choice for multimodal models, and the current evidence on it is the weakest of the remaining open choices. This run exploits the strongest region of the search space while reducing that uncertainty, and the result guides all remaining multimodal runs. Transformer aggregation (config_050) is the natural next follow-up.

1. Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been run, so nothing is known yet about which design choices matter. These include modality (RNA, image, or both), single vs. multi-profile input, encoder type, aggregation, and fusion. 2. What this tests: config_018 is a central, simple reference point. It is multimodal with multiprofile input, uses the simplest encoders (PCA RNA and ResNet50 image), and uses the simplest aggregation (avgpool) and fusion (concat). Each later experiment can change one factor from this baseline: drop a modality (config_002 or config_011), switch to single-profile (config_016), use transformer aggregation (config_020), use weighted fusion (config_019), or swap in a stronger encoder such as scGPT or ViT-L. 3. Why now: Under a limited budget, starting from a mid-complexity baseline allows clean one-factor-at-a-time comparisons for the highest-level choices. It also has a reasonable chance of performing well already. Starting at an extreme, such as the simplest single-modality model or the most complex combination, would make the follow-up comparisons harder to interpret.

1. Evidence: there is only one completed result. The multimodal, multiprofile setup (PCA RNA + ResNet50, avgpool, concat) reached 0.536 accuracy and 0.516 F1. Its absolute level gives no information about which components are responsible for that performance. 2. What this tests: config_002 drops only the image branch. It keeps the same PCA RNA encoder, multiprofile setting and avgpool aggregation. This gives a clean one-factor ablation of whether the image modality, and therefore fusion, adds value over RNA alone. 3. Why now: the modality question decides how to spend the rest of the budget. If RNA-only matches or beats the multimodal result, further work on image encoders and fusion types is unlikely to pay off, and effort should shift to RNA encoders and aggregation. If it clearly underperforms, multimodal exploration is justified, and the next tests should vary the image encoder, RNA encoder or aggregation.

1) Evidence and uncertainty: The two completed runs share the same PCA RNA encoder, multiprofile setting and avgpool aggregation. Adding ResNet50 images with concat fusion (0.536 acc, 0.516 F1) did not beat RNA alone (0.540 acc, 0.524 F1). The gap is small and could be noise, so it is unclear whether the image modality carries little signal or whether concat fusion fails to use it. 2) What this tests: An image-only run with the same ResNet50, multiprofile and avgpool settings completes a clean three-way ablation (RNA-only, image-only, fused). It shows how much signal images carry on their own. 3) Why it is the best next use of budget: Most of the remaining search space is multimodal. If image-only performs near chance, the budget should shift to RNA encoders and aggregation. If it performs reasonably well, the fusion method and image encoder (weighted fusion, ViT-L) become the key levers to test next.

1. Evidence: RNA-only (pca_n2000, avgpool) reached 0.540 accuracy and 0.524 F1. Image-only resnet50 was much weaker at 0.471. Adding resnet50 images via concat gave 0.536, no better than RNA alone. So RNA carries most of the signal, and the RNA encoder has only been tested with PCA. 2. This run swaps only the RNA encoder to scGPT, keeping multiprofile and avgpool fixed. That makes it a controlled comparison with config_002 on what is likely the most influential design choice: a pretrained foundation-model embedding versus a linear PCA embedding. 3. Since RNA dominates performance, the RNA encoder choice will shape every later multimodal configuration. Settling it early, before spending budget on image encoder, fusion or aggregation variants, is the most informative use of the next experiment. It also has a real chance of improving on the current best.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: Among completed runs, PCA RNA-only with avgpool is the strongest (0.540 acc, 0.524 F1). Multimodal concat with ResNet50 did not improve on it (0.536). Image-only (0.471) and scGPT (0.427) are clearly weaker. Every run so far used avgpool, so we know nothing about whether transformer aggregation over multiple profiles helps. That choice affects almost every multiprofile configuration still available. 2. What this tests: config_003 changes only the aggregation (avgpool to transformer) on the best-performing setup. That gives a clean, controlled read on this design axis. 3. Why it is the best next use of budget: The aggregation result will guide many later choices across unimodal and multimodal configurations. Because it builds on the current best setup, it is also a reasonable bet for immediate gains. Fusion type, scVI and ViT-L are also open questions, but they are best tested once the aggregation choice is better understood.

Evidence: the clearest signal so far is aggregation. Switching RNA-only pca_n2000 from avgpool to transformer raised accuracy from 0.540 to 0.678, with F1 rising from 0.524 to 0.646. With avgpool, multimodal concat (0.536) performed about the same as RNA-only (0.540), so adding resnet50 images showed no benefit. Image-only (0.471) and scGPT RNA-only (0.427) were weaker. Question: config_020 keeps the multimodal concat setup and changes only the aggregation to transformer. This tests whether the transformer gain carries over to the fused model, and whether images add value once a stronger aggregator is used. Comparing it with config_003 isolates whether adding the image modality helps. Comparing it with config_018 shows whether the transformer effect holds across model settings. Why now: it builds on the strongest effect found so far while resolving the main open question of whether multimodal fusion is worth pursuing. That answer will decide how much of the remaining budget should go to the many multimodal configurations versus RNA-only refinements such as the scVI encoder.

1) Evidence: the best result so far is RNA-only with PCA and transformer aggregation (0.678 acc / 0.646 F1). Transformer aggregation gave a large gain for RNA-only (+0.14 over avgpool). Adding ResNet50 images with concat fusion did not help under avgpool (0.536 vs 0.540). Under transformer aggregation, concat fusion collapsed to 0.332. Image-only is weak (0.471). The open uncertainty is whether multimodal fusion is harmful in itself or whether naive concat is the problem, for example by letting weaker or noisy image features dominate or destabilize transformer training. 2) Test: config_021 keeps everything from the collapsed config_020 (PCA, ResNet50, multiprofile, transformer) and changes only concat to weighted fusion. This cleanly isolates the fusion choice in the best-performing aggregation regime. If weighted fusion recovers to RNA-only level or beyond, multimodal remains a viable direction and fusion becomes a key design factor. If it also fails, adding images under transformer aggregation is likely harmful, and the budget should shift toward RNA-encoder and RNA-only refinements. 3) Why now: this single controlled comparison decides whether the large multimodal half of the search space deserves further budget. That makes it more informative than marginal RNA-only variations at this stage.

1. Evidence: Transformer aggregation is the strongest signal so far. It raised RNA-only PCA from 0.540 to 0.678 accuracy, with F1 rising in step, and RNA-only PCA + transformer is the current best. Multimodal runs have not beaten it. Concat fusion with a transformer collapsed (0.332), and weighted fusion reached only 0.635. The RNA encoder looks like a major factor, since scGPT was much worse than PCA under avgpool, but scVI has never been tested. 2. Question: Swapping PCA for scVI under the best-known setup (RNA-only, multiprofile, transformer) isolates whether scVI is a better RNA representation. 3. Why this experiment: It exploits the strongest direction while closing the biggest untested gap in a high-leverage design choice. The result also guides which RNA encoder to carry into later multimodal and weighted-fusion experiments, instead of spending budget on more image or fusion variants that have so far lagged.

Evidence: transformer aggregation is the strongest design choice so far. RNA-only PCA with a transformer (0.678 acc / 0.646 F1) beats avgpool (0.540). Among multimodal transformer runs, weighted fusion (0.635) far outperformed concat (0.332), so weighted fusion looks necessary when adding images. Multimodal still trails RNA-only. One reason may be the weak ResNet50 image features, since image-only avgpool reached only 0.471. The alternative image encoder (imagenet_vit_l) is completely untested. This experiment keeps the best-supported settings (PCA RNA, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) and swaps only the image encoder to ViT-L. That isolates whether a stronger image representation lets multimodal fusion match or beat the RNA-only best. It is the best use of the budget because it builds on the promising transformer-plus-weighted direction while resolving a major open question (the image encoder choice). Either outcome is informative: a gain shows multimodal is worth pursuing with ViT-L, and no gain suggests the image modality adds little beyond PCA RNA.

1) Evidence: Every completed run used the multiprofile setting. The best result so far is RNA-only PCA with transformer aggregation (0.678 acc, 0.646 F1), clearly ahead of PCA with avgpool (0.540). Adding images has not helped. Weighted fusion reached 0.635, and concat with a transformer collapsed to 0.332. So aggregation matters, but whether multiprofile input helps at all is untested. 2) Test: config_001 runs the best RNA encoder (PCA) on a single profile with no aggregation. This gives a baseline for the profile-setting decision. If it scores near or above the avgpool result, the gain comes from transformer aggregation rather than from multiple profiles. If it scores well below, multiprofile input has value in itself. 3) Why now: Profile setting is an entire unexplored axis covering many of the remaining configurations, including all the singleprofile multimodal ones. Testing it with the strongest, simplest RNA encoder isolates the effect cheaply and tells us whether those singleprofile configurations are worth budget, which is more informative than another small fusion or encoder tweak.

1. Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been run, so we know nothing yet about which design choices matter. The open questions are modality (RNA, image or multimodal), single vs. multi-profile input, encoder choice, aggregation and fusion. 2. What this tests: config_030 is a central anchor in the search space. It is multimodal and multi-profile, and it uses the simpler option on several axes: avgpool aggregation, concat fusion, scVI as a mid-complexity RNA encoder and ResNet50 for images. Its result gives a reference point for likely competitive performance. Later runs can then change one factor at a time from it: drop to RNA-only or image-only, switch to single-profile, use transformer aggregation or weighted fusion, or swap encoders. 3. Why it is the best next step: Starting from a central, moderately strong configuration makes every later one-factor comparison easy to interpret. That is more budget-efficient than starting at an extreme corner such as the simplest RNA-only baseline or the most complex transformer and weighted-fusion model.

1) Evidence/uncertainty: Only one result exists. The multimodal setup (scVI-200 RNA + ResNet50 image, avgpool, concat) reached 0.532 accuracy and 0.516 F1. With no baseline, we cannot tell whether the image modality adds anything. 2) What this tests: config_005 keeps the same scVI-200 RNA encoder, multiprofile setting and avgpool aggregation, but drops the image branch. It is a one-factor ablation of modality. 3) Why it is the best next experiment: The modality question is the most important early design decision, because it determines whether budget should go toward multimodal variants (image encoders, fusion) or RNA-side choices (encoders, aggregation). Changing only one factor makes the comparison easy to interpret.

1. Evidence: With the scVI RNA encoder and avgpool held fixed, adding ResNet50 image features through concat fusion lowered performance. Accuracy fell from 0.586 to 0.532 and F1 from 0.574 to 0.516. This is only one comparison. The drop could mean the image modality adds noise, or it could mean naive concatenation lets weak image features drown out the stronger RNA signal. 2. Test: config_031 keeps every setting the same as config_030 except fusion, which changes from concat to weighted. This cleanly measures the effect of fusion. If weighted fusion recovers or beats RNA-only, the problem was the concat strategy and multimodal fusion stays worth exploring. If it still trails RNA-only, that strengthens the case that ResNet50 image features add little value. 3. Why now: the fusion choice affects about half of the remaining multimodal configurations. Resolving it early tells us whether to keep investing in multimodal models or shift the budget toward RNA-only options such as encoder and aggregation choices.

1) Evidence so far: with scvi_n200, resnet50 and avgpool held fixed, weighted fusion (0.650 acc, 0.628 F1) clearly beat concat (0.532), which fell below RNA-only (0.586). So the fusion strategy matters, and weighted fusion lets the image modality add value over RNA alone. Aggregation has not been varied at all, and it is a major design axis for multiprofile models. 2) This experiment keeps the best configuration (config_031) and changes only avgpool to transformer aggregation. It tests whether learned set aggregation over profiles improves on simple averaging when paired with the stronger fusion method. 3) This single-factor change exploits the strongest direction found so far while resolving a key uncertainty. The result can then guide later tests of the image encoder (ViT-L) and RNA encoder (scGPT) under the better aggregation choice.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_031 (scVI + ResNet50, avgpool, weighted fusion), with 0.650 accuracy and 0.628 F1. It beats both RNA-only (0.586) and concat fusion (0.532), so weighted fusion over avgpool looks like a useful backbone. Transformer aggregation collapsed (0.224), so that branch is currently unattractive. The image encoder has never been varied: ResNet50 is the only one tested. 2. Test: config_037 keeps the best backbone (scVI, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted) and swaps only the image encoder to ImageNet ViT-L. Changing one factor isolates whether a stronger image representation adds to the multimodal gain. 3. Why now: this exploits the most promising direction while resolving uncertainty about a major untested design choice. The result will tell us whether later experiments should use ViT-L or ResNet50 as the image encoder.

1) Evidence: the best result so far is config_031 (scvi_n200 + resnet50, avgpool, weighted fusion), at 0.650 accuracy and 0.628 F1. It beats RNA-only scvi (0.586) and concat fusion (0.532), so weighted fusion looks useful. 1) Evidence: config_031 (scVI + ResNet50, avgpool, weighted fusion, multiprofile) is the best result so far at 0.650 accuracy and 0.628 F1. Each single change from it has hurt. Concat fusion dropped accuracy to 0.532, scGPT to 0.518, a ViT-L image encoder to 0.260 and transformer aggregation to 0.224. Weighted multimodal fusion also beats RNA-only (0.586). One major design axis is still untested: every completed run used multiprofile inputs, so we have no evidence on whether multiprofile aggregation helps at all. 1. Evidence: Adding ResNet50 image features to the scVI RNA model with concat fusion (config_022) dropped validation accuracy from 0.619 to 0.208, with F1 falling similarly. This is a severe degradation, and it is unclear whether the cause is a weak image signal or a fusion problem, such as concat letting noisy image features dominate. 2. Test: An image-only ResNet50 model under the same multiprofile setting and avgpool aggregation (config_002) isolates how much the image modality contributes on its own. 3. Why now: If image-only is also near chance, image features themselves are the bottleneck, and the next steps should be a different image encoder (ViT-L) or more RNA-side exploration. If image-only is reasonably good, the failure points to the concat fusion, which justifies testing weighted fusion (config_024). Either way, this single-variable baseline efficiently resolves the most important uncertainty before spending budget on further multimodal variants.

1. Evidence: The multimodal scVI + ResNet50 avgpool model with concat fusion (config_022) reached only 0.208 accuracy. That is far below RNA-only (0.619) and image-only (0.422) using the same encoders and aggregation. So the drop comes from how the modalities are combined, not from weak inputs. The likeliest cause is concat fusion, though one run alone does not prove it. 2. Test: config_024 keeps everything identical and changes only concat to weighted fusion. If accuracy recovers toward or above the RNA-only baseline, concat is the bottleneck. If it stays low, the problem is more general to multimodal training in this setup. 3. Why now: Most remaining configurations are multimodal and split between concat and weighted fusion. This single controlled comparison tells us which half of the space is worth the budget before we explore RNA encoders or aggregation further.

Evidence: the RNA-only scvi_n200 avgpool multiprofile model is clearly the best so far (acc 0.619, F1 0.610). It beats image-only (0.422) and both multimodal variants. Weighted fusion (0.535) did far better than concat (0.208), but adding images has not yet helped. Every run so far used avgpool, so we have no evidence on aggregation, which affects all multiprofile configurations. Test: config_014 changes only avgpool to transformer on the current best RNA-only setup. That isolates whether learned cross-profile aggregation improves on simple pooling. Why now: it builds on the strongest result while settling an untested design choice in a single controlled comparison. The answer will guide which aggregation to use in later RNA-encoder, profile-setting and fusion experiments.

1) Evidence and uncertainty: All five completed experiments used the multiprofile setting. The best result so far is RNA-only with scvi_n200 and avgpool (config_037: 0.619 accuracy, 0.610 F1). It beats image-only (0.422) and both multimodal fusions (concat 0.208, weighted 0.535). Within RNA-only, avgpool also beat the transformer (0.525). The singleprofile setting has never been tested, so we do not know whether multiprofile aggregation helps at all. 2) What this tests: config_050 keeps the best configuration's modality (RNA-only) and encoder (scvi_n200) and changes only the profile setting to singleprofile, which has no aggregation step. This directly isolates the effect of profile setting against config_037. 3) Why it is the best next experiment: Profile setting is a major design axis with zero evidence so far, and the answer will shape the rest of the search. If singleprofile matches or beats multiprofile, the many untested singleprofile configurations become promising. If it underperforms, the search can focus on multiprofile and its aggregation choices. Testing RNA encoders (scgpt or pca) is also useful, but it is better done after this more fundamental question is answered.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is RNA-only, multiprofile, scVI with avgpool (acc 0.619, F1 0.610). It beats the scVI single-profile model (0.573), the transformer aggregation (0.525), image-only (0.422) and both multimodal fusions (concat 0.208, weighted 0.535). Every RNA experiment so far used scVI, so the choice of RNA representation is completely untested, even though RNA appears to be the main source of signal. 2. What this tests: config_015 keeps the best configuration fixed and changes only the encoder from scVI to scGPT. This isolates the effect of the RNA representation. 3. Why it is the best next step: It exploits the strongest direction found so far while answering a key open question. The answer will shape later multimodal and fusion experiments, because those depend on the best RNA backbone. If scGPT does better, it becomes the new base. If not, scVI is supported and the budget can shift to the PCA encoder or to fusion refinements.

1) Evidence: RNA-only multiprofile with avgpool is the strongest setting so far. With scVI it reached 0.619 accuracy and 0.610 F1, and with scGPT 0.586 accuracy and 0.574 F1. Image-only lags at 0.422, and multimodal fusion has not beaten RNA-only. Weighted fusion reached 0.535 and concat collapsed to 0.208. Avgpool beat transformer for scVI (0.619 vs 0.525). The RNA representation is the factor that most drives performance, yet pca_n2000 has never been tested. 2) Test: config_035 changes only the RNA encoder to pca_n2000 and keeps the best-known setup (RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool). Evidence: the best result so far is RNA-only scvi_n200 multiprofile avgpool (0.619 acc, 0.610 F1). Adding the only image encoder tested, resnet50, lowered performance: weighted fusion reached 0.535 and concat collapsed to 0.208. Image-only resnet50 gave just 0.422. The second image encoder, imagenet_vit_l, is completely untested, so we cannot tell whether the image modality is weak in general or only with resnet50. This experiment keeps image-only, multiprofile and avgpool fixed and swaps only the encoder, so it directly compares against config_002 (0.422). That isolates the effect of the image representation. It is the best use of the budget because the answer decides whether the many remaining vit_l multimodal configurations are worth exploring. A clearly stronger image-only result would justify trying vit_l with weighted fusion (config_045). A weak result would point the search back toward refining the RNA-only models.

Evidence: the best result so far is RNA-only, multiprofile, scVI, avgpool (0.619 accuracy, 0.610 F1). Multimodal models have not beaten it. With scVI and ResNet50 under multiprofile avgpool, weighted fusion reached 0.535 and concat fell to 0.208. So weighted fusion is the only workable fusion, but adding images hurt in the multiprofile setting. Profile setting has only been compared for RNA-only, where multiprofile scored 0.619 and singleprofile 0.573. It is still unknown whether image fusion behaves differently without multiprofile aggregation. What this tests: config_048 keeps scVI, ResNet50 and weighted fusion and only switches to singleprofile. That isolates the profile-setting effect within multimodal weighted fusion, using config_024 as the reference. It also gives a direct image-addition comparison against singleprofile RNA-only (config_050, 0.573). Why now: it answers whether image signal can add value in a simpler, non-aggregated setting, or whether multimodal fusion is consistently worse than RNA alone. That decides whether the remaining budget should go to multimodal variants or to refining RNA-only models.

1. Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been run yet, so we know nothing about which design choices matter. Representation, profile setting, aggregation and fusion are all open questions. 2. What this tests: config_001 is a simple, mid-complexity anchor. It uses RNA only, multiple profiles, the compact scVI encoder and plain average pooling, with no image branch and no fusion. It gives a reference score that later experiments can be compared against by changing one factor at a time: profile setting (config_043, single profile), aggregation (config_014, transformer), RNA encoder (config_018 scGPT, config_024 PCA), or adding images (config_003 weighted and config_031 concat, both ResNet50). 3. Why it is the best next experiment: Starting with a simple, interpretable baseline avoids assuming that multimodal or more complex models win. Because it has a one-factor neighbor along every major design axis, it makes each later experiment a cleaner comparison, which matters most when the budget is limited.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: only one experiment has been run, an RNA-only multiprofile model with scvi_n200 and avgpool (acc 0.650, F1 0.628). We do not yet know whether the image modality adds useful signal, and that is the most consequential open design question. 2. What this tests: config_003 keeps the RNA encoder, profile setting and aggregation the same. It adds a ResNet50 image branch with weighted fusion. The comparison therefore mostly isolates the effect of going multimodal against the existing baseline. Fusion type is the one unavoidable extra change. 3. Why this is the best next experiment: the result tells us whether the budget should go mainly toward multimodal configurations, which make up most of the untested list, or toward tuning RNA-only and image-only models. A drop or no gain would be equally informative, because it would argue against assuming fusion helps. Questions about the profile setting (e.g. config_043) and the aggregation method (e.g. config_014) can be addressed afterwards with similarly controlled single changes.

1. Evidence: RNA-only (scVI, multiprofile, avgpool) reached 0.650 accuracy. Adding ResNet50 images with weighted fusion, with everything else unchanged, collapsed accuracy to 0.208. With only two runs, it is unclear whether the cause is uninformative ResNet50 image features or a failure of the weighted fusion mechanism. 2. Test: the image-only ResNet50 model under the same multiprofile and avgpool setting provides the missing unimodal baseline. If it also scores near 0.2, the image features are weak and are dragging the fused model down. If it scores reasonably well, the fusion step is the likely culprit, and concat fusion (config_031) becomes the logical next test. 3. Why now: this baseline anchors every later decision about the image modality, including whether to try ViT-L, alternative fusion, or abandon multimodal models. It changes only the modality setting relative to the existing runs, so it best reduces the largest current uncertainty.

1. Evidence: Under multiprofile avgpool, RNA-only scVI reaches 0.650 accuracy and image-only ResNet50 reaches 0.523. Yet multimodal scVI+ResNet50 with weighted fusion collapses to 0.208, far below either modality alone. That points to a fusion failure rather than a lack of complementary signal, but one run cannot tell us whether the cause is the weighted fusion mechanism or multimodal training in general. 2. This experiment keeps everything identical to config_003 (scVI, ResNet50, multiprofile, avgpool) and changes only the fusion to concat. It directly isolates the effect of the fusion method. 3. Whether multimodal models are viable decides how much of the remaining budget goes to the many multimodal configurations. If concat recovers performance near or above RNA-only, weighted fusion is the problem and concat multimodal configurations deserve exploration. If concat also fails, multimodal integration is likely broken in this setup and the budget should shift toward unimodal RNA variants such as encoder, aggregation and profile choices. A single controlled comparison answers this high-impact question efficiently.

Evidence: the best result so far is RNA-only (scVI, multiprofile, avgpool) at 0.650 accuracy and 0.628 F1. It beats concat multimodal (0.591) and image-only ResNet50 (0.523). Weighted fusion collapsed (0.208), so multimodal gains are uncertain and depend heavily on fusion. All four runs so far used avgpool, so we know nothing yet about whether transformer aggregation helps. Test: config_014 keeps the best configuration fixed and changes only avgpool to transformer. Any difference can therefore be attributed to aggregation alone. Why now: aggregation applies to every multiprofile configuration, RNA-only and multimodal alike. One controlled run tells us which aggregation to carry forward in later comparisons of RNA encoders, profile setting and fusion. It also builds on the strongest current direction, so it is a reasonable bet for immediate gains as well as for learning.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: RNA-only scVI with multiprofile avgpool is the best result so far (0.650 accuracy, 0.628 F1). It beats image-only (0.523), multimodal concat (0.591) and multimodal weighted (0.208). Avgpool also beat transformer aggregation for RNA (0.519). However, every experiment so far has used the multiprofile setting, so whether multiprofile aggregation helps at all is completely unknown. 2. What this tests: config_043 keeps the best modality and encoder (RNA-only, scVI) and switches only to the singleprofile setting. This isolates the effect of profile setting against the current best baseline. 3. Why it is the best next experiment: profile setting is a top-level design choice that affects every later branch, including encoder and fusion choices. A single, low-cost, cleanly controlled comparison resolves the largest remaining gap before we spend budget on encoder swaps such as PCA or scGPT. It could also find a better configuration if multiprofile aggregation is adding noise.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is RNA-only, multiprofile, scVI with avgpool (0.650 acc / 0.628 F1). Within scVI RNA-only runs, avgpool beat transformer aggregation (0.519) and multiprofile beat singleprofile (0.507). Multimodal models have not beaten RNA-only: concat reached 0.591 and weighted fusion collapsed to 0.208. Image-only with resnet50 reached 0.523. The RNA encoder choice is completely untested, since every RNA run used scVI, yet RNA looks like the dominant signal. 2. What this tests: config_024 swaps only the RNA encoder from scVI to PCA (n2000) and keeps the best setting otherwise (rna_only, multiprofile, avgpool). This isolates whether the representation drives performance and whether a simple higher-dimensional baseline matches or beats learned scVI embeddings. 3. Why it is the best next experiment: It is a one-factor comparison against the current best, so it is cleanly interpretable. Evidence: RNA representation looks like the most influential choice so far. Under the same rna_only, multiprofile, avgpool setting, pca_n2000 reached 0.725 accuracy and 0.685 F1, versus 0.650 and 0.628 for scvi_n200. Other changes hurt: transformer aggregation dropped to 0.519, singleprofile to 0.507, and adding resnet50 images (concat 0.591, weighted 0.208) underperformed RNA-only. The third RNA encoder, scgpt, has never been tested. Test: config_018 changes only the encoder to scgpt and keeps the best-known rna_only, multiprofile, avgpool setting. This completes a controlled comparison of all three RNA representations with nothing else varying. Why now: if scgpt beats pca_n2000, it becomes the new base for later fusion experiments. If it does not, pca_n2000 is confirmed as the RNA backbone, and later multimodal tests (e.g., pca_n2000 with concat fusion) can build on it. Either outcome removes the largest remaining uncertainty about the factor that has mattered most, for a single experiment.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is RNA-only with pca_n2000, multiprofile, and avgpool (0.725 acc, 0.685 F1). It clearly beats the scVI and scGPT RNA encoders under the same setting. With scVI, adding ResNet50 images through concat fusion gave 0.591 acc, below RNA-only's 0.650. Weighted fusion collapsed to 0.208. So whether images help at all is still uncertain, and it may depend on RNA representation quality. 2. Test: This experiment adds ResNet50 images with concat fusion to the best configuration (config_024). Everything else stays the same: pca_n2000, multiprofile, avgpool. That makes it a clean one-variable test of whether multimodal fusion helps once the RNA representation is strong. It also replicates the scVI fusion comparison (config_001 vs config_031) with a second RNA encoder, so we can see whether the fusion penalty is consistent. 3. Why now: Whether to pursue multimodal models at all is the most consequential open decision. It determines whether the remaining budget should go to image encoders and fusion variants or to refining RNA-only models. Using the stronger concat fusion and the known ResNet50 encoder avoids mixing in other untested changes, such as ViT-L or transformer aggregation.

1. Evidence: PCA_n2000 is clearly the strongest RNA encoder so far (RNA-only avgpool reached 0.725 accuracy, above scVI at 0.650 and scGPT at 0.599). Avgpool beat transformer aggregation (0.650 vs 0.519 for scVI), and multiprofile beat singleprofile (0.650 vs 0.507). Concat fusion was far more stable than weighted fusion (0.591 vs 0.208 for scVI+ResNet50). Adding ResNet50 to PCA with concat (config_009, 0.715) roughly matched RNA-only PCA but did not beat it. The image branch has only been tested with ResNet50, which was weak alone (0.523). The image encoder is therefore the largest untested design choice. 2. Test: config_013 differs from config_009 only in swapping ResNet50 for imagenet_vit_l. This isolates the effect of image representation within the best-performing multimodal setup. It also clarifies whether the image modality can add value beyond RNA, or whether ResNet50 features were the bottleneck. 3. Value: a single-variable change in the strongest context does two things at once. It reduces uncertainty about an unexplored design axis, and it has a realistic chance of exceeding the current best. A clear gain would point toward ViT-L-based multimodal extensions. No gain would strengthen the case that RNA-only PCA is sufficient.

1. Evidence: no experiments have been run yet, so we know nothing about which design choices matter. The first run should be a reference point that later runs can each change in only one way. 2. Test: config_031 is a simple multimodal setup: multiprofile, PCA RNA encoder, ResNet50 image encoder, avgpool aggregation and concat fusion. Almost every design choice can then be tested by changing one thing. Aggregation: config_010 uses a transformer. Fusion: config_017 uses weighted fusion. Image encoder: config_027 uses ViT-L. RNA encoder: config_013 uses scVI and config_040 uses scGPT. Profile setting: config_012 is singleprofile. Modality: config_030 is RNA-only and config_006 is image-only. 3. Why now: under a limited budget, starting from this low-complexity hub lets each later experiment isolate one effect cleanly. It avoids assuming that complex choices such as transformers, weighted fusion or foundation-model encoders will win, and it still gives a reasonable performance baseline.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: only one experiment exists. The multimodal, multiprofile model (PCA-2000 RNA, ResNet50 image, avgpool, concat) reached 0.411 accuracy and 0.378 F1. We cannot yet tell whether the image branch adds anything or whether RNA alone drives this result. 2. What this tests: config_030 is the matching RNA-only model. It keeps the PCA-2000 encoder, the multiprofile setting and avgpool aggregation, and drops only the image modality. Comparing it with config_031 isolates the contribution of images and concat fusion. 3. Why it is the best next use of budget: whether multimodality is worth having is the most consequential open question. If RNA-only matches or beats the multimodal result, the search should shift toward RNA encoders and profile or aggregation choices. If it clearly underperforms, later work on image encoders and fusion methods is justified. This single-factor ablation answers a major design question more cleanly than changing encoders or aggregation now.

1. Evidence: with PCA-2000 RNA, multiprofile and avgpool held fixed, RNA-only (0.471 acc, 0.442 F1) beat multimodal ResNet50 concat (0.411 acc, 0.378 F1). Adding images through concat therefore lowered performance. We cannot yet tell whether the image features carry little signal or whether concat fusion is a poor way to combine two useful modalities. 2. Test: config_006 is image-only ResNet50 with multiprofile avgpool, the same setup otherwise. It completes the three-way modality comparison and measures how much signal the images carry on their own. If image-only is near chance, the multimodal drop is mainly noise from a weak modality, and RNA-side choices (encoder, aggregation) should get priority. If image-only is competitive, the fusion method is the likely bottleneck, which makes weighted fusion (e.g., config_017) the logical next test. 3. Why now: it changes only the modality, uses the configuration already shared by both completed runs, and determines whether the remaining budget should go to RNA-only refinement or to fusion and image-encoder choices.

1) Evidence: with multiprofile, PCA RNA, ResNet50 and avgpool held fixed, image-only scored best (acc 0.532, F1 0.516), RNA-only was next (0.471/0.442), and concat fusion was worst (0.411/0.378). The multimodal model did worse than both of its unimodal parts. That suggests naive concatenation is harming learning, for example through modality imbalance or the weaker RNA features adding noise, rather than multimodality being useless. 2) config_017 changes only the fusion from concat to weighted, with every other choice the same as config_031. This isolates the fusion effect and tests whether a learned modality weighting can recover at least image-only performance or surpass it. 3) Most of the remaining search space is multimodal, so finding out early whether the fusion strategy is the bottleneck tells us whether multimodal configurations are worth further budget. Because it is a single-variable change, the result will be directly interpretable.

1. Evidence: Image-only (ResNet50, multiprofile, avgpool) is the best result so far (acc 0.532, F1 0.516). RNA-only PCA comes next (0.471). Both multimodal fusions with the same encoders did worse than either single modality (concat 0.411, weighted 0.332). So naive fusion currently hurts, and the image branch is the strongest signal. None of the other design axes have been tested yet: image encoder, aggregation and profile setting are all open. 2. Test: Keep everything from the best configuration (image-only, multiprofile, avgpool) and swap only the image encoder from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L. This isolates the effect of image representation on the strongest branch. 3. Why now: The image encoder affects both the unimodal and multimodal configurations, so a clean one-variable comparison tells us which backbone later fusion and aggregation experiments should build on. It also exploits the most promising direction, so it is both informative and has a good chance of improving on the current best. Transformer aggregation and singleprofile can then be tested on the stronger backbone.

1. Evidence: Image-only models lead so far. ViT-L reached 0.540 accuracy (F1 0.524) and ResNet50 reached 0.532, so the two image encoders are nearly tied. Multimodal fusion with PCA RNA features has underperformed both single-modality baselines, with concat at 0.411 and weighted at 0.332. Every completed run used avgpool aggregation, so the effect of aggregation is entirely untested. 2. Question: Swapping avgpool for transformer aggregation on the current best configuration (image-only, multiprofile, ViT-L) changes only one variable. It directly tests whether learned aggregation across profiles improves on simple pooling. 3. Why now: Aggregation is an untested design choice that could affect every multiprofile configuration. Testing it on the strongest branch gives a clean comparison against config_014 and has a reasonable chance of improving the best result. A gain would justify carrying transformer aggregation into the multimodal runs; no gain would let us drop it and save budget.

1. Evidence: Image-only models lead so far. ViT-L with avgpool scored 0.540 accuracy (F1 0.524) and ResNet50 with avgpool scored 0.532. RNA-only PCA reached 0.471. Both multimodal PCA+ResNet50 fusions did worse than either single modality (0.41 with concat, 0.33 with weighted). Transformer aggregation lowered ViT-L to 0.485. Every experiment so far has used the multiprofile setting, so we do not know whether multiprofile aggregation helps at all. 2. This experiment changes only the profile setting, comparing single-profile against the current best (config_014: image-only, ViT-L). It shows whether aggregating multiple profiles adds value or whether a simpler single-profile model is as good or better. That could also help explain why transformer aggregation hurt. 3. It isolates one variable against the strongest baseline. It probes a design dimension that has not been tested at all. It is also a credible candidate for the best result, so it is both informative and potentially high-performing. Tests of RNA encoder choice and fusion with ViT-L can follow once the profile-setting question is settled.

1) Evidence: single-profile image-only ViT-L (config_024, 0.713 accuracy) is far better than every multiprofile run, all of which score 0.33-0.54. In the multiprofile setting, adding PCA RNA hurt image-only results (0.41 concat, 0.33 weighted vs 0.53 image-only), but that was never tested in the single-profile regime. 2) This run takes the best configuration and adds only PCA_n2000 RNA with concat fusion. PCA is the only RNA encoder tested so far, and concat beat weighted fusion earlier. This isolates whether RNA fusion helps or hurts when profiles are not aggregated. 3) It is a direct, low-confound extension of the strongest result. It could beat the current best, and if it does not, it confirms that the multimodal penalty holds across profile settings. That would justify focusing the remaining budget on single-profile image-only variants, such as ResNet50 (config_043).

1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is image-only singleprofile with ViT-L (0.713 accuracy, 0.695 F1), far above every multiprofile run (at most 0.54). Every multimodal run with PCA RNA has done worse than the unimodal runs. The singleprofile multimodal run with PCA and ViT-L fell to 0.328. We have no singleprofile RNA-only baseline, so we cannot tell whether that drop comes from weak PCA RNA features in singleprofile or from the fusion itself. 2. What this tests: config_038 is RNA-only, singleprofile, PCA. Compared with config_030 (the same setup in multiprofile, 0.471), it isolates the profile-setting effect for RNA. It also gives the missing unimodal baseline for interpreting config_049. 3. Why it is the best next experiment: It is a single-factor change that resolves two uncertainties at once. These are whether the singleprofile gain holds beyond images, and whether PCA RNA is what drags down multimodal models. If RNA-only singleprofile turns out weak, the next step is to try other RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT) before spending more budget on fusion variants. If it is strong, the problem lies in the fusion design instead.

1. Evidence: Singleprofile has beaten multiprofile in both modalities tested: image ViT-L 0.713 vs 0.540, and RNA PCA 0.586 vs 0.471. Image-only ViT-L singleprofile is the best result so far. Every multimodal run used PCA RNA features, and all of them fell below the unimodal baselines; the singleprofile ViT-L+PCA concat run reached only 0.328. The RNA encoder is the biggest gap in our knowledge, because only pca_n2000 has been tried. In contrast, ResNet50 and ViT-L were nearly tied in multiprofile (0.532 vs 0.540), so the image encoder is less uncertain. 2. Test: Running rna_only with scvi_n200 in the stronger singleprofile setting changes only the RNA encoder relative to config_038 (PCA, 0.586). This isolates whether a learned latent representation improves RNA performance. 3. Why this is the best next experiment: The result shapes the next multimodal steps. If scVI clearly beats PCA, multimodal runs pairing scVI with ViT-L become worth testing, since weak PCA features may explain the poor fusion results. If scVI does not help, it is more evidence that multimodal fusion adds little here and that image-only singleprofile is the direction to refine. Either outcome saves budget compared with testing more PCA-based multimodal variants.

1. No experiments have been run, so we have no evidence about whether any design choice helps: modality, multiprofile aggregation, encoder type or fusion. 2. This tests the simplest setup: RNA-only, single-profile, PCA (2000 components), with no aggregation or fusion. It sets a reference accuracy and F1 that every later experiment can be compared against. Each future change (adding images, switching to multiprofile with avgpool or transformer aggregation, or using scVI or scGPT encoders) can then be added one at a time from this point. 3. With a limited budget, a cheap and easy-to-interpret anchor is more useful than jumping to a complex multimodal configuration. If a complex model did well first, we could not tell which component caused the result. This baseline also guards against assuming that more complex multimodal models are better.

1) Evidence: there is only one result so far. The RNA-only, single-profile PCA baseline reached 0.512 accuracy and 0.477 F1. Avgpool is the simplest aggregation and so the least confounded choice for this test. 3) Why now: profile setting runs through most of the remaining configurations, so learning its effect early will guide many later choices. 1. Evidence: With the PCA RNA-only setup, single-profile reached 0.512 accuracy and 0.477 F1. Multiprofile with avgpool dropped sharply to 0.332 accuracy and 0.315 F1. It is unclear whether multiprofile input itself hurts, or whether simple average pooling is the problem by washing out profile-specific signal. 2. Test: config_039 keeps everything from config_002 (RNA-only, PCA, multiprofile) and changes only aggregation from avgpool to transformer. This directly isolates the effect of aggregation. If transformer recovers or beats single-profile performance, multiprofile remains viable and avgpool is the weak point. If it stays low, multiprofile is likely harmful in this setting. 3. Value: Most remaining configurations are multiprofile with avgpool or transformer aggregation. 1. Evidence: Only PCA RNA-only models have been tested. Aggregation clearly matters: multiprofile with avgpool fell to 0.332 accuracy, while multiprofile with transformer reached 0.520 accuracy (F1 0.498), slightly above singleprofile at 0.512 (F1 0.477). The image modality is entirely untested, so whether images add useful signal is the biggest open question. 2. Test: config_022 keeps the best setup so far (PCA, multiprofile, transformer) and adds the ViT-L image encoder with the simplest fusion, concat. Compared directly with config_039, it largely isolates the effect of adding images under a known-good aggregation, though it necessarily also fixes a choice of image encoder and fusion method. 3. Why now: Whether multimodality helps is one of the most important design questions for the rest of the search.
