1) No experiments have been run yet, so we know nothing about which design choices matter. 2) config_022 (multimodal, multiprofile, scGPT, ViT-L, avgpool, concat) is a central anchor. Most other options differ from it in only one factor, so each can be compared against it cleanly: fusion (weighted, config_005), aggregation (transformer, config_007), image encoder (ResNet50, config_012), RNA encoder (PCA, config_036; scVI, config_044) and profile setting (singleprofile, config_020). Its unimodal counterparts (RNA-only, config_001; image-only, config_002) use the same encoders and aggregation, so they can later show whether fusion actually helps. 3) Starting from this hub makes every later experiment a one-factor comparison. It also gives a reasonable early baseline without assuming in advance that the complex multimodal model will win.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: Only one experiment has been run. The multimodal, multiprofile model (scGPT + ViT-L, avgpool, concat) reached 0.535 accuracy and 0.519 F1. Without a baseline, we cannot tell whether combining modalities helps, or whether the RNA or image branch is doing most of the work. 2. What this tests: config_001 keeps everything the same (multiprofile, scGPT, avgpool) but drops the image modality. This isolates the contribution of imaging and fusion. If RNA-only matches or beats 0.535, fusion adds little and the search should focus on RNA encoders and aggregation. If it falls clearly short, multimodality is justified and fusion and image choices deserve more of the budget. 3. Why it is the best next use: Whether multimodality matters is the most basic design question and shapes how the remaining budget is spent. A single-variable ablation answers it more cleanly than changing aggregation or fusion first. It also keeps image_only (config_002) as a natural follow-up to complete the modality picture.

1. Evidence: Only two experiments are complete. Both use multiprofile and avgpool, and both use scGPT for RNA. Multimodal with ViT-L and concat fusion (0.535 acc / 0.519 F1) slightly beats RNA-only (0.520 / 0.498). With a single run each, this ~1.5-point gap is small. We have no image-only measurement, so we cannot tell whether the multimodal gain comes from complementary information or from the image branch carrying most of the signal. 2. Test: config_002 is image-only with ViT-L, multiprofile and avgpool, matching the other two runs on every other setting. It completes a clean three-way modality ablation. If image-only matches or beats multimodal, fusion adds little and later runs should focus on image representations. If it falls clearly below, fusion is genuinely helping. 3. Why now: Modality contribution is the most basic open question, and its answer determines how to spend the rest of the budget across encoders, aggregation and fusion. Settling it first with a single-variable comparison is more useful than tuning secondary choices built on an untested assumption.

1. Evidence: the image-only ViT-L multiprofile avgpool model is the clear leader (acc 0.591, F1 0.573). It beats both RNA-only scGPT (0.520) and the concat multimodal model (0.535). So the image branch appears to carry most of the signal, and naive concat fusion with RNA seems to hurt. Aggregation has only ever been tested as avgpool, so its effect is completely unknown. 2. This experiment swaps avgpool for transformer aggregation while keeping everything else in the best configuration fixed. That isolates the aggregation effect and shows whether learned attention over profiles beats mean pooling. 3. It exploits the strongest direction found so far and answers an open design question with a single-variable change. The result will also guide which aggregation to carry into the remaining multimodal and RNA experiments.

1. Evidence: Image-only ViT-L is clearly the strongest branch so far (0.591 with avgpool, 0.599 with transformer). Transformer's edge over avgpool is too small to trust. Multimodal concat with scGPT (0.535) and RNA-only scGPT (0.520) both trail image-only. Every run so far used the multiprofile setting, so the effect of profile setting is completely unknown. 2. This run tests the single-profile version of image-only ViT-L, keeping the modality and encoder of the best model. Comparing it with config_002 and config_030 isolates whether multiprofile aggregation actually helps or whether single-profile inputs do as well. 3. With a limited budget, this answers the biggest open design question within the most promising direction. It also tells us whether later runs, including multimodal ones, should focus on multiprofile or single-profile settings.

Evidence: image-only multiprofile with imagenet_vit_l is the strongest direction so far, at 0.599 accuracy with transformer aggregation and 0.591 with avgpool. That aggregation gap is small, so I don't treat it as conclusive. Multiprofile clearly beat singleprofile for image-only (0.591 vs 0.525). Concat fusion with scGPT RNA (0.535) and RNA-only (0.520) both underperformed image-only. The largest untested axis in the dominant modality is the image encoder, since resnet50 has never been tried. Test: config_016 differs from the best run (config_030) only in swapping imagenet_vit_l for resnet50. This isolates whether the image representation drives performance. Why now: image features appear to carry most of the signal, so knowing which encoder is better guides nearly all remaining configurations, including multimodal ones. That makes this single-variable comparison a high-value use of the next experiment, ahead of retuning fusion or RNA encoders.

Evidence: the best result so far is image-only, multiprofile, ResNet50 with transformer aggregation (config_016, acc 0.653, F1 0.628). ResNet50 beat ViT-L by about 0.054 under the same transformer setup. Transformer aggregation was only slightly better than avgpool for ViT-L (0.599 vs 0.591). The one multimodal run (config_022, scGPT + ViT-L, avgpool, concat) scored 0.535, below its image-only counterpart (0.591), and scGPT RNA-only was weak (0.520). The main open question is whether adding RNA ever helps, or whether concat fusion simply dilutes a strong image signal. That rests on a single comparison made with the weaker image setup. Test: config_015 keeps the best image setup (multiprofile, ResNet50, transformer) and adds scGPT RNA with concat fusion. Against config_016, the only difference is adding the RNA branch. Against the earlier config_002 vs config_022 pair, it shows whether the multimodal penalty holds with a stronger backbone and aggregator. Why now: this answers the highest-value design question, multimodal vs image-only, at the current best operating point, so the result is useful either way. If RNA still hurts, the budget can go to image-side refinements (e.g., config_046 or single-profile ResNet). If it helps or matches, follow-ups on fusion type (config_049) and RNA encoder (config_050 or config_018) become well motivated.

1. Evidence: the best result so far is image-only ResNet50 with transformer aggregation (0.653 accuracy). Adding scGPT RNA with concat fusion (config_015) slightly lowered accuracy to 0.635. scGPT RNA-only was weak (0.520). Every RNA result so far uses scGPT, so it is unclear whether RNA adds little in general or whether scGPT is simply a poor RNA representation here. 2. Test: config_018 changes only the RNA encoder from scGPT to scVI. Everything else matches config_015 (multiprofile, ResNet50, transformer aggregation, concat fusion). This isolates the effect of RNA representation in the strongest region found so far. 3. Why now: this is the largest open uncertainty, and the answer decides where the remaining budget should go. If scVI closes or reverses the gap to image-only, RNA and multimodal fusion are worth exploring further. If it still trails, focus can shift to image-only refinements or fusion type with more confidence.

1) Evidence and uncertainty: ResNet50 with multiprofile transformer aggregation is the strongest setting so far. Image-only config_016 reached 0.653 accuracy, and multimodal scVI concat (config_018) reached 0.650, statistically indistinguishable. Concat fusion has not shown clear value from adding RNA, and weighted fusion has never been tested, so fusion is the largest open design choice. 2) What this tests: config_043 differs from config_018 only in fusion (weighted instead of concat). It therefore isolates whether learned modality weighting lets RNA add complementary signal, or at least avoid diluting the strong image features. 3) Why it is the best next experiment: it explores an untested dimension while staying in the highest-performing region, so it has good odds of a new best result. Either outcome is informative about whether multimodal fusion is worth pursuing over image-only models.

1. Evidence: The strongest setup so far is multiprofile + resnet50 + transformer aggregation. Image-only (config_016) reached 0.653 accuracy. Adding scVI RNA with concat fusion (config_018) gave 0.650, and adding scGPT RNA (config_015) gave 0.635. So the RNA encoder appears to matter, but no RNA representation has yet beaten image-only. The pca_n2000 RNA encoder has not been tested at all. Weighted fusion collapsed in its one trial (0.427), so concat is the safer fusion choice. 2. Test: This run keeps profile setting, image encoder, aggregation and fusion fixed at the best-known values and changes only the RNA encoder to pca_n2000. Compared with config_015 and config_018, it completes a clean three-way comparison of RNA encoders. Compared with config_016, it shows whether any RNA representation adds value over image-only. 3. Why now: It explores the one untested encoder while staying inside the best-performing region. It changes a single factor, so the result is directly interpretable. It also has a reasonable chance of beating the current best.

1) No experiments have been run, so there is no evidence yet about which design choices matter: modality, profile setting, RNA or image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. 2) config_051 (RNA-only, single-profile, scVI with 200 dimensions, no aggregation or fusion) is the simplest reasonable configuration. It sets a reference accuracy and F1. Later runs that change one factor can then be compared against it: adding images (e.g., config_045 or config_050), switching to multiprofile (config_042 for avgpool, config_002 for transformer), or changing the RNA encoder (config_038 for PCA, config_015 for scGPT). 3) Under a limited budget, starting with a cheap, low-complexity anchor avoids assuming that multimodal or multiprofile models are better. It makes every later experiment interpretable as a one-factor change, rather than starting from a complex configuration where any result would be hard to attribute.

1) Evidence: there is only one result so far. The RNA-only, single-profile scVI baseline (config_051) reached 0.713 accuracy and 0.695 F1, so nothing is yet known about which design choices matter. 2) What this tests: config_042 keeps the modality (RNA-only) and encoder (scvi_n200) fixed. It changes only the profile setting to multiprofile, using the simplest aggregation (avgpool). This gives a clean, one-factor test of whether aggregating multiple profiles helps, without confounding it with a more complex transformer aggregator, image features or fusion choices. 3) Why now: profile setting is a key structural decision that most remaining configurations depend on. Resolving it early with a minimal change gives the most interpretable information per experiment, and it tells us whether multiprofile variants such as transformer aggregation and multimodal fusion are worth pursuing next.

1. Evidence: With the scVI RNA-only setup, single-profile reached 0.713 accuracy (F1 0.695). Multi-profile with avgpool fell to 0.520 (F1 0.498). That large drop could mean multi-profile input is harmful in itself, or that avgpool is a poor way to combine profiles. Two runs cannot tell these apart. 2. Test: config_002 keeps model setting (RNA-only), profile setting (multi-profile) and encoder (scVI) fixed and changes only the aggregation, from avgpool to transformer. If accuracy recovers toward or above 0.71, avgpool was the bottleneck and multi-profile designs remain viable. If it stays near 0.52, the multi-profile setting itself is likely the problem. 3. Value: Most of the remaining search space uses multi-profile input with either avgpool or transformer aggregation, including many multimodal configurations. This one-variable comparison therefore tells us whether that large region deserves budget before we spend runs on encoder or image modality choices.

1. Evidence: all three runs so far are RNA-only with scvi_n200. The single-profile model is best (acc 0.713, F1 0.695). Multiprofile underperformed it with both aggregators: transformer reached 0.635 and avgpool only 0.520. So single-profile looks like the stronger setting for now. The biggest open question is whether imaging adds anything, since no image-based configuration has been tested. 2. Test: config_050 keeps the best configuration unchanged (single-profile, scvi_n200, no aggregation) and adds only a ResNet50 image encoder with simple concat fusion. Any change in accuracy or F1 can therefore be attributed to adding image features, not to profile setting or RNA encoder. 3. Why now: whether to fuse modalities shapes the rest of the search, since most untested configurations are multimodal. A one-variable comparison against the current best answers this efficiently. If fusion helps, it points toward exploiting multimodal single-profile variants. If it does not, the budget can shift to RNA encoder comparisons such as scgpt or pca_n2000 in the single-profile setting.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is single-profile RNA-only with scVI (0.713 accuracy, 0.695 F1). Multiprofile aggregation lowered accuracy (transformer 0.635, avgpool 0.520). Concat fusion with ResNet50 images in the single-profile setting failed badly (0.227). Every run so far has used scVI, so we do not know whether the RNA representation itself is a major factor. 2) Test: Keep the strongest setting (RNA-only, single-profile) and change only the RNA encoder to PCA with 2000 components. This isolates the effect of representation without the confounds of image features or fusion. 3) Why now: It exploits the best-performing direction while answering a key open design question with a clean one-factor comparison. A PCA result above or below scVI tells us whether to keep scVI or switch encoders in all later experiments, including any multimodal ones. That is a better use of the budget than more multimodal runs, which so far show strong negative evidence.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is the simplest model, RNA-only single-profile scVI (0.713 acc, 0.695 F1). The RNA encoder clearly matters: PCA in the same setting scored only 0.421. Multiprofile underperformed in both tests, though the transformer (0.635) beat avgpool (0.520). Multimodal concat with ResNet50 collapsed to 0.227. The scGPT encoder is still completely untested. 2) Test: Running scGPT in the best-performing setting changes only the RNA encoder. It shows whether a foundation-model representation beats scVI, which is the most influential design choice observed so far. 3) Why now: It extends the strongest configuration while removing the largest remaining uncertainty about RNA representation. It is a clean single-variable comparison. Its result will also tell us which RNA encoder to carry into later multiprofile and fusion experiments. Questions about weighted fusion or image-only signal are better answered once the best RNA backbone is known.

1) Evidence: scVI single-profile RNA-only is the clear leader (0.713 acc / 0.695 F1). Adding ResNet50 images with concat fusion (config_050) collapsed performance to 0.227. That collapse could come from concat fusion letting weak image features swamp the RNA signal, or from ResNet50 features being harmful in general. This is a single result, so it should not yet be read as proof that multimodal models fail. 2) This experiment keeps everything from config_050 fixed (scVI, ResNet50, single-profile) and changes only the fusion from concat to weighted. If weighted fusion recovers to near or above the RNA-only baseline, fusion was the problem and multimodal models remain viable. If it stays poor, the image features themselves are the likely problem, and image-only or ViT-L tests become the logical next step. 3) It is the best next use of the budget because it is a clean one-variable comparison of a design choice that affects every multimodal configuration, which is most of the remaining options. It also has a reasonable chance of matching or beating the current best, since a learned weighting can down-weight an uninformative modality.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is RNA-only single-profile scVI (0.713 accuracy). Adding ResNet50 image features lowered accuracy, to 0.619 with weighted fusion and 0.227 with concat. The image modality has never been tested alone, so it is unclear whether the images carry little signal or whether the fusion methods are the problem. 2. Test: Image-only, single-profile, ResNet50 isolates how much signal ResNet50 image features carry, using the same image encoder and profile setting as the multimodal runs. 3. Why now: A weak result would suggest images are mostly noise, so the search should focus on RNA, especially aggregation (transformer beat avgpool). A moderate or strong result would support further work on fusion and image encoders (ViT-L). Either way, this one run settles a key uncertainty that affects a large share of the remaining configurations.

1) Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is RNA-only single-profile scVI (0.713 acc, 0.695 F1). Adding ResNet50 images with weighted fusion lowered accuracy to 0.619, and concat fusion collapsed to 0.227. Multiprofile aggregation also hurt RNA, though transformer (0.635) beat avgpool (0.520). Image-only ResNet50 reached 0.535. The ImageNet ViT-L image encoder has never been tested, yet it appears in about half of the remaining configurations, so the quality of the image representation is the largest unresolved design choice. 2) What this tests: config_046 is image-only, single-profile ViT-L, which differs from config_040 (image-only ResNet50) only in the image encoder. It therefore isolates whether ViT-L gives a stronger image representation, without fusion or aggregation effects mixed in. 3) Why it is the best next experiment: If ViT-L clearly beats ResNet50, multimodal weighted fusion with scVI and ViT-L (config_011) becomes a credible way to surpass the RNA-only baseline. If it does not, most ViT-L multimodal configurations can be deprioritized, which saves budget either way.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is the simplest model, scVI RNA-only single-profile (0.713 accuracy, 0.695 F1). For multiprofile RNA, transformer aggregation clearly beat avgpool (0.635 vs 0.520). For multimodal single-profile, weighted fusion far outperformed concat (0.619 vs 0.227), though it still trailed RNA-only. The two image encoders performed about the same on their own (0.535 vs 0.532). 2. Test: This configuration pairs the best-performing choices, transformer aggregation and weighted fusion, in a multiprofile multimodal model with scVI and ResNet50. Compared with config_045, it adds multiprofile with transformer aggregation. Compared with config_002, it adds the image modality through weighted fusion. It is still a two-variable change against each anchor, so if it underperforms we cannot tell which addition caused it. 3. Why now: Whether multiprofile multimodal modeling can beat the simple RNA-only baseline is the main open question about the whole multimodal and multiprofile direction. Answering it is more valuable than swapping image encoders, which showed no difference on their own. It also stays within the configuration space the evidence favors.

1. Evidence: no experiments have been run yet, so there is no information on whether modality, encoder, profile setting, aggregation or fusion matters, or what accuracy level is achievable. 2. Test: config_033 (RNA-only, single-profile, PCA with 2000 components, no aggregation or fusion) is the simplest configuration available. It sets a reference baseline. Each later comparison can then change one factor against it: image-only (config_006/014), multimodal fusion (config_001/018), multiprofile aggregation (config_026/048) or learned RNA encoders (config_031/036). 3. Why now: without an anchor, gains from more complex multimodal or multiprofile models cannot be read reliably. A cheap, interpretable baseline makes every later experiment more informative under the limited budget, and it guards against assuming complexity helps.

1. Evidence: only one result exists. The RNA-only, single-profile PCA baseline (config_033) reached 0.328 accuracy and 0.288 F1. We do not yet know whether imaging adds any signal, and modality is likely the most consequential design choice. 2. Test: config_001 keeps the same RNA encoder (pca_n2000) and profile setting (singleprofile), and adds an image encoder (imagenet_vit_l) through simple concat fusion. Comparing it with config_033 isolates the effect of adding the image modality. 3. Why now: this one-factor change answers the highest-level question first, whether multimodal input helps at all. That answer decides whether later budget should go to fusion, image-encoder and multiprofile variants, or to RNA-side improvements. Concat is the simplest fusion, so it is a clean first test, and later image-only runs can help attribute any gain.

Evidence: the multimodal PCA+ViT-L concat model (0.586 acc, 0.574 F1) far outperforms RNA-only PCA (0.328 acc). This shows the image modality adds a lot, but we cannot yet tell whether fusion helps or whether images alone explain the gain. What it tests: image-only ViT-L in the single-profile setting differs from config_001 only in removing RNA. It therefore isolates RNA's contribution to the multimodal result. Why now: whether multimodal fusion beats a strong unimodal image baseline is the most important unresolved design question. Its answer decides whether later budget should go to fusion, aggregation and RNA encoder choices, or mainly to image-based and multiprofile extensions.

Evidence: in single-profile mode, multimodal PCA plus ViT-L with concat fusion (config_001, acc 0.586, F1 0.574) clearly beats image-only ViT-L (0.519) and RNA-only PCA (0.328). Fusing the two modalities helps, and image features carry most of the signal. Profile setting is still completely untested, and it may be one of the most consequential design choices. Test: config_043 keeps the best configuration's encoders (PCA, ViT-L) and fusion (concat) and switches only to multiprofile. It uses avgpool, the simplest aggregation, so the comparison against config_001 mainly isolates whether multiprofile input helps. Why now: this exploits the strongest known configuration while answering a high-impact open question with a near-single-variable change. If multiprofile helps, later runs can compare transformer against avgpool aggregation (config_039) and weighted against concat fusion. If it does not, the budget can go to single-profile refinements such as encoder or fusion swaps.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is single-profile multimodal (PCA + ViT-L, concat) at 0.586 accuracy and 0.574 F1. Moving to multiprofile with avgpool, with every other choice the same, dropped performance to 0.471 / 0.442. That drop could come from the multiprofile setting itself or from avgpool, which may wash out useful information across profiles. This is the largest unresolved effect in the history. 2. Test: config_039 keeps PCA, ViT-L and concat fixed and changes only avgpool to transformer aggregation. If the transformer recovers or beats 0.586, multiprofile is still worth pursuing with learned aggregation. If it stays low, multiprofile can be deprioritized and the budget focused on single-profile encoder and fusion choices. 3. Why now: This one-variable comparison settles whether a whole branch of the search space (multiprofile configurations) deserves further budget. That is more valuable than a small exploit tweak such as a fusion or encoder swap in the single-profile setting.

1. Evidence: the single-profile multimodal model (PCA + ViT-L, concat; config_001) is best so far at 0.586 accuracy and 0.574 F1. It beats image-only (0.519) and RNA-only PCA (0.328). Both multiprofile variants scored lower (avgpool 0.471, transformer 0.331), so single-profile is the promising direction for now. The RNA branch looks weak with PCA, and the RNA encoder is still untested. 2. Test: config_032 keeps everything in config_001 the same (single-profile, ViT-L, concat) and swaps only the RNA encoder from PCA to scVI. This isolates whether a learned RNA representation adds more to fusion than PCA does. 3. Why now: it exploits the best context while testing a major untested design choice with a single change. A gain would point to RNA representation as a key lever. No gain would suggest the RNA contribution is limited regardless of encoder.

1) Evidence: the best result so far is the single-profile multimodal model with PCA RNA and ViT-L image features using concat fusion (config_001, acc 0.586, F1 0.574). It beats image-only (0.519) and RNA-only (0.328), so fusing both modalities seems to help. Multiprofile aggregation did worse in both forms tried (avgpool 0.471, transformer 0.332). Swapping PCA for scVI also lowered accuracy (0.523). Fusion strategy is the one major design choice not yet tested: every multimodal run used concat. 2) This experiment keeps config_001 fixed and changes only concat to weighted fusion. Any difference can therefore be attributed to the fusion method. 3) Under a limited budget, this one-factor change exploits the strongest configuration while closing the largest untested gap. Weighted fusion may also cope better with the weaker RNA modality. Either outcome tells us whether fusion should be explored further, for example in the multiprofile settings.

Evidence: the best result so far is config_028 (single-profile, PCA RNA, ViT-L image, weighted fusion) at 0.725 accuracy and 0.685 F1. Switching concat to weighted fusion gave a large gain (0.586 to 0.725). Image-only (0.519) far outperforms RNA-only (0.328), so the image representation appears to be the main source of signal. However, every experiment so far has used ViT-L, so the effect of the image encoder is still unknown. Test: config_008 changes only the image encoder (ViT-L to ResNet50) and keeps the rest of the best configuration fixed. This isolates the image-encoder effect within the strongest setup. Why now: because image features drive most of the performance, the choice of image encoder is the most important design decision left untested. This one-variable comparison either confirms ViT-L as the backbone to keep exploiting or reveals a better option. It is more informative than retrying multiprofile variants, which have performed poorly, or testing RNA-encoder swaps, which matter less given RNA's weak standalone signal.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_028 (single-profile, PCA + ViT-L, weighted fusion; accuracy 0.725, F1 0.685). Switching fusion from concat (config_001, 0.586) to weighted was the largest gain observed. Among RNA encoders, scVI underperformed PCA under concat (0.523 vs 0.586), and scGPT has never been tested, so RNA representation is the biggest remaining unknown. Multiprofile runs have only been tried with concat and did poorly (0.471 avgpool, 0.332 transformer). 2) Test: config_044 keeps the best setup and changes only the RNA encoder to scGPT. This isolates whether a pretrained foundation-model RNA representation improves on PCA when paired with the strongest fusion. 3) Why now: it explores a completely untested design choice while staying anchored to the best-known setup, so it could yield a new best. Even if it does not, it shows whether RNA representation matters under weighted fusion. Testing whether weighted fusion rescues multiprofile (config_004) is a sensible follow-up, but current evidence on multiprofile is negative, so resolving the unexplored encoder is the better use of this experiment.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_028 (PCA + ViT-L, single profile, weighted fusion; 0.725 accuracy, 0.685 F1). Weighted fusion clearly beat concat with the same encoders (0.725 vs 0.586). PCA has beaten scVI and scGPT so far. Multiprofile has only been tried with concat fusion. There it underperformed single profile (avgpool 0.471, transformer 0.332 vs 0.586). That leaves open whether multiprofile fails on its own or only fails with weak concat fusion. 2) Test: config_004 keeps the best encoders and weighted fusion and moves to the multiprofile setting with avgpool aggregation. Avgpool was the better multiprofile aggregation in earlier runs. This isolates the profile-setting question under the strongest known fusion. 3) Why now: Profile setting is an important design choice whose current evidence is confounded with the weaker fusion method. The encoder evidence already consistently favors PCA, so another encoder run would teach less. This run is a logical extension of the best configuration and also directly reduces a key uncertainty.

1) No experiments have been run, so we know nothing yet about representation, profile setting, aggregation or fusion. 2) config_002 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, concat) is a central anchor. Each design factor can be isolated from it with one change: fusion (config_027), aggregation (config_021), RNA encoder (config_011, config_017), image encoder (config_030), profile setting (config_024) and modality (config_001 image-only, config_009 RNA-only). 3) Starting here gives a reference point for controlled one-factor comparisons and a plausible estimate of how well a full-featured model performs. Later unimodal and single-profile runs can then test whether the added complexity is actually needed, without assuming it is.

1. Evidence: only one experiment has run. It is a multimodal, multiprofile model (scVI n200 + ImageNet ViT-L, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) reaching 0.512 accuracy and 0.477 F1. We have no reference point, so we don't know whether adding RNA helps. 2. Test: config_001 removes only the RNA branch and fusion. The image encoder (ViT-L), the multiprofile setting and the transformer aggregation stay the same. This isolates RNA's contribution to the multimodal result. 3. Why now: whether multimodality adds value is a top-level design question. If image-only matches or beats 0.512, later experiments can focus on image encoders and aggregation instead of spending budget on RNA encoders and fusion variants. If it underperforms, that supports continuing to explore the multimodal space. A single-factor ablation is the most informative use of the next experiment.

1. Evidence: Image-only (ViT-L, multiprofile, transformer) reached 0.678 accuracy. Adding scVI RNA with concat fusion, with everything else fixed, dropped accuracy to 0.512 and F1 by a similar amount. We cannot tell whether the drop comes from weak RNA signal (scVI features) or from naive concat fusion letting a noisy modality dominate. 2. Test: config_009 is the RNA-only counterpart (scvi_n200, multiprofile, transformer). It completes a clean three-way modality ablation under the same profile and aggregation settings. If RNA alone is far below image, the problem is RNA quality, and later experiments should look at other RNA encoders (scGPT, PCA) or weighted fusion. If RNA alone is reasonably strong, the failure points to concat fusion, and weighted fusion (config_027) becomes the logical next test. 3. Why now: it changes only one factor and resolves the main uncertainty about whether to invest in the multimodal direction at all. That makes it the most informative use of the next experiment, even though it is unlikely to be the top performer.

1) Evidence: Both unimodal transformer-multiprofile models do well (RNA scVI 0.688, image ViT-L 0.678). Combining exactly those encoders with concat fusion drops sharply to 0.512, with F1 also lower (0.477). So the multimodal failure most likely comes from how the modalities are combined, not from weak encoders. 2) Test: config_027 keeps everything from config_002 the same (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI, ViT-L, transformer) and changes only fusion from concat to weighted. This isolates whether concat fusion caused the drop, and whether a learned weighting can recover or exceed unimodal performance. 3) Why now: Whether fusion can make multimodal models competitive is the key unresolved question, and it shapes how roughly two-thirds of the remaining space (the multimodal configs) should be explored. A single-factor comparison against an existing baseline is the most interpretable use of one experiment. 1. Evidence: with multiprofile transformer aggregation, RNA-only (scVI, 0.688 acc) and image-only (ViT-L, 0.678 acc) clearly beat both multimodal variants (concat 0.512, weighted 0.471). Why now: the profile setting is a structural choice that affects most of the remaining configurations, since many are multiprofile. Settling it early with a clean one-variable comparison is the most informative use of the next experiment. The result can then guide follow-ups on aggregation (config_006), RNA encoder, or adding images.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: Only RNA-only PCA models have been tested so far. Moving from singleprofile to multiprofile with avgpool gave a modest accuracy gain (0.507 to 0.523) and a larger F1 gain (0.455 to 0.508). That makes multiprofile/avgpool with PCA the current best base. The biggest open question is whether the image modality adds anything, and nothing tested so far addresses it. 2. What this tests: config_032 keeps the best base unchanged (PCA RNA encoder, multiprofile, avgpool) and adds a ResNet50 image encoder with simple concat fusion. Concat is the least complex way to add the image, so any change in accuracy or F1 mostly reflects the effect of the image itself. 3. Why this is the best next experiment: whether multimodal helps decides how a large share of the remaining configurations should be prioritized, so answering it is worth more than first tuning aggregation (transformer) or the RNA encoder (scVI/scGPT). A clear gain would justify exploring image encoders and fusion types next; no gain or a drop would steer the budget back toward RNA-only refinements.

1. Evidence: Multiprofile avgpool RNA-only (PCA) reached 0.523 accuracy. Adding ResNet50 images with concat fusion raised this to 0.579 accuracy and 0.563 F1, a gain of about 5.6 points. We have not yet tested images alone, so we cannot tell whether that gain comes from combining the two modalities or simply from the image features being stronger. 2. This experiment runs image-only ResNet50 with multiprofile avgpool, matching config_032 exactly except that RNA is removed. If it reaches about 0.58 or more, RNA adds little and later experiments should focus on image encoders. If it clearly falls below 0.579, the two modalities are complementary, and tuning fusion, RNA encoder and aggregation is justified. 3. This baseline changes only one factor and determines how the rest of the limited budget should be split between image-focused and fusion-focused experiments. That makes it more informative right now than small variations on fusion or aggregation.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is multimodal, multiprofile, PCA RNA encoder, ResNet50 image encoder, avgpool aggregation and concat fusion (config_032: accuracy 0.579, F1 0.563). It clearly beats RNA-only (0.523) and image-only (0.494). Multiprofile with avgpool gave only a modest accuracy gain over singleprofile for RNA (0.523 vs 0.507), though F1 improved more. So it is still unclear whether simple averaging is limiting the benefit of multiple profiles. 2. Test: This experiment keeps everything in config_032 fixed and changes only avgpool to transformer aggregation. It isolates whether learned aggregation across profiles improves on mean pooling in the current best setup. 3. Why now: Aggregation affects every multiprofile model, so the answer will guide many later choices. It is a controlled one-factor extension of the strongest configuration, so it can both improve performance and reduce a key uncertainty before testing encoder or fusion variants.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_032 (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA RNA, ResNet50 image, avgpool, concat) at 0.579 accuracy and 0.563 F1. It clearly beats both unimodal multiprofile baselines (RNA 0.523, image 0.494). Swapping avgpool for transformer aggregation lowered accuracy to 0.519, so avgpool currently looks preferable. 1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is config_035 (pca_n2000 + imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, concat; acc 0.632, F1 0.607). Replacing resnet50 with ViT-L gave a clear gain (0.579 to 0.632), and avgpool beat transformer aggregation with resnet50. Multimodal fusion also beat both unimodal baselines. However, every experiment so far has used pca_n2000, so the effect of the RNA encoder is completely unknown. That makes it the largest remaining uncertainty among the main design choices. 2. What this tests: config_020 changes only the RNA encoder (pca_n2000 to scvi_n200) and keeps the best image encoder, aggregation and fusion fixed. This isolates whether a learned probabilistic RNA representation improves on PCA in the strongest setting. 3. Why it is the best next use of budget: It is a clean single-factor comparison against the current best, so it is both exploitative and informative. If scVI helps, it points to a new best direction. If it does not, PCA is confirmed as a strong default and the remaining budget can go to fusion type, scGPT, or image-only ViT ablations.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_035 (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA RNA, ViT-L image, avgpool, concat) at 0.632 accuracy and 0.607 F1. Swapping ResNet50 for ViT-L improved results, and avgpool beat the transformer. Every experiment so far has used concat fusion, so we know nothing yet about how fusion type matters. 2. Test: config_021 changes only the fusion, from concat to weighted, and keeps every other setting of the best configuration fixed. This directly isolates the effect of fusion. 3. Why now: It answers an important unexplored design question with a clean single-variable comparison. It is also a strong exploitation candidate, since weighted fusion may beat the current best. 1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_035 (PCA + ViT-L, avgpool, concat; acc 0.632, F1 0.607). The RNA encoder choice clearly matters. Swapping PCA for scVI in the same setup collapsed performance to 0.208 (config_020). scGPT, however, has never been tested in any setting, so it is the largest unresolved gap in the representation axis. 2) Test: config_022 changes only the RNA encoder, from PCA to scGPT, and keeps everything else from the best configuration. 1) Evidence: The best result so far is scGPT + ViT-L with avgpool and concat fusion (0.721 acc, 0.681 F1). Swapping in PCA RNA gives 0.632, and swapping in scVI collapses to 0.208. So the RNA representation appears to drive large differences. However, scGPT has never been tested without images, so we cannot tell whether the gain comes from scGPT alone or from its fusion with ViT-L. 2) Test: config_036 runs scGPT RNA-only with multiprofile and avgpool, the same setting as the best model minus the image branch. It also parallels the existing PCA RNA-only multiprofile run (0.523). This isolates both the scGPT-versus-PCA representation effect without images and the added value of the ViT-L image modality on top of scGPT. 3) Why now: This is a single-factor ablation of the leading configuration. It shows whether further budget should go into image and fusion variants (if the multimodal gain is large) or into RNA-only and aggregation refinements of scGPT (if scGPT alone is competitive).

1) No experiments have been run yet, so there is no evidence about which design choice matters: modality, profile setting, RNA or image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. 2) config_005 (multimodal, single-profile, scVI RNA, ResNet50 image, concat fusion) is a central reference point that differs by exactly one factor from many other options. These include RNA-only (config_004), image-only (config_002), weighted fusion (config_001), the ViT-L image encoder (config_006), scGPT (config_011) or PCA (config_047) RNA encoders, and multiprofile with avgpool (config_019). 1. Evidence and uncertainty: Only one experiment is complete. config_005 (multimodal, singleprofile, scVI_n200 + ResNet50, concat) scored 0.525 accuracy and 0.498 F1. We have no evidence yet about any major design axis. 2. What this tests: config_019 keeps the same encoders and concat fusion but switches from singleprofile to multiprofile with avgpool. Avgpool is the simplest aggregation, and some aggregation is required for multiprofile, so this is the closest controlled comparison available. It shows whether pooling multiple profiles per sample improves on the single-profile baseline. 3. Why it is the best next experiment: Profile setting is likely one of the most influential and costly choices, and it decides which half of the search space to prioritize. Measuring it first gives the most useful guidance for later choices. Those include encoder swaps (e.g., ViT-L vs ResNet50), fusion type, transformer aggregation, and unimodal ablations.

1. Evidence: with scVI_n200 + ResNet50 + concat fusion, singleprofile reached 0.525 accuracy (F1 0.498). Multiprofile with avgpool aggregation reached only 0.411 (F1 0.378). That is a large drop, but it rests on one comparison, and the cause is unclear. Multiprofile itself may hurt, or simple average pooling may wash out informative per-profile signal. 2. Test: config_023 keeps the same encoders, multiprofile setting and concat fusion, and changes only the aggregation from avgpool to transformer. This isolates whether the multiprofile deficit comes from the aggregation method. 3. Why now: multiprofile configurations make up most of the remaining search space. Ruling them in or out early, and learning whether learned aggregation matters, shapes the rest of the budget more than tuning encoders or fusion in the singleprofile branch. If transformer aggregation closes the gap, multiprofile remains a promising direction. If it does not, the evidence favors concentrating on singleprofile and running modality ablations next.

1. Evidence: Within the scVI + ResNet50 + concat family, the single-profile model (config_005) reached 0.525 accuracy and 0.498 F1. Both multi-profile variants were clearly worse: avgpool scored 0.411 and transformer scored 0.427. This suggests single-profile is the stronger setting for now. However, we have no unimodal baseline, so we do not know whether the image branch actually adds anything. 2. Test: config_004 is RNA-only, single-profile, with the scVI encoder. It is a single-change ablation of config_005 that removes only the image branch. Its result shows how much of the 0.525 comes from the RNA side. If it scores about the same or higher, multimodal fusion is not adding value. If it scores clearly lower, the image modality contributes, and tuning the image encoder or the fusion method becomes worthwhile. 3. Value: Whether multimodal helps over unimodal is a basic design question that shapes the rest of the search. It is better to settle it before spending budget on secondary choices such as fusion type or image encoder.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is single-profile multimodal (scVI + ResNet50, concat) at 0.525 accuracy and 0.498 F1. Single-profile RNA-only scVI reached only 0.260 accuracy. Both multiprofile variants were worse (0.41 and 0.43), so single-profile looks like the stronger setting for now. The large gap between RNA-only and multimodal suggests the image modality drives most of the performance. However, we have not tested image-only, so we cannot tell whether RNA adds anything beyond images. 2. Test: The single-profile image-only ResNet50 run differs from config_005 only by removing RNA, and from config_004 only by swapping the modality. It directly isolates the image contribution and the value of fusion. 3. Why now: This result decides where the remaining budget should go. If image-only roughly matches 0.525, we should prioritise image encoders (e.g., ViT-L) and image-only or aggregation variants. If it falls clearly short, fusion is adding real value, and testing RNA encoders and fusion types within multimodal is justified.

Evidence: image-only singleprofile ResNet50 (config_002) is clearly best at 0.706 accuracy and 0.667 F1. Adding scVI RNA by concat fusion lowered performance to 0.525, RNA-only was weak at 0.260, and the multiprofile multimodal variants were lower still at about 0.41-0.43. The image signal dominates, yet the image encoder has never been varied, so it is the main untested design choice. Question: does swapping ResNet50 for ImageNet ViT-L help or hurt, with everything else held at the best configuration? This changes only one factor from config_002. Why now: it isolates the effect of the image representation, the factor most likely to matter given the results so far. It may also directly improve on the current best. The answer tells us which image encoder to carry into later tests of profile setting, aggregation and fusion, which is a better use of the limited budget than more multimodal or RNA-heavy variants.

1. Evidence: Image-only models perform best so far (ViT-L 0.721, ResNet50 0.706). Adding scVI RNA by concat fusion lowered accuracy sharply (0.525), and RNA-only was weak (0.260). Multiprofile multimodal runs were worse still (avgpool 0.411, transformer 0.427), but those runs also included the weak RNA branch. So we cannot tell whether multiprofile aggregation itself hurts or whether the RNA modality was dragging those results down. 2. Test: This keeps the best setup (image-only, ViT-L) and changes only the profile setting, from single to multiprofile, using transformer aggregation. Transformer slightly outperformed avgpool in the multimodal comparison on both accuracy and F1. The run isolates the effect of multiprofile aggregation on the strongest modality and may improve on 0.721. 3. Why now: Profile setting is a major design choice that remains confounded. Resolving it on the leading branch has both exploration value and a plausible chance of a new best. Testing fusion variants for the weak RNA branch is less likely to pay off right now.

1) Evidence: image-only single-profile models are clearly best (ViT-L 0.721, ResNet50 0.706). Adding scVI RNA by concat fusion drops ResNet50 single-profile accuracy sharply, to 0.525. RNA-only scVI is weak (0.260). Multiprofile variants have been consistently worse than single-profile ones. The main open question is why multimodal fusion hurts. It could be the concat fusion design, or the RNA signal itself may degrade predictions. 2) Config_001 changes only the fusion, from concat to weighted, while keeping the config_005 setup otherwise identical (single-profile, scVI, ResNet50). This isolates the fusion effect. If weighted fusion recovers most of the image-only performance or exceeds it, then fusion design matters and multimodal search is worth continuing. If it stays near 0.525, the RNA modality or encoder is the likely bottleneck. 3) This single-variable comparison resolves a key design choice before more budget goes into multimodal configurations, such as ViT-L pairings or other RNA encoders. It avoids changing several factors at once.

1. Evidence: Single-profile image-only models are clearly best (ViT-L 0.721, ResNet50 0.706). Adding scVI RNA features lowered accuracy (concat 0.525, weighted 0.471), and scVI RNA-only reached just 0.260. Multiprofile settings were worse across every combination tried. The main open question is whether RNA is truly uninformative here or whether the scVI n200 embedding is simply a poor representation. 2. Test: config_043 keeps the RNA-only single-profile setup of config_004 and changes only the encoder, from scVI n200 to PCA n2000. This isolates the effect of RNA representation without confounds from fusion, aggregation, or the image encoder. 3. Why now: If PCA RNA is much stronger than 0.26, multimodal models using PCA or scGPT with ViT-L become worth testing and could beat image-only. Either result prunes a large part of the space, which makes this the most efficient use of the next experiment.

1. Evidence: Single-profile image-only models are clearly best so far (ViT-L 0.721, ResNet50 0.706). Multiprofile settings have consistently hurt performance. Multimodal models built on scVI have underperformed image-only, plausibly because scVI is a weak RNA representation: RNA-only scVI scored 0.260, while RNA-only PCA scored 0.523. The open question is whether multimodality itself is unhelpful or whether the weak RNA encoder caused the drop. 2. Test: config_012 adds PCA RNA features to the best image-only setup (ViT-L, single profile) with concat fusion. Compared directly against config_036, it isolates whether a stronger RNA representation adds complementary signal to the best image model. 3. Rationale: This is both exploitative and informative. It combines the best-performing image encoder, profile setting and RNA encoder, and either outcome answers the most consequential remaining design question: whether adding RNA is worth pursuing at all once the RNA representation is strong.

1. No experiments have been run yet, so we know nothing about which design choices matter. 2. Config_009 (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA-2000 RNA, ResNet50 image, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) is a strong central anchor. Almost every design factor can be isolated from it with one-change comparisons: config_002 changes aggregation to avgpool, config_028 changes fusion to weighted, config_007 changes the image encoder to ViT-L, config_013 and config_039 change the RNA encoder to scVI and scGPT, config_005 switches to single-profile, and config_008 and config_004 drop to RNA-only and image-only. 3. Starting from this hub with simple, standard components gives a reasonable baseline. 1) Evidence and uncertainty: Only one experiment is complete. config_009 (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA RNA + ResNet50 image, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) reached 0.260 accuracy and 0.222 F1. A single result cannot show which components drive performance. The most basic open question is whether the image modality adds value over RNA alone. 2) What this tests: config_008 keeps everything the same (multiprofile, PCA_n2000, transformer aggregation) but drops the image encoder and fusion. Comparing it with config_009 isolates the contribution of the ResNet50 image features and concat fusion. 3) Why this is the best next use of budget: Whether multimodal fusion beats a unimodal baseline determines whether later budget should go to tuning image encoders and fusion, or to RNA representation, profile setting and aggregation. It is a clean one-factor comparison. Its result is informative either way, and we should not assume the multimodal model is better.

1. Evidence: The RNA-only model (multiprofile, pca_n2000, transformer) reached 0.713 accuracy and 0.695 F1. Adding resnet50 images with concat fusion, with everything else the same, dropped this to 0.260 accuracy and 0.222 F1. So adding images in this way badly hurt performance, but we cannot yet tell why. Either the image features carry little signal, or naive concatenation is drowning out or destabilizing the strong RNA signal. 2. Test: config_028 matches config_009 exactly except that fusion is weighted instead of concat. This isolates the effect of the fusion strategy. If weighted fusion recovers performance near or above RNA-only, the problem was concat fusion and multimodal models remain worth exploring. If it stays low, the resnet50 image branch itself is likely harmful, and the search should favor RNA-only models or other image encoders. 3. Why now: This is a single-variable change on the most important open question, whether and how to fuse modalities. That decision determines which large part of the remaining space deserves the limited budget.

1) Evidence and uncertainty: RNA-only (pca_n2000, multiprofile, transformer) is the best result so far at 0.713 accuracy and 0.695 F1. Adding resnet50 images lowered accuracy, slightly with weighted fusion (0.678) and sharply with concat (0.260). The open question is why: either the resnet50 image features carry little signal for this task, or the image signal is real but the fusion step is failing to use it. 2) What this tests: an image-only resnet50 run under the same multiprofile transformer setting measures how much signal the image branch has on its own, with fusion removed from the picture. 3) Why it is the best next run: if image-only is near chance, many resnet50 multimodal configurations can be deprioritized and the budget can shift to RNA encoders, aggregation and the imagenet_vit_l encoder. If image-only is reasonably strong, the problem lies in fusion, and improving fusion becomes the priority. Multimodal weighted fusion came close but did not exceed it (0.678). Concat fusion nearly collapsed (0.260). Image-only was clearly weaker (0.537). 1. Evidence: The RNA encoder has the largest observed effect so far. Within RNA-only multiprofile transformer models, pca_n2000 scored 0.713 accuracy and 0.695 F1, while scvi_n200 scored 0.586 and 0.574. RNA-only PCA is also the best model overall, ahead of weighted-fusion multimodal (0.678), image-only (0.537) and concat fusion (0.260, which looks broken). The main untested option on this key axis is scGPT. 2. Test: config_017 keeps the leading setup fixed (rna_only, multiprofile, transformer) and changes only the RNA encoder to scgpt. This cleanly completes the three-way encoder comparison. 3. Why now: Representation appears to be the dominant design factor, so settling the best RNA encoder first has the highest information value. It could also directly beat the current best. Aggregation (config_018) and profile setting (config_047) remain important single-factor ablations for later. They are best run once we know which encoder to build on.

1. Evidence: Every run so far is multiprofile with transformer aggregation. The best results are RNA-only scGPT (0.721 acc) and PCA (0.713 acc), while scVI is clearly weaker (0.586). Adding images has not helped yet: concat fusion collapsed (0.26), and weighted fusion (0.678) still trailed RNA-only. Profile setting is completely untested, and it is a major design axis. 2. Test: config_020 keeps the strongest RNA-only scGPT setup and switches only multiprofile to singleprofile (aggregation then drops out as a consequence). This shows whether multiprofile aggregation actually adds value. 3. Why now: Results suggest RNA drives performance, so knowing whether multiprofile helps decides where to spend the remaining budget. If singleprofile matches it, simpler models become competitive. If it falls clearly behind, I can focus on multiprofile aggregation and fusion variants (avgpool, scGPT-based weighted fusion).

1) Evidence: the two best runs are both RNA-only, multiprofile, with transformer aggregation: scGPT (0.721 acc) and PCA (0.713 acc). Multiprofile clearly beat single-profile for scGPT (0.721 vs 0.650). Adding images has not helped so far. Weighted fusion fell to 0.678 and concat fusion collapsed to 0.26. 1. Evidence and uncertainty: Among RNA-only multiprofile transformer models, scGPT (0.721) and PCA (0.713) are best. Transformer aggregation clearly beats avgpool, and multiprofile beats singleprofile for scGPT. Fusion is the main open question. With PCA + ResNet50, weighted fusion (0.678) still trailed RNA-only PCA (0.713), and concat fusion collapsed (0.260). Image-only ResNet50 was weaker (0.537). 2. What this tests: config_034 swaps only the RNA encoder in the weighted-fusion multimodal setting (scGPT instead of PCA, versus config_028). It also pairs directly with config_017, the best model so far, which differs only by adding ResNet50 images through weighted fusion. This shows whether the fusion penalty seen with PCA persists with a stronger RNA representation, or whether scGPT combines better with image features. 3. Why it is the best next use: it exploits the strongest component choices (scGPT, multiprofile, transformer, the non-collapsing weighted fusion) while changing one factor at a time against two existing baselines. Either outcome is informative: it decides whether multimodal fusion deserves more budget or whether the search should concentrate on RNA-only models and on image-encoder quality (e.g., ViT-L).

1. Evidence: The best results so far are RNA-only, multiprofile, transformer models (scGPT 0.721 accuracy, PCA 0.713). Within scGPT, transformer aggregation clearly beat avgpool, and multiprofile beat singleprofile. Every multimodal run has fallen below the best RNA-only result. 1. Evidence and uncertainty: there is only one result so far. config_011 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI, ViT-L, avgpool, concat) reached 0.536 accuracy and 0.516 F1. 1) Evidence: RNA-only (scVI, multiprofile, avgpool) reached 0.713 accuracy. Image-only (ViT-L) reached 0.537. Multimodal concat with the same encoders reached 0.536, which is essentially image-only performance. 1. Evidence: The RNA-only model (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool) is the clear leader at 0.713 accuracy and 0.695 F1. Image-only ViT-L is weak at 0.537. Concat fusion performs no better than image-only (0.536), and weighted fusion (0.650) recovers only part of the gap to RNA-only. So the RNA representation appears to drive performance. However, only one RNA encoder has been tested, so the biggest open question is whether scVI is the right representation. 2. Test: config_033 changes only the RNA encoder, from scvi_n200 to pca_n2000, while keeping RNA-only, multiprofile and avgpool fixed. This isolates the effect of RNA representation against the current best model. 3. Why now: The RNA encoder choice affects every RNA-only and multimodal configuration, so this answer will guide most remaining experiments. Aggregation (transformer) and profile-setting ablations can follow once the encoder is settled.

1) Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is RNA-only scVI with multiprofile avgpool (config_032, acc 0.713, F1 0.695). 1) Evidence: The best result so far is RNA-only scVI with multiprofile avgpool (0.713 accuracy, 0.695 F1). 1. Evidence: The best result so far is RNA-only, multiprofile, scVI with avgpool (0.713 accuracy, 0.695 F1). Within that same setting, PCA scored much lower (0.514), so the choice of RNA representation clearly matters. scGPT, the third RNA encoder, has never been tested. Other findings are less relevant to this question: multimodal fusion (0.536 with concat, 0.650 with weighted) has not beaten RNA-only, while transformer aggregation (0.227) and single-profile (0.328) performed poorly. 2. Test: Swapping only the RNA encoder to scGPT in the best-performing setting isolates the encoder effect. It shows whether scVI's lead holds or whether scGPT is better. 3. Why now: This fills the largest remaining gap on the most influential design choice, using the strongest known setup. Either outcome guides later multimodal runs, since it tells us which RNA encoder to pair with image features, so the result is useful whether or not scGPT wins.

1) Evidence: RNA-only multiprofile avgpool is the strongest setting so far, with scVI at 0.713 and scGPT at 0.706. Adding imagenet_vit_l images lowered accuracy, to 0.650 with weighted fusion and 0.536 with concat. Image-only vit_l reached just 0.537, close to concat's 0.536, which suggests concat fusion is dominated by a weak image signal. The resnet50 image encoder has never been tested, so it is unclear whether the image modality is weak in itself or only weak under vit_l. 2) This run is image-only, multiprofile, avgpool with resnet50. It differs from config_028 only in the image encoder, so it directly measures whether resnet50 gives a better image representation. 3) This one result decides which branch of roughly half the remaining search space is worth spending budget on. If resnet50 clearly beats 0.537, multimodal resnet50 configs (e.g., config_041 with weighted fusion) become promising follow-ups. If it does not, the budget should go to refining RNA-only and scGPT variants, accepting that images add little.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is RNA-only multiprofile avgpool with scVI (0.713 accuracy; scGPT is close at 0.706). Among image-only models, ResNet50 (0.639) clearly beats ViT-L (0.537). Both multimodal runs used the weaker ViT-L encoder. Weighted fusion (0.650) beat concat (0.536), but both fell below RNA-only, so it is unclear whether fusion is hurting or the image encoder is the limit. 2. Test: This run keeps scVI, multiprofile, avgpool and weighted fusion fixed and swaps only the image encoder to ResNet50. That isolates the image representation's effect inside multimodal fusion and checks whether a stronger image signal lets fusion beat the RNA-only baseline. 3. Why now: It is a single-variable change built on the best-supported settings (avgpool aggregation, the scVI encoder and weighted fusion). It has a realistic chance of a new best, and either outcome tells us whether multimodality is worth more budget.

1. Evidence: no experiments have been run, so there is no reference point for how much any design choice matters. 2. Test: this is the simplest configuration (RNA-only, single profile, PCA-2000 encoder, no aggregation or fusion). It sets a baseline for validation accuracy and F1. Later experiments can then change one factor at a time against it: RNA encoder (scVI, scGPT), profile setting (multiprofile with avgpool or transformer), modality (image-only, multimodal) and fusion type. 3. 1) Evidence: there is only one result so far, the single-profile RNA-only PCA baseline (config_001: accuracy 0.518, F1 0.484). It uses avgpool, the simplest aggregation, which multiprofile requires. This isolates whether pooling multiple profiles improves on single-profile input, without mixing in a new encoder, a new modality or a learned transformer aggregator. 3) Why now: profile setting affects every later branch (RNA-only, image-only and multimodal). 1. Evidence: Both completed runs are RNA-only with PCA features. Single-profile reached 0.518 accuracy and 0.484 F1. Multi-profile with avgpool reached 0.514 accuracy and 0.498 F1. Switching to multi-profile with simple pooling changed little, so profile setting does not look like a major lever for now. The biggest open question is whether the image modality adds anything at all. 2. Test: config_020 keeps config_001's single-profile setting and PCA RNA encoder and adds ImageNet ViT-L image features with simple concat fusion. Its result against config_001 directly measures what adding images contributes. 3. Why now: This is one of the most consequential open questions in the search space, since most remaining configurations are multimodal. Answering it early decides whether the remaining budget should go to fusion and aggregation choices or to RNA encoder choices within RNA-only models. Concat fusion and single-profile input keep confounders low, so a gain or loss can be attributed mainly to the added modality.

1) Evidence and uncertainty: The multimodal single-profile model (PCA + ImageNet ViT-L, concat; config_020) reached 0.619 accuracy and 0.610 F1. That is a large jump over RNA-only (about 0.51-0.52 accuracy for both single- and multi-profile), and multiprofile avgpool did little for RNA-only. It differs from config_020 only by removing the RNA branch, so it isolates the RNA contribution to the fusion result. If image-only matches about 0.62, RNA adds little and the search should focus on image encoders and aggregation. If it falls well short, fusion is genuinely useful and refining fusion (weighted fusion, multiprofile multimodal) is the better path. 3) Why now: this single controlled comparison resolves the most important open question, which modality drives performance. 1. Evidence: The best result so far is multimodal single-profile PCA + ViT-L with concat fusion (config_020, acc 0.619, F1 0.610). It beats image-only (0.591) and RNA-only (0.518), so fusion appears to help. The effect of multiprofile is still unclear. The only test, in RNA-only (config_022), changed accuracy slightly (-0.004) and F1 slightly (+0.014), which is too small to interpret, and it used the weakest modality. 2. Test: config_050 changes only the profile setting, from single-profile to multiprofile with avgpool, while keeping the RNA encoder, image encoder and concat fusion of the best configuration. This isolates the effect of multiprofile in the strongest setting. 3. Why now: Multiprofile and aggregation decide a large share of the remaining search space. 1. Evidence: Single-profile multimodal (ViT-L + PCA, concat) is the best so far at 0.619 accuracy. Image-only ViT-L at 0.591 beats RNA-only PCA at 0.518. Multiprofile avgpool behaves differently by setting. For RNA-only it was roughly neutral (0.514 vs 0.518 accuracy, F1 slightly higher). For multimodal concat it collapsed to 0.227. We do not yet know whether that collapse comes from image-side multiprofile avgpool aggregation or from combining multiprofile aggregation with fusion. 2. Test: image-only, multiprofile, ViT-L, avgpool changes only the profile setting and aggregation relative to config_014 (0.591). If it performs well, the collapse is specific to multiprofile fusion, and fusion or aggregation alternatives (e.g., transformer, weighted) become the next targets. If it also collapses, the problem lies in image multiprofile avgpool. 3. Why now: Multiprofile accounts for most of the remaining configurations. Diagnosing the anomaly with one controlled comparison will guide many later choices, which is more valuable than a small exploit tweak of the single-profile multimodal model.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is singleprofile multimodal (PCA + ViT-L, concat) at 0.619 accuracy and 0.610 F1. Its multiprofile counterpart with avgpool and concat collapsed to 0.227 accuracy. That is far below either unimodal model. In the unimodal runs, multiprofile avgpool performed about the same as singleprofile (RNA 0.514 vs 0.518; image 0.586 vs 0.591). So avgpool aggregation alone does not explain the failure. The likely cause is how multiprofile aggregation interacts with concat fusion, but this is uncertain. 2. Test: config_035 keeps the collapsed configuration and changes only the fusion, from concat to weighted. If accuracy recovers to around 0.6 or higher, concat fusion of pooled multiprofile features is the culprit. If it stays low, the problem lies in multimodal multiprofile avgpool more generally, and aggregation (e.g. transformer) should be tested next. 3. Why now: Profile setting and fusion are central design choices, and the multiprofile multimodal family covers most of the remaining configurations. Running a one-variable control first tells us whether that family is worth spending budget on. That is more useful than a small exploitative tweak to the current best.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is singleprofile multimodal PCA + ViT-L with concat fusion (config_020: acc 0.619, F1 0.610). It beats image-only ViT-L (0.591) and RNA-only PCA (0.518), so fusion appears to help. Multiprofile has not helped in any modality setting. RNA-only and image-only multiprofile were slightly lower, multimodal multiprofile avgpool with concat collapsed (0.227), and the weighted variant reached only 0.532. The RNA encoder is still completely untested: every RNA-containing run so far used PCA with 2000 components. 2. What this tests: config_025 keeps the best configuration fixed (multimodal, singleprofile, ViT-L, concat) and changes only the RNA encoder to scVI with 200 dimensions. This isolates whether a learned, lower-dimensional RNA representation improves fusion. It could also balance the RNA and image contributions in concat. 3. Why this is the best next experiment: It addresses the largest unexplored design factor with a single controlled change, and it builds on the strongest configuration so far. It also avoids spending more budget on the multiprofile direction, where evidence is currently weak.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_020 (multimodal, singleprofile, PCA + ViT-L, concat fusion) at 0.619 accuracy and 0.610 F1. It beats image-only (0.591) and RNA-only (0.518), so fusion appears to help in the single-profile setting. Fusion choice also mattered a lot in the multiprofile setting: concat collapsed to 0.227, while weighted fusion recovered to 0.532. It is still unknown whether weighted fusion also helps, or hurts, when concat already works well. 2. Test: config_008 keeps everything from the current best and changes only concat to weighted fusion. This isolates the effect of fusion in the strongest setting. 3. Why now: This one-variable change both exploits the most promising configuration and answers a key design question. We learn whether weighted fusion is generally better or only a fix for the unstable multiprofile concat models. That is worth more than testing a less promising branch such as scVI, ResNet50 or transformer aggregation.

Evidence: image features carry most of the signal. ViT-L image-only (0.591) far exceeds PCA RNA-only (0.518), and the best result so far, single-profile PCA+ViT-L concat (0.619), is only about 3 points above image-only. Multimodal results look unstable, ranging from 0.227 to 0.619 depending on fusion, profile setting and RNA encoder. The image encoder has never been varied, since every image run used ViT-L, so resnet50 is a fully untested option on the dominant modality. This experiment swaps only the encoder (ViT-L to resnet50) against config_014, in the simplest setting: image-only, single-profile, with no aggregation or fusion. That gives an unconfounded read on whether the image representation matters, without the noise seen in multimodal runs. Why it is the best use of the budget: image quality appears to be the main performance driver, so this result tells us whether the many resnet50 configurations are worth pursuing or can be deprioritized. If resnet50 is competitive, the logical next step is to test it inside the best fusion pipeline (config_047).

1. Evidence: no experiments have been run, so we have no baseline and no idea how hard the task is or whether any added complexity (images, multiple profiles, aggregation, fusion) is worth it. 2. What this tests: the simplest available configuration, an RNA-only, single-profile model with a PCA (2000 components) RNA encoder and no aggregation or fusion. It sets a reference accuracy and F1 for the RNA modality alone. 3. Why it is the best next step: under a limited budget, a clean baseline makes every later result interpretable. Single-factor follow-ups can then isolate one design choice each: adding images (config_003), switching to multiple profiles (config_037), or changing the RNA encoder (config_034 for scVI, config_022 for scGPT). This avoids assuming that multimodal or multiprofile models will help, and avoids confounding several design choices in the first run.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: Only one experiment has been run, the RNA-only single-profile PCA baseline (accuracy 0.494, F1 0.453). Every other design axis is still untested: image modality, profile setting, aggregation, fusion and RNA encoder. The most basic open question is whether adding imaging data improves performance at all. 2. What this tests: config_003 keeps the RNA encoder (pca_n2000) and the single-profile setting fixed. It adds only a ResNet50 image encoder with simple concat fusion. Comparing it with config_005 therefore isolates the effect of adding the image modality, with no aggregation confound. 3. Why this is the best next experiment: Modality choice probably determines which large part of the search space is worth exploring. A clear gain would justify a focus on multimodal configurations. Little or no gain would point the search toward RNA-only variants and RNA encoder choices. Concat and ResNet50 are the simplest options, so the result is easy to interpret and gives a clean anchor for later tests of fusion type, image encoder and multiprofile aggregation.

1. Evidence: Adding ResNet50 image features to the PCA RNA baseline (single profile, concat fusion) raised validation accuracy from 0.494 to 0.715, with F1 rising similarly from 0.453 to 0.687. This leaves open whether the gain comes from true multimodal complementarity or whether the image modality simply carries most of the signal on its own. 2. Test: An image-only ResNet50 single-profile model is the missing third leg of this comparison, since it matches config_003 except for removing RNA. If it reaches about 0.70, RNA adds little and later effort should go to image encoders and profile aggregation. If it falls well below 0.715, fusion is adding real value, and RNA encoder and fusion choices deserve priority. 3. Why now: With only two runs, the most important uncertainty is which modality drives performance. This one-variable change resolves it cheaply and guides how to spend the rest of the budget. Testing multiprofile or other encoders first would compound changes before we know what matters.

1. Evidence: Fusion has been tested, but the profile setting has not. Multimodal single-profile PCA+ResNet50 with concat fusion (0.715 acc / 0.687 F1) clearly beats RNA-only (0.494) and image-only (0.536) with the same encoders. That makes combining modalities the strongest signal so far. All three runs are single-profile, so we have no evidence on whether multiprofile inputs help. 2. Test: config_002 keeps the best configuration's encoders (PCA n2000, ResNet50) and fusion (concat). It switches only to multiprofile, using avgpool, the simplest aggregation. This isolates the profile-setting effect against config_003 as directly as the design space allows. 3. Why now: Profile setting is a major structural choice that applies to most of the remaining configurations. Knowing whether multiprofile helps will guide whether to spend the remaining budget on aggregation choices (transformer vs avgpool) or on single-profile encoder and fusion tweaks. Those tweaks, such as weighted fusion or a ViT image encoder, are likely smaller refinements that can be tested afterward.

1) Evidence: Single-profile multimodal fusion (PCA + ResNet50, concat; config_003) scored 0.715 accuracy and 0.687 F1. That is far above RNA-only (0.494) and image-only (0.536), so fusion clearly helps. The same model in the multiprofile setting with avgpool aggregation (config_002) collapsed to 0.520 / 0.479. We cannot yet tell whether multiprofile input is inherently harmful or whether simple average pooling washes out profile-specific signal. 2) Test: config_008 keeps everything identical to config_002 (PCA, ResNet50, concat, multiprofile) and changes only the aggregation from avgpool to transformer. This isolates the effect of aggregation. If accuracy recovers toward or above 0.715, the multiprofile branch of the search space stays viable and attention-based aggregation matters. If it stays near 0.52, multiprofile can be deprioritized and the remaining budget focused on single-profile encoder and fusion refinements. 3) Why now: a large share of the untested configurations are multiprofile. Resolving whether the config_002 drop came from the aggregation or from the profile setting itself will guide many later choices, which makes it more valuable than a small single-profile tweak right now.

1. Evidence: Multimodal fusion clearly beats either modality alone (about 0.72 vs 0.49 for RNA-only and 0.54 for image-only). Multiprofile with transformer aggregation (config_008, 0.721) roughly matches singleprofile (config_003, 0.715), and transformer aggregation is far better than avgpool (0.520). Every run so far used pca_n2000 RNA and a resnet50 image encoder, so the effect of representation choice is entirely unknown. 2. Test: config_004 keeps the best configuration (config_008: multiprofile, transformer, concat, pca_n2000) and changes only the image encoder to imagenet_vit_l. Any difference can therefore be attributed to the image representation. 3. Why now: Representation is the largest untested design axis. A stronger image encoder could plausibly raise the weak image-only signal and, with it, multimodal performance. This single-variable change exploits the current best setup while answering an important open question, and it is more informative than tuning fusion type first.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is config_008 (multiprofile, transformer aggregation, PCA RNA, ResNet50, concat) at 0.721 accuracy. It is roughly tied with the single-profile ResNet50 concat model (0.715). Two design choices are already fairly clear. Avgpool aggregation was much worse (0.520). Swapping ResNet50 for ViT-L was also much worse (0.507). The RNA encoder, however, is completely untested: every run so far used PCA, and PCA alone was weak in the RNA-only model (0.494). 2. What this tests: config_039 changes only the RNA encoder, from PCA to scVI, while keeping the best-performing setup fixed. This isolates whether a learned RNA representation improves fusion performance. 3. Why it is the best next use of budget: The RNA encoder is a major unexplored axis, so this result has high information value. It also has a real chance of improving on the current best, because it extends the strongest configuration rather than a weak one. Fusion type (weighted vs. concat) is a secondary question that can be tested afterwards on whichever RNA encoder proves better.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is config_008 (multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) at 0.721 accuracy. It is roughly tied with the singleprofile version, config_003, at 0.715. Several single-factor changes away from these settings clearly hurt: avgpool instead of transformer (0.520), ViT-L instead of ResNet50 (0.507) and scVI instead of PCA (0.579). Fusion, however, has never been varied; every multimodal run used concat. 2. What this tests: config_011 keeps config_008 exactly and switches only concat to weighted fusion. Any change in accuracy or F1 can therefore be attributed to the fusion method alone. 3. Why it is the best next run: It isolates a completely untested design choice while staying in the strongest region found so far. It is a reasonable candidate for improving the best result, and even a negative result tells us whether fusion matters. That makes it a better use of budget than retesting choices that already show clear negative signals.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_008 (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA RNA, ResNet50 image, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) at 0.721 accuracy. The single-profile PCA/ResNet50/concat model (config_003) is close behind at 0.715 accuracy, with slightly higher F1. Within the multiprofile setting, three single-factor swaps from config_008 each hurt badly: avgpool instead of transformer (0.520), ViT-L instead of ResNet50 (0.507), and weighted instead of concat fusion (0.537).
