Its result will tell us whether fusion is likely to help and whether image encoder choice deserves more experiments. 3) Most of the remaining search space is multimodal, so settling the value of the image modality early is the most informative next step. If images are weak, we can shift budget to RNA encoders and multiprofile aggregation. If they are strong or comparable, multimodal fusion becomes the priority. ResNet50 is the simpler image encoder, which makes it the right single-profile reference point before trying ViT-L.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_002 tested an image-only, single-profile model with a ResNet50 image encoder and no aggregation or fusion, as a modality counterpart to the RNA-only PCA baseline (llm_summary_001). It reached a validation accuracy of 0.411 (primary metric) and a validation F1 of 0.378, about 0.06 below the RNA-only baseline on both metrics (0.471 / 0.442). This suggests that image features from ResNet50 carry measurable but possibly weaker signal than PCA-encoded RNA in the single-profile setting. The comparison changes the encoder along with the modality (ResNet50 vs. PCA-2000), and each result comes from a single run with no variance or chance-level reference, so it remains uncertain whether the gap reflects the modality itself, the encoder choice (e.g., ViT-L might do better), or run-to-run noise, and whether the image signal is complementary enough to RNA for fusion to help.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence so far: two single-profile unimodal baselines. RNA-only PCA-2000 reached 0.471 accuracy and 0.442 F1. Image-only ResNet50 reached 0.411 and 0.378. Both modalities carry signal, but we do not know whether the image signal adds anything beyond RNA or is redundant with it. 2. This experiment adds the image features to RNA through simple concatenation. Config_016 keeps profile setting (single), RNA encoder (PCA-2000), image encoder (ResNet50) and aggregation (none) fixed. Both of its components already have measured baselines, so any change from 0.471 can be attributed mainly to fusion itself, without confounding from a new encoder or from multiprofile aggregation. 3. Whether fusion helps is the decision that splits the search space most: about two-thirds of the remaining configurations are multimodal. A clear gain would justify exploring fusion variants, weighted fusion and multiprofile versions. No gain or a loss would point the budget toward stronger unimodal options, such as other RNA encoders or multiprofile RNA. Concat is the least complex fusion, so it is the logical first test before trying weighted fusion. A single run cannot settle this, but it is a cleanly attributable first comparison.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_003 tested multimodal, single-profile fusion by concatenating PCA-2000 RNA features with ResNet50 image features, with no aggregation. Every other setting matched the two unimodal baselines, so the only change was combining the modalities via concat. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.260 (primary metric) and F1 of 0.222. That is well below both RNA-only (0.471 / 0.442) and image-only (0.411 / 0.378), so in this setup naive concatenation degraded performance rather than adding complementary signal. A drop below even the weaker unimodal baseline is unexpected, and this is a single run with no variance estimate. It remains uncertain whether the loss reflects concat fusion itself or fixable factors such as feature-scale or dimensionality imbalance between the two feature sets, optimization or training instability, or a pipeline issue. This result alone should not be taken as evidence that multimodal fusion in general, including weighted fusion or multiprofile variants, cannot help.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: In single runs, RNA-only PCA-2000 (0.471 acc / 0.442 F1) beat image-only ResNet50 (0.411 / 0.378). Concat fusion of the two dropped to 0.260 / 0.222, below either modality alone. That drop is anomalous. It could come from concat itself (for example, scale or dimensionality imbalance between 2000-d PCA and ResNet features), from optimization problems, or from multimodal fusion simply not helping here. 2) What this tests: config_017 keeps everything from config_016 the same (single-profile, PCA-2000, ResNet50) and changes only the fusion method from concat to weighted. If weighted fusion recovers to or above the RNA-only baseline, the failure was specific to concat. If it also collapses, that points to a broader problem with combining modalities in this pipeline. 3) Why it is the best next use of budget: Most of the remaining configurations (35 of 48) are multimodal and use either concat or weighted fusion. Settling whether fusion can work at all, and which method to prefer, is the single biggest source of uncertainty for pruning the search space. It is also a clean one-variable comparison. Encoder and multiprofile questions, such as config_002 and config_004, remain good follow-ups after this.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_004 repeated the multimodal, single-profile PCA-2000 RNA + ResNet50 image configuration from llm_summary_003 with no aggregation, changing only the fusion method from concat to weighted. That makes it a one-variable test of whether the earlier fusion collapse was specific to concat. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.332 (primary metric) and an F1 of 0.315. This is above concat fusion (0.260 / 0.222), so the concat failure may have been partly method-specific. It is still well below both image-only (0.411 / 0.378) and RNA-only (0.471 / 0.442), so neither fusion method has yet shown complementary benefit. All results are single runs with no variance estimate, so the size of the weighted-vs-concat gain is uncertain. It also remains unclear whether multimodal underperformance comes from the fusion design, from feature-scale or dimensionality imbalance or optimization problems common to both fusion runs, or from a pipeline issue. This calls for caution before investing heavily in the many remaining single-profile multimodal configurations, though multiprofile or other encoder variants are untested.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: RNA-only PCA-2000 single-profile is the best result so far (0.471 acc / 0.442 F1). Image-only ResNet50 is lower (0.411 / 0.378). Both single-profile fusion attempts fell below either unimodal baseline (concat 0.260, weighted 0.332), so fusion currently looks like a poor investment until the stronger components are better understood. Profile setting and aggregation are completely untested. 2. Test: config_002 keeps the best configuration (RNA-only, PCA-2000) and changes only the profile setting to multiprofile, using the simplest aggregation (avgpool). This isolates whether aggregating multiple profiles improves on the single-profile baseline. 3. Why now: multiprofile is a major design axis. It appears in many of the remaining configurations, including multimodal ones, so learning its effect cheaply informs a large share of the search space. It also builds directly on the strongest result so far, which balances learning with the chance of improving performance. Avgpool sets a clean reference before trying transformer aggregation or swapping RNA encoders.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_005 kept the best prior configuration (RNA-only, PCA-2000 encoder, no image or fusion) and changed only the profile setting from singleprofile to multiprofile, aggregating profiles with simple average pooling. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.725 (primary metric) and an F1 of 0.685. That is a large improvement over the single-profile RNA-only baseline from llm_summary_001 (0.471 / 0.442) and makes this the best result so far. Because this was a near one-variable comparison, multiprofile input with avgpool is strongly associated with the gain, though multiprofile and its aggregation method cannot be separated, and both results are single runs with no variance estimate. It remains untested whether the benefit transfers to image-only or multimodal multiprofile settings, whether transformer aggregation or other RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT) improve on avgpool/PCA, and whether multiprofile evaluation is directly comparable to single-profile evaluation (e.g., the effective number or grouping of validation samples may differ).

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: Moving RNA-only PCA-2000 from single-profile to multiprofile with avgpool raised validation accuracy from 0.471 to 0.725 (F1 0.442 to 0.685). This is by far the largest effect seen so far, but it comes from one run on one modality. It is unclear whether the gain reflects multiprofile aggregation in general, something RNA-specific, or a change in how multiprofile evaluation is done. Both single-profile fusion runs fell below the unimodal baselines. 2. What this tests: config_011 changes only the profile setting for the image-only ResNet50 baseline (0.411 / 0.378), from single-profile to multiprofile with avgpool. A similarly large gain would show that the multiprofile effect is modality-general. A small or no gain would point to an RNA-specific benefit or an evaluation artifact. It also creates the matched unimodal reference needed to read any multiprofile multimodal result (e.g., config_019). 3. Why now: Profile setting is the design choice with the most evidence of mattering. Checking whether it generalizes clarifies the main driver of performance at the cost of one experiment. It also tells us whether multiprofile fusion is worth budget, which avoids spending runs on the many multimodal configurations blindly. Testing transformer aggregation (config_003) is a reasonable follow-up once this is known.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_006 changed only the profile setting of the image-only ResNet50 baseline (llm_summary_002) from singleprofile to multiprofile with avgpool aggregation, to test whether the large multiprofile gain seen for RNA-only PCA-2000 generalizes across modalities. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.537 (primary metric) and F1 of 0.518, up from 0.411 / 0.378 (about +0.13 accuracy, +0.14 F1). This indicates that the multiprofile benefit is not RNA-specific, though it is roughly half the RNA gain (+0.25 accuracy), so image-only multiprofile remains well below RNA-only multiprofile (0.725 / 0.685) and the modality gap widened from about 0.06 to about 0.19. Uncertainties: these are single runs with no variance estimate; multiprofile input and avgpool aggregation cannot be separated; and a shared change in multiprofile evaluation (e.g., sample grouping) could still inflate both gains, so an evaluation artifact is not ruled out. Matched multiprofile unimodal references now exist for interpreting multiprofile fusion (e.g., config_019), but given the earlier single-profile fusion collapse and the weaker image signal, it is untested whether multiprofile fusion can beat RNA-only multiprofile, and whether transformer aggregation (e.g., config_003) improves on avgpool.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: Multiprofile input with avgpool gave the largest gains so far. RNA-only PCA-2000 rose from 0.471 to 0.725 accuracy, and image-only rose from 0.411 to 0.537. That makes RNA-only multiprofile (config_002) the clear leader. However, the aggregation method has never been varied, so the multiprofile benefit cannot be separated from avgpool specifically. Single-profile fusion underperformed both unimodal baselines, which argues for caution before spending heavily on multimodal runs. 2) Test: config_003 changes only the aggregation of the best configuration, from avgpool to transformer. This is a clean one-variable test of whether learned attention over profiles beats simple averaging. 3) Value: It exploits the strongest direction found so far. Its answer also bears on every remaining multiprofile configuration, unimodal and multimodal, which is about half the search space. That will help direct later choices, such as whether multiprofile fusion runs should use avgpool or transformer. It is also a cleaner and more broadly informative use of one experiment than jumping to fusion now.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_007 kept the leading configuration (RNA-only, multiprofile, PCA-2000 encoder, no image or fusion; llm_summary_005) and changed only the aggregation method from avgpool to transformer. This made it a one-variable test of whether learned attention over profiles beats simple averaging. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.706 (primary metric) and an F1 of 0.667, slightly below avgpool (0.725 / 0.685; about -0.019 accuracy and -0.018 F1). Transformer aggregation therefore gave no improvement here, and avgpool RNA-only multiprofile remains the best result so far. Both results come from single runs with no variance estimate, so this small gap may fall within run-to-run noise and should not be read as evidence that transformer aggregation is reliably worse. It is also untested whether the result holds for image-only or multimodal multiprofile settings, or with transformer tuning (e.g., capacity, regularization, number of profiles). The test does show that the large multiprofile gain does not depend specifically on avgpool, since both aggregators performed far above the single-profile baseline (0.471). However, a shared multiprofile evaluation artifact (e.g., differences in sample grouping) is still not ruled out.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: Multiprofile input with avgpool gave large gains for both RNA-only (0.725 / 0.685, the best so far) and image-only (0.537 / 0.518). Transformer aggregation did not beat avgpool for RNA (0.706). Multimodal fusion has only been tested in the single-profile setting, where it fell below both unimodal baselines. Weighted fusion (0.332) did better there than concat (0.260). The key open question is whether fusion can add complementary signal when the inputs are the much stronger multiprofile representations. 2. Test: config_019 uses the same PCA-2000 RNA and ResNet50 image encoders and the same multiprofile avgpool aggregation as config_002 and config_011, and switches to multimodal with weighted fusion. This is a clean comparison against matched unimodal references. It also uses the better-performing fusion method and aggregator, so it gives fusion its fairest test. 3. Why now: Fusion is the design axis behind most of the remaining configurations. A positive result (beating 0.725) would point toward exploiting multimodal multiprofile variants. A negative result would show that the single-profile fusion failure persists, which would justify moving the budget to RNA-encoder tests (scVI, scGPT) on the RNA-only multiprofile setup. Either outcome sharply narrows the search, whereas an encoder swap alone would leave this larger question unresolved.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_008 (config_019) tested multimodal weighted fusion of PCA-2000 RNA and ResNet50 image features under multiprofile avgpool aggregation, a matched comparison against the RNA-only (llm_summary_005; 0.725 / 0.685) and image-only (llm_summary_006; 0.537 / 0.518) multiprofile references, to see whether fusion adds complementary signal when both inputs are strong. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.573 (primary metric) and an F1 of 0.573. That is a large improvement over single-profile weighted fusion (0.332 / 0.315) and modestly above image-only multiprofile, but about 0.15 accuracy below RNA-only multiprofile, so fusion again failed to beat the best unimodal model and RNA-only multiprofile avgpool remains the best result so far. This is consistent with the single-profile fusion underperformance persisting under multiprofile input and supports shifting budget toward RNA-encoder tests (scVI, scGPT) on RNA-only multiprofile. However, these are single runs with no variance estimate, concat fusion, transformer aggregation, and other encoders are untested in multiprofile multimodal settings, and it remains unclear whether the gap reflects fusion design, feature-scale or dimensionality imbalance, optimization issues, or a pipeline problem; a shared multiprofile evaluation artifact also remains unruled out.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: Multiprofile input is the dominant factor so far. RNA-only PCA-2000 rose from 0.471 to 0.725 accuracy, image-only from 0.411 to 0.537, and avgpool slightly beat transformer aggregation (0.725 vs 0.706, likely within noise). Fusion has underperformed the best unimodal model in every run, including multiprofile weighted fusion (0.573). The RNA encoder has only ever been PCA-2000, so it is the largest untested design choice on the leading branch. 2) This test: config_005 keeps the best configuration (RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool) and changes only the encoder from PCA-2000 to scVI-200. That isolates whether a learned, lower-dimensional probabilistic RNA representation beats linear PCA. 3) Why now: it exploits the strongest direction while settling a key representation question with a clean one-variable change. The result will also guide whether later multimodal runs should use scVI, which matters given the open hypothesis that PCA-2000 dimensionality imbalance hurts fusion. The scGPT counterpart (config_008) is a natural follow-up.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_009 kept the leading configuration (RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool, no image or fusion; llm_summary_005) and changed only the RNA encoder from PCA-2000 to scVI-200, a one-variable test of whether a learned, lower-dimensional probabilistic representation beats linear PCA. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.512 (primary metric) and F1 of 0.477, far below PCA-2000 under the same setup (0.725 / 0.685; about -0.21 accuracy) and even below image-only multiprofile (0.537 / 0.518). In this setup scVI-200 therefore did not help, and RNA-only multiprofile avgpool with PCA-2000 remains the best result. This argues against simply adopting scVI-200 for later multimodal runs to address the suspected dimensionality imbalance. However, this is a single run with no variance estimate. The encoder swap changes dimensionality (200 vs 2000) and representation type together, so these cannot be separated. It is also untested whether scVI training or tuning (e.g., latent size, gene selection, normalization), a pipeline issue, or the shared multiprofile evaluation setup explains the drop. scGPT (config_008) remains an open comparison.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: RNA-only multiprofile with avgpool and PCA-2000 is the clear leader (0.725 / 0.685). Transformer aggregation was not better (0.706). Fusion has so far failed to beat the best unimodal model (0.573). Swapping PCA for scVI-200 dropped sharply (0.512). The RNA encoder therefore matters a great deal, but only two encoder types have been compared, and each is a single run. scGPT, a pretrained foundation-model representation, is the remaining untested RNA encoder. 2. What it tests: config_008 keeps the leading setup (RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool) and changes only the encoder to scGPT. It asks whether PCA's advantage is specific to scVI's weaknesses, or whether linear PCA-2000 is generally hard to beat for this task. 3. Why it is the best next use of budget: it is a clean one-variable comparison on the strongest pipeline, so it can directly improve on the best result. It also tells us which RNA encoder to carry into later multimodal runs, which is the dominant modality's key unresolved choice. Image-encoder tests (e.g., ViT-L in config_014) matter less given image's weaker signal and the fusion results so far.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_010 (config_008) kept the leading configuration (RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool, no image or fusion; llm_summary_005) and changed only the RNA encoder from PCA-2000 to scGPT. This made it a one-variable test of whether a pretrained foundation-model representation beats linear PCA. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.421 (primary metric) and F1 of 0.412. That is far below PCA-2000 (0.725 / 0.685; about -0.30 accuracy), below scVI-200 (0.512 / 0.477) and image-only multiprofile (0.537 / 0.518), and even below the single-profile PCA baseline (0.471). Both learned encoders tested so far have therefore underperformed PCA-2000 in this setup, so PCA-2000 remains the best RNA encoder candidate to carry forward, and RNA-only multiprofile avgpool with PCA-2000 remains the best result. However, each result is a single run with no variance estimate, and scGPT differs from PCA in representation type, dimensionality, and pretraining domain together. The size of the drop also leaves open whether it reflects the encoder itself or fixable factors, such as how scGPT embeddings were extracted, gene-vocabulary overlap, normalization, lack of fine-tuning, or a pipeline issue. A shared multiprofile evaluation artifact also remains unruled out.

selection_reason: 1) No experiments have been run yet, so we know nothing about the task's difficulty, which modality carries the signal, or whether multiprofile aggregation, stronger encoders, or fusion help. 2) config_001 (RNA-only, single-profile, PCA with 2000 components) is the simplest and cheapest configuration. It gives a reference point: later runs can each change one factor from it, such as the encoder (scVI or scGPT), profile setting (avgpool or transformer), or modality (adding images), so their effects can be read directly. 3) With a limited budget, a simple, interpretable baseline is the most efficient first step. It avoids assuming that complex multimodal models are better, and it anchors every later comparison. The image-only baseline (config_010) is a natural next step to compare modalities.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_001 tested the simplest configuration, an RNA-only, single-profile model using a PCA encoder with 2000 components and no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It reached validation accuracy 0.650 and validation F1 0.628. This shows the RNA modality alone carries meaningful predictive signal, but no prior experiments exist for comparison, so the result is only an initial baseline. It remains unknown whether other RNA encoders (e.g., scVI, scGPT), multiprofile aggregation (avgpool, transformer), the image modality alone (e.g., config_010), or multimodal fusion would do better or worse. Later runs that each change one factor from this configuration are needed to isolate those effects.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: there is only one result so far, the RNA-only single-profile PCA baseline (accuracy 0.650, F1 0.628). It shows RNA carries useful signal. We have no information yet about the image modality, which every multimodal configuration depends on. 2) Test: config_010 runs the image-only single-profile model with a ResNet50 encoder. Holding the single-profile setting fixed and swapping modality from RNA to image tells us how predictive the image modality is on its own, relative to the RNA baseline. 3) Why now: the modality question is the broadest open uncertainty. If images are weak, budget should go to RNA encoder and aggregation choices. If images are comparable or stronger, multimodal fusion becomes much more promising. Starting with ResNet50, the simplest image encoder, gives a clean reference point before we compare image encoders or test fusion.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_002 tested an image-only, single-profile model with a ResNet50 image encoder and no RNA encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It reached validation accuracy 0.532 and validation F1 0.517, both below the RNA-only single-profile PCA-2000 baseline (0.650 / 0.628 in llm_summary_001), so this image configuration carries some predictive signal but less than the RNA baseline. The comparison changes modality and encoder together (PCA on RNA versus ResNet50 on images), and each is a single run, so it does not cleanly show that the image modality is inherently weaker; other image encoders could narrow the gap. It also remains unknown whether image features add complementary information when fused with RNA, or how multiprofile aggregation affects either modality.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: Single-profile RNA-only with PCA-2000 reached 0.650 accuracy and 0.628 F1. Single-profile image-only with ResNet50 reached 0.532 and 0.517. So both modalities carry signal and RNA is stronger, but it is unknown whether image features complement RNA or only add noise. 2. Test: config_016 fuses exactly these two tested encoders (PCA-2000 RNA plus ResNet50 image) by simple concatenation, with single-profile input and no aggregation. Any change relative to the two unimodal baselines is therefore attributable to multimodal fusion alone, not to a new encoder or profile setting. 3. Why now: Whether to fuse the modalities is a top-level design question that determines whether the 36 multimodal configurations are worth exploring. Concat is the simplest fusion and gives a clean reference point for later weighted-fusion, encoder, and multiprofile comparisons. If fusion fails to beat RNA-only, the budget can shift toward RNA encoders and aggregation instead.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_003 tested a multimodal, single-profile model that concatenates the same two encoders used in the earlier unimodal baselines: PCA-2000 for RNA and ResNet50 for images, with no aggregation. It reached validation accuracy 0.507 and F1 0.455, below both RNA-only (0.650 / 0.628, llm_summary_001) and image-only (0.532 / 0.517, llm_summary_002). So in this setup, adding image features by simple concatenation was associated with lower performance rather than complementary gains. Because the encoders and profile setting match the baselines, the drop is tied to this particular concat fusion. However, each configuration is a single run, so variance cannot be ruled out, and the evidence does not show whether fusion itself is unhelpful. Untested explanations include feature-scale or dimensionality imbalance between the concatenated features, other fusion methods (e.g., weighted), other encoders, or multiprofile aggregation, any of which could change the outcome.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: RNA-only single-profile PCA-2000 (config_001) is the strongest result so far (0.650 accuracy / 0.628 F1). Image-only ResNet50 scored lower (0.532 / 0.517), and simple concat fusion scored lower still (0.507 / 0.455). Each is a single run, so these gaps are suggestive rather than settled. Profile setting has not been tested at all, yet most remaining configurations depend on it. 2) What this tests: config_002 changes only the profile setting, from single-profile to multiprofile with avgpool, on the best-known baseline. This isolates whether aggregating multiple profiles helps, using the simplest aggregator before trying the transformer. 3) Why now: it builds on the strongest current direction while answering a broad design question. The result will guide whether later RNA, image and multimodal experiments should focus on multiprofile variants. Testing weighted fusion or other encoders can follow once the profile-setting effect is known.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_004 kept the best-known RNA-only PCA-2000 baseline (llm_summary_001) fixed and changed only the profile setting, from single-profile to multiprofile with avgpool aggregation. It reached validation accuracy 0.523 and F1 0.508, well below the single-profile baseline (0.650 / 0.628), so in this setup multiprofile-with-avgpool was associated with lower performance. Because profile setting and aggregator change together, the evidence cannot separate whether multiprofile input itself is unhelpful or whether simple mean pooling discards useful per-profile signal; a transformer aggregator remains untested. Each configuration is a single run, so variance cannot be ruled out, and it is unknown whether this pattern carries over to image-only or multimodal settings.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: the best result so far is the simplest model, RNA-only single-profile PCA-2000 (0.650 acc / 0.628 F1). Three changes to it all did worse: switching to image-only ResNet50 (0.532), concat fusion with images (0.507), and multiprofile with avgpool (0.523). One axis is still completely untested: the RNA representation. Every RNA run so far has used PCA-2000. 2) Test: config_004 keeps the best configuration fixed and changes only the RNA encoder to scVI (200 dimensions). This isolates whether a learned, lower-dimensional latent space beats or matches PCA for the strongest modality. 3) Why this is the best use of the budget: the RNA encoder choice affects most of the remaining configurations, since many multimodal and multiprofile runs use scVI or scGPT. If scVI is better, it raises the baseline and gives a stronger RNA backbone for later aggregation and fusion tests. If it is worse, PCA is confirmed as the RNA representation to build on. A single-factor change from the current best gives a cleaner answer than testing the transformer aggregator or weighted fusion first, because both of those alternatives currently sit on weaker branches.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_005 kept the best-known RNA-only, single-profile configuration (llm_summary_001) fixed and changed only the RNA encoder, from PCA-2000 to scVI with a 200-dimensional latent. It reached validation accuracy 0.471 and F1 0.442, well below the PCA-2000 baseline (0.650 / 0.628) and the lowest accuracy of any run so far. Because this was a single-factor change, the drop is attributable to the encoder swap in this setup, which supports keeping PCA-2000 as the RNA backbone for now. However, each configuration is a single run, so variance cannot be ruled out. It is also unclear whether the gap comes from scVI as a method, the much lower dimensionality (200 vs 2000), or its training and hyperparameter settings. This result does not show how scVI behaves in multiprofile or multimodal configurations, and scGPT remains untested.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: Concat fusion of PCA-2000 and ResNet50 (config_016, 0.507 / 0.455) scored below both unimodal baselines: RNA-only at 0.650 / 0.628 and image-only at 0.532 / 0.517. Falling below both unimodal models suggests the fusion method itself may be the problem, for example scale or dimensionality imbalance between the concatenated features, rather than images adding nothing. This is a single run, though. 2) Test: config_017 keeps the encoders and the single-profile setting identical to config_016 and changes only the fusion, from concat to weighted. This cleanly isolates whether a learned modality weighting recovers or exceeds RNA-only performance. 3) Why now: Most of the remaining search space is multimodal, so knowing whether any fusion method can beat RNA-only largely decides whether to keep exploring that space or focus on RNA-only options such as scGPT (config_007) and transformer aggregation (config_003). It is the single-factor experiment with the highest information value per run.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_006 kept the multimodal single-profile setup of llm_summary_003 (PCA-2000 RNA + ResNet50 image, no aggregation) and changed only the fusion from concat to weighted. It reached validation accuracy 0.635 and F1 0.618, well above concat fusion (0.507 / 0.455) and image-only (0.532 / 0.517). Because this was a single-factor change, the gain is tied to weighted versus concat fusion in this setup, which fits the idea that simple concatenation was the problem rather than images being uninformative. However, it still fell slightly short of the RNA-only PCA-2000 baseline (0.650 / 0.628), so there is no evidence yet that images add complementary signal. The weighted model may simply be down-weighting the image branch, and the learned modality weights were not reported. Each configuration is a single run, so the small gap to RNA-only may be within variance. Other fusion methods, other encoders, and multiprofile or transformer aggregation remain untested for multimodal models.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: RNA-only single-profile PCA-2000 is the best result so far (0.650 accuracy / 0.628 F1). Switching to multiprofile with avgpool dropped it sharply (0.523 / 0.508). That earlier run changed the profile setting and the aggregator together, so we cannot tell whether multiprofile input is unhelpful or whether mean pooling discards useful per-profile signal. 2. What this tests: config_003 keeps the RNA-only multiprofile PCA-2000 setup of config_002 and changes only the aggregator, from avgpool to transformer. If it recovers to or beats the single-profile baseline, avgpool was the bottleneck and multiprofile is worth pursuing. If it stays low, that is evidence against multiprofile in this task. 3. Why it is the best next use of budget: most of the remaining untested configurations are multiprofile, so settling this one question decides whether a large share of the search space deserves budget. The test uses the strongest known RNA backbone and changes a single factor. It also has a plausible chance of producing a new best result, so it balances exploration with exploitation better than encoder swaps such as scGPT or ViT-L, which can follow afterward.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_007 kept the RNA-only multiprofile PCA-2000 setup of llm_summary_004 and changed only the aggregator from avgpool to transformer. It reached validation accuracy 0.494 and F1 0.453, below avgpool (0.523 / 0.508) and well below the single-profile PCA-2000 baseline (0.650 / 0.628). A better aggregator did not recover performance in this setup, so the low multiprofile results are not explained by mean pooling alone, and both multiprofile runs are now well below single-profile. This adds evidence against multiprofile input for RNA-only PCA-2000, but each configuration is a single run, so variance cannot be ruled out. The transformer's capacity, training, and hyperparameter settings are also untested, and it remains unknown whether multiprofile behaves differently for image-only, multimodal (e.g., weighted fusion), or other-encoder configurations.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: The RNA-only single-profile PCA-2000 baseline (0.650 acc / 0.628 F1) is still the best run. Multiprofile aggregation hurt RNA-only with both avgpool (0.523) and transformer (0.494). Weighted fusion with ResNet50 images came close (0.635) but did not beat RNA alone. scVI-200 did much worse (0.471), but scGPT, the third RNA encoder, is untested. So the main open question about the strongest modality's representation is unanswered. 2. What this tests: config_007 changes only the RNA encoder, from PCA-2000 to scGPT, keeping the best-performing single-profile RNA-only setup. It shows whether a pretrained foundation-model embedding beats PCA, or whether the scVI result reflects a general weakness of learned embeddings here. 3. Why it is the best next use: It is a clean single-factor comparison against the current best configuration, so it is both exploratory and potentially exploitative. Its result also guides the many untested multimodal scGPT configurations (config_040 to config_051). It tells us whether scGPT is worth combining with weighted fusion or whether PCA-2000 should remain the RNA backbone for later fusion and image-encoder tests, such as ViT-L in config_013 or config_023.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_008 kept the best-known RNA-only, single-profile configuration (llm_summary_001) fixed and changed only the RNA encoder, from PCA-2000 to scGPT. It reached validation accuracy 0.537 and F1 0.518, well below the PCA-2000 baseline (0.650 / 0.628) but above scVI-200 (0.471 / 0.442, llm_summary_005). Because this was a single-factor change, the drop is tied to the encoder swap in this setup, and with both learned embeddings (scVI, scGPT) now below PCA-2000, the evidence supports keeping PCA-2000 as the RNA backbone for later fusion and image-encoder tests. However, each configuration is a single run, so variance cannot be ruled out, and it remains unclear whether scGPT's shortfall reflects the embedding itself, its dimensionality, or its extraction and downstream-training settings. It is also unknown how scGPT behaves with weighted fusion or in the untested multimodal scGPT configurations (config_040 to config_051).

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: single-profile RNA-only PCA-2000 is the best run so far (0.650 / 0.628). Multiprofile aggregation (avgpool and transformer) and the alternative RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT) all performed clearly worse. Weighted fusion with ResNet50 recovered to 0.635 but did not beat RNA-only, likely because ResNet50 image features are weak (image-only 0.532). The image encoder is now the main design choice not yet tested, and imagenet_vit_l has never been run. 2) This experiment keeps the image-only single-profile ResNet50 setup (config_010) and changes only the encoder to ViT-L. It cleanly measures whether a stronger image representation carries more signal, without fusion effects mixed in. 3) This one run tells us whether it is worth pursuing the untested ViT-L multimodal configurations. If ViT-L clearly beats ResNet50, the logical next step is weighted fusion with PCA-2000 and ViT-L (config_023), which could exceed RNA-only. If it does not, the budget can stay focused on RNA-centric configurations.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_009 kept the image-only, single-profile setup of llm_summary_002 and changed only the image encoder, from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L. It reached validation accuracy 0.520 and F1 0.498, slightly below ResNet50 (0.532 / 0.517) and well below the RNA-only PCA-2000 baseline (0.650 / 0.628). So in this setup the larger ViT-L encoder did not provide a stronger image representation, and the image modality still trails RNA. The small gap to ResNet50 is a single-run comparison and may be within variance. This result weakens the case for prioritizing ViT-L multimodal runs such as weighted fusion with PCA-2000 (config_023), but does not rule out that ViT-L could behave differently under fusion, with other pretraining or fine-tuning, or with different downstream-training settings.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: Single-profile setups lead so far. RNA-only PCA-2000 scored 0.650 accuracy / 0.628 F1, and PCA-2000 + ResNet50 with weighted fusion scored 0.635 / 0.618. Both RNA-only multiprofile runs were much worse (avgpool 0.523, transformer 0.494). Whether multiprofile also hurts once images are added and fused with weights is untested, and most remaining configurations are multiprofile multimodal. 2) Test: config_019 keeps the best multimodal setup (config_017: PCA-2000 + ResNet50, weighted fusion) and changes only the profile setting, to multiprofile with avgpool. Avgpool was the better of the two RNA multiprofile aggregators. This isolates whether the multiprofile penalty carries over to multimodal weighted fusion, or whether per-profile image signal becomes useful when pooled with RNA. 3) Why now: The result decides a large share of the remaining space. If multiprofile again drops sharply, the multiprofile multimodal branches can be deprioritized and the budget focused on single-profile refinements such as config_023. If it matches or beats config_017, it opens the most promising direction for exceeding the RNA-only baseline. Either outcome is informative from a single-factor change, unlike swapping the image encoder to ViT-L, which trailed ResNet50 in image-only runs and so seems unlikely to change conclusions.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_010 kept the best multimodal setup (llm_summary_006: PCA-2000 RNA + ResNet50 image, weighted fusion) and changed only the profile setting, from single-profile to multiprofile with avgpool aggregation. It reached validation accuracy 0.639 and F1 0.620. That is essentially level with the single-profile weighted model (0.635 / 0.618) and far above the RNA-only multiprofile avgpool run (0.523 / 0.508). So the large multiprofile penalty seen for RNA-only did not appear in this multimodal weighted-fusion setup, which supports keeping multiprofile multimodal branches in consideration rather than deprioritizing them. The result still sits slightly below the RNA-only single-profile baseline (0.650 / 0.628), so there is no evidence yet that images or multiple profiles add complementary signal. Each configuration is a single run, so the small differences may be within variance. The learned modality weights were not reported, so the model may simply be relying mostly on one branch. It is also unclear why multiprofile is tolerated here but not for RNA-only, and whether a transformer aggregator or other encoders would behave differently in this setting.

selection_reason: 1) No experiments have been run, so there is no evidence about which modality, encoder, profile setting, aggregation, or fusion choice matters. 2) config_001 (RNA-only, single-profile, PCA-2000) is the simplest, cheapest configuration. It sets a reference level for validation accuracy and F1, and later experiments that change one factor at a time can be compared against it: RNA encoder (scVI, scGPT), profile setting and aggregation (avgpool, transformer), image modality, and fusion. 3) With a limited budget and no prior information, starting with a simple, interpretable baseline is the most informative choice. It avoids assuming that multimodal or multiprofile models will win, and it makes later gains attributable to specific design choices.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_001 tested the simplest configuration: an RNA-only, single-profile model with a PCA (n=2000) RNA encoder and no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It reached validation accuracy 0.2266, with a lower validation F1 of 0.1907, which may point to uneven performance across classes. This is the first completed experiment, so the result is a reference baseline, not evidence that any design choice helps or hurts. The number of classes and chance-level accuracy are not given, so it is unclear how strong this baseline is. It is also not yet known whether other RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), multiprofile aggregation, the image modality, or fusion would improve on it, so future experiments should change one factor at a time relative to this configuration.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: there is only one result so far, an RNA-only single-profile PCA baseline (acc 0.227, F1 0.191). It is a reference point, and no design choice has been tested yet. 2) This experiment changes one factor. It moves from single-profile to multiprofile and uses the simplest aggregator (avgpool), keeping the PCA RNA encoder and RNA-only setting fixed. That isolates whether pooling multiple profiles helps, without the extra capacity of a transformer aggregator getting in the way. 3) Profile setting affects most of the remaining configurations, including every multimodal multiprofile one, so settling it early tells us which part of the search space to prioritize. Using avgpool gives a clean, low-risk test of the multiprofile effect, and transformer aggregation can be compared against it afterward. Testing other RNA encoders (scVI or scGPT) or the image-only baselines are good follow-ups.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_002 kept the RNA-only PCA (n=2000) setup from llm_summary_001 but switched from single-profile to multiprofile input with average-pooling aggregation. Validation accuracy rose from 0.2266 to 0.5136 and validation F1 from 0.1907 to 0.4982, and the smaller accuracy–F1 gap may mean performance is more even across classes. Because the encoder and modality were held fixed, this is a fairly clean comparison suggesting that multiprofile input with avgpool helps this RNA-only baseline. However, the effect of using multiple profiles cannot be separated from the choice of avgpool, and each configuration has only one run with no variance estimate. It also remains unknown whether the gain holds for other RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), image or multimodal settings, or transformer aggregation, which is the natural next comparison against this avgpool reference.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: So far only the RNA-only PCA setup has been tested. Switching from single-profile to multiprofile with avgpool raised validation accuracy from 0.227 to 0.514, and F1 rose with it. That makes multiprofile avgpool the current reference. The biggest unknown is the image modality. It appears in 42 of the 51 configurations, through the image-only and multimodal options, yet we have no data on it. 2. What this tests: config_011 keeps the multiprofile avgpool setting and swaps RNA for image, using the simpler resnet50 encoder. Comparing it with config_002 shows whether image features alone carry useful signal under the setup that worked for RNA. It also checks whether the multiprofile setting stays strong in a second modality, although that still needs an image single-profile run to confirm. 3. Why this is the best next experiment: if images are weak, most image-only and multimodal options can be deprioritized. If images are strong, fusion becomes a promising direction to exploit. That decision affects most of the remaining search, so it is worth more than smaller refinements such as avgpool versus transformer aggregation or comparing RNA encoders, which can follow.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_003 kept the multiprofile avgpool setup from llm_summary_002 but replaced the RNA PCA (n=2000) encoder with an image-only ResNet50 encoder. It reached validation accuracy 0.5232 and F1 0.5084, slightly above the RNA-only multiprofile result (0.5136 / 0.4982). This initial observation suggests image features alone carry useful signal, at a level comparable to RNA under this setup, so image-only and multimodal options should not be deprioritized and fusion looks worth testing. The ~0.01 difference comes from single runs with no variance estimate, so it should not be read as image outperforming RNA. It is also unknown whether multiprofile avgpool helps images as it did RNA, since no image single-profile run exists, and other image encoders, transformer aggregation, and fusion remain untested.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: Multiprofile avgpool gave a large gain over single-profile for RNA PCA (0.227 to 0.514 accuracy). Image-only ResNet50 under the same multiprofile avgpool setup reached a similar level (0.523 accuracy, 0.508 F1). So both modalities carry comparable signal on their own. Whether combining them adds anything is still untested. 2) Test: config_018 keeps everything from the two completed unimodal runs (PCA n2000, ResNet50, multiprofile, avgpool) and adds simple concat fusion. Any change in accuracy or F1 can therefore be attributed fairly cleanly to fusing the modalities. A clear gain would mean RNA and image carry complementary information. Little or no gain would mean they are redundant and that encoder or aggregation choices matter more. 3) Why now: Whether to pursue multimodal models decides how to spend most of the remaining budget, because most of the untested configurations are multimodal. Concat with avgpool is the simplest fusion baseline, and it gives a reference for later tests of weighted fusion or transformer aggregation. Single runs with no variance estimate mean small differences should not be overread, but a large effect either way would be informative.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_004 combined the two completed unimodal multiprofile avgpool runs (RNA PCA n2000 and image ResNet50) using simple concat fusion, so fusion was the only design change. It reached validation accuracy 0.4275 and F1 0.4166. That is about 0.09 below both RNA-only (0.5136 / 0.4982) and image-only (0.5232 / 0.5084), so this naive concat multimodal model did not benefit from combining modalities and appears to have lost performance. The drop is large enough to be informative despite single runs with no variance estimate. Because it is not known whether the cause is redundant modalities, poor fusion (e.g., feature-scale or dimensionality imbalance between 2000-dim PCA and ResNet50 features), overfitting, or optimization issues, this does not show that multimodal modeling is inherently unhelpful. Weighted fusion, transformer aggregation, other encoders, and normalization of the inputs to concatenation remain untested and could change the conclusion.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: Multiprofile avgpool gave similar results for RNA-only PCA (0.514) and image-only ResNet50 (0.523). Combining them with naive concat fusion (config_018) fell to 0.427, about 0.09 below either unimodal model, which is a large and informative drop. The main open question is whether this drop reflects the concat fusion mechanism (for example, scale or dimensionality imbalance between 2000-dim PCA and ResNet50 features) or a real lack of benefit from combining modalities. 2. Test: config_019 keeps everything from config_018 the same (multiprofile, PCA n2000, ResNet50, avgpool) and changes only the fusion from concat to weighted. This isolates the effect of the fusion method. If weighted fusion recovers or exceeds unimodal performance, fusion design is a key lever and the multimodal space is worth exploring with other encoders and aggregations. If it also underperforms, multimodal configurations can be deprioritized in favor of unimodal encoder and aggregation searches. 3. Budget: The multimodal configurations make up most of the remaining search space, so settling whether fusion choice explains the multimodal failure is the most valuable single experiment for allocating the rest of the budget. It is a clean one-factor comparison against an existing result.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_005 repeated the multimodal multiprofile setup of llm_summary_004 (RNA PCA n2000 + ResNet50 image, avgpool aggregation) but changed only the fusion, from concat to weighted. It reached validation accuracy 0.6530 and F1 0.6283. That is about 0.23 above concat fusion (0.4275 / 0.4166) and about 0.13 above the best unimodal run (image-only ResNet50, 0.5232 / 0.5084). Because fusion was the only factor changed, this is a fairly clean comparison suggesting that fusion design is a key lever, that the earlier multimodal drop likely reflected the concat mechanism rather than a lack of complementary signal, and that the multimodal space is worth further exploration. Uncertainties remain: each configuration has a single run with no variance estimate. It is unknown which aspect of weighted fusion matters, for example whether it corrects scale or dimensionality imbalance or acts more like learned modality selection. It is also untested whether the gain holds with other RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), other image encoders, transformer aggregation, or a normalized-concat baseline.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: Multiprofile input with avgpool clearly beat single-profile for RNA (0.227 to 0.514). Weighted fusion of PCA and ResNet50 gave the best result so far (0.653 accuracy, 0.628 F1), well above concat and both unimodal runs. Aggregation is the largest untested design choice: every multiprofile run has used avgpool, and transformer aggregation has never been tried. 2. What this tests: config_021 keeps the best configuration (config_019) fixed and changes only avgpool to transformer. This isolates whether learned attention across profiles adds value beyond simple averaging, within the multimodal weighted-fusion setting that currently performs best. 3. Why it is the best next use of budget: it exploits the strongest direction while answering an open design question in a single-variable comparison. If transformer helps, it may set a new best. If it hurts, that is evidence avgpool is sufficient here, and later runs can focus on the encoder (scVI, scGPT, ViT-L) against a settled aggregation choice.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_006 kept the best configuration, llm_summary_005 (multimodal multiprofile, RNA PCA n2000 + ResNet50 image, weighted fusion), and changed only the aggregation from avgpool to transformer. Validation accuracy fell from 0.6530 to 0.4849 and F1 from 0.6283 to 0.4639, leaving it below both unimodal avgpool runs (~0.51–0.52) and only modestly above concat fusion (0.4275). Because aggregation was the only factor changed, this is a fairly clean single-run comparison suggesting that transformer aggregation, as configured here, performs worse than avgpool in this setting, and that avgpool is a reasonable default for upcoming encoder comparisons (scVI, scGPT, ViT-L). It remains uncertain whether the drop reflects transformer aggregation itself or under-tuning, overfitting, limited data, or optimization difficulties. There is no variance estimate, and transformer aggregation has not been tested in unimodal or other fusion settings, so it should not be ruled out entirely.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_019 (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA n2000 + ResNet50, avgpool, weighted fusion) at 0.653 accuracy and 0.628 F1. Two single-factor changes from nearby configurations were clean and informative. Switching concat to weighted fusion gained about 0.23. Switching avgpool to transformer aggregation lost about 0.17. Encoder choice is the main design axis not yet tested anywhere: no scVI, scGPT or ViT-L run exists. Image-only ResNet50 was the strongest unimodal model (0.523), so image representation quality may strongly affect the fused result. 2. Test: config_025 keeps the best configuration fixed and changes only the image encoder, from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L. This isolates whether a stronger pretrained image representation improves the weighted-fusion multimodal model. 3. Why now: It exploits the best known setup while answering an open question about representation in a single controlled comparison. Either outcome guides the next step. If ViT-L helps, encoder upgrades become a priority. If it does not, the RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT) become the next lever to test under the same fusion and aggregation settings.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_007 kept the best prior configuration, llm_summary_005 (multimodal multiprofile, RNA PCA n2000, avgpool aggregation, weighted fusion), and changed only the image encoder from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L. Validation accuracy rose from 0.6530 to 0.7207 and F1 from 0.6283 to 0.6815, making this the new best configuration. Because the image encoder was the only factor changed, this is a fairly clean single-run comparison suggesting that a stronger pretrained image representation improves the weighted-fusion multimodal model, which makes encoder choice a promising lever. Uncertainties remain. There is no variance estimate, and the source of the ~0.07 gain is unknown: it could come from model capacity, the ViT architecture, pretraining, or feature dimensionality, and it may interact with weighted fusion. ViT-L has not been tested image-only, so its unimodal contribution is unknown, and RNA encoder alternatives (scVI, scGPT) remain untested under this setup.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_025 (PCA n2000 + ViT-L, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted fusion; 0.7207 acc / 0.6815 F1). Several choices have fairly clean single-factor support. Multiprofile beat single-profile, weighted fusion beat concat, avgpool beat transformer, and ViT-L beat ResNet50. The RNA encoder is the one major design choice that has never been varied; every RNA-containing run used PCA n2000. 2) Test: config_037 keeps the best configuration fixed and swaps only the RNA encoder from PCA n2000 to scVI n200. This isolates whether a learned, lower-dimensional RNA representation improves the fused model. It may help if 2000-dim PCA features are noisy or poorly balanced against image features. 3) Why now: This is a single-factor change on the current best setup, so it can improve performance while also resolving the largest remaining gap in the search. If scVI helps or hurts, the next logical step is to test scGPT (config_049) or check ViT-L image-only (config_014) to measure each modality's contribution.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_008 kept the best configuration, llm_summary_007 (multimodal multiprofile, ImageNet ViT-L image encoder, avgpool aggregation, weighted fusion), and changed only the RNA encoder from PCA n2000 to scVI n200, the first variation of the RNA encoder in the search. Validation accuracy fell from 0.7207 to 0.6352 and F1 from 0.6815 to 0.6183. The result is also slightly below the ResNet50 + PCA weighted-fusion run (0.6530 / 0.6283), although the smaller accuracy–F1 gap may mean performance is somewhat more even across classes. Because only the RNA encoder changed, this is a fairly clean single-run comparison suggesting that scVI n200, as configured here, performs worse than PCA n2000 in this fused setup. It remains uncertain whether the drop reflects the learned scVI representation itself, its lower dimensionality, scVI training or tuning choices, or an interaction with weighted fusion. There is no variance estimate, scVI has not been tested RNA-only, and scGPT and ViT-L image-only (needed to measure each modality's contribution) remain untested.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_025 (PCA n2000 + ViT-L, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted fusion; 0.7207 accuracy / 0.6815 F1). In clean one-factor comparisons, weighted fusion beat concat, avgpool beat transformer aggregation, and ViT-L beat ResNet50. The RNA encoder is the least-resolved important choice. scVI n200 lowered accuracy to 0.6352, and scGPT is completely untested. It is unclear whether PCA is genuinely the better RNA representation or whether scVI's low dimensionality or tuning was the problem. 2) Test: config_049 keeps the best setup and changes only the RNA encoder to scGPT. This shows whether a pretrained foundation-model RNA representation helps or hurts relative to PCA under the strongest fusion and aggregation settings. 3) Why now: It is the only remaining RNA encoder and could plausibly set a new best, so it serves both exploitation and exploration. It also completes the three-way RNA encoder comparison in a single controlled step. An image-only ViT-L run (config_014) would clarify modality contributions, but it cannot improve on the current best, so it is a lower priority under the limited budget.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_009 kept the best configuration, llm_summary_007 (multimodal multiprofile, ImageNet ViT-L, avgpool, weighted fusion; 0.7207 / 0.6815), and changed only the RNA encoder from PCA n2000 to scGPT, which completes the three-way RNA encoder comparison. Validation accuracy fell sharply to 0.4224 (F1 0.4051). That is below scVI n200 (0.6352), below both unimodal multiprofile runs (RNA PCA 0.5136, image ResNet50 0.5232), and near the concat-fusion run (0.4275). As a fairly clean single-run, one-factor comparison, this suggests the RNA encoder ranking in this fused setup is PCA n2000 > scVI n200 > scGPT, and that scGPT features as configured here appear to actively degrade the fused model rather than just add less signal. It remains uncertain whether this reflects scGPT's representation itself or other factors such as embedding extraction, gene-vocabulary or preprocessing mismatch, dimensionality, lack of fine-tuning, or an interaction with weighted fusion; there is also no variance estimate, scGPT has not been tested RNA-only, and the ViT-L image-only run needed to gauge each modality's contribution is still missing.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is config_025 (PCA n2000 + ImageNet ViT-L, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted fusion), at 0.7207 accuracy and 0.6815 F1. Switching the image encoder from ResNet50 to ViT-L added about 0.07 accuracy. However, ViT-L has never been run image-only, so we cannot tell whether that gain came from complementary RNA signal through weighted fusion or simply from much stronger image features. The modality-contribution question has been flagged repeatedly in earlier summaries. 2. What this tests: Config_014 is the image-only counterpart of config_025, differing only in dropping RNA and fusion. It isolates ViT-L's unimodal performance under the same multiprofile avgpool setting. It also gives a ViT-L vs ResNet50 image-only comparison against config_011 (0.5232). If ViT-L alone approaches 0.72, the fused model adds little and the search should focus on image representations. If it stays well below, that confirms real multimodal complementarity and justifies further fusion and RNA-side exploration. 3. Why it is the best use of budget: Encoder, aggregation and fusion axes already have clean one-factor comparisons around the best configuration. The largest remaining gap in understanding is how much each modality contributes to the top model, and this single run addresses it directly and cheaply.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_010 tested an image-only ImageNet ViT-L model (multiprofile, avgpool, no RNA or fusion), the image-only counterpart of the best configuration llm_summary_007 (PCA n2000 + ViT-L, weighted fusion; 0.7207 accuracy / 0.6815 F1), and reached 0.5399 validation accuracy and 0.5245 F1. That is far below the fused model (about 0.18 lower accuracy) and only slightly above image-only ResNet50 (0.5232 / 0.5084), which suggests the top model's performance depends substantially on combining PCA RNA with images through weighted fusion rather than on ViT-L image features alone; continued work on fusion and the RNA side therefore looks justified. The results also hint at an interaction: ViT-L improved over ResNet50 by about 0.07 in the fused setting but by only about 0.02 image-only, and scGPT fusion (0.4224) fell below this image-only baseline, while scVI fusion (0.6352) exceeded it. All comparisons are single runs with no variance estimate, so the small ViT-L vs ResNet50 image-only gap may not be meaningful, and why ViT-L features combine better with RNA (feature dimensionality, how weighted fusion uses them, or another factor) remains untested.

selection_reason: 1) No experiments have been run, so there is no evidence on whether RNA, image, multiprofile aggregation, or fusion helps. 2) config_001 (RNA-only, single-profile, PCA-2000) is the simplest, lowest-complexity configuration. It sets a reference point for validation accuracy and F1 that later experiments can be compared against, each changing one factor at a time: the RNA encoder (config_004/007), the profile setting and aggregation (config_002/003), the image modality (config_010), or multimodal fusion (config_016/017). 3) With a limited budget, a clean simple baseline comes first. It avoids assuming that complex multimodal or multiprofile models are better, and it makes every later single-factor comparison interpretable.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_001 tested the simplest configuration: an RNA-only, single-profile model with a PCA (2000-component) RNA encoder and no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.5136 (primary metric) and a validation F1 of 0.4982. F1 sits slightly below accuracy, which may point to somewhat uneven performance across classes. No other experiments have been completed, so this result is only an initial baseline and reference point. It provides no evidence yet on whether other RNA encoders, multiprofile aggregation, the image modality, or multimodal fusion would improve performance, and later single-factor comparisons (e.g., config_004/007, 002/003, 010, 016/017) are needed to assess each design choice.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: there is only one result, an RNA-only single-profile PCA baseline at 0.514 accuracy and 0.498 F1. We know nothing yet about the image modality, which half of the remaining configurations depend on. 2) Test: config_010 is the image-only single-profile ResNet50 model, the simplest image counterpart to the baseline. Comparing it with config_001 measures how informative images are on their own relative to RNA, with profile setting, aggregation and fusion held fixed (none). 3) Why now: modality is the highest-level design choice and sets priorities for the rest of the budget. If images are weak, multimodal and image-encoder experiments can be deprioritized in favor of RNA encoder and multiprofile tests. If images are competitive, the fusion configurations (e.g., config_016/017) become well-motivated. An RNA encoder comparison (config_004/007) or a multiprofile test (config_002) is also useful, but each would refine only the RNA branch. config_010 also provides the second reference point that any later fusion result needs to be interpreted against.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_002 tested an image-only, single-profile model with a ResNet50 image encoder and no RNA encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.2239 (primary metric) and an F1 of 0.1843, well below the RNA-only PCA single-profile baseline (llm_summary_001: 0.5136 accuracy, 0.4982 F1). Its larger F1-accuracy gap may point to more uneven performance across classes. This is an initial observation that this image-only setup is much less informative than the RNA-only baseline, but the comparison changes both modality and encoder at once (single runs, no variance estimates, chance level unknown), so it cannot separate a modality effect from a ResNet50-specific limitation. It also does not show whether images would add complementary value in fusion (e.g., config_016/017) or perform better with other image encoders or multiprofile aggregation.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: RNA-only PCA single-profile (0.514 acc, 0.498 F1) clearly beats image-only ResNet50 single-profile (0.224 acc, 0.184 F1). So RNA looks like the stronger modality, though this rests on single runs. We have no evidence yet on profile setting, aggregation, RNA encoder or fusion. 2) config_002 changes only one factor from the best baseline: single-profile becomes multiprofile with simple avgpool aggregation, keeping the PCA RNA encoder. This isolates whether pooling multiple profiles helps in the strongest modality. Avgpool is the simplest aggregator, so it tests the profile effect before adding transformer complexity. 3) Most remaining configurations are multiprofile, so learning whether multiprofile helps tells us which large part of the search space deserves budget. Later steps can then compare transformer aggregation (config_003) or alternative RNA encoders (config_004/007) against a clearer reference.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_003 tested an RNA-only multiprofile model with a PCA (2000-component) RNA encoder and simple avgpool aggregation. It differs from the RNA-only single-profile baseline (llm_summary_001: 0.5136 accuracy, 0.4982 F1) only in profile setting, since avgpool aggregation is required to combine multiple profiles. It reached 0.5856 validation accuracy (primary metric) and 0.5745 F1, about +0.07 on both metrics, with a similarly small F1-accuracy gap. This is suggestive evidence that multiprofile input with avgpool helps the PCA RNA model, but it rests on single runs with no variance estimates. It cannot separate the benefit of extra profiles from the specific aggregator, and it is not yet known whether the gain carries over to transformer aggregation (config_003), other RNA encoders (config_004/007), the image modality, or fusion.

selection_reason:
1. Evidence and uncertainty: RNA-only PCA is the strongest setting so far. Moving from single-profile (0.514 accuracy) to multiprofile with avgpool (0.586 accuracy) gave about +0.07 on both accuracy and F1. That is our most promising direction, but it is unclear whether the gain comes from using multiple profiles or from the specific aggregator. Image-only ResNet50 was weak (0.224), so adding images is a lower-priority bet for now.
2. What this tests: config_003 keeps the RNA-only, multiprofile, PCA setup fixed and swaps only avgpool for transformer aggregation. This isolates the effect of the aggregation method.
3. Why it is the best next experiment: it builds directly on the best result with a single-factor change, so either outcome is easy to interpret. It tells us which aggregator to carry into later encoder and fusion comparisons, and it may also raise the best accuracy.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_004 tested an RNA-only multiprofile model with a PCA (2000-component) RNA encoder and transformer aggregation. It differs from llm_summary_003 (avgpool: 0.5856 accuracy, 0.5745 F1) only in the aggregator. It reached 0.4710 validation accuracy (primary metric) and 0.4419 F1. That is about -0.11 accuracy and -0.13 F1 relative to avgpool, below even the single-profile baseline (llm_summary_001: 0.5136), with a slightly larger F1-accuracy gap. This single-factor comparison is initial evidence that, in this setup, avgpool works better than transformer aggregation and is the safer choice to carry forward. However, it rests on single runs with no variance estimates or tuning details, so the transformer's underperformance may reflect optimization, capacity, or data-size issues rather than an inherent limitation. It also remains unclear whether the multiprofile gain seen with avgpool comes from the extra profiles themselves, and whether this ranking holds for other RNA encoders, the image modality, or fusion.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: RNA is clearly the stronger modality so far (PCA single-profile 0.514 vs ResNet50 image-only 0.224). Multiprofile with avgpool is the current best at 0.586 accuracy and 0.574 F1. Transformer aggregation underperformed avgpool (0.471). However, every RNA result so far uses PCA, so the RNA encoder is a major untested design choice. 2. What this tests: config_008 keeps the best setup (RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool) and changes only the RNA encoder from PCA to scGPT. This isolates whether a pretrained foundation-model representation improves on PCA. 3. Why it is the best next use of budget: it exploits the strongest direction found so far while answering a key representation question that carries over to all fusion configurations. Testing fusion with the weak ResNet50 image features now would mix two factors before the best RNA encoder is known. If scGPT does not beat PCA, that still clarifies which RNA encoder to carry into the multimodal comparisons.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_005 tested an RNA-only multiprofile model with avgpool aggregation and a pretrained scGPT RNA encoder. It differs from the current best configuration (llm_summary_003, PCA-2000: 0.5856 accuracy, 0.5745 F1) only in the RNA encoder. It reached 0.4348 validation accuracy (primary metric) and 0.4234 F1, about -0.15 on both metrics, which is also below the PCA single-profile baseline (0.5136). This single-factor comparison is initial evidence that, in this setup, scGPT embeddings underperform PCA and that PCA is the stronger RNA encoder to carry into the multimodal comparisons. Uncertainty remains because these are single runs with no variance estimates, and the result may reflect how the scGPT embeddings were extracted or adapted (e.g., frozen vs fine-tuned, gene-vocabulary overlap, preprocessing) rather than an inherent limitation; it is also unknown whether the gap holds with single-profile input, other aggregators, or fusion.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: The best result so far is RNA-only multiprofile PCA with avgpool (config_002: 0.586 accuracy, 0.574 F1). Single-factor comparisons suggest avgpool beats transformer and PCA beats scGPT. Image-only ResNet50 was weak (0.224), but nothing has tested whether images add complementary information when fused with RNA. That is the main untested design question. 2. Test: config_018 keeps every setting of config_002 (PCA-2000, multiprofile, avgpool) and only adds ResNet50 image features with the simplest fusion, concat. Any difference can therefore be attributed to adding the image modality. 3. Why now: Whether multimodal fusion helps over the strongest unimodal model determines how much of the remaining budget should go to the large multimodal space (image encoder, fusion type). A gain would justify exploring weighted fusion and ViT-L next. No gain or a drop would shift effort toward RNA-side refinements such as scVI (config_005). This makes it the most decision-relevant experiment. It is also a reasonable exploitation step, since it builds directly on the current best configuration.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_006 tested a multimodal multiprofile model that keeps the current best RNA-only setup (llm_summary_003: PCA-2000, multiprofile, avgpool; 0.5856 accuracy, 0.5745 F1) and changes only one thing: it adds ResNet50 image features through simple concat fusion. It reached 0.6776 validation accuracy (primary metric) and 0.6464 F1, the best result so far. That is about +0.09 accuracy and +0.07 F1 over the RNA-only counterpart, even though image-only ResNet50 was weak (llm_summary_002: 0.2239). Because this is a single-factor comparison, it is initial evidence that adding the image modality helps in this setup, which supports further exploration of the multimodal space, such as other fusion types and image encoders. Uncertainty remains for several reasons. These are single runs with no variance estimates. The gain could partly reflect added feature dimensionality or capacity rather than truly complementary image information. The F1-accuracy gap widened slightly (about 0.031 vs 0.011), which may hint at less even per-class performance. It is also unknown whether weighted fusion, stronger image encoders (e.g., ViT-L), or other RNA encoders would increase or reduce the gain.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA-2000, ResNet50, avgpool, concat), at 0.678 accuracy and 0.646 F1. Adding ResNet50 image features gave about +0.09 accuracy over the matching RNA-only model, even though ResNet50 alone was weak (0.224). This suggests the image signal is useful but limited by the encoder. The image encoder is still the least explored important choice, since no ViT-L run exists yet. 2. What this tests: config_024 keeps config_018 exactly and changes only the image encoder to ImageNet ViT-L. This isolates whether a stronger image representation increases the multimodal gain. 3. Why it is the best next use of budget: It is a clean single-factor extension of the best configuration, so it combines exploitation and exploration. Its result will directly guide the many remaining multimodal configurations that depend on the image encoder. Weighted fusion (config_019) is also worth testing, but it is a finer refinement and can follow once the image encoder choice is settled.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_007 kept the best configuration so far (llm_summary_006: multimodal, multiprofile, PCA-2000, avgpool, concat; 0.6776 accuracy, 0.6464 F1) and changed only the image encoder, from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L. It reached 0.5176 validation accuracy (primary metric) and 0.4837 F1, about -0.16 on both metrics. That is below the matching RNA-only multiprofile model (llm_summary_003: 0.5856) and roughly at the single-profile RNA-only baseline (0.5136). This single-factor comparison is initial evidence that, in this concat setup, ViT-L features did not strengthen the multimodal gain and may actively hurt fusion, so ResNet50 remains the image encoder to carry forward. Uncertainty remains for several reasons. These are single runs with no variance estimates, and no image-only ViT-L run exists to show whether its standalone features are weaker or stronger. The drop could also reflect fusion-specific issues such as the higher feature dimensionality of ViT-L overwhelming the RNA signal under plain concat, feature scaling or normalization, or optimization and overfitting, rather than poor image information. Whether weighted fusion or other fusion schemes would change this ranking is still unknown.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA-2000, ResNet50, avgpool, concat; 0.6776 acc, 0.6464 F1). It beat its RNA-only counterpart by about +0.09 accuracy. Swapping in ViT-L under concat hurt badly (0.5176). Fusion type is the one major design axis still completely untested, and the ViT-L drop raises a specific question: does plain concat mishandle the imbalance between the modality feature spaces? 2) Test: config_019 changes only the fusion method, from concat to weighted, and keeps everything else fixed at the best configuration. This isolates the fusion effect and checks whether learned modality weighting adds to the image benefit. It also checks whether weighting reduces the widened F1-accuracy gap. 3) Why now: it is a clean single-factor comparison on the strongest branch, so it serves both exploitation (it may set a new best) and exploration (it resolves fusion uncertainty). The result will guide later choices, for example whether to revisit ViT-L with weighted fusion (config_025). That makes it a better use of the limited budget than revisiting directions with negative evidence (transformer aggregation, scGPT) or the still-untested scVI encoder.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_008 kept the best configuration so far (llm_summary_006: multimodal, multiprofile, PCA-2000, ResNet50, avgpool; 0.6776 accuracy, 0.6464 F1) and changed only the fusion method, from concat to weighted. It reached 0.6287 validation accuracy (primary metric) and 0.5993 F1, about -0.05 on both metrics, with a similar F1-accuracy gap (about 0.029 vs 0.031), so weighting did not narrow the gap. This single-factor comparison is initial evidence that, in this setup, weighted fusion does not improve on concat and that concat remains the fusion to carry forward. Weighted fusion still beat the RNA-only multiprofile counterpart (llm_summary_003: 0.5856), so the image benefit persisted under both fusion types. Uncertainty remains for several reasons: these are single runs with no variance estimates, the weighting scheme's implementation, learned weights, and tuning are unknown, and it is unclear whether weighted fusion would behave differently with ViT-L, where concat performed poorly.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA-2000, ResNet50, avgpool, concat; 0.678 accuracy, 0.646 F1). Single-factor changes from it all scored lower: ViT-L dropped to 0.518, and weighted fusion dropped to 0.629. Transformer aggregation also lost to avgpool in the RNA-only comparison (0.471 vs 0.586). The RNA encoder axis is only partly explored. scGPT underperformed PCA, but scVI-200 has never been tested in any setting, so it is the largest remaining unknown among the design choices. 2. What this tests: config_030 keeps the best configuration and swaps only the RNA encoder from PCA-2000 to scVI-200. It asks whether a compact, batch-aware latent representation beats or complements ResNet50 image features better than PCA does. scVI's lower dimensionality (200) may also balance the two modalities better under plain concat. That would bear on the earlier concern that feature dimensionality affects concat fusion. 3. Why this is the best next experiment: it is a clean one-variable comparison against the current best. It explores the only fully untested level of a major design factor, and it still has a realistic chance of improving the best score. Other options are less useful right now. Single-profile multimodal runs or further ViT-L and transformer variants either target smaller questions or extend directions that have so far performed worse.
