experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_009 kept the best configuration so far (llm_summary_006: multimodal, multiprofile, ResNet50, avgpool, concat; 0.6776 accuracy, 0.6464 F1) and changed only the RNA encoder, from PCA-2000 to scVI-200, the first test of scVI in any setting. It reached 0.7150 validation accuracy (primary metric) and 0.6872 F1, the new best result, about +0.04 on both metrics, with a similar F1-accuracy gap (about 0.028 vs 0.031). This single-factor comparison is initial evidence that, in this multimodal concat setup, scVI-200 is a stronger RNA encoder than PCA-2000 and should be carried forward. Uncertainty remains for several reasons. These are single runs with no variance estimates, and the margin is modest. No RNA-only scVI run exists, so it is unclear whether the gain comes from better standalone RNA features or from better modality balance under concat because of scVI's lower dimensionality. It is also unknown whether scVI changes the earlier rankings for fusion type, image encoder (e.g., ViT-L), aggregator, or single-profile input.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is config_030 (scVI-200, ResNet50, multiprofile, avgpool, concat) at 0.715 accuracy and 0.687 F1, about +0.04 over its PCA counterpart. scVI has never been tested without images, so we cannot tell whether the gain comes from better standalone RNA features or from better modality balance, since scVI's lower dimensionality may help under concat. 2. What this tests: The RNA-only scVI-200 multiprofile avgpool model differs from config_002 (PCA, 0.586) only in RNA encoder. It also differs from config_030 only in dropping the image modality. It therefore answers two questions: whether scVI beats PCA as a standalone RNA representation, and how much ResNet50 images add on top of scVI. If the image gain shrinks, the multimodal benefit may partly reflect dimensionality or balance effects rather than complementary image information. 3. Why it is the best use of the budget: Single-factor comparisons are already in place on both sides. The result will guide whether to keep investing in multimodal variants (for example, scVI with ViT-L or weighted fusion) or to focus on the RNA representation. This reduces key uncertainty more than another incremental multimodal tweak would.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_010 tested an RNA-only multiprofile avgpool model with a scVI-200 RNA encoder. It differs from llm_summary_003 (PCA-2000: 0.5856 accuracy, 0.5745 F1) only in the RNA encoder, and from llm_summary_009 (scVI-200 + ResNet50 concat, current best: 0.7150 accuracy, 0.6872 F1) only in dropping images. It reached 0.4214 validation accuracy (primary metric) and 0.4124 F1, with a small F1-accuracy gap (about 0.009). That is about -0.16 below the PCA RNA-only counterpart, below the single-profile PCA baseline (0.5136), and similar to scGPT (0.4348). These single-factor comparisons are initial evidence that scVI-200 is a weaker standalone RNA representation than PCA-2000 in this setup. Adding ResNet50 images gives a much larger gain with scVI (about +0.29) than with PCA (about +0.09), so the advantage of scVI in llm_summary_009 does not appear to come from better standalone RNA features but from how scVI interacts with image features under concat. Uncertainty remains for several reasons. These are single runs with no variance estimates, and scVI training details are unknown. The evidence cannot separate complementary image information from dimensionality or modality-balance effects; for example, a low-dimensional PCA control (e.g., PCA-200 + ResNet50) or a multiprofile image-only run would help. It is also unknown whether this scVI-image synergy holds with weighted fusion, ViT-L, or single-profile input.

selection_reason: 1) No experiments have been run, so there is no evidence yet about which modality, encoder, profile setting, aggregation or fusion matters. 2) config_001 (RNA-only, single-profile, PCA-2000) is the simplest, lowest-complexity configuration. It gives a reference accuracy and F1 against which each later design choice can be compared by changing one factor at a time: RNA encoder via config_004/007, multiprofile aggregation via config_002/003, image modality via config_010, and fusion via config_016/017. 3) Starting from a minimal baseline gives the most interpretable anchor for the limited budget. It avoids assuming that multimodal or multiprofile complexity helps, and it makes every subsequent single-factor comparison informative.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_001 tested the simplest configuration: RNA-only, single-profile, with a PCA (2000-component) RNA encoder and no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.525 and a supporting validation F1 of 0.498. This is the first completed experiment, so the result is a baseline reference only. It does not show whether any design choice helps or hurts. Still unknown: whether other RNA encoders (e.g., config_004/007), multiprofile aggregation (config_002/003), adding the image modality (config_010), or fusion strategies (config_016/017) would improve on it, and how much the result would vary across runs, since only a single run is available.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: there is only one result so far. RNA-only, single-profile, PCA-2000 reached 0.525 accuracy and 0.498 F1. No design choice has been tested yet. 2. Test: config_002 changes one factor from this baseline, single-profile to multiprofile, using the simplest aggregation (avgpool) and keeping the same RNA-only PCA setup. Any difference can therefore be attributed to profile setting. 3. Why now: profile setting runs through roughly two-thirds of the remaining configurations, so learning early whether multiprofile helps will guide where the rest of the budget goes. Avgpool is a lower-variance first check than the transformer. A gain would justify testing transformer aggregation and other encoders under multiprofile next. A loss would point toward single-profile and encoder or modality comparisons instead. Since this is one run, a small difference should be treated as weak evidence rather than a settled answer.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_002 tested RNA-only, multiprofile input with mean-pooled (avgpool) aggregation, keeping the PCA-2000 RNA encoder and the no-image, no-fusion setup of the llm_summary_001 baseline. It reached 0.532 validation accuracy (supporting F1 0.516), versus 0.525 accuracy (F1 0.498) for the single-profile baseline. That is a small gain of about 0.007 in accuracy and a somewhat larger gain of about 0.018 in F1. Because each configuration has only one run and run-to-run variance is unknown, this is weak evidence that multiprofile with avgpool helps slightly. The effect of multiprofile input also cannot be separated from the addition of avgpool aggregation, since the two change together. Still untested: transformer aggregation under multiprofile (e.g., config_003), other RNA encoders, the image modality, fusion strategies, and whether this small margin would hold across repeated runs.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: Only two RNA-only PCA-2000 runs exist. The single-profile baseline reached 0.525 accuracy, and multiprofile with avgpool reached 0.532 (F1 0.516 vs 0.498). That is a small gain from single runs and is weak evidence. The image modality is completely untested, yet over two-thirds of the search space (image-only and multimodal configurations) depends on whether images carry useful signal. 2) What this tests: An image-only, single-profile ResNet50 run gives a clean baseline for the image modality, directly comparable to the single-profile RNA baseline (config_001). Its result shows whether images alone are predictive and how they compare to RNA. That indicates whether multimodal fusion is worth pursuing and suggests which modality may dominate. 3) Why this is the best next use of budget: Aggregation (config_003) and RNA encoder (config_004/007) comparisons refine a single branch and would likely yield small differences. The modality question has the largest effect on where the remaining budget should go, so resolving it first reduces the most uncertainty about the overall design.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_003 established the first image-only baseline: single-profile input with a ResNet50 image encoder and no RNA encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It reached 0.260 validation accuracy (supporting F1 0.222), well below the single-profile RNA-only PCA-2000 baseline (llm_summary_001: 0.525 accuracy, F1 0.498). From single runs, this is an initial observation that this image pipeline carries clearly less predictive signal than RNA in this setup. The gap of about 0.27 accuracy is large compared with the 0.007 multiprofile difference seen in llm_summary_002, so it is less likely to be explained by run-to-run noise alone. Still uncertain: whether images add complementary signal when fused with RNA (multimodal configurations), whether other image encoders or multiprofile aggregation would raise image-only performance, and how much these single-run results vary, so multimodal fusion should not be ruled out on this evidence.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence so far: RNA-only PCA-2000 gives about 0.525–0.532 accuracy. Image-only ResNet50 is far weaker (0.260). It is still unknown whether images add complementary signal when combined with RNA. 2) config_016 tests exactly that. It adds ResNet50 images to the single-profile PCA-2000 baseline (config_001) with simple concat fusion, and keeps every other choice fixed. The comparison isolates the effect of adding the image modality. 3) This is the best use of the next experiment because most remaining configurations are multimodal. Knowing early whether fusion helps, is neutral, or hurts relative to RNA-only will decide whether the budget should go to multimodal variants or to RNA encoders and aggregation. Either outcome is informative.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_004 added ResNet50 image features to the single-profile PCA-2000 RNA baseline (llm_summary_001) using simple concat fusion, with all other choices held fixed. It reached 0.224 validation accuracy (supporting F1 0.184), far below the RNA-only baseline (0.525 accuracy, F1 0.498) and even below image-only ResNet50 (llm_summary_003: 0.260 accuracy, F1 0.222). In this single run, adding images through concat fusion was strongly harmful; the drop of about 0.30 accuracy is too large to be easily explained by run-to-run noise, given the roughly 0.007 differences seen elsewhere. Because performance fell below both unimodal baselines, the result may reflect a problem with how this concat pipeline combines the modalities (e.g., feature scale or dimensionality imbalance, or optimization issues) rather than images lacking complementary signal, and the current evidence cannot tell these apart; other fusion strategies (e.g., config_017), feature normalization, multiprofile multimodal settings, and repeated runs remain untested, so multimodal approaches should not be ruled out, though naive concat with these encoders looks unpromising.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: RNA-only PCA-2000 is the strongest result so far (about 0.525–0.532 accuracy). Image-only ResNet50 is much weaker (0.260). Concat fusion of the two (config_016: 0.224 accuracy, 0.184 F1) fell below both unimodal baselines. That pattern suggests the concat pipeline itself is failing, for example through scale or dimensionality imbalance, rather than images simply adding no signal. One run cannot tell these explanations apart. 2) What this tests: config_017 keeps everything from config_016 the same (single-profile, PCA-2000, ResNet50) and changes only the fusion method from concat to weighted. This isolates the effect of fusion. If weighted fusion recovers to near or above the RNA-only baseline, the concat result was a fusion artifact and multimodal remains a live direction. If it also collapses, adding ResNet50 images is likely harmful in this setup. 3) Why it is the best next experiment: multimodal settings make up most of the remaining search space, and whether fusion can work at all is currently the largest open question. A single one-variable comparison settles whether to keep exploring that space or redirect the budget to RNA-only questions such as the scVI and scGPT encoders and transformer aggregation. It is more informative than a small RNA-only tweak at this stage.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_005 repeated the single-profile multimodal setup of llm_summary_004 (PCA-2000 RNA plus ResNet50 images) and changed only the fusion method, from concat to weighted. It reached 0.523 validation accuracy (supporting F1 0.508), a large recovery from concat fusion (0.224 accuracy, F1 0.184) and roughly equal to the single-profile RNA-only baseline (llm_summary_001: 0.525 accuracy, F1 0.498). Because fusion was the only variable changed, this single-run comparison suggests the concat collapse was a fusion artifact rather than proof that images are inherently harmful, so multimodal configurations remain viable. However, there is no evidence yet that images add complementary signal: accuracy is about 0.002 below RNA-only, and the roughly 0.010 F1 gain is within the margins seen elsewhere. It is also unknown whether weighted fusion simply down-weights the image branch, how large run-to-run variance is, and whether multiprofile multimodal settings, other encoders, or other fusion strategies would improve on RNA-only performance (best so far: llm_summary_002, multiprofile avgpool, 0.532 accuracy).

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: RNA is clearly the dominant source of signal. RNA-only reached about 0.525 accuracy, against 0.260 for image-only. Weighted multimodal fusion only matched RNA-only (0.523), and multiprofile avgpool gave just a small gain (0.532, single run). Every RNA result so far uses PCA-2000, so the choice of RNA encoder, probably the most important design lever here, is completely untested. 2. What this tests: config_004 swaps PCA-2000 for scVI-200 in the single-profile RNA-only baseline (config_001) and changes nothing else. Any difference can therefore be attributed to the RNA representation alone. 3. Why it is the best next use of budget: Further fusion or aggregation tweaks look likely to give only small margins near noise level. The encoder result will shape which RNA backbone carries into later multiprofile and multimodal experiments, so it reduces the largest remaining uncertainty at low cost.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_006 changed only the RNA encoder in the single-profile RNA-only baseline (llm_summary_001), replacing PCA-2000 with scVI-200. It reached 0.471 validation accuracy (supporting F1 0.442), about 0.054 accuracy and 0.056 F1 below the PCA-2000 baseline (0.525, F1 0.498). Because the encoder was the only variable changed, this single-run comparison suggests that this scVI-200 setup is a weaker RNA representation than PCA-2000 here. The gap is larger than the roughly 0.002 to 0.007 differences seen elsewhere but has not been checked against run-to-run variance. Still uncertain: whether the deficit comes from scVI itself or from its smaller latent size or training and hyperparameter choices (other scVI dimensions or encoders such as config_007 are untested), and whether the ranking would hold under multiprofile or multimodal settings. For now, PCA-2000 remains the stronger RNA backbone, with the best overall result still llm_summary_002 (multiprofile avgpool, 0.532 accuracy).

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: the best result so far is multiprofile avgpool with PCA-2000 (config_002, 0.532 accuracy, F1 0.516). It is only slightly above single-profile (0.525). The aggregation method has not been tested on its own, because the multiprofile gain could not be separated from avgpool. PCA-2000 is the strongest RNA encoder so far (scVI-200 was about 0.054 lower). Images have not yet added signal: concat collapsed, and weighted fusion matched RNA-only. 2) Test: config_003 changes only the aggregation, from avgpool to transformer, on the current best RNA-only multiprofile PCA-2000 setup. This shows whether a learned set aggregator can extract more from multiple profiles than mean pooling, or whether the small multiprofile gain is all this setting offers. 3) Why now: it is a single-variable extension of the current best configuration, so it exploits the promising direction while settling a design choice that affects every multiprofile configuration, unimodal and multimodal. Its answer will guide later choices between avgpool and transformer when testing scGPT, ViT-L, or multiprofile fusion.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_007 took the previous best setup (llm_summary_002: RNA-only, multiprofile, PCA-2000) and changed only the aggregation, from avgpool to a learned transformer set aggregator. It reached 0.706 validation accuracy (supporting F1 0.667), up from 0.532 accuracy (F1 0.516), a gain of about 0.174 accuracy and 0.151 F1, which makes it the new best configuration by a wide margin. Because aggregation was the only variable changed, this single-run comparison suggests that how multiple profiles are combined matters much more than the small avgpool gain over single-profile (about 0.007) implied, and that transformer aggregation extracts substantially more signal from multiprofile input. Still uncertain: run-to-run variance (only one run, though the gap far exceeds the 0.002 to 0.007 differences seen elsewhere), whether the gain comes from the attention mechanism itself or from added capacity or training choices, sensitivity to transformer hyperparameters, and whether the advantage carries over to other RNA encoders (e.g., scGPT), image-only multiprofile, or multiprofile multimodal fusion, none of which has been tested.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: Transformer aggregation over multiprofile PCA-2000 RNA (config_003) is the clear best result at 0.706 accuracy and 0.667 F1. Its gain of about 0.17 over avgpool far exceeds the 0.002 to 0.007 differences seen elsewhere. In single-profile runs, adding ResNet50 images with weighted fusion (config_017) recovered from the concat collapse but only matched RNA-only (0.523 vs 0.525). So it is still unknown whether images add complementary signal, especially once the model can aggregate across profiles. 2. Test: config_021 keeps the best setup (multiprofile, PCA-2000, transformer) and adds ResNet50 images through weighted fusion, the fusion method already shown to avoid the concat failure. Comparing it with config_003 isolates whether the image modality helps or hurts on top of the strongest RNA pipeline. 3. Why now: This exploits the strongest evidence by extending the best configuration with a single, well-motivated addition. It also answers a central design question, whether multimodality is worth it, in the setting most likely to reveal a benefit. Running it before encoder or image-only multiprofile sweeps is the most efficient use of the next experiment.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_008 took the best configuration (llm_summary_007: RNA-only, multiprofile, PCA-2000, transformer aggregation; 0.706 accuracy, F1 0.667) and changed only one thing: it added ResNet50 image features through weighted fusion. It reached 0.530 validation accuracy (supporting F1 0.515), a drop of about 0.176 accuracy and 0.152 F1 that wipes out the transformer gain and lands near the multiprofile avgpool RNA-only level (llm_summary_002: 0.532). Because the image branch was the only variable changed, this single-run comparison suggests that adding images this way strongly hurts in the multiprofile transformer setting. That contrasts with single-profile, where weighted fusion roughly matched RNA-only (llm_summary_005: 0.523 vs 0.525). The cause remains uncertain: images may lack complementary signal, or the drop may come from how weighted fusion interacts with transformer aggregation (e.g., fusion placement relative to aggregation, modality scale imbalance, optimization or capacity issues), and run-to-run variance, other fusion strategies, image normalization, and image-only multiprofile performance are all untested, so for now the RNA-only multiprofile transformer remains the best and most reliable configuration.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is config_003 (RNA-only, multiprofile, PCA-2000, transformer aggregation) at 0.706 accuracy and 0.667 F1. Transformer aggregation was by far the largest effect seen. Adding images hurt in both concat and weighted fusion, and scVI-200 was weaker than PCA-2000 in the single-profile setting. The scGPT encoder is the main design choice not yet tested at all. 2. What this tests: config_009 changes only the RNA encoder, from PCA-2000 to scGPT, within the best setup. It shows whether a pretrained foundation-model representation adds signal beyond PCA once profiles are combined by the transformer. It also checks whether the transformer gain depends on the encoder. 3. Why it is the best next use of budget: It is a clean one-variable comparison against the strongest configuration, so it both explores the untested encoder and could produce a new best. Further multimodal tests look lower-value until the RNA backbone is settled.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_009 took the best configuration (llm_summary_007: RNA-only, multiprofile, transformer aggregation, PCA-2000; 0.706 accuracy, F1 0.667) and changed only the RNA encoder, from PCA-2000 to the pretrained scGPT encoder. It reached 0.536 validation accuracy (supporting F1 0.516), a drop of about 0.170 accuracy and 0.151 F1. That leaves it only marginally above the multiprofile avgpool PCA level (llm_summary_002: 0.532), so this single-run comparison suggests the scGPT representation, as configured here, adds no signal beyond PCA and does not keep the transformer aggregation gain. Together with the weaker scVI-200 result (llm_summary_006), PCA-2000 remains the strongest tested RNA backbone. Still uncertain: whether the deficit reflects scGPT itself or setup choices (e.g., frozen versus fine-tuned embeddings, embedding extraction, dimensionality or normalization mismatch, transformer hyperparameters tuned for PCA inputs), run-to-run variance, and how scGPT performs in single-profile or avgpool settings, which would show whether the problem is specific to its interaction with transformer aggregation.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: The RNA-only multiprofile transformer is clearly best (config_003: 0.706 accuracy, F1 0.667). Adding ResNet50 images through weighted fusion in that same setting dropped it to 0.530 (config_021). In single-profile, weighted fusion roughly matched RNA-only (0.523 vs 0.525). We only know image-only performance for single-profile (0.260), so we cannot tell why images hurt the multiprofile transformer. The images may simply carry little signal, or the problem may come from how fusion interacts with transformer aggregation. 2) What this tests: Image-only, multiprofile, ResNet50 with transformer aggregation changes only the profile/aggregation setting relative to config_010. It shows whether transformer aggregation over multiple profiles also lifts image-only performance, as it did for RNA (+0.17 over avgpool). A strong gain would point to a fixable fusion problem as the cause of the multimodal drop, which would justify exploring other fusion variants. Little or no gain would support deprioritizing ResNet50 multimodal configurations. 3) Why it is the best use of budget: It resolves the main open question about whether the large multimodal branch of the search space is worth pursuing. It does this with a single-variable comparison and without stacking changes to encoder and fusion.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_010 tested image-only ResNet50 with multiprofile input and transformer aggregation. It reached 0.586 validation accuracy (supporting F1 0.574), far above the single-profile image-only baseline (llm_summary_003: 0.260, F1 0.222) but still below the best configuration, the RNA-only PCA-2000 multiprofile transformer (llm_summary_007: 0.706, F1 0.667). Because profile setting and aggregation changed together, this single run cannot separate the effect of multiprofile input from transformer aggregation (image-only avgpool is untested). Even so, it suggests ResNet50 images carry substantial signal when multiple profiles are aggregated. It also outperforms the multimodal weighted-fusion transformer (llm_summary_008: 0.530), so that multimodal drop is more plausibly a fusion or integration problem (e.g., fusion placement, modality scaling, optimization) than a lack of image signal, which makes alternative fusion variants in the multiprofile transformer setting worth exploring. Still uncertain: run-to-run variance, whether images add complementary signal beyond RNA under a better fusion scheme, and whether other image encoders or aggregation choices would do better.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been run, so we know nothing yet about the value of modality, representation, profile setting, aggregation, or fusion. 2. What this tests: config_001 (RNA-only, single-profile, PCA n2000, no aggregation or fusion) is the simplest configuration in the space. It sets a baseline that later experiments can each change along one axis: encoder (scVI, scGPT), profile setting (multiprofile with avgpool or transformer), and modality (image-only, multimodal). 3. Why it is the best use of budget: Without a simple reference point, gains from more complex models cannot be judged. This baseline makes every later comparison a clean single-variable test, and it avoids assuming that multimodal or multiprofile models will help.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_001 established the first baseline: an RNA-only, single-profile model using a PCA (n=2000) RNA encoder with no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It reached validation accuracy of 0.4348, with validation F1 of 0.4234, so performance is moderate and roughly consistent across classes. This is the only completed experiment, so no comparison yet shows whether other RNA encoders (e.g., scVI, scGPT), multiprofile aggregation, image-only inputs, or multimodal fusion would help or hurt. The result serves as a reference point for later single-axis comparisons, but its run-to-run variability and how far it sits above chance are still unknown.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: The only result so far is the RNA-only, single-profile PCA baseline (accuracy 0.435, F1 0.423). We know nothing yet about whether the imaging modality carries useful signal, and the image and multimodal configurations make up most of the remaining search space. 2. What this tests: An image-only, single-profile ResNet50 model (no aggregation, no fusion) gives a matched baseline for the second modality. It keeps the profile setting and the simplest pipeline the same and swaps only the input modality. 3. Why it is the best next use of budget: This result shapes how we prioritise most later experiments. If image features alone are competitive or complementary, multimodal fusion becomes a strong direction. If they are weak, the budget should go to RNA encoders and multiprofile aggregation instead. The profile-setting and RNA-encoder comparisons stay simple single-axis follow-ups for afterwards.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_002 tested an image-only, single-profile model with a ResNet50 image encoder and no RNA encoder, aggregation, or fusion, as a matched second-modality baseline to the RNA-only PCA run (llm_summary_001). It reached validation accuracy of 0.7250 and F1 of 0.6847, well above the RNA-only baseline (0.4348 accuracy, 0.4234 F1). This suggests the imaging modality, at least as encoded by ResNet50, carries substantial class signal, so image-based and multimodal configurations look like promising directions. Because modality and encoder changed together, the gap cannot be attributed to modality alone: it may partly reflect PCA being a weak RNA encoder. Also unknown are run-to-run variance, whether RNA adds complementary signal under fusion, the effect of multiprofile aggregation, and whether other image or RNA encoders would change the picture. The somewhat lower F1 relative to accuracy may point to uneven performance across classes.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: Image-only ResNet50 (0.725 acc, 0.685 F1) clearly beats RNA-only PCA (0.435 acc, 0.423 F1). We still do not know whether RNA adds complementary signal on top of the strong image representation, or whether it just adds noise. 2. What this tests: config_016 takes the best configuration so far (single-profile ResNet50) and adds only one thing, PCA RNA features through simple concat fusion. Profile setting and image encoder stay the same, so any gain or loss in accuracy or F1 can be attributed to adding the RNA modality. 3. Why it is the best next use of budget: Whether multimodality helps determines whether roughly 36 of the remaining multimodal configurations are worth exploring. A clean, single-axis test of this question is therefore highly informative. It also has a reasonable chance of improving on the current best, while follow-ups on image encoder, profile setting, or aggregation can still be run afterward.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_003 tested whether adding RNA helps the best configuration so far. It took the single-profile ResNet50 image model and added only PCA (n=2000) RNA features via simple concat fusion, with no aggregation. Validation accuracy fell to 0.6501 and F1 to 0.6275, below image-only ResNet50 (0.7250 / 0.6847) but well above RNA-only PCA (0.4348 / 0.4234). Because this was a single-axis change, the drop is associated with adding PCA RNA under concat fusion in this setting. It does not show that multimodality is unhelpful in general: PCA may be a weak RNA encoder, naive concat may let the noisier RNA features dilute the image signal, and other fusion methods, RNA encoders (e.g., scVI, scGPT), or multiprofile aggregation were not tested. Each result also comes from a single run with unknown run-to-run variance, so the size and reliability of the gap are uncertain.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: image-only ResNet50 single-profile is clearly the best so far (0.725 accuracy, 0.685 F1). It beats RNA-only PCA (0.435) by a wide margin. Adding PCA RNA via concat lowered performance (0.650). The profile-setting axis (single-profile vs multiprofile aggregation) has not been tested in any modality, and it affects most of the remaining configurations. 2) This run changes only one thing from the best configuration: single-profile becomes multiprofile with avgpool aggregation, keeping the image-only ResNet50 setup. It will show whether pooling multiple profiles adds signal on top of the strongest single-modality baseline. Avgpool is the simpler aggregator, so it gives a clean first read before trying transformer aggregation. 3) It exploits the most promising direction (image features) while settling a broad design question. The answer will guide whether later image-only and multimodal experiments should favor multiprofile settings. That makes it more informative per experiment than testing a fusion or encoder variant on the weaker multimodal path.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_004 tested the profile-setting axis for the first time. It took the best configuration so far (image-only ResNet50, single-profile) and changed only one thing: single-profile became multiprofile with avgpool aggregation. Validation accuracy was 0.7150 and F1 was 0.6872, essentially matching the single-profile baseline (0.7250 / 0.6847): accuracy was about 0.01 lower and F1 marginally higher. Simple average pooling over multiple profiles therefore showed no clear gain in this setting. Several things remain uncertain: whether the small differences exceed run-to-run variance (each result comes from a single run), whether a learned aggregator such as a transformer would extract more from multiple profiles, and whether multiprofile settings behave differently for RNA-only or multimodal configurations.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: Image-only ResNet50 single-profile is the best result so far (0.725 acc / 0.685 F1). Adding PCA RNA via concat fusion lowered performance. Multiprofile avgpool gave no clear gain (0.715 / 0.687). The image encoder axis has never been tested, even though imaging carries most of the signal seen so far. 2. Test: Swapping only the image encoder from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L, keeping image-only and single-profile fixed, isolates the effect of image representation on the strongest modality. 3. Why now: The image encoder choice applies to every image-only and multimodal configuration remaining, so the answer is useful across most of the search space. It is also a direct, single-axis extension of the current best, so it may give the highest immediate gain while resolving a key uncertainty. RNA encoder comparisons (scVI, scGPT) remain important and can follow once the stronger image backbone is known.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_005 tested the image-encoder axis for the first time by swapping ResNet50 for an ImageNet-pretrained ViT-L in the image-only, single-profile configuration that had performed best so far, with no RNA encoder, aggregation, or fusion. Validation accuracy fell sharply to 0.5266 and F1 to 0.5104, compared with 0.7250 / 0.6847 for ResNet50. Because only the encoder changed, the drop is associated with using ImageNet ViT-L in this setup, and ResNet50 remains the stronger image backbone among those tried. It is still uncertain whether the gap reflects the architecture itself or setup factors such as input resolution, preprocessing, which features are extracted, or how well the pretrained ViT features transfer to cellular images, and whether it would hold across repeated runs, in multimodal or multiprofile settings, or for other image encoders (e.g., domain-specific or self-supervised models).

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: Adding PCA RNA to ResNet50 through concat fusion (config_016: 0.650 accuracy / 0.628 F1) scored below image-only ResNet50 (0.725 / 0.685). It is unclear whether naive concat dilutes the stronger image signal or whether PCA RNA simply adds nothing useful. 2) Test: This keeps everything from config_016 the same (single-profile, PCA n=2000, ResNet50) and changes only concat to weighted fusion. That isolates the fusion axis, which has not been tested yet. If weighted fusion recovers or beats image-only performance, the earlier drop was due to the fusion method, and the multimodal direction stays viable. If it still trails image-only, PCA RNA is more likely the limiting factor, which points next to stronger RNA encoders such as scVI or scGPT. 3) Why now: It is a clean one-variable comparison against an existing result. It answers a central question about whether multimodality can help in this study. It also has a realistic chance of matching or exceeding the current best, because weighted fusion can down-weight the weaker modality.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_006 kept the single-profile multimodal setup of llm_summary_003 (PCA n=2000 RNA + ResNet50, no aggregation) and changed only concat fusion to weighted fusion, isolating the fusion axis. Validation accuracy was 0.6530 and F1 was 0.6283, essentially identical to concat (0.6501 / 0.6275) and still well below image-only ResNet50 (0.7250 / 0.6847). Weighted fusion therefore did not recover the image-only performance, and concat versus weighted fusion made no meaningful difference in this setting. This is consistent with, but does not prove, the view that PCA RNA features are the limiting factor rather than the fusion method. It remains uncertain whether stronger RNA encoders (e.g., scVI, scGPT) or other fusion schemes (e.g., attention or gated fusion) would let RNA add complementary signal, why weighted fusion did not simply down-weight RNA toward image-only performance (which could reflect how the weighting is learned or constrained), and whether these small differences exceed run-to-run variance, since each result comes from a single run.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: Image-only ResNet50 is the best result so far (0.725 accuracy / 0.685 F1). Adding PCA RNA lowered performance under both concat fusion (0.650) and weighted fusion (0.653). RNA-only PCA was weak (0.435). The prior summaries suggest the PCA RNA encoder, not the fusion method, may be the bottleneck. However, the RNA-encoder axis has never been tested, and about two thirds of the remaining configurations depend on it. 2) What this tests: Swapping only PCA (n=2000) for scVI (n=200) in the RNA-only, single-profile baseline (config_001) isolates the effect of the RNA representation. It shows whether a stronger RNA encoder carries substantially more class signal. 3) Why this is the best next experiment: If scVI clearly beats PCA, the logical follow-up is scVI plus ResNet50 multimodal (config_028/029), to see whether RNA can then add complementary signal. If scVI does not help, that supports deprioritizing RNA and multimodal runs in favor of image-side refinements such as transformer aggregation (config_012). Testing this in the RNA-only setting avoids confounding encoder quality with fusion behavior, so either outcome redirects the remaining budget.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_007 tested the RNA-encoder axis for the first time. It took the RNA-only, single-profile baseline (llm_summary_001) and swapped only the PCA (n=2000) encoder for scVI (n=200), with no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. Validation accuracy rose from 0.4348 to 0.5856 and F1 from 0.4234 to 0.5745, so in this isolated comparison scVI is associated with substantially more class signal than PCA. This supports the earlier view that PCA was a weak RNA representation, though scVI RNA-only remains well below image-only ResNet50 (0.7250 / 0.6847). It is still uncertain whether scVI RNA would add complementary signal when fused with ResNet50 rather than diluting it as PCA did (0.650–0.653), how other RNA encoders (e.g., scGPT) or multiprofile settings would compare, and how large run-to-run variance is, since each result comes from a single run.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: image-only ResNet50 is the best configuration so far (0.725 accuracy / 0.685 F1). Adding PCA RNA lowered performance to about 0.650–0.653 accuracy, whether fusion was concat or weighted. That suggests fusion method is not the bottleneck and points to the weak PCA RNA features instead. scVI then raised RNA-only accuracy from 0.435 to 0.586, so the stronger RNA representation is now known. What remains open is whether any RNA encoder adds complementary signal to images rather than diluting it. 2. What this tests: config_028 is config_016 (PCA + ResNet50, single-profile, concat) with only the RNA encoder changed to scVI. This isolates the RNA encoder within the multimodal setting. If it approaches or beats 0.725, multimodal fusion is worth pursuing with better RNA features. If it still falls below image-only, RNA appears to dilute the image signal even with a stronger encoder. Concat is used because it matches the existing PCA baseline and fusion type showed no difference. 3. Why now: this result decides how to spend much of the remaining budget, since most untested configurations are multimodal. A clear answer here tells us whether to invest in multimodal variants (scVI or scGPT, aggregation) or to focus on image-only refinements.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_008 took the single-profile PCA + ResNet50 concat setup (llm_summary_003) and changed only the RNA encoder to scVI (n=200), isolating the RNA encoder in the multimodal setting. Validation accuracy collapsed to 0.4214 and F1 to 0.4124. That is far below image-only ResNet50 (0.7250 / 0.6847) and PCA + ResNet50 concat (0.6501 / 0.6275). It is also below scVI RNA-only (0.5856 / 0.5745) and slightly below PCA RNA-only (0.4348 / 0.4234). So in this isolated comparison, the stronger RNA-only encoder was associated with much worse multimodal performance, and this concat model did worse than either of its unimodal components. Because a fused model scoring below both of its unimodal parts is anomalous, the cause is highly uncertain. Possible explanations include a training or optimization failure, feature-scale or dimensionality mismatch between scVI latents and ResNet50 features under naive concat, or a pipeline issue. Since this is a single run with unknown variance, verifying the result (for example, a rerun, feature normalization, or weighted fusion with scVI) would be prudent before concluding that RNA cannot add complementary signal or redirecting the remaining budget away from multimodal variants.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: ResNet50 image-only is the best model so far (0.725 accuracy). Adding PCA RNA lowered performance under both concat (0.650) and weighted fusion (0.653), so fusion type made little difference with PCA. scVI is clearly the stronger RNA-only encoder (0.586 vs 0.435). Yet scVI+ResNet50 concat collapsed to 0.421, below either of its unimodal parts. That anomaly could be a concat-specific failure, such as feature-scale or dimensionality mismatch between scVI latents and ResNet50 features, or a broader problem with scVI fusion. 2) What this tests: config_029 changes only concat to weighted fusion in the scVI+ResNet50 single-profile setup. If accuracy recovers to about 0.65 or higher, the collapse was concat-specific, and scVI may still add complementary signal. If it stays near 0.42, the problem lies with scVI in fusion or the pipeline. 3) Why it is the best use of the budget: the conclusion about whether RNA helps when fused depends on resolving this anomaly. That decides whether the many remaining scVI and multimodal configurations are worth exploring, so this single-axis verification is more informative than further image-only tuning.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_009 took the scVI (n=200) + ResNet50 single-profile concat setup (llm_summary_008) and changed only concat to weighted fusion, as a check on whether that model's collapse was specific to concat. Validation accuracy was 0.2596 and F1 was 0.2217. That is even lower than scVI + ResNet50 concat (0.4214 / 0.4124) and far below image-only ResNet50 (0.7250 / 0.6847), scVI RNA-only (0.5856 / 0.5745), and PCA + ResNet50 weighted fusion (0.6530 / 0.6283), so a concat-specific failure does not explain the anomaly. Both scVI fusion runs now score below either unimodal component, while PCA fusion runs did not. This points to a problem specific to combining scVI features with ResNet50 in this pipeline, but the available evidence cannot distinguish feature-scale or normalization mismatch, an optimization or training failure, misalignment of scVI latents with image samples in the fused pipeline, or a code bug. Each result also comes from a single run, so diagnostics would be prudent before deprioritizing scVI multimodal configurations or concluding that RNA cannot add complementary signal; useful checks include a rerun, normalizing scVI features before fusion, and verifying the fused data pipeline.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: image-only ResNet50 is clearly the strongest direction so far (single-profile 0.725 accuracy, multiprofile avgpool 0.715 accuracy with marginally higher F1). Every multimodal fusion run has scored below image-only, and the scVI fusion runs behaved anomalously, so it is unclear whether RNA helps at all in this pipeline. The aggregation axis is only half explored: simple average pooling gave no clear gain, and the transformer aggregator has never been tested in any setting. 2. Test: switching config_011's avgpool to transformer aggregation, with everything else unchanged, isolates whether a learned aggregator can extract more signal from multiple profiles than mean pooling. 3. Why now: this extends the best-performing branch, so it may raise the top score, and it resolves an important design choice at the same time. If the transformer beats avgpool, multiprofile becomes a priority for later multimodal runs. If it does not, multiprofile settings can reasonably be deprioritized, which saves budget. It is more informative now than further multimodal runs, which remain confounded by the unexplained scVI fusion failures.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_010 took the image-only, multiprofile ResNet50 avgpool setup (llm_summary_004) and changed only the aggregator to a transformer, testing for the first time whether a learned aggregator extracts more from multiple profiles than mean pooling. Validation accuracy fell to 0.4849 and F1 to 0.4639. That is far below avgpool (0.7150 / 0.6872) and single-profile ResNet50 (0.7250 / 0.6847), and close to the RNA-only PCA baseline (0.4348 / 0.4234). Because only the aggregator changed, the drop is associated with transformer aggregation in this setup, and avgpool remains the better multiprofile aggregator among those tried, though neither has beaten single-profile. The size of the drop could reflect undertraining or optimization difficulty, too little data for a learned aggregator, hyperparameter choices, or a pipeline issue (as with the anomalous scVI fusion runs), rather than an inherent limit of learned aggregation; given these possibilities and single-run results with unknown variance, it is uncertain whether multiprofile settings in general should be deprioritized or how transformer aggregation would behave in RNA-only or multimodal configurations.

selection_reason: 1) No experiments have been run, so there is no evidence yet about which modality, encoder, profile setting, aggregation or fusion matters. 2) config_001 (RNA-only, single-profile, PCA-2000) is the simplest, most standard baseline. It sets a reference accuracy and F1 that later experiments can be compared against one variable at a time: scVI or scGPT encoders, multiprofile with avgpool or transformer, image-only, and multimodal fusion. 3) Under a limited budget, anchoring the search with a cheap, interpretable baseline is the most efficient first step. It avoids assuming that complex multimodal or multiprofile models help, and every later result becomes a clean single-factor comparison rather than a confounded one.
experiment_summary: The first experiment (llm_summary_001) tested the simplest baseline: an RNA-only, single-profile model with a PCA (n=2000) RNA encoder, with no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.706 (primary metric), and the supporting validation F1 of 0.667 is somewhat lower, possibly reflecting uneven per-class performance. Because no other configurations have been run, this is only an initial reference point. It says nothing yet about whether alternative RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), multiprofile aggregation (avgpool, transformer), image-only models, or multimodal fusion would perform better or worse. Run-to-run variance is also unknown, so later comparisons against this baseline should be treated cautiously, ideally with replicates and single-variable changes.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: The only result so far is the RNA-only, single-profile PCA baseline (config_001), with accuracy 0.706 and a lower F1 of 0.667. We know nothing yet about whether imaging adds useful signal, even though multimodal configurations make up most of the remaining search space (36 of 50). 2. What this tests: config_016 keeps the RNA encoder (PCA) and the single-profile setting the same and adds only a ResNet50 image branch with the simplest fusion, concatenation. Comparing it with config_001 isolates whether adding the image modality improves accuracy and F1. 3. Why now: Whether multimodality helps is the design choice that decides how much of the remaining budget should go to multimodal versus unimodal configurations. Answering it early with a clean change to one design choice gives the most information. Encoder choice, multiprofile aggregation and fusion type can then be explored conditional on this result. One caveat is that run-to-run variance is unknown, so a small difference between the two runs should be read cautiously.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_002 added a ResNet50 image branch with concatenation fusion to the RNA-only single-profile PCA (n=2000) baseline (llm_summary_001), leaving everything else unchanged so that adding imaging was the only change. Validation accuracy fell from 0.706 to 0.507 (primary metric), and F1 fell from 0.667 to 0.455. This gap of about 0.2 is large enough that it is probably not run-to-run noise, although variance is still unmeasured. This suggests that adding images this way (ResNet50 features plus plain concatenation) hurts rather than helps, but it does not show that the image modality is uninformative in general. The drop could instead come from how features are combined, such as scale or dimensionality imbalance or the image features overwhelming the RNA signal, from the choice of image encoder, or from training dynamics. Next steps could include an image-only run to gauge the image signal on its own, alternative fusion methods, feature normalization, or replicates to estimate variance.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: the RNA-only single-profile PCA baseline (config_001) reached 0.706 accuracy and 0.667 F1. Adding a ResNet50 image branch with concat fusion (config_016) dropped accuracy to 0.507 and F1 to 0.455. We cannot yet tell whether this drop comes from weak ResNet50 image features or from how concat fusion combined the two modalities. 2) Test: an image-only ResNet50 single-profile run measures the image signal on its own, holding the encoder and profile setting fixed. If it scores near or below 0.5, ResNet50 features are weak and adding them dilutes the RNA signal. If it scores well, the fusion method is the likely problem, which would point toward weighted fusion (config_017). 3) Why now: this one run resolves the main open question about the image modality before we spend budget on the many multimodal configurations. It also sets the reference point for later comparisons with ViT-L and multiprofile image models.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_003 tested an image-only, single-profile model with a ResNet50 image encoder and no RNA encoder, aggregation, or fusion, to measure the image signal on its own after concat fusion (llm_summary_002, 0.507 accuracy) underperformed the RNA-only PCA baseline (llm_summary_001, 0.706). It reached a validation accuracy of 0.411 (primary metric) and F1 of 0.378, the lowest of the three runs and below the 0.5 threshold the run was designed around. This suggests that ResNet50 single-profile image features carry relatively weak signal in this setup, consistent with the hypothesis that adding them diluted the RNA signal, and the concat model scoring between image-only and RNA-only fits that picture. It does not rule out fusion-method effects, though, since weighted fusion (config_017) and normalization are untested, and chance level (number of classes), run-to-run variance, and whether other image encoders (e.g., ViT-L) or multiprofile image aggregation would extract stronger image signal all remain unknown.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: RNA-only single-profile PCA is clearly the strongest so far (0.706 accuracy, 0.667 F1). Adding ResNet50 images by concatenation dropped this to 0.507, and image-only reached just 0.411. So the RNA branch carries most of the signal, and profile setting and aggregation are completely untested. 2) This run changes one thing from the best baseline: single-profile to multiprofile with simple avgpool aggregation, keeping PCA RNA and no images. It isolates whether pooling multiple profiles improves the dominant RNA signal, without confounds from image encoder or fusion choices. 3) Profile setting affects a large share of the remaining search space (RNA-only, image-only and multimodal variants). Avgpool is the simplest aggregation, so it is the cleanest first test before the transformer. Building on the best direction is likely to perform well, and either outcome will narrow the space for later choices of encoder, aggregation and fusion.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_004 kept the best configuration so far, the RNA-only PCA (n=2000) model with no images (llm_summary_001, 0.706 accuracy / 0.667 F1), and switched from single-profile to multiprofile input with avgpool aggregation. Validation accuracy fell sharply to 0.421 (primary metric), with F1 at 0.412. That is roughly the image-only level (llm_summary_003, 0.411) and below the multimodal concat run (llm_summary_002, 0.507). The roughly 0.28 drop is large enough that it is probably not run-to-run noise, though variance is still unmeasured, so multiprofile with avgpool appears clearly worse than single-profile in this RNA-only setup. However, the profile setting and the aggregation method changed together, so it is unclear whether the drop comes from multiprofile input itself (for example, different sample counts or label structure), from mean-pooling washing out informative profile-level variation, or from implementation or training issues. Transformer aggregation, multiprofile runs with other encoders or modalities, chance level, and replicates remain untested.

selection_reason: Evidence: the RNA-only single-profile PCA baseline (config_001, 0.706 acc / 0.667 F1) is the best so far. Switching to multiprofile with avgpool (config_002) dropped accuracy sharply to 0.421. That change altered profile setting and aggregation together, so we cannot tell whether multiprofile input is inherently worse or mean-pooling discarded useful profile-level variation. Test: config_003 keeps everything from config_002 (RNA-only, PCA n2000, multiprofile) and changes only the aggregation, from avgpool to transformer. This isolates the effect of aggregation on multiprofile input. Why now: roughly half the remaining grid is multiprofile. If transformer aggregation recovers toward or beyond the 0.706 baseline, those configurations stay worth exploring. If it stays near 0.42, we can confidently deprioritize multiprofile and focus the budget on single-profile RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT) and fusion methods. This is a clean single-variable comparison against the best modality setting, so it resolves a high-leverage uncertainty more efficiently than testing a new encoder first.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_005 kept the multiprofile RNA-only PCA (n=2000) setup of llm_summary_004 and changed only the aggregation, from avgpool to transformer. This was a single-variable test of whether mean-pooling caused the drop from the single-profile baseline (llm_summary_001, 0.706 acc / 0.667 F1). Validation accuracy was 0.435 (primary metric) with F1 0.423, only marginally above avgpool (0.421 / 0.412) and far below the single-profile baseline. This suggests the choice between these two aggregators is not the main cause of the multiprofile drop, which points to something about the multiprofile setting itself, its data or label structure, or the pipeline, and weakens the case for further multiprofile runs with this encoder. Still uncertain: whether the ~0.013 gain is real given unmeasured run-to-run variance, whether the transformer aggregator was adequately tuned or trained, the chance level, and whether multiprofile input behaves differently with other RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), image inputs, or fusion. A brief check for implementation issues or data/label differences in multiprofile mode may be warranted before deprioritizing it entirely.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: the single-profile RNA-only PCA (n=2000) baseline is clearly the strongest run so far (0.706 acc / 0.667 F1). Adding ResNet50 images with concat fusion (0.507), image-only ResNet50 (0.411) and multiprofile RNA with either aggregator (0.421 and 0.435) all fell well below it. The RNA encoder is the main untested design choice in the best-performing branch, since every RNA run so far used PCA. 2) This run keeps the best setting fixed (RNA-only, single-profile, no aggregation or fusion) and changes only the encoder from PCA to scVI (n=200). That isolates whether a learned, lower-dimensional latent captures RNA signal better or worse than PCA. 3) This is a low-confounding, single-variable test on the most promising branch, so it serves both exploitation and exploration. Its result will guide later choices, such as comparing scGPT and deciding which RNA encoder to carry into further fusion or multiprofile runs. Further multiprofile or image-heavy runs now look less promising than resolving this choice.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_006 kept the best configuration so far (RNA-only, single-profile, no aggregation or fusion; llm_summary_001, 0.706 acc / 0.667 F1) and changed only the RNA encoder, from PCA (n=2000) to scVI (n=200). Validation accuracy fell to 0.532 (primary metric), with F1 at 0.517. This is still above the image-only and multiprofile runs (0.411–0.435) and about level with multimodal concat (0.507). The ~0.17 drop is large enough that it is probably not run-to-run noise, though variance is unmeasured, so this scVI setup appears clearly worse than PCA here and PCA (n=2000) remains the strongest RNA encoder tested. The run does not show whether the gap comes from the learned scVI latent itself, its much lower dimensionality (200 vs 2000), or scVI training and tuning choices, and scGPT, a higher-dimensional scVI, replicates, and the chance level all remain untested.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: Single-profile RNA-only PCA (config_001, 0.706 acc / 0.667 F1) is clearly the best so far. Adding ResNet50 images with concat fusion (config_016) dropped accuracy to 0.507. Image-only ResNet50 (config_010) reached only 0.411, so the image signal looks weak and concat may let it dilute or overwhelm the RNA features. It is still unclear whether the multimodal drop reflects an uninformative modality or just the fusion method. 2) What this tests: config_017 is identical to config_016 except that fusion changes from concat to weighted. This isolates the fusion effect. If weighted fusion recovers to near or above 0.706, the concat drop was a fusion artifact and multimodal remains a viable direction. If it stays well below 0.706, that is strong evidence against ResNet50 multimodal fusion, and we can deprioritize most of the remaining multimodal ResNet50 configurations. 3) Why this is the best next use of budget: it is a clean single-variable comparison on the central design question of whether multimodal fusion can beat the strong RNA-only baseline. Either outcome prunes a large part of the remaining search space. Testing scGPT single-profile (config_007) is a close alternative and a sensible follow-up.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_007 repeated the multimodal single-profile PCA (n=2000) + ResNet50 setup of llm_summary_002 and changed only the fusion, from concat to weighted. This was a single-variable test of whether the multimodal drop was a fusion artifact. Validation accuracy rose from 0.507 to 0.653 (primary metric), and F1 rose from 0.455 to 0.628. This suggests the fusion method substantially affects multimodal performance and that much of the concat drop was likely due to how features were combined, though variance is unmeasured. However, the result is still about 0.05 below the RNA-only PCA baseline (llm_summary_001, 0.706 / 0.667), so there is still no evidence that adding ResNet50 images helps. Weighted fusion may simply be down-weighting a weak image signal (image-only was 0.411). Still uncertain: whether the ~0.05 gap to RNA-only is beyond run-to-run noise, what weights the fusion learned, whether stronger image encoders (e.g., ViT-L) or tuning or normalization could let multimodal fusion beat RNA-only, and the chance level.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: RNA carries most of the signal. RNA-only single-profile PCA (n=2000) is the best run so far (0.706 acc / 0.667 F1). Every other change has hurt performance: images (image-only 0.411; best multimodal, weighted fusion, 0.653), multiprofile aggregation (0.421–0.435) and scVI (0.532). The RNA encoder is the one major axis still only partly explored, since scGPT is untested. 2. Test: config_007 keeps the best configuration and changes only the RNA encoder to scGPT. This shows whether a pretrained foundation-model embedding beats or trails PCA. It also helps explain the scVI drop: if scGPT also underperforms, simple high-dimensional PCA features may be better suited to this task than learned latents. 3. Why now: RNA dominates performance, so the RNA encoder choice is likely to have the most leverage. A clean one-variable comparison against the current best finishes the encoder comparison. Its result also decides whether later multimodal runs should use PCA or scGPT, which makes it more efficient than probing ViT-L image runs first.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_008 kept the best configuration so far (RNA-only, single-profile, no aggregation or fusion; llm_summary_001, PCA n=2000, 0.706 acc / 0.667 F1) and changed only the RNA encoder to scGPT. Validation accuracy fell to 0.485 (primary metric), with F1 at 0.464. That is below scVI (llm_summary_006, 0.532 / 0.517) and multimodal concat (0.507), and above only the image-only and multiprofile runs (0.411–0.435). The ~0.22 drop from PCA is large enough that it is probably not run-to-run noise, though variance is unmeasured. Both learned or pretrained encoders tested (scVI, scGPT) now trail PCA (n=2000), which is consistent with, but does not prove, the hypothesis that simple high-dimensional PCA features suit this task better. PCA should likely stay the default RNA encoder for later multimodal runs. Still uncertain: whether scGPT's underperformance reflects the embedding itself, how it was extracted (e.g., cell vs. gene-token pooling, gene-vocabulary overlap), the lack of fine-tuning, its dimensionality, or the downstream head and tuning, along with the chance level and replicate variance.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: RNA-only single-profile PCA (config_001, 0.706 acc / 0.667 F1) is still the best run. Weighted fusion recovered most of the multimodal loss (config_017, 0.653 vs 0.507 with concat). However, ResNet50 image features look weak (image-only 0.411), so the image encoder may be the bottleneck. ViT-L is the main untested design choice that could plausibly make multimodal fusion beat RNA-only. Multiprofile, scVI and scGPT all look clearly worse and are lower priority. 2. Test: config_023 keeps the best multimodal setup (single-profile, PCA n=2000, weighted fusion) and changes only the image encoder from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L. This isolates whether a stronger image representation adds information beyond RNA. 3. Why now: it is a clean single-variable extension of the most promising multimodal direction. It has a realistic chance of a new best result and directly answers whether imaging helps at all. If it still trails RNA-only, an image-only ViT-L run (config_013) can then show whether the image signal itself is the limit.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_009 kept the best multimodal setup (single-profile, PCA n=2000 RNA, weighted fusion; llm_summary_007, 0.653 acc / 0.628 F1) and changed only the image encoder from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L, to test whether a stronger image representation could let fusion beat the RNA-only PCA baseline (llm_summary_001, 0.706 / 0.667). Validation accuracy collapsed to 0.227 (primary metric), with F1 at 0.191. This is the lowest result of all runs, far below the ResNet50 weighted run, the RNA-only baseline, and even the ResNet50 image-only run (0.411), so ViT-L in this pipeline clearly did not help and appears harmful. Because a fusion model with the strong PCA RNA branch scored well below RNA-only and image-only levels, the drop may reflect a feature-extraction, normalization or scale, dimensionality, or training or optimization failure rather than ViT-L features being inherently less informative, and the evidence cannot separate these explanations. Still uncertain: the chance level, the fusion weights learned, replicate variance, and how ViT-L performs on its own; an image-only ViT-L run (config_013) and a sanity check of the ViT-L feature pipeline would help diagnose the result before ViT-L is ruled out.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: PCA n=2000 single-profile RNA-only is the best run (0.706). Weighted fusion with ResNet50 reached 0.653. Swapping in ImageNet ViT-L under the same weighted fusion collapsed accuracy to 0.227, below even ResNet50 image-only (0.411). That result is hard to explain if ViT-L features are merely weak, since the PCA branch should have kept accuracy near RNA-only. So the collapse could come from the ViT-L features themselves or from a pipeline, scale, or optimization failure. 2) This run tests image-only single-profile ViT-L. It differs from the ResNet50 image-only run (config_010) only in the image encoder, so it isolates ViT-L's standalone signal. If it matches or beats 0.411, ViT-L features are informative and the collapse points to fusion or scale problems. If it is near chance or far below 0.411, the ViT-L features or their extraction are the problem. 3) Why this is the best next run: ViT-L appears in about half of the remaining multimodal and image configurations. Resolving whether it is viable or broken will guide many future choices, which makes this the most uncertainty-reducing experiment for the budget. Multiprofile and alternative RNA encoders already show consistent large deficits and offer less to learn.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_010 tested an image-only, single-profile model with an ImageNet ViT-L image encoder and no RNA encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It differs from the ResNet50 image-only run (llm_summary_003, 0.411 acc / 0.378 F1) only in the image encoder, so it isolates ViT-L's standalone signal after the ViT-L weighted-fusion collapse (llm_summary_009, 0.227). It reached 0.715 validation accuracy (primary metric) with F1 0.687, far above ResNet50 image-only and marginally above the RNA-only PCA n=2000 baseline (llm_summary_001, 0.706 / 0.667), making it the best run so far. This indicates that ViT-L features are highly informative and that ViT-L itself was likely the source of the large image-only gain. It also implies the llm_summary_009 collapse more likely came from the fusion, scale or normalization, or optimization interaction than from weak ViT-L features, though that run's failure has not been directly diagnosed. Still uncertain: whether the ~0.01 edge over RNA-only exceeds run-to-run noise, why PCA + ViT-L weighted fusion failed so badly, and whether fixes such as feature normalization, concat or other fusion, or retuning could let ViT-L + PCA fusion beat either single modality. Replicate variance, chance level, and ViT-L in multiprofile settings also remain untested.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been run, so we have no data on any design choice. That includes whether RNA or image carries more signal and whether multiprofile aggregation or fusion add value. 2. What this tests: config_001 (RNA-only, single-profile, PCA with 2000 components) is the simplest configuration, with no aggregation or fusion. It sets a reference baseline that later changes can be compared against one factor at a time: RNA encoder (scVI, scGPT), profile setting (avgpool, transformer), modality (image-only), and fusion. 3. Why now: Under a limited budget, a simple, low-variance baseline makes every later comparison interpretable. Starting with a complex multimodal model would mix several factors together and leave us unable to attribute any gain or loss. Choosing this config does not assume complexity is unhelpful; it is the point that later experiments, such as an image-only single-profile run or multimodal concat, will be measured against.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_001 tested the simplest configuration as the reference baseline: RNA-only, single-profile, PCA RNA encoder with 2000 components, and no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It reached validation accuracy 0.520 (primary metric) and validation F1 0.479. The lower F1 may mean uneven performance across classes, but this is not confirmed. Because no other experiments have been completed, this is only an initial baseline and supports no conclusions about whether RNA or image carries more signal, or whether alternative RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), multiprofile aggregation (avgpool, transformer), or fusion add value. Those questions need one-factor-at-a-time comparisons against this run. Run-to-run variance is also unknown, so small differences from future runs should be interpreted cautiously.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: We have only one result. RNA-only, single-profile, PCA reaches 0.520 accuracy and 0.479 F1. We do not yet know whether the image modality carries comparable, weaker, or stronger signal, and that is the most important unknown for the whole search. Every multimodal configuration (016–051) depends on it, and no other single factor determines more of the remaining space. 2. What this tests: config_010 runs image-only, single-profile, ResNet50. It keeps the single-profile setting and the absence of aggregation and fusion from the baseline, so it isolates the modality as cleanly as the design allows. It gives a direct RNA-vs-image reference point. 3. Why this is the best use of budget: Knowing the standalone image signal tells us whether fusion is worth pursuing and how much effort image encoders deserve. Comparing RNA encoders or adding aggregation would refine a single branch first, before we know whether that branch is the right focus. ResNet50 is the simpler image encoder, so it is a sensible first image reference before testing ViT-L.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_002 tested image-only, single-profile, ResNet50 image encoder with no RNA encoder, aggregation, or fusion, as the first image reference against the RNA-only PCA (n=2000) baseline (llm_summary_001: accuracy 0.520, F1 0.479). It reached validation accuracy 0.514 (primary metric) and validation F1 0.498. That is about 0.006 lower in accuracy but about 0.019 higher in F1 than the RNA baseline, which suggests the two single-modality setups carry roughly comparable signal and that the image model may perform somewhat more evenly across classes. Because modality and encoder both changed together (ResNet50 vs PCA) and run-to-run variance is unknown, this gap cannot be attributed to modality alone and may be within noise. Whether ViT-L or other RNA encoders change the balance, and whether fusion or multiprofile aggregation adds value over either single modality, remains untested.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: The two single-modality baselines are nearly tied. RNA-only PCA reached accuracy 0.520 and F1 0.479. Image-only ResNet50 reached accuracy 0.514 and F1 0.498. Neither clearly dominates, and their accuracy/F1 profiles differ, which hints that they may capture partly complementary signal. Whether fusion adds value over either modality alone is the largest open question. 2) Test: config_016 combines exactly the two components already measured (PCA n2000 RNA and ResNet50 image) with simple concat fusion, single-profile and no aggregation. Fusion is the only new factor, so it gives a clean comparison against both baselines. 3) Why now: Whether multimodality helps determines whether roughly 36 multimodal configurations are worth exploring or whether the budget should go to single-modality encoder and aggregation choices. Concat is the simplest fusion and gives a reference for later weighted-fusion tests. Any gain should be judged cautiously, since run-to-run variance is unknown.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_003 tested multimodal concat fusion of the two components already measured alone: PCA (n=2000) RNA plus ResNet50 image, single-profile, no aggregation. This makes fusion the only new factor relative to the RNA-only (llm_summary_001: accuracy 0.520, F1 0.479) and image-only (llm_summary_002: accuracy 0.514, F1 0.498) baselines. It reached validation accuracy 0.713 (primary metric) and F1 0.695, about 0.19 above either single-modality run on both metrics. This gain is much larger than the earlier ~0.006 gap between modalities and is consistent with the two modalities carrying complementary signal, which supports exploring the multimodal configuration space further. Uncertainties remain: run-to-run variance is unknown (though it seems unlikely to explain a gain this large), this is a single run with one encoder pair and the simplest fusion, and it is untested whether other RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), ViT-L, weighted fusion, or multiprofile aggregation would add to or change this gain.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: Multimodal concat fusion (config_016: accuracy 0.713, F1 0.695) beat both single-modality baselines (about 0.52 and 0.51 accuracy) by about 0.19 on both metrics. That makes the multimodal PCA plus ResNet50 setup the clear anchor for further search. Every other axis is still untested: profile setting, aggregation, fusion type and encoders. Profile setting (single vs multiprofile) is arguably the largest structural choice left. 2. Test: config_018 changes only the profile setting, from singleprofile to multiprofile with the simplest aggregation (avgpool). Encoders and concat fusion stay fixed. This isolates whether pooling information across multiple profiles adds signal on top of the strong multimodal baseline. Using avgpool rather than a transformer keeps the comparison clean. A transformer would add learned capacity, which would confound the effect of multiprofile input itself. 3. Why now: This is a one-factor change from the best configuration, so it exploits the promising direction while answering a high-impact design question. If multiprofile helps, it opens the 12-plus multiprofile multimodal configurations as the main search space and motivates a later avgpool vs transformer comparison. If it doesn't help, the remaining budget can go to single-profile encoder and fusion comparisons such as ViT-L, scVI/scGPT and weighted fusion.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_004 changed the best configuration so far (llm_summary_003: multimodal PCA n=2000 RNA + ResNet50 image, concat fusion, single-profile; accuracy 0.713, F1 0.695) from single-profile to multiprofile input, which also required adding the simplest aggregation (avgpool). It reached validation accuracy 0.573 (primary metric) and F1 0.573. That is about 0.14 below the single-profile multimodal anchor, though still about 0.05 above the single-modality baselines (llm_summary_001: 0.520; llm_summary_002: 0.514). F1 now essentially matches accuracy, which may indicate more even performance across classes, but this is unconfirmed. Because multiprofile input and avgpool aggregation were introduced together, the drop cannot be attributed to multiprofile input itself rather than to avgpool possibly diluting profile-level signal, and run-to-run variance is unknown. It remains untested whether a learned aggregator such as a transformer, or other encoders and fusion types, would recover or exceed the single-profile result, so single-profile multimodal remains the stronger observed direction for now.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: Single-profile multimodal concat (PCA n=2000 + ResNet50) is the best result so far, at 0.713 accuracy and 0.695 F1. Moving to multiprofile with avgpool (config_018) dropped accuracy to 0.573. Multiprofile input and avgpool were introduced together, so it is unclear whether multiprofile input hurts or whether avgpool dilutes profile-level signal. This ambiguity affects a large part of the remaining search space, since about half of the untested configurations are multiprofile. 2. What this tests: config_020 is identical to config_018 except that avgpool is replaced by the learned transformer aggregator. It therefore isolates the aggregation effect. If accuracy recovers to near or above 0.713, multiprofile remains viable and avgpool was the bottleneck. If it stays near 0.57, multiprofile input itself likely underperforms here, and the budget can shift toward single-profile variants such as fusion type and encoder choice. 3. Why it is the best next step: It is a one-factor comparison against an existing run and resolves the largest open question, a 0.14 swing, more than marginal fusion or encoder tweaks would. It also has a plausible chance of producing a new best result.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_005 kept the multiprofile multimodal setup of llm_summary_004 (PCA n=2000 RNA + ResNet50 image, concat fusion) and changed only the aggregator, replacing avgpool with a learned transformer, so it is a one-factor test of aggregation. It reached validation accuracy 0.715 (primary metric) and F1 0.687, recovering the full ~0.14 drop seen with avgpool (0.573 / 0.573). This suggests avgpool, rather than multiprofile input itself, was mainly responsible for that drop, and that multiprofile configurations remain viable. Against the single-profile multimodal anchor (llm_summary_003: 0.713 / 0.695), accuracy is nominally the highest so far but only about 0.002 higher, while F1 is about 0.008 lower. With unknown run-to-run variance and single runs, this is effectively a tie, so there is no evidence yet that multiprofile input adds value over single-profile. It also remains untested whether other encoders (scVI, scGPT, ViT-L) or weighted fusion would separate the two profile settings.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: Fusing modalities gave the largest gain so far. Multimodal PCA (n=2000) + ResNet50 with concat reached about 0.713 accuracy, versus about 0.52 for either single modality. Swapping avgpool for a transformer aggregator recovered multiprofile performance to 0.715. That is a tie with single-profile (0.713), and single-profile has the slightly higher F1. So fusion matters, but only the simplest fusion type (concat) has been tested. Fusion type is a binary choice that affects every multimodal configuration remaining in the space. 2. What this tests: config_017 keeps the single-profile multimodal anchor (config_016) unchanged and swaps only concat for weighted fusion. Any difference can therefore be attributed to fusion type alone. 3. Why it is the best next use of budget: Single-profile is the simpler anchor, avoids aggregation as a confound, and performs as well as multiprofile. The result will tell us which fusion type to carry forward into later encoder tests (ViT-L, scVI, scGPT), so those comparisons can each vary one factor on the stronger fusion setting.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_006 kept the single-profile multimodal anchor (llm_summary_003: PCA n=2000 RNA + ResNet50 image, no aggregation, concat fusion; accuracy 0.713, F1 0.695) and changed only concat to weighted fusion, making it a one-factor test of fusion type. It reached validation accuracy 0.525 (primary metric) and F1 0.498. That is about 0.19 below the concat anchor and essentially at the single-modality baselines (RNA-only 0.520 / 0.479; image-only 0.514 / 0.498), so in this run weighted fusion erased the entire multimodal gain, and concat remains the observed fusion setting to carry forward. Because the drop matches the earlier fusion gain almost exactly, it may reflect the weighted fusion collapsing onto one modality or failing to train in this implementation, not an inherent limit of weighted fusion.
