This is unconfirmed, as are run-to-run variance and whether weighted fusion behaves differently with multiprofile transformer aggregation or with other encoders (scVI, scGPT, ViT-L).

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: Concat fusion of PCA (n=2000) RNA and ResNet50 image is the clear winner so far. Single-profile reached 0.713 accuracy and 0.695 F1, about 0.19 above either single modality. Multiprofile with transformer aggregation ties it (0.715 / 0.687), while avgpool and weighted fusion both lost most or all of the gain. Encoder choice is now the largest untested design dimension, since every run so far used PCA and ResNet50. 2) Test: config_022 keeps the single-profile concat anchor (config_016) and changes only the image encoder from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L. This isolates whether a stronger image representation adds to the multimodal gain. 3) Why now: The design choices we can keep fixed are already settled enough (concat; single-profile as the simpler of two tied settings), so the most uncertain remaining factor is representation. The single-profile anchor is the cleanest and cheapest baseline for a one-factor encoder test. ViT-L is the only alternative image encoder, so one run fully answers the image-encoder question. Alternative RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT) would need two runs, so they can follow next using the same design.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_007 kept the single-profile multimodal concat anchor (llm_summary_003: PCA n=2000 RNA + ResNet50 image, no aggregation; accuracy 0.713, F1 0.695) and changed only the image encoder from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L, making it a one-factor test of image representation. It reached validation accuracy 0.678 (primary metric) and F1 0.646, about 0.036 and 0.048 below the anchor but still well above the single-modality baselines (RNA-only 0.520 / 0.479; image-only ResNet50 0.514 / 0.498). In this setup ViT-L did not add to the multimodal gain and nominally reduced it, so ResNet50 remains the observed image encoder to carry forward. Uncertainties remain: the gap is moderate and run-to-run variance is unknown, ViT-L was never tested image-only (so its standalone quality is unmeasured), and the drop could reflect an interaction with PCA RNA features or concat fusion, for example the larger embedding dimension unbalancing the concatenation, rather than ViT-L being inherently weaker; whether it behaves differently with multiprofile transformer aggregation or with scVI/scGPT RNA encoders is also untested.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: profile setting, aggregation, fusion and image encoder have each had a one-factor test around the multimodal concat anchor. Single-profile concat (config_016: 0.713/0.695) and multiprofile transformer (config_020: 0.715/0.687) are effectively tied. Avgpool, weighted fusion and ViT-L each did worse. The RNA encoder is the only major design choice not yet tested: every RNA-containing run used PCA n=2000, so whether scVI or scGPT changes the multimodal gain is unknown. 2. What this tests: config_028 keeps the single-profile ResNet50 concat anchor and changes only the RNA encoder from PCA n=2000 to scVI n=200. This isolates the effect of RNA representation in the best-performing setup. It also bears on the open hypothesis that embedding-dimension balance matters for concat fusion, since scVI's embedding is much smaller. 3. Why it is the best next use of budget: it fills the largest remaining gap with a clean comparison. It has a realistic chance of beating the current best, and it tells us which RNA encoder to carry into later scGPT or multiprofile-transformer runs. The single-profile anchor is used because it is simpler and cheaper and performed as well as multiprofile.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_008 kept the single-profile multimodal concat anchor (llm_summary_003: ResNet50 image, no aggregation; accuracy 0.713, F1 0.695) and changed only the RNA encoder from PCA n=2000 to scVI n=200, making it the first one-factor test of RNA representation. It reached validation accuracy 0.629 (primary metric) and F1 0.599. That is about 0.084 and 0.095 below the anchor and also below the ViT-L variant (llm_summary_007: 0.678 / 0.646), but still about 0.11 above the single-modality baselines (RNA-only PCA 0.520 / 0.479; image-only ResNet50 0.514 / 0.498). In this setup scVI n=200 retained part of the multimodal gain but reduced it, so PCA n=2000 remains the observed RNA encoder to carry forward, and a much smaller RNA embedding did not help concat fusion here. Uncertainties remain: run-to-run variance is unknown, scVI was never tested RNA-only, and the encoder type and embedding dimension changed together, so the evidence cannot separate weaker scVI features from a dimension or balance effect in concat. scGPT, other scVI sizes, and scVI with multiprofile transformer aggregation are also untested.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: The PCA n=2000 + ResNet50, concat, single-profile anchor (0.713 accuracy / 0.695 F1) is effectively tied with its multiprofile-transformer version (0.715 / 0.687). Every one-factor change so far has scored lower: weighted fusion, ViT-L, scVI and avgpool. scGPT is the only encoder option not yet tested anywhere, so it is the largest remaining gap in the RNA representation axis. 2. What this tests: config_040 changes only the RNA encoder, from PCA to scGPT, while keeping ResNet50, single-profile input, no aggregation and concat fusion. Any difference from the anchor can therefore be attributed to RNA representation. Together with the scVI result (0.629), it shows whether pretrained or learned RNA embeddings help or hurt concat fusion relative to PCA. 3. Why it is the best use of budget: It closes the last unexplored encoder level using the cheapest, best-understood fusion setting, before spending runs on multiprofile or fusion combinations. It is a direct exploitation candidate that could beat the anchor, and it is informative either way, since a drop would strengthen the case that PCA is the RNA encoder to carry forward.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_009 kept the single-profile multimodal concat anchor (llm_summary_003: PCA n=2000 RNA + ResNet50 image, no aggregation; accuracy 0.713, F1 0.695) and changed only the RNA encoder from PCA to scGPT, completing the one-factor survey of RNA encoders alongside scVI n=200 (llm_summary_008: 0.629 / 0.599). It reached validation accuracy 0.422 (primary metric) and F1 0.405. That is about 0.29 below the anchor, the lowest result so far, and roughly 0.09–0.10 below even the single-modality baselines (RNA-only PCA 0.520 / 0.479; image-only ResNet50 0.514 / 0.498), so in this setup scGPT erased the multimodal gain and appears to have degraded the image signal as well. Together with the scVI result, this strengthens the case for carrying PCA n=2000 forward as the RNA encoder for concat fusion. Uncertainties remain: run-to-run variance is unknown, scGPT was never tested RNA-only, and its embedding dimension and preprocessing differ from PCA, so the evidence cannot separate weak scGPT features from a concat imbalance, a preprocessing mismatch, or a training failure. The fact that it fell below image-only suggests one of these interactions or failures may be involved, though this is unconfirmed; scGPT with multiprofile transformer aggregation is also untested.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: The two best runs are effectively tied. Multiprofile with transformer aggregation (config_020) scored 0.715 accuracy / 0.687 F1. Single-profile (config_016) scored 0.713 / 0.695. Both use PCA n=2000 + ResNet50 with concat fusion. So we still do not know whether multiprofile input with a learned aggregator adds any real signal. The multimodal gain may be masking or absorbing its effect. Encoder swaps (ViT-L, scVI, scGPT) and weighted fusion all underperformed the anchor, so profile setting and aggregation are the main open design questions. 2. What this tests: Running RNA-only, multiprofile, transformer aggregation with the same PCA n=2000 encoder compares directly against the RNA-only single-profile baseline (config_001: 0.520 / 0.479). Only the profile setting and its required aggregator change, and the transformer is the aggregator already shown to avoid the avgpool collapse. A clear gain would show that multiprofile aggregation carries real signal, motivating further multiprofile multimodal extensions. No gain would suggest the tie in the multimodal setting reflects no added value, so single-profile, the simpler option, could be preferred. 3. Why this is the best use of the budget: Most remaining multimodal variants combine choices that have already underperformed, so they are unlikely to resolve the profile-setting question. This low-complexity experiment tackles the most important unresolved factor directly and uses the cleanest available reference.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_010 changed the RNA-only single-profile PCA n=2000 baseline (llm_summary_001: accuracy 0.520, F1 0.479) to multiprofile input with transformer aggregation. Only the profile setting and its required aggregator changed, so this tests whether multiprofile aggregation adds signal without image features. It reached validation accuracy 0.512 (primary metric) and F1 0.477, about 0.008 and 0.002 below the baseline. That is effectively a tie or a negligible drop, which matches the multimodal tie between multiprofile transformer (llm_summary_005: 0.715 / 0.687) and single-profile concat (llm_summary_003: 0.713 / 0.695), so there is still no evidence that multiprofile transformer aggregation adds value, and the simpler single-profile setting is a reasonable default. Uncertainties remain: run-to-run variance is unknown, these are single runs with only the PCA encoder, and the transformer's configuration was not varied, so a benefit of multiprofile input under other aggregator settings, image-only multiprofile, or other encoders cannot be ruled out.

selection_reason: 1) No experiments have been run, so we know nothing yet about which modality, encoder, profile setting, aggregation, or fusion choice matters. 2) config_001 (RNA-only, single-profile, PCA-2000) is the simplest, cheapest baseline. It sets a reference accuracy and F1 that every later change can be compared against one factor at a time: the encoder (scVI, scGPT), the profile setting (multiprofile with avgpool or transformer), the modality (image-only), and multimodal fusion. 3) With a limited budget, starting from a minimal baseline makes each later result easier to interpret. It also checks whether a simple model is already competitive, rather than assuming that complex multimodal setups will win.
experiment_summary: The first experiment (llm_summary_001) tested an RNA-only, single-profile model using a PCA encoder with 2000 components (pca_n2000), with no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It was chosen as the simplest, cheapest reference point so that later experiments can change one factor at a time. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.471 and a validation F1 of 0.442. The F1 is slightly lower than the accuracy, which may mean performance is uneven across classes, though per-class results were not reported. Because no other experiments exist yet, this is only an initial baseline. It remains unknown whether other RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), multiprofile aggregation (avgpool, transformer), image-only models, or multimodal fusion would improve on it, and we cannot yet say whether 0.471 is competitive or how much it would vary with different random seeds or data splits.

selection_reason: 1) The only result so far is an RNA-only, single-profile PCA baseline (acc 0.471, F1 0.442). We know nothing yet about the image modality. Modality is the largest open question, because it determines whether the many multimodal configurations are worth exploring. 2) config_010 is image-only, single-profile, with a ResNet50 encoder and no aggregation or fusion. It mirrors the baseline's simplicity and gives a reference for the image modality on its own. Comparing it with config_001 shows how informative images are relative to RNA. 3) That comparison, together with the RNA baseline, is the natural reference for judging any later multimodal fusion gain. It also guides whether to spend budget on RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), image encoders, or fusion. Changing the RNA encoder or profile setting first would refine a single branch while the modality question stays open. This single-profile, low-cost run therefore removes the most uncertainty per experiment.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_002 tested an image-only, single-profile model with a ResNet50 image encoder and no RNA encoder, aggregation, or fusion, as an image-modality reference to compare with the RNA-only PCA baseline (llm_summary_001). It reached a validation accuracy of 0.678 and an F1 of 0.646, well above the RNA-only pca_n2000 baseline (0.471 accuracy, 0.442 F1). This is an initial sign that the image branch is at least as informative as the RNA branch in this setup. However, the two runs differ in both modality and encoder type (ResNet50 vs. PCA), so the gap cannot be attributed to modality alone. It is also based on single runs without seed or split variability estimates, and F1 again trails accuracy slightly, which may mean some class imbalance in performance. Still unknown: whether stronger RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT) would narrow the gap, whether multiprofile aggregation helps, and whether multimodal fusion adds anything beyond the image-only result, which now serves as the stronger reference point for judging fusion gains.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: Only two single-profile runs exist. The image-only ResNet50 model (0.678 accuracy, 0.646 F1) clearly beats the RNA-only PCA model (0.471, 0.442). It is still unknown whether RNA adds complementary information on top of images. This matters because 36 of the 49 remaining configurations are multimodal. 2. Test: config_016 adds the already-tested PCA RNA branch to the already-tested ResNet50 image branch with simple concat fusion, keeping single-profile and both encoders fixed. Any change relative to config_010 can then be attributed to adding RNA through fusion. Concat is the simplest fusion choice, so it gives the cleanest test. 3. Why now: this result decides how much of the budget should go to the large multimodal part of the space. A clear gain would justify exploring encoder, aggregation and fusion variants within multimodal models. No gain or a loss would suggest focusing on image-side improvements (ViT-L, multiprofile aggregation) and stronger RNA encoders before fusion. One run is not definitive, so a small difference in either direction should be confirmed later.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_003 tested a single-profile multimodal model that combines the previously tested pca_n2000 RNA branch with the ResNet50 image branch using simple concat fusion and no aggregation. This lets it be compared directly with the image-only ResNet50 run (llm_summary_002) and the RNA-only PCA run (llm_summary_001). It reached 0.512 validation accuracy and 0.477 F1. That is far below image-only (0.678 / 0.646) and only slightly above RNA-only (0.471 / 0.442), an initial sign that adding PCA RNA through naive concat fusion hurts rather than helps in this setup. Because this is a single run, and only concat with these two encoders was tested, it remains unclear whether the drop reflects RNA adding little complementary signal or a problem with this fusion design (for example, the 2000-dimensional PCA features dominating or causing training issues). It is also unknown whether stronger RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), other fusion methods, or multiprofile aggregation would reverse this, so multimodal configurations should not yet be ruled out.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: image-only ResNet50 (0.678 accuracy / 0.646 F1) clearly beats RNA-only PCA (0.471 / 0.442). Yet multimodal concat with the same two encoders fell to 0.512 / 0.477, far below image-only. That drop could mean the PCA RNA features add little useful signal. It could also mean naive concat lets the 2000-dimensional PCA input swamp the image features. A single run cannot tell these apart. 2. What this tests: config_017 keeps everything from config_016 the same (single profile, pca_n2000, ResNet50) and changes only concat to weighted fusion. If weighted fusion recovers or beats image-only accuracy, the problem was the fusion design and multimodal remains a viable direction. If it stays well below image-only, that points to the PCA RNA branch, and the next step should be stronger RNA encoders or image-only extensions. 3. Why it is the best use of budget: more than half of the remaining configurations are multimodal, and they split between concat and weighted fusion. Knowing whether the fusion method causes the drop will shape how that large part of the search space is prioritized. This one-factor comparison answers that question at the same low cost as single-profile runs.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_004 tested a single-profile multimodal model identical to llm_summary_003 (pca_n2000 RNA, ResNet50 image, no aggregation) except that concat fusion was replaced by weighted fusion. The goal was to tell whether the multimodal drop came from the fusion design or from the PCA RNA branch. It reached only 0.208 validation accuracy and 0.172 F1, far below concat (0.512 / 0.477), image-only (0.678 / 0.646), and even RNA-only (0.471 / 0.442). Because only the fusion method changed, this one-factor comparison suggests that weighted fusion performed worse than concat for this encoder pair, but it rests on single runs without seed or split variability estimates. Falling below both unimodal baselines is not what weak but harmless RNA features would be expected to produce, and it hints at a training or optimization problem with weighted fusion in this setup (for example, collapsed or poorly learned modality weights or scale mismatch). That possibility was not verified, so the result neither cleanly confirms that the PCA RNA branch is the bottleneck nor that weighted fusion is inherently worse. It remains unknown whether weighted fusion behaves differently with stronger RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), feature normalization, or multiprofile aggregation, so weighted-fusion configurations should be treated cautiously rather than ruled out.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: image-only ResNet50 single-profile is clearly the strongest result so far (0.678 accuracy / 0.646 F1). Both fusion attempts with PCA RNA fell below it, with weighted fusion collapsing to 0.208. The profile setting (single vs. multiprofile) and aggregation have not been tested at all, so we have no evidence on this major design axis. 2) What this tests: config_011 changes only the profile setting, from single-profile to multiprofile with avgpool aggregation, while keeping the image-only ResNet50 setup fixed. Comparing it with config_010 isolates the effect of multiprofile aggregation in the best-performing modality. It also avoids the confounds seen in the multimodal runs (weak PCA RNA features and unstable fusion). Avgpool is the simplest aggregator, so it gives a clean first read before trying the transformer aggregator. 3) Why it is the best use of the budget: it explores an entirely untested factor and exploits the strongest branch, so it may improve the best score. Whatever the outcome, it tells us whether multiprofile settings deserve further budget, including in later multimodal runs.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_005 tested an image-only ResNet50 model with multiprofile input and avgpool aggregation. It differs from the best run so far, llm_summary_002 (image-only, ResNet50, single-profile), only in the profile/aggregation setting, and is the first test of that design axis. It reached 0.639 validation accuracy and 0.620 F1, below single-profile llm_summary_002 (0.678 / 0.646) but well above all RNA-only and multimodal runs. This one-factor comparison is an initial sign that multiprofile with avgpool did not help, and may have slightly hurt, in the image-only setting. The F1 gap below accuracy was somewhat smaller (0.020 vs. 0.031), but that difference is too small to interpret. Because multiprofile and avgpool were changed together, the drop cannot be attributed to multiprofile input itself rather than to simple mean pooling. A gap of about 0.04 from single runs without seed or split variability estimates may also not be robust. It therefore remains unknown whether a learned aggregator (transformer) or multiprofile settings in combination with stronger RNA encoders or fusion would perform differently.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: Image-only ResNet50 single-profile is the best run so far (0.678 acc / 0.646 F1). RNA-only PCA (0.471) and both PCA-based multimodal runs (concat 0.512, weighted 0.208) are clearly worse. Multiprofile with avgpool slightly underperformed single-profile (0.639). The image encoder axis has not been tested at all, and it is the modality carrying most of the signal. 2) This run changes only the image encoder (ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L) and keeps the best setting otherwise: image-only, single-profile, no aggregation or fusion. That isolates whether a stronger pretrained image representation improves on the best result. 3) It is the best next use of the budget because it exploits the strongest direction while answering an important open design question. Its answer will also guide which image encoder to carry into later aggregation (transformer) and fusion experiments. The RNA encoder question (scVI or scGPT) remains a high-priority follow-up.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_006 tested an image-only, single-profile model with an ImageNet ViT-L image encoder and no aggregation or fusion. It differs from the best run so far, llm_summary_002 (ResNet50, 0.678 acc / 0.646 F1), only in the image encoder. It reached 0.525 validation accuracy and 0.498 F1, well below ResNet50 and also below image-only multiprofile avgpool (0.639), though still above RNA-only PCA (0.471). This one-factor comparison is an initial sign that ImageNet ViT-L, as configured here, underperformed ResNet50 in this setup, so it does not support the hypothesis that a larger pretrained image encoder helps. However, it is a single run without seed or split variability estimates, and possible causes were not checked. These include an ImageNet domain mismatch for cellular images, input resolution or preprocessing incompatibility, embedding dimensionality, or an optimization or training issue. ResNet50 therefore remains the default image encoder for later aggregation and fusion experiments, but it is unknown whether other image encoders (for example, domain-specific or differently tuned ViTs) would do better.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: every RNA result so far uses the PCA (pca_n2000) encoder. RNA-only PCA was weak (0.471 accuracy / 0.442 F1). Both multimodal PCA runs fell below image-only ResNet50, which is the current best at 0.678 / 0.646. So we cannot tell whether RNA adds little useful signal or whether the PCA representation is the bottleneck. The RNA encoder is the largest untested design axis, and many remaining configurations depend on it. 2) What this tests: scVI (scvi_n200) RNA-only, single-profile, compared directly against config_001. Only the RNA encoder changes, so any difference can be attributed to the encoder. A clear gain would mean the multimodal results with PCA understate what RNA can contribute, which would justify scVI+ResNet50 concat fusion (config_028) next. No gain would suggest RNA is weakly informative, so the budget should go toward image-side choices such as transformer aggregation (config_012). 3) Why now: it is a cheap, unimodal, one-factor experiment. It reduces uncertainty about whether multimodal fusion is worth pursuing at all, which makes it more informative than jumping to a more complex configuration that changes several factors at once.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_007 tested an RNA-only, single-profile model with the scVI (scvi_n200) RNA encoder. It differs from the RNA-only baseline llm_summary_001 (pca_n2000, 0.471 acc / 0.442 F1) only in the RNA encoder. It reached 0.632 validation accuracy and 0.607 F1, a large one-factor gain over PCA that suggests the PCA representation, not RNA itself, was a major bottleneck. It also puts RNA-only close to, though still below, the best image-only ResNet50 run (0.678 / 0.646). This makes it plausible that the earlier multimodal results with PCA (concat 0.512, weighted 0.208) understate what RNA can add, which supports testing scVI+ResNet50 concat fusion (config_028) next. However, these are single runs without seed or split variability estimates, and it remains unknown whether scVI features are complementary to image features rather than redundant, how scVI behaves under different fusion methods or multiprofile aggregation, and whether other RNA encoders (e.g., scGPT) would do better.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: scVI greatly improved RNA-only results over PCA (0.632 vs 0.471 accuracy), coming close to the best run, image-only ResNet50 (0.678 / 0.646). Every multimodal run so far used PCA RNA and fell below image-only (concat 0.512, weighted 0.208). So it is still unclear whether fusion fails because of weak PCA RNA features or because RNA adds little beyond images. 2) Test: config_028 changes only the RNA encoder relative to config_016 (PCA to scVI, with ResNet50, single-profile, concat). It isolates whether a strong RNA representation lets concat fusion beat both unimodal baselines, which would show the two modalities are complementary. Concat is used because weighted fusion looked unstable. Single-profile is kept because avgpool multiprofile did not help for images. 3) Why now: this is the most important open question, whether multimodality is worth pursuing at all. It also has a realistic chance of producing a new best result, and its outcome decides whether the remaining budget should go to scVI or scGPT fusion variants or to refining unimodal image models.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_008 tested a single-profile multimodal model that fuses scVI RNA (scvi_n200) with ResNet50 image features by concat. It differs from llm_summary_003 (PCA+ResNet50 concat, 0.512 acc / 0.477 F1) only in the RNA encoder, and its goal was to see whether a stronger RNA representation lets fusion beat the unimodal baselines. It reached only 0.227 validation accuracy and 0.191 F1, far below scVI RNA-only (0.632 / 0.607), ResNet50 image-only (0.678 / 0.646, still the best run), and PCA concat, and close to the failed weighted-fusion run (0.208). In this one-factor comparison, swapping PCA for scVI was followed by a large drop rather than a gain, so this concat fusion setup did not benefit from the stronger RNA encoder. Because the result falls far below both branches that worked well on their own, it more likely points to an unverified training or optimization problem in the fusion pipeline (for example, feature-scale or dimensionality mismatch, missing normalization, or one branch dominating) than to evidence that RNA is redundant with images. This is a single run without seed or split variability estimates and the cause was not diagnosed, so whether the two modalities are complementary remains unanswered, and sanity checks of the fusion implementation and feature normalization may be warranted before more multimodal variants (scGPT, other fusion methods) are tried or multimodality is abandoned.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: ResNet50 image-only single-profile is the best run so far (0.678 acc / 0.646 F1). Multiprofile with avgpool scored somewhat lower (0.639 / 0.620). That earlier test changed profile setting and aggregation together, so we cannot tell whether multiprofile input itself hurts or only simple mean pooling does. Every multimodal run collapsed, including scVI+ResNet50 concat at 0.227. Those failures more likely reflect an undiagnosed fusion or training problem than a lack of complementary signal. More multimodal variants are unlikely to be informative until that is resolved. 2. What this tests: config_012 differs from config_011 only in using a learned transformer aggregator instead of avgpool. This isolates the effect of aggregation on the strongest encoder and shows whether multiprofile input can match or beat single-profile when aggregation is learned. 3. Why it is the best next experiment: it is a clean one-factor comparison on a stable, well-performing pipeline. It has a realistic chance of improving the best accuracy. It also answers a question that carries over to later RNA and multimodal multiprofile experiments: should transformer aggregation be preferred to avgpool, or should multiprofile be set aside? Completing the RNA encoder axis with scGPT (config_007) is a strong candidate for a follow-up experiment.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_009 tested an image-only ResNet50 model with multiprofile input and a learned transformer aggregator. It differs from llm_summary_005 (multiprofile avgpool, 0.639 acc / 0.620 F1) only in the aggregation method, so the comparison isolates aggregation on the strongest encoder. It reached 0.653 validation accuracy and 0.628 F1, a modest gain over avgpool (about +0.014 acc and +0.009 F1) but still below the best run, single-profile ResNet50 llm_summary_002 (0.678 / 0.646). This is an initial sign that transformer aggregation may do slightly better than mean pooling, yet multiprofile input did not match or beat single-profile in this image-only setting. All differences come from single runs without seed or split variability estimates, so the roughly 0.01 aggregation gain and the roughly 0.025 remaining gap to single-profile may not be robust. It remains unknown whether the multiprofile shortfall is inherent to multiprofile input or reflects aggregator capacity, tuning, or training, and whether transformer aggregation would help RNA or multimodal pipelines. Multimodal runs remain blocked by the undiagnosed fusion collapse.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: The RNA encoder is the design choice with the largest one-factor effect so far. Swapping PCA for scVI raised RNA-only accuracy from 0.471 to 0.632, close to the best run (ResNet50 image-only, 0.678). scGPT, the third RNA encoder, has never been tested. Multiprofile aggregation has given only small differences, and both remained below single-profile image-only. Multimodal fusion has collapsed below the unimodal baselines several times (0.208, 0.227, 0.512) for undiagnosed reasons, so more fusion runs are hard to interpret. 2. What this tests: config_007 (scGPT, RNA-only, single-profile) changes only the RNA encoder relative to the scVI run (config_004). It shows whether a pretrained foundation-model RNA representation beats scVI, and possibly whether RNA-only can match or exceed the image-only best. 3. Why it is the best use of the budget: It is a clean single-model comparison on the axis with the biggest observed effect, and it avoids the confounded fusion pipeline. The result also decides which RNA encoder should go forward to any later multiprofile or fusion experiments once fusion is debugged.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_010 tested an RNA-only, single-profile model with the pretrained scGPT RNA encoder, with no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. Relative to the scVI run llm_summary_007 (0.632 acc / 0.607 F1), only the RNA encoder changed, so this is a clean one-factor test of whether a foundation-model RNA representation beats scVI. It reached 0.421 validation accuracy and 0.412 F1. That is well below scVI, below even the PCA baseline (0.471 / 0.442), and far below the best run, ResNet50 image-only (0.678 / 0.646). This is an initial sign that scGPT, as configured here, is the weakest RNA encoder tested, so scVI remains the preferred RNA encoder for any later multiprofile or fusion experiments, but several things are still unknown: these are single runs without seed or split variability estimates; the underperformance was not diagnosed (possible causes include gene-vocabulary or preprocessing mismatch, how embeddings were extracted, frozen rather than fine-tuned use, or a domain gap with scGPT's pretraining data), so it does not show that foundation-model RNA representations are inherently worse; and multimodal runs remain blocked by the undiagnosed fusion collapse.

selection_reason: 1) No experiments have been run yet, so there is no evidence about which modality, encoder, profile setting, aggregation, or fusion choice matters. 2) config_001 is the simplest RNA-only single-profile model with a standard PCA encoder. It sets a baseline for validation accuracy and F1 that later experiments can be compared against. Encoders (scVI, scGPT), multiprofile aggregation (avgpool, transformer), image-only models and multimodal fusion can each be tested as a one-factor change from it. 3) With a limited budget, a clean, cheap reference point is the most efficient first experiment. It makes later comparisons interpretable and avoids assuming that more complex multimodal or multiprofile models will help.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_001 tested the simplest configuration as a baseline: an RNA-only, single-profile model with a PCA encoder (pca_n2000) and no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.421 (primary metric), with a similar validation F1 of 0.412, which suggests performance is fairly balanced across classes rather than driven by a few. This is the first completed experiment, so it serves only as a reference point. It shows nothing yet about whether other RNA encoders (e.g., scVI, scGPT), multiprofile aggregation, image-only models, or multimodal fusion would do better or worse. Variance across runs or seeds is also unknown, so small future differences from this baseline should be read cautiously, and one-factor changes from this configuration would give the most interpretable comparisons.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: The only result so far is the RNA-only, single-profile PCA baseline (config_001), with accuracy 0.421 and F1 0.412. We know nothing yet about the image modality, even though most of the remaining space (image-only and all multimodal configurations) depends on it. 2. What this tests: config_010 is the simplest image baseline (resnet50, single-profile, no aggregation or fusion). It keeps the profile setting fixed and changes only the input modality, so it compares directly against the RNA baseline. It shows whether images alone carry signal comparable to, weaker than, or stronger than RNA. 3. Why it is the best next experiment: Knowing the relative strength of each modality is the most decision-relevant question for the budget. It tells us whether multimodal fusion is worth exploring and which modality should anchor later experiments. Encoder and profile-setting comparisons can then be prioritized within whichever modality looks most promising.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_002 tested the simplest image baseline: an image-only, single-profile model with a ResNet50 encoder and no aggregation or fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.535 (F1 0.519), above the RNA-only PCA single-profile baseline (llm_summary_001: accuracy 0.421, F1 0.412). This is an initial observation that this image configuration carries at least as much usable signal as this RNA configuration. However, the comparison changes both the modality and the specific encoder (ResNet50 vs. pca_n2000), so the gap cannot be attributed to modality alone and may reflect encoder choice; seed and run variance is also unknown, and whether fusion, multiprofile aggregation, or other RNA or image encoders would change this ranking remains untested.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: we have two single-profile, unimodal baselines. Image-only ResNet50 reached 0.535 accuracy (F1 0.519) and RNA-only PCA reached 0.421 (F1 0.412). This suggests images carry more usable signal in these setups. It is still unknown whether RNA adds complementary information or just weaker, redundant signal. 2. What this tests: config_016 keeps the two completed baselines' encoders (pca_n2000 and resnet50) and profile setting (single-profile). It adds only simple concat fusion. Each unimodal baseline therefore differs from it only by adding the other modality. This cleanly isolates whether combining modalities helps, using the simplest fusion and no aggregation as confounds. 3. Why it is the best next step: whether multimodality is worth pursuing is the decision with the most leverage over the rest of the search space, since most remaining configurations are multimodal. If concat does not beat 0.535, effort should shift toward image encoders and profile aggregation. If it does, later runs can probe weighted fusion, other RNA encoders, and multiprofile settings. Any small difference from 0.535 should be read cautiously, since run-to-run variance is unknown.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_003 tested a multimodal, single-profile model that concatenates the two baseline encoders (pca_n2000 RNA and ResNet50 image) with no aggregation. Relative to the image-only baseline it differs only by adding RNA, and relative to the RNA-only baseline it differs only by adding images. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.540 (F1 0.524), far above RNA-only (llm_summary_001: 0.421 / 0.412) but only about 0.005 above image-only (llm_summary_002: 0.535 / 0.519), with F1 moving in the same direction. This suggests concat fusion with RNA is at least not harmful, but the gain over image-only is small enough that it may fall within run-to-run noise, since seed variance is unknown. It therefore remains uncertain whether RNA contributes complementary signal or is largely redundant under this fusion, and whether other fusion methods, RNA encoders, or multiprofile aggregation would widen the gap; repeated seeds would help clarify whether the multimodal edge is real.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: Image-only ResNet50 single-profile (0.535 acc / 0.519 F1) clearly beats RNA-only PCA (0.421 / 0.412). Adding PCA RNA via concat fusion gave only about +0.005 (0.540 / 0.524), which may be noise. So image features carry most of the usable signal. Profile setting (single vs. multiprofile) and aggregation are still completely untested. 2. Test: Switching the strongest simple model (image-only ResNet50) from singleprofile to multiprofile with avgpool aggregation changes only one design factor relative to config_010. Any change in accuracy or F1 can then be attributed to multiprofile aggregation itself, without RNA or fusion effects confounding it. 3. Why now: Profile setting is a major untested axis and could matter more than the small fusion effect seen so far. Testing it on the dominant modality first is both informative and plausibly high-performing. Avgpool is the simplest aggregator, so it gives a clean baseline before trying transformer aggregation or extending multiprofile to the multimodal models.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_004 tested an image-only ResNet50 model with the profile setting switched from singleprofile to multiprofile, using avgpool aggregation and no RNA or fusion, which makes it a near one-factor change from the image-only single-profile baseline (llm_summary_002: 0.535 acc / 0.519 F1). It reached a validation accuracy of 0.512 (F1 0.477), about 0.023 lower in accuracy and about 0.042 lower in F1. The larger F1 drop suggests performance may have become somewhat less balanced across classes. This is an initial observation that multiprofile with avgpool did not help, and may have hurt, in this image-only setting. However, multiprofile and avgpool aggregation change together, so the drop cannot be attributed to multiprofile input itself rather than to simple mean pooling. Seed variance is also unknown, and it remains untested whether a learned aggregator (e.g., a transformer), other image encoders, or multiprofile combined with multimodal fusion would reverse this result.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: Image carries most of the signal so far. Image-only ResNet50 scored 0.535 accuracy, versus 0.421 for RNA-only PCA. Adding PCA RNA via concat gave only a small, possibly noise-level gain (0.540). Multiprofile with avgpool hurt slightly (0.512, with a larger F1 drop). The image encoder, which drives performance, has only been tested as ResNet50. 2. Question: config_013 changes one factor from config_010, swapping ResNet50 for imagenet_vit_l in the image-only single-profile setting. This isolates how much image representation quality matters. 3. Why now: Because image dominates, the image encoder choice likely affects every downstream multimodal and multiprofile configuration. Settling it now lets later fusion and aggregation tests build on the stronger backbone. It is also a plausible route to a higher-accuracy model. Testing RNA encoders or transformer aggregation remains useful but seems less likely to shift results across the search space.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_005 swapped the ResNet50 image encoder for imagenet_vit_l in the image-only, single-profile setting with no aggregation or fusion, a clean one-factor change from llm_summary_002 (0.535 acc / 0.519 F1). It reached a validation accuracy of 0.532 (F1 0.516), about 0.004 lower in accuracy and 0.003 lower in F1. So in this setup the larger ViT backbone gave no measurable gain over ResNet50. The difference is small enough that it may fall within run-to-run noise, and seed variance is unknown, so the two encoders are best treated as roughly equivalent here rather than ResNet50 being clearly better. It remains untested whether other image encoders (e.g., domain-specific ones) would change this, and whether imagenet_vit_l would behave differently in multimodal fusion or multiprofile settings. Because swapping the image backbone did not shift performance here, the image encoder may not be the main bottleneck, but this is uncertain.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: image-only ResNet50 is the strongest single modality (0.535 acc). Switching to multiprofile with avgpool lowered accuracy to 0.512, and F1 fell more, to 0.477. But in that run the multiprofile input and the simple mean-pooling aggregator changed together, so the cause of the drop is unclear. Swapping the image backbone to ViT-L changed little, which suggests the encoder is not the main lever. 2. Test: config_012 keeps everything from config_011 fixed (image-only, ResNet50, multiprofile) and changes only avgpool to transformer aggregation. If it recovers or beats the single-profile baseline, the earlier drop came from naive pooling. If it stays low, multiprofile input itself is likely not useful here. 3. Why now: about half of the remaining space, including most multimodal configurations, uses multiprofile with avgpool or transformer aggregation. Resolving whether learned aggregation rescues multiprofile in the best-performing modality will efficiently guide whether to keep pursuing multiprofile branches or prune them under the limited budget.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_006 tested an image-only, multiprofile ResNet50 model with transformer aggregation. It is a clean one-factor change from llm_summary_004, swapping avgpool for transformer aggregation (0.512 acc / 0.477 F1). It reached a validation accuracy of 0.532 (F1 0.517), about 0.020 higher in accuracy and 0.040 higher in F1 than avgpool. This brings it roughly back to the image-only single-profile baseline (llm_summary_002: 0.535 / 0.519) without exceeding it, and it remains slightly below multimodal single-profile concat (llm_summary_003: 0.540 / 0.524). This suggests the earlier multiprofile drop was linked to the avgpool aggregator rather than to multiprofile input itself, but learned aggregation gave no measurable gain over using a single profile in this image-only setting. Seed variance is unknown, so the small gaps to the single-profile baselines may be noise, and it remains untested whether multiprofile with transformer aggregation adds value when combined with RNA in multimodal fusion.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: Image encoders look interchangeable (ResNet50 0.535 vs ViT-L 0.532). Multiprofile gave no gain over single-profile, even with transformer aggregation (0.532). Adding PCA RNA via concat gave only a marginal gain over image-only (0.540 vs 0.535). The largest untested axis is the RNA encoder. Only pca_n2000 has been tried, and it is weak alone (0.421). We cannot yet tell whether RNA is truly redundant or just poorly represented by PCA. 2. What this tests: swapping pca_n2000 for scGPT in the RNA-only, single-profile setting is a clean one-factor change from config_001. It measures whether a foundation-model RNA representation carries much more class signal. This is easier to detect without the image branch dominating. 3. Why it is the best use of budget: the result decides how to spend the remaining multimodal experiments. A large gain would justify scGPT-based fusion runs (e.g., config_040) as the most promising route past the image-only ceiling. Little or no gain would suggest RNA adds limited value, so further effort should go to fusion or aggregation choices instead.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_007 swapped the pca_n2000 RNA encoder for scGPT in the RNA-only, single-profile setting with no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. This is a clean one-factor change from llm_summary_001 (0.421 acc / 0.412 F1). It reached a validation accuracy of 0.586 (F1 0.574), about 0.164 higher in accuracy, with F1 rising similarly. It is also the best result so far, above image-only ResNet50 (llm_summary_002: 0.535 / 0.519) and the pca+ResNet50 concat model (llm_summary_003: 0.540 / 0.524). This gap is far larger than the roughly 0.005 differences seen elsewhere, so it suggests the earlier weak RNA results reflected the PCA representation rather than RNA being inherently uninformative. Seed variance is still unknown, and it remains untested whether scGPT keeps its edge when combined with images (e.g., concat or other fusion), whether images add complementary signal on top of scGPT, and whether other RNA encoders (e.g., scVI) or multiprofile aggregation would perform similarly or better.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: scGPT RNA-only is the best result so far (0.586 acc / 0.574 F1), about 0.16 above PCA RNA-only. Image-only ResNet50 reaches 0.535. With weak PCA features, concat fusion gained only about 0.005 over image-only, which may be noise, so it is unclear whether images add complementary signal once RNA features are strong. The image encoders (ResNet50 vs ViT-L) and multiprofile transformer aggregation have shown no clear gains. 2) Test: config_040 adds ResNet50 images to scGPT with concat fusion in the single-profile setting. That is a one-factor change from config_007 (add the image modality) and from config_016 (swap PCA for scGPT). It asks directly whether multimodal fusion beats the strongest unimodal model. 3) Why now: this exploits the most promising direction, the scGPT representation, while answering the central open question of whether fusion is worth it. It uses the cheapest, best-understood fusion, encoder, and profile setting, so the result can be interpreted cleanly. It also sets the reference point for later tests of weighted fusion, multiprofile aggregation, or scVI.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_008 tested multimodal, single-profile concat fusion of scGPT RNA features with ResNet50 image features and no aggregation. It is a one-factor change from scGPT RNA-only (llm_summary_007: 0.586 acc / 0.574 F1) by adding images, and from pca+ResNet50 concat (llm_summary_003: 0.540 / 0.524) by swapping PCA for scGPT. It reached only 0.260 validation accuracy (F1 0.222), about 0.33 below scGPT RNA-only, about 0.28 below image-only ResNet50 (llm_summary_002: 0.535), and far below every earlier run. A combination performing much worse than either of its unimodal parts looks more like a failed or unstable training run, or an integration issue, than evidence that images harm scGPT. Possible explanations include feature-scale or dimensionality mismatch between scGPT embeddings and ResNet50 features under concat, optimization or hyperparameter problems, or a pipeline bug, but none of these is isolated here. So whether images add complementary signal to strong scGPT features is still unanswered. Seed variance is unknown, and this result should be verified before ruling out scGPT-based fusion, for example by rerunning, normalizing or projecting each modality before concat, or trying other fusion methods.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: scGPT RNA-only is the best result so far (0.586 acc / 0.574 F1). Adding ResNet50 images with concat fusion collapsed to 0.260 / 0.222, far below either modality alone. That pattern suggests a fusion or integration failure, such as a feature-scale or dimensionality mismatch, rather than images genuinely hurting performance. 2. What this tests: config_041 keeps scGPT, ResNet50 and the single-profile setting fixed and changes only the fusion from concat to weighted. If weighted fusion recovers to scGPT-level or better, the collapse was specific to concat, and scGPT-based multimodal models stay viable. If it also fails, the problem more likely lies with combining scGPT and image features in general, or with the pipeline. 3. Why it is the best use of the budget: the most promising region of the search space is scGPT-based models, and whether images add complementary signal to scGPT is the central open question. This clean one-factor comparison directly addresses that anomaly and may also produce the top-performing configuration. Testing multiprofile or scVI variants first would leave the scGPT fusion question unresolved.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_009 tested multimodal, single-profile fusion of scGPT RNA and ResNet50 image features with weighted fusion and no aggregation, a clean one-factor change from the concat version (llm_summary_008: 0.260 acc / 0.222 F1). It reached 0.427 validation accuracy (F1 0.417), well above concat, which suggests part of the earlier collapse was specific to concat. However, it remains far below both of its unimodal parts, scGPT RNA-only (llm_summary_007: 0.586 / 0.574) and image-only ResNet50 (llm_summary_002: 0.535 / 0.519), and only about level with the PCA RNA-only baseline (0.421), so combining scGPT with images still appears to fail under both fusion methods tried. Seed variance is unknown, and the cause is not isolated: it could be feature-scale or dimensionality mismatch, optimization or hyperparameter issues, or a pipeline bug. So whether images add complementary signal to scGPT is still unanswered, and checks such as per-modality normalization or projection, reruns, or other fusion methods are needed before ruling out scGPT-based multimodal models.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: scGPT RNA-only single-profile is clearly the best result (0.586 acc / 0.574 F1). That margin over PCA (+0.16) is much larger than the ~0.005 differences seen elsewhere. Both scGPT+ResNet50 fusions failed badly (0.260 concat, 0.427 weighted), which looks like an integration or optimization problem rather than real evidence about complementarity. Multiprofile input has only been tested in the image-only setting. There, avgpool hurt and transformer aggregation recovered to roughly single-profile level, so whether multiprofile helps RNA, and especially the strong scGPT representation, is untested. 2) Test: config_009 is a clean one-factor change from the best configuration (config_007), switching single-profile to multiprofile with transformer aggregation. Transformer is used because avgpool already appeared to harm performance. This isolates whether aggregating multiple profiles adds value on top of the strongest representation. 3) Why now: it exploits the most promising direction while resolving an important open design question, profile setting for RNA. It avoids the confounded and unstable scGPT fusion pipeline. Fusion diagnostics (e.g., PCA weighted fusion or other scGPT fusion variants) remain worthwhile later.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_010 tested scGPT RNA-only with multiprofile input and transformer aggregation (no images or fusion). The selection rationale framed it as a one-factor change from the best prior run, scGPT RNA-only single-profile (llm_summary_007: 0.586 acc / 0.574 F1), although that run used no aggregation, so profile setting and the transformer aggregator change together. It reached 0.632 validation accuracy (F1 0.607), about 0.046 higher in accuracy and 0.032 higher in F1, making it the new best result and well above all fusion attempts (best: llm_summary_009 at 0.427) and image-only runs (~0.53). This is an initial observation that multiprofile input with transformer aggregation helps scGPT RNA, in contrast to the image-only setting, where the same change only matched single-profile (llm_summary_006: 0.532 vs llm_summary_002: 0.535). However, the effect of multiprofile input cannot be separated from the effect of the transformer aggregator, seed variance is unknown, and it remains untested whether avgpool or other aggregators, other RNA encoders (e.g., scVI), or a working scGPT-image fusion pipeline would add further gains.

selection_reason: 1) No experiments have been run, so we know nothing yet about how representation, profile setting, aggregation, or fusion affect performance. 2) config_001 (RNA-only, single-profile, PCA-2000) is the simplest, cheapest baseline. It has no aggregation or fusion components, so it isolates RNA signal with a standard representation. Later experiments can then change one factor at a time against it: scVI or scGPT encoders, multiprofile avgpool or transformer aggregation, image-only models, or adding the image modality. 3) Under a limited budget, a clean reference point makes every later comparison easier to interpret. We should not assume that complex multimodal or multiprofile models win before we know how a simple model performs.
experiment_summary: The first experiment (llm_summary_001) tested an RNA-only, single-profile model with a PCA-2000 RNA encoder and no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It was chosen as the simplest reference configuration. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.3275, with a supporting validation F1 of 0.2884. The slightly lower F1 hints that performance may be uneven across classes. With no prior experiments to compare against, this is only a baseline: it does not yet show whether other RNA encoders (e.g., scVI, scGPT), multiprofile aggregation, image-only models, or multimodal fusion would do better or worse. It is also unknown how much of the gap from perfect accuracy reflects limits of PCA-2000, the single-profile setting, or the task itself, and the run-to-run variance of this estimate is unknown.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: There is only one data point so far. The RNA-only, single-profile PCA-2000 baseline reached 0.3275 accuracy and 0.2884 F1. We know nothing yet about the image modality, and most of the remaining search space (image-only and all multimodal configurations) depends on whether images carry useful signal for this task. 2. What this tests: The image-only, single-profile ResNet50 model is the simplest image counterpart to the baseline. It keeps the single-profile setting with no aggregation or fusion, so the comparison isolates modality: RNA via PCA versus images via ResNet50. It tells us whether images are weaker, comparable, or stronger than RNA on their own. 3. Why it is the best next use of budget: This result is a prerequisite for interpreting any later fusion experiment. If images perform poorly, multimodal gains are less likely and the budget should go to RNA encoders and profile aggregation. If images are competitive, fusion becomes a strong direction to pursue. Either way, one simple run reduces uncertainty across a large part of the space, more than tuning the RNA branch first would.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_002 tested an image-only, single-profile model with a ResNet50 image encoder and no RNA encoder, aggregation, or fusion, as the simplest image counterpart to the RNA-only PCA-2000 baseline (llm_summary_001: 0.3275 accuracy, 0.2884 F1). It reached 0.5375 validation accuracy, with a supporting F1 of 0.5184, roughly 21 points higher on both metrics. This suggests the image modality carries substantial signal and makes image-based and multimodal fusion configurations worth exploring. However, the comparison changes the modality and the encoder at once (PCA on RNA vs. ResNet50 on images), so it cannot separate modality from encoder choice; it is also a single run each with unknown variance, and it remains untested whether stronger RNA encoders (e.g., scVI, scGPT), other image encoders, multiprofile aggregation, or fusion would narrow, widen, or build on this gap.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: With single-profile settings, image-only ResNet50 (0.5375 acc, 0.5184 F1) beat RNA-only PCA-2000 (0.3275 acc, 0.2884 F1) by about 21 points. So images carry strong signal. It is still unknown whether the weaker RNA modality adds complementary information or only adds noise. 2. Test: config_016 fuses exactly the two encoders already tested (PCA-2000 and ResNet50) by simple concatenation, still in the single-profile setting. Both unimodal reference points exist, so any change can be credited to adding RNA through fusion, not to a new encoder or to aggregation. Accuracy, with F1 as support, will show whether multimodality helps, is neutral, or hurts. 3. Why now: Whether to fuse modalities is the largest structural decision in the search space. Most remaining configurations are multimodal, so this result decides whether the budget should go to fusion variants or to stronger image-only models, such as ViT-L or multiprofile aggregation. I chose concat over weighted fusion as the simplest baseline, to avoid changing several design choices at once.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_003 tested a multimodal, single-profile model that fused the two encoders already tested alone, PCA-2000 for RNA and ResNet50 for images, by simple concatenation with no aggregation. Its purpose was to see whether adding the weaker RNA modality complements or degrades image signal. It reached 0.4214 validation accuracy (F1 0.4124). That is about 11.6 points below image-only ResNet50 (llm_summary_002: 0.5375 acc, 0.5184 F1) and about 9.4 points above RNA-only PCA-2000 (llm_summary_001: 0.3275 acc, 0.2884 F1). This suggests that, in this setup, adding RNA through naive concat fusion hurt rather than helped relative to images alone. However, it does not show that multimodality is inherently harmful: the drop could reflect concat-specific issues such as feature scale or dimensionality imbalance, missing normalization, or weighting and optimization effects that weighted or other fusion schemes might fix. With single runs and unknown variance, it also remains untested whether stronger RNA encoders (e.g., scVI, scGPT), alternative fusion methods, or multiprofile aggregation would make fusion competitive with or better than image-only models.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: Image-only ResNet50 single-profile is clearly best so far (0.5375 acc, 0.5184 F1). It beats RNA-only PCA-2000 by about 21 points and concat multimodal by about 12 points. The profile setting (single vs. multiprofile with aggregation) has not been tested at all, yet it applies to most of the remaining search space. 2) Test: This experiment changes one factor of the best configuration, switching from single-profile to multiprofile with avgpool aggregation. It isolates whether pooling multiple profiles adds signal for the strongest modality. Avgpool is the simplest aggregator, so it gives a clean first read before trying the transformer aggregator. 3) Why now: It exploits the most promising direction while answering a design question that affects roughly two-thirds of the untested configurations. The fusion question (weighted vs. concat, config_017) also matters, but it currently concerns a weaker branch. If multiprofile helps here, it is a strong reason to carry aggregation into later image and multimodal runs.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_004 tested an image-only ResNet50 model using multiprofile input with avgpool aggregation. Profile setting was the only change from the previous best configuration (llm_summary_002: image-only ResNet50, single-profile, 0.5375 acc, 0.5184 F1). It reached 0.7150 validation accuracy (F1 0.6872), about 17.8 points higher on accuracy and 16.9 points higher on F1, making it the best configuration so far. Because this comparison isolates the switch from single-profile to multiprofile with avgpool, it suggests that pooling multiple profiles adds substantial signal for the image modality in this setup. However, each configuration was run once with unknown variance, and several questions remain untested: whether a transformer aggregator would do better than avgpool, whether the gain carries over to RNA-only or multimodal models (including whether it could rescue the weaker concat fusion of llm_summary_003), and how the gain depends on the number or selection of profiles pooled.

selection_reason: Evidence: Moving from single-profile to multiprofile with avgpool was the largest gain so far. Image-only ResNet50 rose from 0.5375 to 0.7150 accuracy, with F1 rising from 0.518 to 0.687, which makes aggregation the most promising design axis. Only avgpool has been tried, so it is unknown whether a learned aggregator captures more signal from multiple profiles. Test: config_012 changes only the aggregator, from avgpool to transformer, on the current best configuration (image-only ResNet50, multiprofile). This cleanly isolates the effect of aggregation method. Why now: Most remaining configurations are multiprofile and must choose between avgpool and transformer, including the RNA-only and multimodal ones. Settling this choice on the strongest and simplest setup therefore informs a large part of the remaining search. It also directly exploits the best-performing direction. Encoder swaps (ViT-L) and revisiting fusion (multiprofile concat or weighted) remain important next steps.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_005 tested an image-only ResNet50 model with multiprofile input and a transformer aggregator. Aggregation was the only change from the current best configuration (llm_summary_004: avgpool, 0.7150 acc, 0.6872 F1), which isolates the aggregation method. It reached 0.5420 validation accuracy (F1 0.4833), about 17.3 points lower in accuracy and 20.4 points lower in F1 than avgpool, and roughly at the level of single-profile image-only ResNet50 (llm_summary_002: 0.5375 acc, 0.5184 F1). The larger drop in F1 suggests performance became more uneven across classes. In this setup, the transformer aggregator therefore gave much lower validation performance than avgpool, so avgpool is the stronger default for the remaining multiprofile configurations. However, each configuration was run once with unknown variance. The poor result may reflect transformer-specific training issues, such as optimization, hyperparameters, data size, or overfitting, rather than an inherent limit of learned aggregation. It also remains untested whether this ranking holds for RNA-only or multimodal multiprofile models, or with other image encoders such as ViT-L.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: The best result so far is image-only ResNet50 with multiprofile avgpool (0.7150 acc, 0.6872 F1). Moving from single-profile to multiprofile avgpool gave about +17.8 points, and a transformer aggregator gave about -17.3 points, so avgpool is the strong default. Image signal clearly dominates RNA PCA-2000. The image encoder is still a major untested choice, because only ResNet50 has been tried. Naive concat fusion with PCA RNA hurt in the single-profile setting. 2) Test: Swapping ResNet50 for ImageNet ViT-L while keeping image-only, multiprofile and avgpool fixed isolates the effect of the image encoder on the current best setup. 3) Why now: This is a one-variable extension of the strongest configuration, so it can either directly improve accuracy or confirm ResNet50 as the backbone. That answer determines which image encoder to carry into the many remaining multimodal configurations, so it should come before testing fusion schemes or RNA encoders. It is a single run, so a small difference should be treated cautiously.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_006 tested swapping the image encoder from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L while keeping the rest of the current best configuration fixed (image-only, multiprofile, avgpool), which isolates the image encoder choice. It reached 0.6501 validation accuracy (F1 0.6275), about 6.5 points lower in accuracy and 6.0 points lower in F1 than ResNet50 (llm_summary_004: 0.7150 acc, 0.6872 F1). That still clearly beats single-profile image-only ResNet50 (llm_summary_002: 0.5375 acc), so in this setup ResNet50 remains the stronger backbone and the preferred default for later multimodal configurations. However, each configuration was run once with unknown variance, and the gap may reflect ViT-L-specific factors such as input resolution, preprocessing, fine-tuning or frozen-feature handling, or hyperparameters rather than an inherent limit of the architecture; other image encoders and whether this ranking holds in multimodal or fusion settings remain untested.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: The best result so far is image-only, multiprofile ResNet50 with avgpool (0.7150 acc, 0.6872 F1). Multiprofile avgpool clearly beat single-profile (+17.8 points), the transformer aggregator (+17.3) and ViT-L (+6.5), so ResNet50 with multiprofile avgpool is a strong base. The open question is whether RNA can add anything. RNA-only PCA was weak (0.3275), and naive concat fusion in the single-profile setting fell well below image-only (0.4214 vs 0.5375). That drop may come from concat-specific problems such as scale or dimensionality imbalance between the modalities. Weighted fusion has not been tested yet. 2) This experiment adds PCA-2000 RNA to the best configuration through weighted fusion, keeping the image encoder, profile setting and aggregation fixed. It tests whether a fusion method that can down-weight the weaker modality lets RNA complement the strongest image pipeline. 3) Why this is the best next use of budget: it extends the strongest direction found so far and directly tests the main remaining design choice (multimodal fusion) at the setting most likely to give the best result. If it beats 0.715, multimodal fusion becomes the main line to pursue. If it does not, that is fairly strong evidence that PCA-based RNA adds little even with adaptive weighting, and later experiments should shift to stronger RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT) or stay image-only. Concat at this setting (config_018) or single-profile weighted fusion (config_017) remain cheap follow-ups to separate the fusion effect if needed.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_007 added PCA-2000 RNA to the best image-only configuration (ResNet50, multiprofile, avgpool; llm_summary_004: 0.7150 acc, 0.6872 F1) through weighted fusion, keeping everything else fixed, to test whether a fusion method that can down-weight the weaker modality lets RNA complement the strongest image pipeline. It reached 0.6776 validation accuracy (F1 0.6464), about 3.7 points lower in accuracy and 4.1 points lower in F1 than image-only, though still well above the earlier single-profile concat fusion (llm_summary_003: 0.4214). Within this setup, adding PCA-based RNA through weighted fusion did not help and slightly reduced performance, which is a second, smaller multimodal drop after the concat result and suggests PCA-2000 RNA adds little even with adaptive weighting. Several points remain uncertain: each configuration was run once with unknown variance, so the 3.7-point gap may partly be noise; concat fusion at this same multiprofile setting (config_018) is untested, so weighted fusion's specific contribution relative to concat cannot be isolated; and whether stronger RNA encoders (e.g., scVI, scGPT), learned fusion weights or tuning would make fusion competitive with image-only is also untested.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: Multiprofile avgpool with ResNet50 is the clear best image pipeline (0.715 acc). Adding RNA has hurt both times it was tried: concat fusion at single-profile, and weighted fusion at multiprofile (config_019: 0.678 acc, -3.7 points). Both runs used PCA-2000, the only RNA encoder tested so far, and PCA RNA alone was weak (0.328). So it is unclear whether multimodality itself fails here or whether the PCA representation is the bottleneck. 2. Test: config_031 differs from config_019 only in the RNA encoder (scVI-200 instead of PCA-2000). It keeps ResNet50, multiprofile, avgpool and weighted fusion fixed, so it isolates whether a stronger RNA representation lets fusion match or beat image-only. 3. Why now: This answers the most consequential open design question, whether the large untested multimodal space (scVI and scGPT variants) is worth pursuing. It also has a realistic chance of producing a new best result. If it still underperforms image-only, that is strong evidence to deprioritize fusion and focus the remaining budget on image-only or RNA-only refinements.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_008 swapped the RNA encoder from PCA-2000 to scVI-200 in the multimodal, multiprofile, ResNet50, avgpool, weighted-fusion configuration, keeping all else fixed (vs. llm_summary_007: 0.6776 acc, 0.6464 F1), which isolates the RNA encoder within this fusion setup. It reached 0.5353 validation accuracy (F1 0.5187), about 14.2 points below the PCA-2000 fusion run, about 18.0 points below the best image-only multiprofile model (llm_summary_004: 0.7150 acc, 0.6872 F1), and roughly at the level of single-profile image-only ResNet50 (llm_summary_002: 0.5375). So in this setup, scVI-200 did not rescue fusion and instead gave a much larger drop, making three multimodal runs that all underperformed image-only, and image-only ResNet50 with multiprofile avgpool remains the strongest configuration. Several points remain uncertain: each configuration was run once with unknown variance; scVI-200 RNA-only performance is untested, so it is unclear whether scVI features are weak on their own or interact poorly with weighted fusion (e.g., through feature scale, dimensionality, or modality weighting that fails to down-weight RNA); and scGPT encoders, concat fusion at multiprofile, and fusion tuning remain untested, so this argues for deprioritizing fusion in its current form rather than ruling out multimodality entirely.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: image-only ResNet50 with multiprofile avgpool is the best run so far (0.7150 acc, 0.6872 F1). Adding RNA through weighted fusion in this exact setup lowered accuracy with PCA-2000 (0.6776) and lowered it much more with scVI-200 (0.5353). So the RNA encoder strongly affects fusion results. scGPT, the third RNA encoder, is completely untested, and it is the main remaining uncertainty about whether multimodality can help. 2) This run swaps only the RNA encoder to scGPT and keeps image encoder, profile setting, aggregation and fusion the same as config_019 and config_031. That gives a clean three-way RNA encoder comparison within the strongest fusion pipeline. It shows whether a pretrained foundation-model RNA representation lets fusion match or beat image-only, or whether the multimodal deficit holds across all encoders. 3) Under a limited budget, this one experiment either finds a new best configuration (exploitation) or gives strong evidence to deprioritize multimodal fusion and focus remaining runs on image-only and aggregation refinements (exploration). Other options answer narrower questions with lower expected payoff: concat vs. weighted fusion (config_018), or whether multiprofile pooling helps RNA-only models.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_009 swapped the RNA encoder to scGPT in the multimodal, multiprofile, ResNet50, avgpool, weighted-fusion configuration and kept everything else fixed. This completes a three-way RNA encoder comparison within this fusion setup: PCA-2000 (llm_summary_007) gave 0.6776 acc and scVI-200 (llm_summary_008) gave 0.5353 acc. scGPT reached 0.4942 validation accuracy (F1 0.4533), the lowest of the three, about 22.1 points below the best image-only multiprofile ResNet50 model (llm_summary_004: 0.7150 acc, 0.6872 F1) and below even single-profile image-only ResNet50 (llm_summary_002: 0.5375). In this setup, all four multimodal runs (all three RNA encoders, plus the earlier single-profile concat run) underperformed image-only, with a consistent ranking PCA-2000 > scVI-200 > scGPT. This supports deprioritizing weighted fusion in its current form and focusing remaining budget on image-only and aggregation refinements. Several points remain uncertain: each configuration was run once with unknown variance; RNA-only performance of scVI and scGPT is untested, so it is unclear whether these encoders are weak on their own or whether weighted fusion fails to down-weight them (e.g., through feature scale, dimensionality, or weighting behavior); scGPT may also depend on preprocessing or fine-tuning choices; and concat fusion at multiprofile and fusion tuning remain untested, so multimodality is not ruled out in general.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: Image-only ResNet50 with multiprofile avgpool is the best configuration so far (0.7150 acc). It came from a +17.8-point gain over single-profile. All four multimodal runs underperformed image-only. The only RNA-only evidence is a single single-profile PCA-2000 run (0.3275). So we do not know whether RNA's weakness is inherent or partly a single-profile limitation. 2) What this tests: config_002 changes only the profile setting for RNA-only PCA-2000 (single-profile to multiprofile avgpool), directly paralleling the config_010 to config_011 comparison. It shows whether the multiprofile and avgpool benefit generalizes beyond images. It also shows how strong RNA is under the same multiprofile setting used in the fusion runs, which helps explain why PCA weighted fusion (0.6776) fell below image-only. 3) Why it is the best use of budget: It resolves a core uncertainty about the RNA modality with a clean one-variable comparison. That informs whether any further fusion or RNA-encoder experiments are worth funding, instead of blindly trying more fusion variants that have consistently underperformed.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_010 tested an RNA-only PCA-2000 model with multiprofile avgpool aggregation, changing only the profile setting from the single-profile RNA-only baseline (llm_summary_001: 0.3275 acc, 0.2884 F1), which isolates the switch to multiprofile avgpool for RNA. It reached 0.5136 validation accuracy (F1 0.4982), about 18.6 points higher in accuracy and 21.0 points higher in F1. This parallels the 17.8-point image-only gain (llm_summary_002 to llm_summary_004) and suggests that, in this setup, the multiprofile avgpool benefit holds across both modalities, so part of RNA's earlier weakness reflected the single-profile setting. RNA-only nonetheless remains about 20.1 points below the best image-only multiprofile ResNet50 model (llm_summary_004: 0.7150 acc) and about 16.4 points below PCA weighted fusion (llm_summary_007: 0.6776), which sits between the two unimodal results; this is consistent with a weaker RNA modality diluting image signal, though the fusion mechanism itself is not isolated. Several points remain uncertain: each configuration was run once with unknown variance; RNA-only multiprofile performance of scVI-200 and scGPT is untested, so it is unclear whether their poor fusion results reflect weak standalone features or fusion behavior; and whether other aggregators or RNA encoders would narrow the gap to images is also untested.

selection_reason: 1) No experiments have been run yet, so there is no evidence about which modality, encoder, profile setting, aggregation, or fusion choice matters. 2) config_001 (RNA-only, single-profile, PCA with 2000 components) is the simplest configuration with no aggregation and no fusion. It sets a baseline on the RNA side. Later experiments can then each change one factor against it: encoder (scVI or scGPT), profile setting (avgpool or transformer multiprofile), or adding the image modality. 3) Under a limited budget, starting with a cheap, interpretable baseline makes every later comparison cleaner. It also guards against assuming that more complex multimodal or multiprofile models will win. If the simple baseline is strong, we learn early that added complexity must beat a high bar.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_001 set the first baseline: an RNA-only, single-profile model with a PCA RNA encoder (n=2000 components), no image modality, no aggregation, and no fusion. It reached validation accuracy 0.6287, with validation F1 0.5993 as supporting evidence. Because no other configurations have been run, this is only a reference point and says nothing yet about whether alternative RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), multiprofile settings (avgpool, transformer), or adding image features would help. Future experiments should change one factor at a time against this baseline. A single run also leaves the effect of run-to-run variance unknown, so small differences from this number should be read cautiously.

selection_reason: 1) The only evidence so far is one RNA-only, single-profile PCA baseline (acc 0.629, F1 0.599). Every other factor is untested: RNA encoder, profile setting, aggregation, image modality and fusion. 2) config_002 changes exactly one factor from that baseline, switching from single-profile to multiprofile. It uses the simplest aggregation (avgpool) and keeps the PCA RNA encoder. This shows whether pooling several profiles per sample helps on its own. 3) Profile setting affects a large share of the remaining search space, so knowing its effect early tells us how to spend the rest of the budget. Avgpool gives a clean, low-complexity test before we try the transformer aggregator. Other one-factor comparisons, such as scVI or scGPT encoders and an image-only baseline, can follow next.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_002 tested an RNA-only, multiprofile model with the PCA RNA encoder (n=2000), avgpool aggregation, no image modality and no fusion. It differs from the single-profile baseline llm_summary_001 only in profile setting, plus the aggregation that multiprofile requires. Validation accuracy was 0.5232 versus 0.6287 for the baseline, and validation F1 was 0.5084 versus 0.5993, so on both metrics multiprofile with avgpool did worse than the single-profile baseline in this initial comparison. Because profile setting and avgpool were introduced together, this result cannot tell us whether multiprofile input itself hurts or whether simple averaging discards useful per-profile information. A transformer aggregator, other RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), or adding image features could change the picture, and with one run per configuration and unknown run-to-run variance, the size of the gap should be treated as provisional.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: with the PCA RNA encoder, multiprofile plus avgpool (0.523 acc, 0.508 F1) did clearly worse than single-profile (0.629 acc, 0.599 F1).
