Multiprofile input and avgpool were introduced together, so we cannot tell whether multiprofile data hurts or whether simple averaging throws away per-profile information. 2) What this tests: config_003 keeps everything from config_002 (RNA-only, multiprofile, PCA n2000) and changes only the aggregation, from avgpool to transformer. If accuracy recovers to near or above the single-profile baseline, avgpool was the bottleneck and learned aggregation is worth carrying forward. If it stays low, multiprofile input itself looks unhelpful for RNA, and later experiments can favor single-profile settings. 3) Why it is the best next use of budget: aggregation and profile setting are crossed with every encoder and fusion option across most of the remaining space. Settling this question cheaply now, before testing other encoders or adding images, can prune or redirect many later experiments. This makes it a high-information, single-factor experiment.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_003 changed only the aggregation of llm_summary_002, from avgpool to transformer, keeping the RNA-only, multiprofile, PCA (n=2000) setup with no image modality or fusion. It reached validation accuracy 0.4214 (F1 0.4124), below avgpool (0.5232 acc, 0.5084 F1) and well below the single-profile baseline llm_summary_001 (0.6287 acc, 0.5993 F1), so learned transformer aggregation did not recover performance and was worse than simple averaging in this single-factor comparison. One reading is that multiprofile input is unhelpful for PCA RNA features, since neither aggregator approached the single-profile result. But no aggregator-free multiprofile control exists, and the transformer may be poorly suited or under-tuned here (for example, overfitting or optimization issues on PCA features), so we cannot yet attribute the gap to multiprofile input itself. With one run per configuration and unknown run-to-run variance, these gaps are provisional, and they may not hold for other RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT) or when image features are added.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: All three experiments so far used PCA RNA features. Single-profile (0.629 acc, 0.599 F1) beat multiprofile with avgpool (0.523) and with transformer (0.421). This suggests single-profile is the stronger setting, at least for PCA RNA, though each result comes from one run. The image modality is completely untested, yet it underlies 42 of the 48 remaining configurations (all image-only and multimodal ones). 2. What this tests: config_010 is an image-only, single-profile ResNet50 model. It measures how much signal images carry on their own, in the profile setting that has worked best so far. That gives a direct modality comparison against the RNA baseline config_001. 3. Why it is the best next step: whether images are informative is the largest open design question and determines whether the multimodal branch is worth budget. If image-only is weak, multimodal fusion is less likely to help, and effort can shift to RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT). If it is competitive, it supports testing single-profile fusion, such as config_016 or config_017, next. One run answers a more important question than another RNA-encoder or aggregation variant would.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_004 gave the first image-modality result: an image-only, single-profile model with a ResNet50 image encoder, no RNA input, no aggregation and no fusion. It reached validation accuracy 0.5321 (F1 0.5172), below the RNA-only single-profile PCA baseline llm_summary_001 (0.6287 acc, 0.5993 F1), so in this initial comparison ResNet50 image features were weaker than PCA RNA features. The comparison changes modality and encoder together, so it reflects these two specific encoders and not modalities in general. The number of classes and the chance-level accuracy are not given, so it is unclear how much label signal the images carry in absolute terms. Whether fusion would help also remains unresolved, because a weaker modality can still add complementary information; this is worth testing with single-profile fusion (e.g., config_016/017) before deprioritizing the multimodal branch. Other image encoders, other RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT) and unknown run-to-run variance (one run per configuration) all leave the size of the gap provisional.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: the best result so far is the single-profile PCA RNA baseline (0.629 acc, 0.599 F1). Single-profile ResNet50 image-only is weaker (0.532 acc, 0.517 F1). Multiprofile with either aggregator hurt RNA performance, so single-profile is the more promising setting for now. Whether fusion helps is untested, and it is a core design question. 2) config_016 adds ResNet50 image features to the best RNA setup with simple concat fusion, keeping the single-profile setting and both encoders that already have unimodal results. Comparing it with config_001 and config_010 isolates the value of adding the image modality, i.e., whether the weaker image features carry complementary signal. 3) Both unimodal reference points already exist, so this is a clean, readable comparison. Its outcome determines whether the large multimodal part of the search space deserves budget. If fusion helps, the next steps are weighted fusion (config_017) and stronger encoders. If it does not, the budget should shift toward RNA encoder comparisons such as scVI (config_004) and scGPT (config_007).
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_005 tested whether ResNet50 image features add useful signal to the best RNA setup: a single-profile multimodal model with the PCA (n=2000) RNA encoder, the ResNet50 image encoder, simple concat fusion and no aggregation. It reached validation accuracy 0.5191 (F1 0.4797), below both unimodal references, the RNA-only PCA baseline llm_summary_001 (0.6287 acc, 0.5993 F1) and the image-only ResNet50 model llm_summary_004 (0.5321 acc, 0.5172 F1). This is an initial observation that naive concat fusion of these two encoders did not exploit any complementary image signal and was in fact worse than either modality alone. Because only one fusion method was tried, it remains unclear whether the image modality itself is unhelpful or whether concat fusion is the problem (for example, feature-scale or dimensionality imbalance between the two encoders, overfitting, or optimization issues), so weighted fusion (config_017) would be the cheapest check before deprioritizing the multimodal branch in favor of RNA encoder comparisons (scVI, scGPT); with one run per configuration and unknown run-to-run variance, the gaps remain provisional.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: RNA-only single-profile PCA (config_001, acc 0.629, F1 0.599) is the best result so far. Every multiprofile variant (avgpool 0.523, transformer 0.421), image-only ResNet50 (0.532) and concat fusion (0.519) did worse. The RNA encoder is still completely untested, even though it is the strongest modality and feeds into most of the remaining configurations. 2) This experiment swaps only the RNA encoder from PCA (n=2000) to scVI (n=200) and keeps everything else identical to the baseline. It cleanly isolates whether a learned, compact RNA representation beats PCA. 3) Under a limited budget, the encoder choice is the highest-leverage open question. It extends the best-performing branch, so there is a real chance of an immediate gain. It also tells us which RNA encoder to carry into any later fusion or multiprofile tests. Weighted fusion (config_017) remains a sensible follow-up, but it builds on a branch that has so far underperformed.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_006 changed only the RNA encoder of the RNA-only, single-profile baseline llm_summary_001, from PCA (n=2000) to scVI (n=200), with no image modality, aggregation or fusion. It reached validation accuracy 0.7062 (F1 0.6671) versus 0.6287 (F1 0.5993) for PCA, the best result so far, so scVI outperformed PCA on both metrics in this one-factor comparison. The encoder swap also changes representation dimensionality (2000 to 200), so it cannot separate whether the gain comes from learned scVI modeling or from a more compact representation, and scGPT remains untested. With one run per configuration and unknown run-to-run variance, the size of the gain is provisional, and it is untested whether scVI also improves the weaker multiprofile (avgpool/transformer) or fusion (concat/weighted) settings, which makes it the natural RNA encoder to carry into those follow-ups.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: The RNA encoder is the strongest lever found so far. Swapping PCA for scVI in the RNA-only single-profile setting raised validation accuracy from 0.629 to 0.706 and F1 from 0.599 to 0.667. In contrast, multiprofile aggregation (avgpool 0.523, transformer 0.421) and concat fusion with ResNet50 (0.519) all hurt relative to the PCA baseline. scGPT is the only RNA encoder not yet tested. 2) Test: config_007 swaps only the RNA encoder to scGPT in the same RNA-only, single-profile setup with no aggregation or fusion. That gives a clean three-way encoder comparison (PCA, scVI, scGPT). It shows whether a pretrained foundation-model representation beats scVI, and which encoder should anchor later multiprofile and fusion tests. 3) Why now: Every downstream branch depends on choosing the best RNA backbone. One cheap, simple experiment settles that choice before spending budget on more complex combinations, whose weaker results so far may partly reflect the PCA encoder. It also has a realistic chance of producing a new best accuracy.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_007 changed only the RNA encoder of the RNA-only, single-profile setup (no image modality, aggregation or fusion) to scGPT, completing a three-way encoder comparison. It reached validation accuracy 0.5375 (F1 0.5184). That is well below scVI (llm_summary_006: 0.7062 acc, 0.6671 F1) and the PCA baseline (llm_summary_001: 0.6287 acc, 0.5993 F1), so in this one-factor comparison the pretrained foundation-model representation did not help and scVI remains the best RNA backbone to carry into multiprofile and fusion follow-ups. It is unclear whether the gap reflects scGPT embeddings being poorly matched to this data, or setup factors such as frozen versus fine-tuned use, embedding dimensionality, preprocessing or gene-vocabulary overlap, or under-tuning. With one run per configuration and unknown run-to-run variance, the size of the gaps is provisional, and how scGPT would behave in multiprofile or fusion settings is untested.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: Concat fusion of PCA and ResNet50 (config_016, 0.519 acc, 0.480 F1) did worse than either modality alone (PCA RNA 0.629, ResNet50 image 0.532). This could mean the image modality adds nothing, or that concat fusion is flawed, for example through scale or dimensionality imbalance or overfitting. Only one fusion method has been tried, so these two causes cannot be told apart. 2. Test: config_017 keeps everything in config_016 fixed and changes only the fusion, from concat to weighted. Weighted fusion can down-weight a weaker or noisy modality, so this directly tests whether the fusion method causes the multimodal deficit. 3. Value: About half of the remaining search space is multimodal, so this result decides whether that branch is worth budget. If weighted fusion matches or beats RNA-only PCA, the next step is the logical extension to the best RNA encoder (scVI with ResNet50, weighted: config_029). If it does not help, multimodal fusion can be deprioritized in favor of scVI-focused experiments. A one-factor diagnostic gives a clearer answer than jumping straight to scVI fusion, which would confound encoder and fusion effects.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_008 (config_017) kept the single-profile multimodal setup of llm_summary_005 (PCA n=2000 RNA encoder, ResNet50 image encoder, no aggregation) and changed only the fusion, from concat to weighted, to test whether concat fusion caused the multimodal deficit. It reached validation accuracy 0.5318 (F1 0.5161). That is a small gain over concat (0.5191 acc, 0.4797 F1), larger on F1 than on accuracy, and essentially the same as image-only ResNet50 (llm_summary_004: 0.5321 acc, 0.5172 F1). It remains well below RNA-only PCA (llm_summary_001: 0.6287 acc, 0.5993 F1) and RNA-only scVI (llm_summary_006: 0.7062 acc). Weighted fusion therefore did not meet the pre-stated criterion of matching or beating RNA-only PCA, which by the planned decision rule argues for deprioritizing the multimodal branch in favor of scVI-focused experiments. Several points remain uncertain: the learned modality weights were not reported, so it is unknown why fusion still underperformed the RNA-only model (possibilities include the fused model leaning on the weaker image features, optimization or overfitting problems, or scale imbalance between the two encoders); whether a stronger RNA encoder (scVI + ResNet50, config_029) would change the outcome is untested; and with one run per configuration and unknown run-to-run variance, the small concat-versus-weighted difference is provisional.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: scVI is clearly the best RNA encoder so far (config_004: 0.706 acc, 0.667 F1), ahead of PCA (0.629) and scGPT (0.537). Multiprofile input has only been tested with PCA, where it hurt badly: avgpool reached 0.523 and transformer 0.421, both below single-profile PCA at 0.629. Multimodal fusion with ResNet50 was no better than image-only, and the earlier decision rule argued for focusing on scVI. It is still unknown whether the multiprofile penalty is general or specific to the 2000-dimensional PCA features. 2) Test: config_005 changes only the profile setting of the current best model, scVI single-profile to scVI multiprofile with avgpool. Avgpool was the better aggregator with PCA. This isolates whether multiprofile hurts with a compact learned representation, or whether it might help. 3) Why this experiment: profile setting splits about two-thirds of the remaining configurations. One clean comparison against the best model will tell us whether to prune or revisit all scVI multiprofile and fusion variants. It also has a reasonable chance of improving on the current best. Testing a ViT-L image encoder remains an important open question for a later experiment.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_009 (config_005) changed only the profile setting of the best model so far, RNA-only scVI (n=200) with no image modality or fusion, from single-profile to multiprofile with avgpool aggregation. It reached validation accuracy 0.3316 (F1 0.3150), far below single-profile scVI (llm_summary_006: 0.7062 acc, 0.6671 F1) and also below multiprofile PCA with avgpool (llm_summary_002: 0.5232 acc), making it the worst result so far. Together with the PCA results, this indicates that the multiprofile penalty is not specific to the 2000-dimensional PCA features: in both RNA-encoder comparisons tested, multiprofile with avgpool performed much worse than single-profile. By the planned decision rule, this argues for deprioritizing the remaining scVI multiprofile and multiprofile-fusion variants. Several points remain uncertain. Multiprofile and aggregation are introduced together, so the evidence cannot separate whether multiprofile input itself hurts or whether averaging discards per-profile signal; scVI with the transformer aggregator is untested, although the transformer was worse than avgpool with PCA. The unusually large drop for the stronger encoder, which falls below even multiprofile PCA, could also reflect pipeline or setup issues in the multiprofile scVI path, such as how scVI embeddings are computed or pooled per profile. With one run per configuration and unknown run-to-run variance, the gap sizes are provisional.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: single-profile RNA-only scVI is clearly the best result so far (0.706 acc, 0.667 F1). Multiprofile has hurt with both RNA encoders tested. Multimodal fusion has only been tried with the weaker PCA encoder, where weighted fusion (0.532) beat concat (0.519) but did not reach RNA-only PCA. So it remains open whether the fusion deficit comes from the image modality itself or from pairing it with a weaker RNA representation. 2) This experiment changes only the RNA encoder of config_017, from PCA to scVI, and keeps ResNet50, single-profile input and the better-performing weighted fusion. Compared with config_004, it is a one-factor test of whether adding ResNet50 image features through weighted fusion helps or hurts the strongest RNA backbone. 3) Best use of budget: it builds on the strongest direction (scVI, single-profile) while settling whether the multimodal branch deserves further budget. If fusion matches or beats scVI alone, follow-ups such as concat fusion (config_028) or ViT-L fusion (config_035) become worthwhile. If it underperforms, that strengthens the case for deprioritizing fusion and focusing on image-encoder or other RNA-centered comparisons.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_010 (config_029) took the best model so far, single-profile RNA-only scVI (n=200; llm_summary_006: 0.7062 acc, 0.6671 F1), and added ResNet50 image features through weighted fusion with no aggregation; it also differs from llm_summary_008 (PCA + ResNet50, weighted) only in the RNA encoder. Validation accuracy was 0.5362 (F1 0.5158), far below RNA-only scVI and essentially the same as PCA + ResNet50 weighted fusion (0.5318 acc, 0.5161 F1) and image-only ResNet50 (llm_summary_004: 0.5321 acc, 0.5172 F1). So in this one-factor comparison, adding ResNet50 through weighted fusion hurt the strongest RNA backbone, and the much stronger RNA encoder gave almost no benefit inside the fusion model; by the planned decision rule, this argues for deprioritizing the fusion branch, including the concat (config_028) and ViT-L (config_035) follow-ups, in favor of RNA-centered work. It remains unexplained why fused models across both RNA encoders converge to roughly image-only performance: possibilities include the fusion weighting leaning on the image branch, feature-scale imbalance, optimization or overfitting problems, or a pipeline issue in the multimodal path, and the learned modality weights were not reported. With one run per configuration and unknown run-to-run variance, all of these gaps are provisional.

selection_reason: 1) No experiments have been run yet, so there is no evidence about which modality, encoder, profile setting, aggregation, or fusion choice matters. 2) config_001 (RNA-only, single-profile, PCA-2000) is the simplest configuration in the space. It sets a reference point for accuracy and F1 without adding encoder complexity, aggregation, or fusion. 3) Each later change can be isolated by changing one factor from this anchor: RNA encoder (scVI, scGPT), profile setting and aggregation (avgpool vs. transformer), modality (image or multimodal), and fusion. With a limited budget, a clean baseline first is the most efficient way to make future comparisons interpretable. It also avoids assuming that more complex models will do better.
experiment_summary: The first experiment (llm_summary_001) tested the simplest configuration in the search space: an RNA-only, single-profile model with a PCA-2000 RNA encoder and no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It was chosen as a clean reference point. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.523 and a validation F1 of 0.508. The close accuracy and F1 values loosely suggest performance is not driven by a few classes, though per-class results were not reported. With no other experiments to compare against, this is only an initial baseline: it says nothing yet about whether alternative RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), multi-profile aggregation (avgpool, transformer), image or multimodal inputs, or fusion would help. Run-to-run variance is also unknown. Future single-factor changes from this anchor are needed to tell which design choices matter.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: there is only one result so far, the RNA-only, single-profile PCA-2000 baseline (accuracy 0.523, F1 0.508). It tells us nothing yet about which design choices matter. 2. What this tests: config_002 changes one factor from that baseline. It moves from single-profile to multiprofile using the simplest aggregation (avgpool), keeping the RNA-only setting and PCA-2000 encoder fixed. Any change in accuracy or F1 can therefore be attributed to multi-profile aggregation itself. This avoids confounding it with encoder or modality changes, and avgpool separates the benefit of extra profiles from the added complexity of a transformer aggregator. 3. Why it is the best use of the budget: profile setting affects most of the remaining search space, including the RNA-only, image-only and multimodal branches. Learning early whether pooling multiple profiles helps will guide many later choices. Single-factor tests of the RNA encoder (scVI, scGPT) and image-only baselines can follow from the same anchor.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_002 changed one factor from the RNA-only PCA-2000 single-profile baseline (llm_summary_001): it switched to multiprofile input with avgpool aggregation, keeping the RNA-only setting and PCA-2000 encoder fixed. Validation accuracy fell from 0.523 to 0.435 and validation F1 from 0.508 to 0.423, so multiprofile with avgpool underperformed single-profile in this RNA-only setting. Because multiprofile and avgpool were introduced together, the drop cannot be assigned to using multiple profiles as such rather than to simple mean pooling, which may wash out per-profile signal. With one run per configuration and unknown run-to-run variance, it also remains uncertain how robust the gap is, whether a learned aggregator (e.g., transformer) would recover or exceed baseline performance, and whether the pattern holds for other RNA encoders or for image and multimodal branches.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: With RNA-only PCA-2000, switching from single-profile (acc 0.523, F1 0.508) to multiprofile with avgpool dropped performance to acc 0.435 and F1 0.423. Multiprofile and avgpool were introduced together, so we cannot yet tell whether multiple profiles hurt or whether mean pooling washes out per-profile signal. 2. What this tests: config_003 keeps everything from config_002 fixed and changes only avgpool to a transformer aggregator. If accuracy recovers toward or above 0.523, the drop came mainly from the aggregator. If it stays near 0.435, multiprofile input itself looks unhelpful in this setting. 3. Why now: aggregation and profile setting recur across most of the remaining search space, including the image-only and multimodal branches. Resolving this question with one clean single-factor experiment helps decide which large blocks of configurations deserve budget. Encoder and modality comparisons (e.g., config_004, config_010) remain important but can follow.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_003 kept the RNA-only, multiprofile, PCA-2000 setup of llm_summary_002 fixed and changed only the aggregator from avgpool to transformer. Validation accuracy rose from 0.435 to 0.579 and F1 from 0.423 to 0.563, also exceeding the single-profile baseline (llm_summary_001: acc 0.523, F1 0.508). Within this single-factor comparison, the earlier multiprofile drop appears tied to avgpool aggregation rather than to multiprofile input as such, and multiprofile input with a transformer aggregator looks promising for RNA-only PCA-2000. However, each configuration was run once and run-to-run variance is unknown, so the size and robustness of the gains are uncertain, and it is untested whether the advantage holds for other RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT) or for image-only and multimodal branches.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: the three runs so far all use RNA-only PCA-2000. Within that setting, multiprofile input with a transformer aggregator (config_003: acc 0.579, F1 0.563) beat both the single-profile baseline (0.523) and avgpool (0.435). The image modality is completely untested, so we do not know how strong image features are on their own. 2) Test: config_012 keeps the best known profile and aggregation setting (multiprofile + transformer) and swaps the RNA branch for an image-only ResNet50 branch. This measures the standalone value of image features. It also shows whether the transformer aggregation advantage carries over to another modality. 3) Why now: the result tells us whether the many multimodal configurations are worth the budget, and it gives a reference for interpreting later fusion results such as config_020. Comparing RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT) is useful but explores a narrower question, so it can wait.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_004 kept the multiprofile input and transformer aggregation of the best run so far (llm_summary_003) and replaced the RNA-only PCA-2000 branch with an image-only ResNet50 branch, isolating the input modality under this setting. Validation accuracy was 0.411 and F1 was 0.378, well below the RNA-only counterpart (llm_summary_003: acc 0.579, F1 0.563) and also below the RNA-only single-profile baseline (llm_summary_001: acc 0.523). This suggests ResNet50 image features alone are substantially weaker than PCA-2000 RNA features here, and the slightly wider accuracy–F1 gap hints at less even per-class performance, though per-class results were not reported. Each configuration was run once and run-to-run variance is unknown; there are no image-only single-profile or avgpool runs, so it is unknown whether transformer aggregation helps for images. It is also untested whether image features add complementary signal when fused with RNA, or whether other image encoders would do better.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: The best run so far is RNA-only PCA-2000 with multiprofile input and transformer aggregation (config_003: acc 0.579, F1 0.563). Image-only ResNet50 under the same multiprofile and transformer setup was much weaker (config_012: acc 0.411, F1 0.378). We still do not know whether image features add complementary signal when combined with RNA, or whether they only add noise. Each configuration was run once, so small differences should be read with caution. 2) Test: config_020 keeps the RNA encoder, profile setting and aggregator of config_003 fixed. It adds the ResNet50 image branch using the simplest fusion, concat. Compared with config_003, it isolates the effect of adding imaging. Compared with config_012, it isolates the effect of adding RNA. 3) Why now: Whether multimodal fusion helps is the central design question, and it controls about two-thirds of the remaining search space. This single-factor extension of the best configuration settles it efficiently. If it beats config_003, later runs can explore fusion type and the image or RNA encoder within the multimodal setting. If it does not, the budget can shift toward RNA encoder comparisons (scVI, scGPT) in the RNA-only setting.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_005 added a ResNet50 image branch with concat fusion to the best configuration so far (llm_summary_003: RNA-only PCA-2000, multiprofile, transformer aggregation), keeping the RNA encoder, profile setting and aggregator fixed. Validation accuracy fell from 0.579 to 0.507 and F1 from 0.563 to 0.455. The run beat image-only under the same setup (llm_summary_004: acc 0.411, F1 0.378) but scored below even the RNA-only single-profile baseline (llm_summary_001: acc 0.523). In this setting, simply concatenating ResNet50 features with PCA-2000 RNA features did not add complementary signal and appears to hurt, and the wider accuracy–F1 gap hints at less even per-class performance, though per-class results were not reported. Each configuration was run once with unknown run-to-run variance. Only concat fusion and one image encoder were tested. It therefore remains uncertain whether the drop reflects image features adding noise or the simple fusion design, and whether other fusion methods, image encoders or RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT) would change the multimodal outcome.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: the best run so far is RNA-only PCA-2000 with multiprofile transformer aggregation (config_003: acc 0.579, F1 0.563). Adding ResNet50 with concat fusion (config_020) dropped accuracy to 0.507 and F1 to 0.455. Only concat fusion has been tested, so we cannot tell whether image features add noise or whether naive concatenation is the problem. 2. What this tests: config_021 changes only the fusion method from concat to weighted, holding the RNA encoder, image encoder, profile setting and aggregator fixed. If weighted fusion recovers or exceeds the RNA-only result, the fusion design was the bottleneck. If it stays below 0.579, ResNet50 image features likely contribute little in this setup. 3. Why now: the answer bears on the large multimodal share of the remaining search space (36 configurations), so a clean single-factor fusion test is high-value. RNA-encoder comparisons such as scVI (config_006) remain natural follow-ups.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_006 kept the multimodal PCA-2000 + ResNet50, multiprofile, transformer-aggregation setup of llm_summary_005 fixed and changed only the fusion method from concat to weighted. Validation accuracy rose from 0.507 to 0.542 and F1 from 0.455 to 0.483, but both stayed below the RNA-only counterpart (llm_summary_003: acc 0.579, F1 0.563); its F1 was also below the RNA-only single-profile baseline (llm_summary_001: F1 0.508). This suggests fusion design matters somewhat, but under both tested fusion methods adding ResNet50 features gave no net benefit over RNA alone, and the persistently wide accuracy–F1 gap hints at uneven per-class performance (not reported). Each configuration was run once with unknown run-to-run variance, so the concat-to-weighted gain may not be robust, and it remains untested whether other fusion methods, image encoders or RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT) would make multimodal input competitive.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: RNA is clearly the strongest modality. The best run so far is config_003 (RNA-only PCA-2000, multiprofile, transformer aggregation), at acc 0.579 and F1 0.563. ResNet50 image-only runs are much weaker, and adding ResNet50 through concat or weighted fusion has not beaten RNA alone. The RNA encoder choice is a major design decision that is still completely untested, since every run so far used PCA-2000. 2) Test: switch only the RNA encoder from PCA-2000 to scGPT, keeping the best RNA-only multiprofile transformer setup fixed. This isolates whether a pretrained foundation-model representation improves on PCA features. 3) Why now: it is a one-factor change from the best configuration, so it has a real chance of exploitation gains. It also reduces uncertainty about which RNA representation later multimodal runs should build on. That makes it a better use of budget than further image or fusion variants built on a modality that has so far underperformed.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_007 kept the best configuration so far (llm_summary_003: RNA-only, multiprofile, transformer aggregation) fixed and changed only the RNA encoder from PCA-2000 to pretrained scGPT. Validation accuracy fell from 0.579 to 0.427 and F1 from 0.563 to 0.417. This was below the RNA-only single-profile PCA-2000 baseline (llm_summary_001: acc 0.523) and roughly level with the multiprofile avgpool PCA-2000 run (llm_summary_002: acc 0.435). Image-only ResNet50 remains the lowest-scoring run (llm_summary_004: acc 0.411). In this single-factor comparison, scGPT features did not improve on PCA-2000 and appear substantially weaker under this setup, so PCA-2000 remains the stronger tested RNA representation for downstream multimodal runs. Each configuration was run once with unknown run-to-run variance. Only this one scGPT setup was tested, with no single-profile or avgpool scGPT runs and no scVI comparison, so it is uncertain whether the gap reflects the scGPT representation itself or its interaction with transformer aggregation or this training setup.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best run so far is RNA-only PCA-2000 with multiprofile input and transformer aggregation (config_003: acc 0.579, F1 0.563). RNA is clearly the dominant signal. Image-only ResNet50 was weak, and adding it through concat or weighted fusion did not help. Swapping PCA-2000 for scGPT hurt badly (acc 0.427). scVI is the only RNA encoder not yet tested, so we do not know whether PCA-2000 is the best RNA representation or whether scGPT's drop reflects pretrained embeddings in general. 2. What this tests: config_006 keeps the best setup fixed and changes only the encoder from PCA-2000 to scVI-200. This isolates the effect of a compact, dataset-trained latent representation against PCA. 3. Why it is the best next use of budget: RNA representation is the most consequential remaining choice. It directly limits the RNA-only ceiling and decides which RNA encoder all later multimodal runs should use. This single-factor run has a real chance of beating the current best and is informative either way. Exploring image encoders like ViT-L is a lower priority given how weak the image signal has been so far.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_008 kept the best configuration so far fixed (llm_summary_003: RNA-only, multiprofile, transformer aggregation) and changed only the RNA encoder from PCA-2000 to scVI-200. Validation accuracy rose from 0.579 to 0.721 and F1 from 0.563 to 0.681, making this the best run to date and well above the scGPT variant (llm_summary_007: acc 0.427). In this single-factor comparison, scVI-200 latents look like the strongest tested RNA representation under this setup and the natural RNA encoder for later multimodal runs. Each configuration was run once with unknown run-to-run variance, so the size of the gain is uncertain. The accuracy–F1 gap is wider than for PCA-2000, which hints at less even per-class performance, though per-class results were not reported. It is also untested whether scVI's advantage holds under single-profile or avgpool settings, or whether pairing it with image features via concat or weighted fusion would still give no net benefit over RNA alone.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: The best run so far is RNA-only scVI-200 with multiprofile input and transformer aggregation (config_006, acc 0.721). Adding ResNet50 image features hurt under both concat and weighted fusion (acc 0.507 and 0.542, against 0.579 for RNA-only PCA-2000). Image-only ResNet50 was weak (acc 0.411). Every image result so far uses ResNet50, so we cannot yet tell whether image data has little value or ResNet50 is simply a poor image encoder. 2) Test: This run keeps the image-only, multiprofile, transformer setup of config_012 fixed and changes only the image encoder from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L. That isolates the effect of the image representation. 3) Why now: About half of the remaining configurations are multimodal runs that depend on the image encoder. If ViT-L is clearly stronger than ResNet50, fusing it with scVI becomes a promising next step. If it is equally weak, we can deprioritize multimodal runs and focus on RNA-side questions. Either result saves budget compared with spending another run on ResNet50 fusion, which has already failed twice.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_009 kept the image-only, multiprofile, transformer-aggregation setup of llm_summary_004 fixed and changed only the image encoder from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L, testing whether the weak image results so far reflected ResNet50 specifically or low image signal in general. Validation accuracy rose only slightly, from 0.411 to 0.421, while F1 rose somewhat more, from 0.378 to 0.412, which hints at more even per-class performance (per-class results not reported). Both image-only runs remain far below every RNA-only multiprofile transformer run (PCA-2000: 0.579; scVI-200, the best run so far: 0.721), so among the two image encoders tested, image features alone look weak regardless of encoder. With one run per configuration and unknown run-to-run variance, the small ViT-L gain may not be robust, and it remains untested whether ViT-L features add complementary signal when fused with scVI or PCA-2000, or whether other image encoders or single-profile/avgpool image settings would differ.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: The best run so far is RNA-only scVI-200 with multiprofile input and a transformer aggregator (config_006, acc 0.721, F1 0.681), well ahead of PCA-2000 (0.579). With the weaker PCA-2000 encoder, adding ResNet50 image features hurt under both fusion methods. Weighted fusion (0.542) did better than concat (0.507). The main open question is whether this negative result for images holds when the RNA representation is much stronger. 2. Test: This run swaps PCA-2000 for scVI-200 in the weighted-fusion multimodal setup of config_021, changing only the RNA encoder. It also differs from config_006 only by adding the ResNet50 branch with weighted fusion. So it gives two clean single-factor comparisons: whether scVI's advantage carries into multimodal models, and whether image features add complementary signal on top of the strongest RNA encoder. I chose ResNet50 over ViT-L to keep a direct match with config_021, since ViT-L was only slightly better as image-only. 3. Value: This answers the central fusion question at the current best operating point, and it could also produce a new best model. If images still give no gain, the remaining budget can shift toward profile and aggregation checks for scVI (e.g., config_004 or config_005) rather than further multimodal variants.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_010 combined the best RNA-only setup (llm_summary_008: scVI-200, multiprofile, transformer aggregation; acc 0.721, F1 0.681) with a ResNet50 image branch and weighted fusion, giving two single-factor comparisons: adding images to llm_summary_008, and swapping PCA-2000 for scVI-200 in the weighted multimodal run llm_summary_006 (acc 0.542, F1 0.483). It reached validation accuracy 0.639 and F1 0.620, so scVI-200 clearly outperformed PCA-2000 within the multimodal setting too, but adding ResNet50 features with weighted fusion still lowered accuracy and F1 relative to RNA-only scVI-200, matching the earlier PCA-2000 finding that this image branch gives no net benefit under concat or weighted fusion. The accuracy–F1 gap was narrower than for RNA-only scVI-200 (about 0.02 vs 0.04), which hints at more even per-class performance, though per-class results were not reported. Each configuration was run once with unknown run-to-run variance, and only ResNet50 with weighted fusion was tested on scVI, so it remains uncertain whether ViT-L, concat or other fusion designs would change the outcome, and whether scVI's advantage holds under single-profile or avgpool settings.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: no experiments have been run, so we know nothing yet about which modality, encoder, profile setting, aggregation or fusion choice matters. 2. Test: config_001 (RNA-only, single-profile, PCA with 2000 components, no aggregation or fusion) is the simplest available setup. It gives a reference accuracy and F1 that later experiments can be compared against by changing one factor at a time: a learned RNA encoder (scVI or scGPT), multiprofile aggregation (avgpool or transformer), the image modality, or fusion. 3. Why now: with a limited budget, a cheap and interpretable baseline is the best first step. It avoids assuming that complex multimodal models help and makes each later result easier to attribute to a specific design choice.
experiment_summary: The first experiment (llm_summary_001) tested the simplest available setup as a baseline: an RNA-only, single-profile model using a PCA encoder with 2000 components, with no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.725 (primary metric) and a validation F1 of 0.685, giving a reference point for later one-factor-at-a-time comparisons. This is an initial observation, and no prior experiments exist to compare it against, so nothing can yet be concluded about whether learned RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), multiprofile aggregation (avgpool, transformer), the image modality, or fusion would help or hurt. The somewhat lower F1 relative to accuracy may hint at uneven performance across classes, but this is unconfirmed, and run-to-run variance is unknown because there is only a single run.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: there is only one result so far, the RNA-only single-profile PCA baseline (acc 0.725, F1 0.685). We know nothing yet about whether the image modality carries useful signal. That question decides whether the 36 multimodal configurations deserve budget at all. 2) Test: config_010 (image-only, single-profile, ResNet50, no aggregation or fusion) gives a clean modality comparison against the baseline, since profile setting, aggregation and fusion all stay fixed. If images alone are competitive, or strong on classes RNA misses (F1 vs accuracy will hint at this), fusion becomes a priority. If images are weak, the budget can shift toward RNA encoders and multiprofile aggregation. 3) Why now: the RNA-encoder (config_004) and multiprofile (config_002) comparisons are also single-factor tests. However, modality is the highest-level branching decision in this search space, so settling it first prunes or prioritizes the largest set of remaining configurations. ResNet50 is the simpler of the two image encoders, which makes it the natural reference point before trying ViT-L.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_002 tested an image-only, single-profile model with a ResNet50 image encoder and no aggregation or fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.507 (F1 0.455), well below the RNA-only PCA-2000 single-profile baseline from llm_summary_001 (accuracy 0.725, F1 0.685), with profile setting, aggregation and fusion held fixed. Because switching modality also switched the encoder (ResNet50 vs PCA), this gap reflects this particular image pipeline rather than the image modality in general; ViT-L is untested, and each result comes from a single run with unknown variance. The result does not show whether image features carry signal that complements RNA, so fusion's value is still open. The F1 being lower than accuracy, as with the RNA baseline, may hint at uneven per-class performance, but per-class comparisons are unavailable.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: we have two single-profile baselines. RNA-only PCA-2000 reached 0.725 accuracy (F1 0.685). Image-only ResNet50 reached 0.507 (F1 0.455). Image features alone are much weaker, but we do not know whether they add information that RNA lacks. That question decides whether the large multimodal half of the search space is worth exploring. 2. What this tests: config_016 adds ResNet50 image features to the exact RNA baseline (PCA-2000, single profile) using simple concat fusion. Since both unimodal components are already measured, this is a clean one-factor test of whether adding the image modality helps or hurts. 3. Why now: a gain would justify further multimodal work. No gain or a drop would let us deprioritize most of the 36 multimodal configurations and focus on RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT) and multiprofile aggregation. Testing an RNA encoder first would also isolate one factor, but it only narrows a smaller branch. This test resolves the largest structural uncertainty with one run, though one run of unknown variance should not be overinterpreted.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_003 added ResNet50 image features to the exact RNA-only PCA-2000 single-profile baseline using concat fusion, with no aggregation, as a one-factor test of whether the image modality adds information. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.208 (F1 0.172), far below both the RNA-only baseline (0.725, F1 0.685) and the image-only ResNet50 model (0.507, F1 0.455). Concat fusion of this pipeline therefore performed much worse than either modality alone in this run. Because the result falls below even the weaker unimodal component, it may reflect a fusion or training problem, such as feature-scale or dimensionality mismatch or optimization failure, rather than images being inherently uninformative or harmful. The run cannot separate the image modality from the concat fusion method, it comes from a single run of unknown variance, and other fusion methods, ViT-L, and other RNA encoders remain untested, so deprioritizing all multimodal configurations on this basis alone would be premature.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: RNA-only PCA-2000 single-profile is the best result so far (accuracy 0.725, F1 0.685), and image-only ResNet50 reached 0.507. Concat fusion of these same two pipelines collapsed to 0.208, below even the weaker single modality. That pattern points to a fusion or optimization failure (for example, mismatched feature scales or dimensions) rather than evidence that images are harmful, but one run cannot tell these apart. 2. What this tests: config_017 keeps everything from config_016 the same (multimodal, single-profile, PCA-2000, ResNet50, no aggregation) and changes only the fusion method from concat to weighted. If weighted fusion recovers to near or above the RNA baseline, the collapse was specific to concat. If it also fails, the image features or the multimodal training setup are the problem. 3. Why this is the best next experiment: multimodal settings make up most of the remaining search space, and the concat-versus-weighted choice appears in nearly all of them. A clean one-factor test of fusion tells us whether that whole region should be pursued or deprioritized, which is more valuable than a further RNA-only exploitation step at this point. RNA-side questions (multiprofile aggregation, scVI or scGPT encoders) stay open for later runs.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_004 repeated the multimodal single-profile PCA-2000 + ResNet50 setup from llm_summary_003 (no aggregation) and changed only the fusion method from concat to weighted. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.527 (F1 0.510), well above concat's 0.208 (F1 0.172). Because fusion was the only factor changed, this suggests the earlier collapse was at least partly specific to concat fusion in this pipeline, though each result comes from a single run of unknown variance. Weighted fusion still fell well below the RNA-only PCA-2000 baseline (0.725, F1 0.685) and only slightly exceeded image-only ResNet50 (0.507, F1 0.455), so in this configuration adding images has not yet helped; it remains unclear whether this reflects weak image features, a fusion that over-weights the image branch (learned weights are not reported), or a multimodal optimization issue, and ViT-L, other RNA encoders, and multiprofile aggregation remain untested in the multimodal setting.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: The RNA-only PCA-2000 single-profile baseline is clearly the strongest result so far (acc 0.725, F1 0.685). Image-only ResNet50 (0.507) and both multimodal fusions (concat 0.208, weighted 0.527) fell well below it. Profile setting (single vs multi), and therefore aggregation, has not been tested in any modality. It is a major design axis that touches 32 of the remaining configurations. 2. Test: This keeps the best-performing pipeline fixed (RNA-only, PCA-2000, no fusion) and changes only the profile setting to multiprofile, using the simplest aggregator (avgpool). It isolates whether pooling multiple profiles helps or hurts classification. 3. Why now: It builds on the strongest arm while resolving uncertainty about a factor that affects many untested configurations. It avoids the confounds of the unstable multimodal pipeline. If avgpool helps, transformer aggregation (config_003) and multiprofile variants of other encoders become logical next steps. If it hurts, the large multiprofile part of the space can be deprioritized. This is a single run of unknown variance, so a small difference should not be overread.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_005 kept the strongest pipeline fixed (RNA-only, PCA-2000, no image encoder or fusion) and changed only the profile setting from single-profile to multiprofile with avgpool aggregation. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.579 (F1 0.563), clearly below the single-profile baseline from llm_summary_001 (0.725, F1 0.685). Because profile setting and aggregation change together, this suggests that multiprofile input with mean pooling hurt this RNA pipeline in this run, but it cannot separate an effect of using multiple profiles from an effect of the simple avgpool aggregator. The gap between accuracy and F1 was smaller than in the baseline, which may hint at more even per-class performance, though per-class results are unavailable. Each result is a single run of unknown variance, and transformer aggregation (config_003), multiprofile variants of other RNA encoders, and multiprofile image or multimodal settings remain untested, so deprioritizing the whole multiprofile space on this basis alone would be premature.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: The RNA-only single-profile PCA-2000 baseline (0.725 accuracy, 0.685 F1) is still the best result. Image-only runs, multimodal runs (concat and weighted) and multiprofile avgpool have all scored lower. The RNA encoder choice, which drives the strongest modality, has never been varied; every RNA run so far used PCA-2000. 2. Test: config_004 changes only the RNA encoder from PCA-2000 to scVI-200 and keeps the rest of the best pipeline fixed (RNA-only, single-profile, no aggregation, no fusion). This cleanly shows whether a learned, lower-dimensional RNA representation beats PCA. 3. Why now: The RNA encoder affects nearly every remaining configuration, including the multimodal ones. Its answer will therefore guide much of the rest of the search, either by finding a better base encoder or by confirming PCA as the reference. Narrower questions, such as transformer versus avgpool aggregation (config_003) or ViT-L images, matter less because those directions have so far trailed the baseline. This is one run of unknown variance, so a small gap in either direction should not be overinterpreted.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_006 kept the best pipeline fixed (RNA-only, single-profile, no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion) and changed only the RNA encoder from PCA-2000 to scVI-200. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.542 (F1 0.483), well below the PCA-2000 baseline from llm_summary_001 (0.725, F1 0.685), so PCA-2000 remains the strongest RNA encoder observed and the best overall result. Because the encoder was the only factor changed, this suggests that this scVI-200 representation underperformed PCA-2000 in this pipeline. However, it is a single run of unknown variance, and the test cannot separate a learned encoder from the much smaller dimensionality (200 vs 2000) or from scVI training or hyperparameter choices. scGPT, other scVI sizes, and scVI in multiprofile or multimodal settings remain untested, so ruling out learned RNA encoders in general would be premature.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: The RNA-only PCA-2000 single-profile baseline (0.725 accuracy, 0.685 F1) is still the best result. Moving to multiprofile with avgpool dropped it to 0.579. That change altered profile setting and aggregation together, so we cannot tell whether multiple profiles hurt or whether mean pooling discarded useful information. 2) Test: config_003 keeps the multiprofile PCA-2000 RNA-only pipeline fixed and changes only the aggregator from avgpool to transformer. If transformer aggregation recovers or beats single-profile performance, avgpool was the bottleneck. If it stays near 0.58, multiprofile input itself likely hurts this task. 3) Why now: About half of the untested configurations (multiprofile RNA, image, and multimodal variants) depend on whether multiprofile input is worthwhile and which aggregator to use. This one-factor experiment on the strongest pipeline resolves that question more cleanly than testing scGPT or ViT-L would, and both of those remain cheap follow-ups.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_007 kept the multiprofile RNA-only PCA-2000 pipeline from llm_summary_005 fixed and changed only the aggregator from avgpool to transformer. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.715 (F1 0.687), well above avgpool's 0.579 (F1 0.563) and close to the single-profile PCA-2000 baseline (0.725, F1 0.685), which remains the best accuracy observed, while this run had a marginally higher F1. Because aggregation was the only factor changed, this suggests the earlier multiprofile drop was largely due to avgpool rather than to multiprofile input itself. However, with transformer aggregation, multiprofile input has not been shown to beat single-profile in this pipeline, and the roughly 0.01 accuracy and 0.003 F1 differences from the baseline are within what single runs of unknown variance could plausibly produce. Transformer aggregation remains untested with other RNA encoders and in image-only or multimodal multiprofile settings.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: RNA-only PCA-2000 single-profile is the best result so far (accuracy 0.725). Every image-based run has used ResNet50, which was weak alone (0.507). The multimodal ResNet50 runs did not beat RNA-only (concat 0.208, weighted 0.527). So we cannot tell whether the image modality is uninformative or only this image encoder is weak. ViT-L is completely untested, and it appears in about half of the remaining multimodal configurations. 2. What this tests: Changing only the image encoder from ResNet50 to ViT-L in the image-only single-profile setting isolates the effect of image representation. No fusion or aggregation is involved to confound the comparison. 3. Why it is the best next experiment: The result decides whether the large multimodal ViT-L subspace is worth further budget. If ViT-L is clearly stronger than ResNet50, ViT-L fusion with PCA-2000 becomes a promising exploit, for example config_023 with weighted fusion. If ViT-L is also weak, we can reasonably deprioritize image-heavy configurations and focus on RNA, such as testing scGPT next. This one cheap, single-factor experiment reduces uncertainty about the largest part of the remaining search space.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_008 kept the image-only single-profile pipeline from llm_summary_002 fixed (no RNA encoder, aggregation, or fusion) and changed only the image encoder from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.586 (F1 0.574), above ResNet50's 0.507 (F1 0.455). Because the encoder was the only factor changed, this suggests ViT-L gives a stronger image representation than ResNet50 in this setting and that the image modality carries some signal. It still falls well below the RNA-only PCA-2000 single-profile baseline (0.725, F1 0.685), which remains the best result. Each result is a single run of unknown variance, and ViT-L has not been tested in multimodal fusion (for example weighted fusion with PCA-2000) or multiprofile settings, so whether its gain carries over to complement RNA is still open; the gap between accuracy and F1 was smaller than for ResNet50, which may hint at more even per-class performance, but per-class results are unavailable.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: The best result is still RNA-only PCA-2000 single-profile (0.725 accuracy, F1 0.685). Multimodal models have only been tried with ResNet50. With that encoder, concat collapsed (0.208) and weighted fusion reached 0.527 (F1 0.510), barely above ResNet50 image-only (0.507). Switching the image-only model from ResNet50 to ViT-L raised accuracy to 0.586 (F1 0.574). So the weak multimodal results may come from the weak ResNet50 features rather than from fusion itself. 2) Test: config_023 keeps config_017 fixed (single-profile, PCA-2000, weighted fusion, no aggregation) and changes only the image encoder to ViT-L. This isolates whether a stronger image representation lets weighted fusion approach or beat the RNA-only baseline. 3) Why now: Whether the image modality can add to RNA is the largest unresolved design question, and it governs about half of the remaining search space. This one-factor comparison uses the best-performing fusion and the best image encoder, so a clear failure would justify deprioritizing multimodal configurations, while a gain would point to an exploitable direction. Untested scGPT and multiprofile image settings are still worth checking but matter less to the overall search.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_009 kept the multimodal single-profile PCA-2000 + weighted-fusion pipeline from llm_summary_004 fixed (no aggregation) and changed only the image encoder from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L, testing whether a stronger image representation lets fusion approach or beat the RNA-only PCA-2000 baseline (0.725, F1 0.685). It reached a validation accuracy of 0.224 (F1 0.184). That is far below the ResNet50 weighted-fusion run (0.527, F1 0.510), below ViT-L image-only (0.586, F1 0.574), and close to the collapsed ResNet50 concat run (0.208, F1 0.172). Because the encoder was the only factor changed, the swap to ViT-L coincided with this collapse. However, the fact that it falls below both unimodal components suggests a fusion or optimization failure, such as feature-scale or dimensionality mismatch between ViT-L and PCA features, unstable fusion weights, or training instability, rather than ViT-L features being uninformative. This is a single run of unknown variance, learned fusion weights and training diagnostics are unavailable, and whether this pipeline is fragile across runs is unknown. Images have still not been shown to add to RNA in any configuration. Multimodal results look unstable, but feature normalization, other fusion variants, multiprofile settings, and other RNA encoders remain untested, so ruling out multimodal configurations entirely would still be premature.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: RNA is clearly the strongest modality so far. RNA-only single-profile PCA-2000 has the best accuracy (0.725, F1 0.685). Transformer multiprofile roughly matches it (0.715, F1 0.687). Images alone are weaker (best 0.586 with ViT-L), and multimodal fusion has been unstable (0.208–0.527). Of the RNA encoders, only scVI-200 has been tested, and it underperformed (0.542). scGPT is completely untested. 2) What this tests: swapping PCA-2000 for scGPT in the best pipeline (RNA-only, single-profile, no aggregation or fusion) is a clean one-factor test. It asks whether a pretrained foundation-model RNA representation beats PCA, or whether the weak scVI result reflects a general disadvantage of learned encoders here. 3) Why it is the best next use of budget: the RNA encoder is the most impactful design choice that remains unresolved. scGPT appears in 15 of the remaining configurations, including multiprofile and multimodal variants, so this result determines whether that large region is worth exploring. Further multimodal runs, by contrast, would mostly probe fusion instability.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_010 kept the best pipeline fixed (RNA-only, single-profile, no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion) and changed only the RNA encoder from PCA-2000 to scGPT. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.540 (F1 0.524), well below the PCA-2000 baseline (0.725, F1 0.685) and roughly matching scVI-200 in accuracy (0.542) with a higher F1 (0.483 for scVI-200), so PCA-2000 remains the strongest RNA encoder and the best result overall. Because the encoder was the only factor changed, this suggests that this scGPT representation underperformed PCA-2000 in this pipeline, and with scVI-200 also underperforming, both learned RNA encoders tested so far trail PCA here. However, each result is a single run of unknown variance, and the test cannot separate the scGPT representation itself from embedding dimensionality, how embeddings were extracted, or downstream training choices. scGPT remains untested in multiprofile settings (for example with transformer aggregation) and in multimodal settings, so the lower priority this suggests for the 15 remaining scGPT configurations is a tentative inference rather than a confirmed conclusion.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been run, so we know nothing about how much each modality, encoder, profile setting, aggregation or fusion choice matters. 2. What it tests: config_001 (RNA-only, single-profile, PCA-2000) is the simplest configuration. It sets a reference point that later changes can be measured against one factor at a time: learned RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), multiprofile aggregation (avgpool, transformer), adding the image modality, and multimodal fusion. 3. Why now: Under a limited budget, a clean baseline makes every later comparison interpretable. It also guards against assuming complex multimodal or multiprofile models are better without evidence. Starting with a complex configuration would mix several design choices and make the result hard to attribute.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_001 tested the simplest configuration, an RNA-only, single-profile model with a PCA (n=2000) RNA encoder and no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It was chosen as a reference point for later one-factor-at-a-time comparisons. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.520, with a supporting validation F1 of 0.479. The somewhat lower F1 may indicate uneven performance across classes, but this is not confirmed. Because no other experiments have been completed, this result is only an initial baseline. It says nothing yet about whether learned RNA encoders (e.g., scVI, scGPT), multiprofile aggregation, adding the image modality, or multimodal fusion would improve performance. Run-to-run variance and the number and balance of classes are also unknown.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: Only one baseline exists, RNA-only single-profile PCA, with accuracy 0.520 and F1 0.479. We do not yet know whether the image modality carries useful signal on its own. That is the biggest open question, because about 42 of the remaining configurations are image-only or multimodal. 2. What this tests: config_010 (image-only, single-profile, ResNet50) gives a matched single-profile, no-aggregation, no-fusion reference for the second modality. Comparing it with config_001 shows how much signal each modality has. That in turn shows whether multimodal fusion is likely to help, and whether RNA encoder choices (scVI, scGPT) deserve most of the remaining budget. 3. Why this is the best next step: An encoder swap within RNA (such as config_004) would refine only one branch of the search space. A first image result reduces uncertainty across the whole space and keeps a clean one-factor contrast with the baseline, since only the modality changes. ResNet50 is the simpler image encoder, so it serves as a reference point before testing ViT-L.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_002 tested an image-only, single-profile model with a ResNet50 image encoder and no RNA encoder, aggregation, or fusion, as a matched reference for the image modality against the RNA-only PCA baseline (llm_summary_001). It reached a validation accuracy of 0.523 and a validation F1 of 0.508. Accuracy is nearly identical to the RNA baseline (0.520; a difference of about 0.003), and F1 is modestly higher (0.479), so the initial observation is that the image modality alone carries signal comparable to RNA-only PCA, possibly with somewhat more even per-class performance. The two runs differ in both modality and encoder, and run-to-run variance is unknown, so this gap cannot be attributed to modality or treated as meaningful; it also remains untested whether the two modalities are complementary under fusion, whether ViT-L or learned RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT) would improve on these baselines, and whether multiprofile aggregation helps.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: Two single-profile baselines exist. RNA-only PCA scored 0.520 accuracy and 0.479 F1. Image-only ResNet50 scored 0.523 accuracy and 0.508 F1. The two modalities carry similar signal, and run-to-run variance is unknown. It is untested whether they are complementary. 2) Test: config_016 combines exactly the encoders already tested (PCA RNA plus ResNet50 image) in a single-profile setting with the simplest fusion, concatenation. Adding the second modality is therefore the only change from either baseline. A clear gain over both baselines would suggest complementary information. Little or no gain would suggest redundancy and point the search toward encoders or multiprofile aggregation. 3) Why now: whether to fuse modalities is a high-level decision that affects most of the remaining configurations (36 of 49 are multimodal). Resolving it early with a cleanly matched comparison is the best use of the limited budget. Encoder swaps and aggregation can be explored afterward within whichever branch looks more promising.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_003 tested a single-profile multimodal model that concatenated the same PCA (n=2000) RNA encoder and ResNet50 image encoder used in the two unimodal baselines. It was a matched test of whether adding a second modality helps. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.507 and F1 of 0.455. Both are slightly below the RNA-only (0.520 / 0.479) and image-only (0.523 / 0.508) baselines, so this initial observation shows no evidence that the two modalities are complementary under simple concatenation fusion. However, run-to-run variance is unknown, so the small drop (about 0.013–0.016 accuracy) may not be meaningful. The result also does not show whether the modalities are truly redundant or whether this specific fusion setup is the limitation, for example through feature-scale imbalance or high dimensionality. Other fusion methods, learned or alternative encoders (scVI, scGPT, ViT-L), and multiprofile aggregation remain untested and could change this conclusion.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence so far: RNA-only PCA (0.520) and image-only ResNet50 (0.523, best F1 0.508) perform about the same. Concat fusion (0.507) did not help. All three runs are single-profile, so the profile setting and aggregation axis has never been tested, and it may matter more than the modality or fusion details. 2) This run changes one factor from the best configuration so far (config_010): it moves from single-profile to multiprofile, using simple avgpool aggregation. That isolates whether pooling across multiple profiles improves image-based classification. 3) This is the best use of the next experiment because it explores a major untested design axis with a clean comparison, builds on the strongest current baseline, and uses the simplest aggregator before trying the more complex transformer. The result will show whether later runs (RNA multiprofile, multimodal multiprofile) should prioritize multiprofile settings. Testing weighted fusion would only refine an axis that has so far shown no gain.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_004 changed one setting from the best prior configuration (image-only ResNet50, llm_summary_002): it moved from single-profile to multiprofile input with simple avgpool aggregation, to test whether pooling across profiles helps. Validation accuracy fell to 0.421 (F1 0.412) from 0.523 (F1 0.508), a drop of about 0.10 that is much larger than any gap seen so far (all prior runs were within about 0.016 of each other). This suggests that multiprofile input with avgpool, as implemented here, hurts image-based classification, although run-to-run variance is still unknown. Because multiprofile input and the avgpool aggregator were introduced together, this run cannot show whether the drop comes from multiprofile input itself or from mean pooling, for example by washing out discriminative per-profile features; untested factors such as a transformer aggregator, RNA-only or multimodal multiprofile settings, or differences in effective sample count or task setup under multiprofile input could change this conclusion.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: all single-profile runs are close together (0.507–0.523 accuracy). Moving the best image-only ResNet50 model to multiprofile with avgpool (config_011) dropped accuracy by about 0.10, far larger than any other gap so far. Because multiprofile input and avgpool were introduced together, it is unclear whether multiprofile input itself hurts or mean pooling washes out discriminative per-profile features. 2) This run changes only the aggregator (avgpool to transformer) relative to config_011, keeping image-only ResNet50 multiprofile fixed. If accuracy recovers to about 0.52 or above, mean pooling was the problem and transformer aggregation is worth pursuing. If it stays near 0.42, the multiprofile setting itself is likely harmful. 3) Multiprofile configurations make up most of the remaining search space, including nearly all multimodal options. Resolving this one question decides whether a large share of the remaining budget should go to multiprofile variants, so it is more valuable now than an encoder swap (ViT-L, scVI, scGPT), which can be tested next on the single-profile baselines.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_005 changed only the aggregator from avgpool to transformer, relative to llm_summary_004, keeping the image-only ResNet50 multiprofile setup fixed, to test whether mean pooling explained the roughly 0.10 accuracy drop from single-profile input. Validation accuracy did not recover (0.411 vs 0.421 with avgpool and 0.523 single-profile), and F1 was lower (0.378 vs 0.412 and 0.508), so the evidence does not support avgpool as the explanation and is more consistent with the multiprofile setting itself, as currently implemented, being harmful for image-only classification. The small avgpool-vs-transformer gap (about 0.011 accuracy) is within the range of differences previously treated as possibly noise, so neither aggregator can be called better. Still uncertain are run-to-run variance, whether the transformer was adequately tuned or trained, whether multiprofile input changes effective sample count or task setup, and whether RNA-only or multimodal multiprofile configurations behave differently; these leave open whether the multiprofile search space is broadly unproductive or only for this image-only setup.

selection_reason: Evidence: in single-profile mode, image-only ResNet50 (0.523 acc / 0.508 F1) and RNA-only PCA (0.520 / 0.479) perform about the same. Concat fusion of the two did not help (0.507 / 0.455). Multiprofile input cut image-only accuracy by about 0.10 with both avgpool (0.421) and transformer (0.411), so the multiprofile setting itself looks harmful. That makes it a low priority for now. The biggest untested design factor is encoder choice: neither ViT-L nor the learned RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT) have been tried. Test: this run swaps only the image encoder (ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L) and keeps the current best setting (image-only, single-profile). It isolates whether a stronger pretrained image representation raises the ceiling. Why now: it builds on the best result while clarifying a design choice that feeds into many remaining multimodal configurations. If ViT-L helps, later fusion experiments should use it. If it does not, encoder effort shifts to the RNA side (scVI or scGPT), which is the planned follow-up comparison.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_006 changed only the image encoder, from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L, in the best prior configuration (image-only, single-profile, no aggregation or fusion; llm_summary_002). The goal was to test whether a stronger pretrained image representation raises the performance ceiling. Validation accuracy rose to 0.713 (F1 0.695) from 0.523 (F1 0.508). This gain of about 0.19 is by far the largest change in the study so far, well above the roughly 0.016 differences previously treated as possible noise. Because this was a one-factor change, it is reasonable evidence that encoder choice is a major driver of performance in this setup and that ViT-L is a strong candidate default image encoder for later experiments. Several questions remain open: run-to-run variance is unknown; it is unclear whether the gain comes from architecture, model scale, or pretraining; it is untested whether ViT-L changes the earlier negative findings for concat fusion and multiprofile input; and learned RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT) have not been tried. The RNA side now trails substantially (PCA 0.520), so whether fusion can add anything beyond ViT-L image-only performance is an open question.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: The largest effect so far came from the encoder. Swapping ResNet50 for ViT-L raised image-only accuracy from 0.523 to 0.713. The RNA side has only been tried with PCA (0.520), and concat fusion with PCA+ResNet50 did not help. Multiprofile input hurt image-only models with both aggregators. The biggest open uncertainty is therefore whether a learned or pretrained RNA representation can close the gap to ViT-L. Without that, fusion has little reason to add value. 2) Test: Swapping only the RNA encoder from PCA to the pretrained scGPT foundation model, relative to config_001 (RNA-only, single-profile), isolates the effect of RNA representation. It directly parallels the ViT-L test on the image side. 3) Why now: The result tells us whether RNA is worth carrying into multimodal ViT-L fusion experiments, and which RNA encoder to use there. That matters more than testing PCA+ViT-L fusion with a weak RNA branch, or retrying multiprofile input, which has already looked unproductive.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_007 changed only the RNA encoder, from PCA (n=2000) to the pretrained scGPT foundation model, in the RNA-only, single-profile baseline (llm_summary_001), to test whether a pretrained RNA representation can close the gap to the ViT-L image-only model. Validation accuracy rose to 0.650 (F1 0.628) from 0.520 (F1 0.479). Because this was a one-factor change and the gain of about 0.13 is far larger than the roughly 0.016 differences previously treated as possible noise, it is reasonable evidence that RNA encoder choice strongly affects performance here and that scGPT is the stronger candidate RNA branch, although it still trails ViT-L image-only (0.713 / 0.695) by about 0.06. Run-to-run variance remains unknown, and it is unclear whether the gain comes from pretraining, architecture, or representation dimensionality. It is also untested whether scGPT+ViT-L fusion adds anything beyond ViT-L alone (the earlier concat result used much weaker encoders), whether other learned RNA encoders such as scVI would do as well, and whether stronger encoders change the earlier negative multiprofile findings.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: Encoder choice is the dominant factor so far. Switching to ViT-L raised image-only accuracy to 0.713, and switching to scGPT raised RNA-only accuracy to 0.650, both far beyond the roughly 0.016 differences treated as noise. The only fusion test (config_016, concat) used the weak PCA and ResNet50 encoders and slightly underperformed both unimodal baselines. That leaves open whether the modalities are redundant or whether the weak encoders were the limitation. 2. Test: This run pairs the two strongest encoders (scGPT + ViT-L) in a single-profile model with concat fusion. It is a direct comparison against ViT-L image-only (config_013) and scGPT RNA-only (config_007), and it keeps the fusion method matched to config_016. It asks whether RNA adds complementary signal once both branches are strong. 3. Value: This is the most decision-relevant open question. A gain would set a new best and justify exploring fusion variants such as weighted fusion. No gain would suggest the search should focus on unimodal ViT-L. Multiprofile input has looked harmful so far, so it is deferred to keep this a clean single-profile comparison.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_008 paired the two strongest encoders so far (scGPT RNA and ImageNet ViT-L image) in a single-profile multimodal model with concat fusion, the same fusion used in llm_summary_003. It tested whether RNA adds complementary signal once both branches are strong, compared directly against ViT-L image-only (0.713 / F1 0.695) and scGPT RNA-only (0.650 / F1 0.628). Validation accuracy was only 0.537 (F1 0.518), about 0.18 below ViT-L alone and 0.11 below scGPT alone, and barely above the weak PCA and ResNet50 baselines. This drop is far larger than the roughly 0.016 differences treated as possible noise, so concat fusion as currently implemented clearly fails to exploit, and appears to degrade, the strong unimodal representations, extending the smaller negative concat result from llm_summary_003. The evidence does not isolate the cause: true modality redundancy, feature-scale or dimensionality imbalance between the encoder outputs, optimization or training issues, or an implementation problem in the fusion pipeline are all possible, and the size of the collapse makes a setup issue plausible. Run-to-run variance is also unknown, so ViT-L image-only remains the best configuration, and alternative fusion methods (e.g., weighted fusion, or fusion with normalized or projected features) remain untested before multimodal fusion can be judged unproductive.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: ViT-L image-only (0.713 / F1 0.695) and scGPT RNA-only (0.650 / 0.628) are the strongest results. Pairing them with concat fusion (config_046) collapsed to 0.537 / 0.518, a drop far larger than the roughly 0.016 differences treated as possible noise. Concat therefore looks like the likely failure point (scale or dimensionality imbalance, or a setup problem), but this has not been confirmed. 2) This run changes only the fusion method, from concat to weighted, while keeping the strongest encoders and single-profile input. If accuracy recovers to near or above ViT-L alone, concat was the problem and multimodal fusion stays worth pursuing. If it collapses again, the evidence points toward modality redundancy or a broader issue in the multimodal pipeline, and the search can focus on ViT-L image-only. 3) It is a clean one-factor comparison on the most decision-relevant open question, whether fusion can add anything, and it also has a plausible chance of producing a new best configuration. Multiprofile tests are lower priority because that setting already hurt image-only ResNet50 under both aggregators.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_009 changed only the fusion method, from concat to weighted, relative to llm_summary_008. Encoders (scGPT RNA, ImageNet ViT-L image) and single-profile input stayed fixed, to test whether concat was the cause of the multimodal collapse. Validation accuracy was 0.527 (F1 0.510), essentially unchanged from concat (0.537 / 0.518; the gap of about 0.011 is within the range treated as possible noise) and far below ViT-L image-only (0.713 / 0.695) and scGPT RNA-only (0.650 / 0.628). The evidence therefore does not support concat specifically as the failure point. It is more consistent with a problem shared by the multimodal pipeline as implemented, such as feature-scale or dimensionality imbalance before fusion, optimization or training issues, an implementation bug, or true modality redundancy. The near-identical results across two fusion methods, both near the weak-baseline level, make a setup issue plausible, but none of these causes is isolated, and run-to-run variance remains unknown. ViT-L image-only is still the best configuration.
